He was filled with distress and saw what had happened: his own lust had taken ten years of his life. He did not blame Menaka. He sent her away kindly, and went north to the Himalayas to begin his penance again, this time by the Kaushiki river. By the account in the Ramayana, he went on to even greater austerities and was tested again, and in the end he became a Brahmarishi. What it shows: In the Gita's words, desire is "all-devouring" (3.37). Even a sage with a thousand years of discipline lost a decade to it. But the story's second half matters just as much: he recognised the cause, did not stay in guilt, and returned to practice. The way back is honest recognition and renewed effort.

Nachiketa and Yama From the Katha Upanishad, first chapter. Nachiketa was a young boy who, in anger at his father's careless offering, ended up in the house of Yama, the lord of death. Yama was away for three days, and when he returned he was ashamed that a guest had gone unattended. As amends, he offered Nachiketa three boons. Nachiketa used the first two on his father's peace and a sacred fire. For the third, he asked the great question: what happens after a person dies? Yama did not want to answer. He tested him, offering instead everything the world could give: sons and grandsons who would live a hundred years, elephants, horses, cattle and gold, and a vast kingdom, as long a life as he wanted, and the most tempting offer, beautiful maidens with chariots and music, such as no mortal could obtain. It is a picture of every pleasure in the world, including desire, placed in front of a young person. A lesser seeker would have taken it. Nachiketa refused. He answered that these things are of a day, that they wear out the vigour of the senses, and that even the longest life is short. "Keep your horses, dances and songs for yourself," he said, and insisted on his question. Yama was impressed. He saw that a person who could not be turned aside by pleasure was ready for the highest knowledge, and he taught him. This is where the text sets out the choice between the pleasant (preyas) and the good (shreyas). What it shows: This is a story of lust not taking hold. Nachiketa saw it for what it was, passing and wasteful, and kept his eyes on what mattered most. The text says that a mind that knows what it wants is not easily bought.

King David and Bathsheba From 2 Samuel 11-12, with Psalm 51. David was Israel's greatest king, a man God chose as one "after his own heart" (1 Samuel 13:14, NIV). One spring, when kings went to war, David stayed home in Jerusalem. One evening, from the roof of his palace, he saw a woman bathing. He found out she was Bathsheba, the wife of Uriah, one of his own soldiers. He sent for her and slept with her. She became pregnant. The problems then multiplied, as the story is careful to show: Cover-up. David called Uriah home from the battlefield, hoping he would go to his wife. Uriah, loyal to the men still at war, refused to enjoy a home comfort while they were in the field. Murder. David wrote to his general to place Uriah in the fiercest fighting and pull back from him. Uriah was killed. David then married Bathsheba. Silence. For a time it seemed to be over. But the narrator states that what David had done displeased the Lord. God sent the prophet Nathan, who told David a story about a rich man who took a poor man's only lamb. David was furious and said the man deserved to die. Nathan answered, "You are the man." David did not argue or have Nathan silenced. He said, "I have sinned against the Lord." Nathan told him he would not die, but that consequences would follow, and the child born to Bathsheba fell ill and died. David wept and fasted, and then rose, worshipped and went on. Later he and Bathsheba had another son, Solomon. Psalm 51 is traditionally read as David's prayer of repentance: "Create in me a pure heart, O God, and renew a steadfast spirit within me." What it shows: It started with a look that was entertained, as James 1:14-15 describes, and grew into adultery, deceit and death. Even a great man falls. But the story shows the way back: being confronted, naming the sin honestly, and asking for mercy. It also shows that forgiveness does not erase every consequence.

Nanda and the Five Hundred Nymphs From the Nanda Sutta (Udana 3.2). Nanda was the Buddha's half-brother, and he had become a monk. But his heart was not in it. He was thinking of a young woman of the Sakyan clan who had asked him to come back soon. He told his fellow monks he wanted to give up the training and return to lay life. The Buddha heard of it and took Nanda aside. By his spiritual power, he took Nanda up to the heaven of the Thirty-three gods, where they saw five hundred celestial nymphs with beautiful pink feet. The Buddha asked: which is lovelier, the Sakyan girl, or these nymphs? Nanda answered that compared with them, she was like a scorched monkey with its ears and nose cut off. The Buddha then said: if you keep to the holy life, I promise you five hundred such nymphs. Nanda agreed eagerly. From then on, the other monks teased him, calling him a hireling who lived the holy life for the sake of nymphs. The comments shamed him, and he went off alone and practised with real effort. Before long he reached arahantship, full awakening. He then released the Buddha from his promise: he no longer wanted anything of the kind. What it shows: The Buddha did not shame or forbid Nanda at first. He showed him that desire always finds something bigger to want, and the "bigger prize" was only a way to stop the mind running in circles. The real freedom came when Nanda saw through the craving itself. The Dhammapada says, "There is no satisfying sensual desires, even with the rain of gold coins" (186). The cure was practice, honest shame that turned into effort, and seeing craving clearly.

Augustine and the Divided Will From Augustine's Confessions*, Book VIII (written about the year 400).* Augustine was a brilliant teacher of rhetoric and a philosopher. By his thirties he was convinced that the Christian message was true. But he could not bring himself to live by it, because he was held by sexual desire. He wrote what became a famous prayer: "Grant me chastity and continency, but not yet." His problem was not that he lacked information. It was the old puzzle Aristotle called akrasia: knowing the good and not doing it. In Book VIII he asks why the mind can order the body to move and be obeyed, but cannot order itself and get the same result. His conclusion is that the will is divided: part of it wants to change, part of it clings to habit. Habit, he writes, had hardened into a chain. The turning point came in a garden in Milan. He was in tears under a fig tree, torn between the two wills. Then he heard a child's voice from a nearby house, chanting "take up and read." He took it as a sign, picked up the book of Paul's letters, and read the first passage he saw: Romans 13:13-14, a call to put aside indulgence and "make not provision for the flesh" (in the translation of Augustine's text that New Advent gives). As he tells it, "by a light, as it were, of security infused into my heart, all the gloom of doubt vanished away." He shared it with his friend Alypius and with his mother Monica, who rejoiced. Augustine left his career, was baptised, and became one of the most influential thinkers in Western history. What it shows: Knowing what is right is not enough. Augustine found that change requires the whole will, not just the intellect, and that a person often needs a decisive moment and a supporting community. His honesty about the divided self is why the account has lasted.

Envy is the pain of seeing someone else have something you want: a quality, a success, a possession or a relationship. It is different from jealousy, which is fear of losing something you have to a rival. Envy involves two people (you and the one you envy); jealousy involves three. Psychologists describe two forms: Benign envy pushes you to improve ("I want that too, and I can work for it"). Malicious envy wants the other person to lose what they have, and may lead to belittling, gossip or sabotage. The sin is mainly the malicious kind. Its everyday signs include: A sting when a friend announces good news. Quietly enjoying someone's failure (schadenfreude). Finding fault with people who are doing well.

The Sanskrit word is matsarya, envy or jealousy of others' good fortune, the sixth of the inner enemies (shadripu). Related words are asuya (finding fault, begrudging) and irshya (jealousy). The Gita names the quality in its portrait of the asuri nature: in 16.18, such people hate the Divine in themselves and in others, and are full of asuya. By contrast, the person dear to Krishna is described as "hating no creature" (12.13), and in 3.31 those who follow the teaching with faith and "without envy" (anasuyantah) are freed from the bonds of action. The wise student is called anasuya ("free from envy") in 9.1 and 18.71.

The Upanishads have no single word for envy. They address it through what lies underneath: seeing others as separate from yourself. The Isha Upanishad opens with "do not covet anyone's wealth" (verse 1) and goes on to the vision that cures it: the one who sees all beings in the Self, and the Self in all beings, "does not shrink from anything" (verse 6). In verse 7, for the one who sees the oneness of all, "what delusion and what sorrow can there be?" The Mundaka (3.1.1-2) and Shvetashvatara (4.6-7) Upanishads give a picture of two birds on one tree. One eats the fruit and is troubled. The other looks on without eating. When the first sees the other, and its greatness, sorrow leaves it. Envy appears here as one form of the sorrow that goes with believing you are separate and lacking. This is related to envy and not identical to it: the texts have no word for begrudging another's good fortune, and speak of the separateness underneath.

Christian tradition calls it envy (Latin invidia): sadness at another's good, and the wish to see them lose it. The Catechism says envy is a capital sin and describes it as sadness at a neighbour's goods and an immoderate desire to have them for oneself, even unjustly (CCC 2538). It is named in the tenth commandment's warning against coveting, and in the Bible's lists of vices (for example Galatians 5:19-21). Proverbs 14:30 says "a tranquil mind gives life to the flesh, but jealousy makes the bones rot" (the older NRSV reads "passion"). Proverbs 27:4 asks, "Who can stand before jealousy?" James 3:16 says that where there is envy and selfish ambition there will be disorder and wickedness of every kind. Augustine called envy the "diabolical" sin, because it is sorrow at another's good, and Aquinas treats it in Summa II-II q.36 as sorrow at someone's good seen as diminishing one's own.

The Pali word is issa, envy or jealousy: a mental state that finds others' success hard to bear. In the traditional lists of mental factors (Abhidhamma) it is an unwholesome factor, rooted in aversion (dosa), and it is often paired with macchariya, stinginess. The Dhammapada says: "One should not despise what one has received, nor envy the gains of others. The monk who envies the gains of others does not attain to meditative absorption" (365, Buddharakkhita translation). The positive counterpart is mudita, sympathetic joy, delight in the good fortune of others. It is one of the four brahmaviharas (divine abidings) alongside loving-kindness, compassion and equanimity, as in MN 7 (Vatthupama Sutta).

Philosophers define envy fairly consistently. Aristotle. In the Rhetoric (2.10) envy is pain at the apparent good fortune of others who are our equals, not to gain anything but because they have it. He separates it from emulation (2.11), which is the pain of lacking what a good person has and so strives to get it. Plato. In the Philebus (47d-50e) envy is a mixed feeling of pain and pleasure at others' misfortune. In the Phaedrus (247a) "jealousy has no place in the celestial choir" (Jowett translation). Kant. In the Metaphysics of Morals (Doctrine of Virtue, sections 36-37), envy, ingratitude and malice are the vices of hatred of humanity, with envy as the tendency to see others' well-being as a loss to oneself. Hume. In the Treatise (2.2.8) envy arises from comparison with someone close to us.

Envy grows from comparison and from what comparison says about you. Social comparison. People judge themselves by looking at others (Festinger's theory). Envy is strongest toward people close to us in age, field and background. Self-relevance. We envy most in areas that matter to our self-image. Nobody envies a stranger's talent in something they don't care about. Low or fragile self-worth. Someone else's success feels like proof of your own shortfall. Feeling blocked. Envy is stronger when we believe the gap can't be closed, and turns malicious when it seems unfair. Social media. Constant, curated views of other people's best moments feed comparison. Some studies link passive scrolling with lower mood.

Hindu thought traces envy to separateness, desire and the guna of rajas. Duality. Seeing "me" and "them" as fundamentally apart makes another's gain feel like my loss. Gita 5.18 praises the sage who sees with an equal eye in all. Unfulfilled desire. Envy follows when desire is aimed at what others have. Gita 2.62-63 describes how fixing the mind on objects leads to desire, anger and delusion. Ego. Gita 16.18 links asuya with ahamkara, power and arrogance. Lack of contentment. Gita 12.19 describes the dear devotee as content with whatever comes. Envy is the opposite. Karma as a lens. Another's fortune is often explained by their past actions, which in tradition is a reason not to resent it.

For the Upanishads, the root is the mistaken sense that you are a separate, lacking self. Fear and lack from a "second." Brihadaranyaka 1.4.2-3 says the Self felt fear because there was a second, and desire for that second. Where there is another, there is comparing and wanting. The two birds. Mundaka 3.1.1-2: the bird caught up in the fruit grieves in its helplessness. The grief belongs to forgetting the other bird, the witness, which is the same Self. Ignorance of unity. Isha 7: for the one who knows all beings have become the Self, there is no delusion or sorrow, so the lack of that knowledge is the cause. Valuing outer things. Katha 2.1.1 says people look outward and not within, so they measure themselves by what they see in others.

Christian writers find envy's roots in pride, a distorted view of one's own worth, and distrust of God's goodness. From pride. Gregory the Great (Moralia 31.45) lists envy as a daughter of vainglory. If I must be the best, another's excellence threatens me. Suspicion of God's fairness. In Matthew 20:1-16 the workers hired first complain about those hired last, and the owner asks, "Are you envious because I am generous?" Envy objects to grace given to someone else. The devil's envy. Wisdom 2:24 says death came into the world through the devil's envy. Zero-sum thinking. The older brother in Luke 15:25-32 sees the father's welcome of his brother as a loss to himself. Disordered love. Aquinas (ST II-II q.36) says we grieve at another's good when we see it as diminishing our own excellence.

Buddhism sees envy as coming from aversion, attachment to self and gain, and attention to comparison. Rooted in aversion. In the Abhidhamma analysis, issa is a factor of the hatred (dosa) family: dislike of another's good. Attachment to gain and status. AN 8.6 lists the eight worldly winds: gain and loss, fame and disrepute, praise and blame, pleasure and pain. A mind pushed by them envies those who get more of what it likes. Conceit. Comparison ("they have more than I") is a form of mana, as in SN 22.89. Stinginess. Macchariya, clinging to what one has, goes with envy at what others have. Not seeing not-self. If you take the self as fixed and in need of defending, others' rise feels like your fall (SN 22.59).

Philosophers see envy as an effect of comparison and of the love of honour. Equals. Aristotle (Rhetoric 2.10) says we envy those near to us in time, place, age and reputation, and those who compete with us for the same honour. Wounded self-love. Kant (Doctrine of Virtue, 36) describes envy as the tendency to view others' well-being as a reproach to ourselves. Relative standing. Hume (Treatise 2.2.8) says envy comes from comparing our situation with that of someone only a little ahead, not with someone far above us. Love of honour and rank. Rousseau's amour-propre (Discourse on Inequality) describes the habit of valuing oneself by how one stands against others. Valuing what is not in our control. Epictetus (Enchiridion 25) says to ask what price the other paid for the honour, and whether you would pay it.

Envy hurts the envier first. Mood. Envy goes with lower well-being, resentment and rumination. Relationships. Resentment of friends and colleagues sours closeness; people feel the coldness even if you say nothing. Behaviour. Malicious envy can lead to gossip, undermining or withholding help. In experiments, people have sometimes paid a cost to bring down a better-off partner. Wasted signal. Benign envy can point to something you value, but malicious envy turns that into spite and wastes the information. Brain. One imaging study found that envy activates a region linked to pain, and that the rival's misfortune activates reward areas.

The Hindu texts name envy as a block to peace and to knowledge. No freedom from bondage. Gita 3.32 says that those who carp at the teaching and do not follow it are "deluded in all knowledge" and lost. 3.31 gives the opposite: faith and freedom from envy bring release. Inner enemy. Matsarya sits among the six shadripu that rob the mind of calm. Falling to lower states. Gita 16.19-20 says the haters and the cruel are cast again and again into demoniac wombs, and fall to the lowest path. Peace for the free. Gita 12.13-15 describes the devotee who hates no one, is friendly and compassionate, and is "not agitated by the world nor agitating it." Epic example. In the Mahabharata, Shishupala's envy of Krishna ends in his death at the Rajasuya.

In the Upanishads the effect of envy is the same as that of any sense of separateness: sorrow. The grieving bird. Mundaka 3.1.2 says the one who is attached "grieves, deluded in his helplessness" until he sees the Lord and his greatness. Fear and delusion. Isha 6-7 says that only the one who sees unity is free from shrinking, delusion and sorrow. The rest keep them. Wandering. Katha 2.1.10 (also Brihadaranyaka 4.4.19) says one goes from death to death who sees difference here. No peace. Katha 2.2.13 says eternal peace belongs to those who perceive the one Self, not to others.

Scripture is stark about what envy does. Wasting the body. Proverbs 14:30: "jealousy makes the bones rot" (older NRSV: "passion"). Disorder. James 3:14-16: where there is envy and selfish ambition, there is disorder and "wickedness of every kind." Violence. Cain's envy of Abel's accepted offering ends in murder (Genesis 4:3-8). Pilate "realized that it was out of jealousy that they had handed him over" (Matthew 27:18). Exclusion from the community's peace. Galatians 5:19-21 lists envy among the works of the flesh, and Galatians 5:26 urges, "Let us not become conceited, competing against one another, envying one another." Contrast. Romans 12:15 asks believers to "rejoice with those who rejoice."

Envy damages the mind, and the community. No concentration. Dhammapada 365 says that a monk who envies others' gains does not attain concentration. Unwholesome action. Envy rooted in aversion leads to harsh speech and harmful acts, which in the teaching on karma bring suffering to oneself and others. Quarrels. Envy and stinginess feed disputes (the "quarrels and disputes" of the Kalahavivada Sutta, Sn 4.11, are traced to what is dear to us and to stinginess). Splits in the Sangha. The tradition's best-known case is Devadatta, whose envy of the Buddha's standing led him to attempt to divide the community (Vinaya, Cullavagga 7). Lost joy. Where mudita is absent, others' happiness is a source of pain, not delight.

Philosophers say envy distorts judgment and corrodes society. Pain with no gain. Aristotle (Rhetoric 2.10) notes that the envious person is pained not for any benefit to themselves but by the other's good. A vice, not an emotion alone. In NE 2.7, Aristotle lists envy (phthonos) among the dispositions that are always bad, with no mean. Enmity. Kant says envy, ingratitude and malice are "diabolical" in being direct hatred of humanity (Doctrine of Virtue 36). Social friction. Hume and Rousseau both see relative comparison as the source of resentment between ranks. Unhappiness. Bertrand Russell (The Conquest of Happiness, ch. 6) calls envy one of the strongest causes of unhappiness, since the envious person takes pain from what they have as well as what others have.

The aim is to turn envy into information and then into goodwill. Name it. Say "this is envy." Unnamed envy shows up as irritation or criticism. Ask what it points to. What do I actually want? A skill, recognition, security? Envy is often a signal of a value. Convert it to a step. If the want is reachable, choose one action (a course, a conversation, a draft). This is the benign form. Cut the fuel. Mute or unfollow accounts that leave you feeling behind, and cut passive scrolling. Remember the unseen. You see their result, not their cost, doubts or luck. Practise active joy. Tell the person congratulations and mean it. Do it even when it's hard. Keep a gratitude list, and compare yourself with your past self.

Hindu practice answers envy with equal vision, friendliness and contentment. Equal vision. Gita 5.18 and 6.9 praise the one who sees all with an equal eye, and 6.32 the one who feels another's joy and sorrow as their own. Friendliness and compassion. Gita 12.13: "adveshta sarva-bhutanam, maitrah karuna eva cha", hating no being, friendly and compassionate. The Yoga Sutras (1.33) recommend friendliness toward the happy, compassion toward the unhappy, gladness toward the virtuous and equanimity toward the wicked. Contentment. Gita 12.19 and Yoga Sutras 2.42 (santosha). Offer your actions. Gita 3.30 and 18.66 teach acting for the Divine and letting go of "mine." Satsang and service, which put attention on others' good.

The Upanishadic cure is to see the one Self in all. See all in the Self. Isha 6-7: the one who sees all beings in the Self and the Self in all beings no longer shrinks, and for them delusion and sorrow end. Do not covet. Isha 1 gives the practice: leave the wealth of others to them and enjoy through renunciation. Take the witness seat. The second bird of Mundaka 3.1.1-2 looks on without eating. Practise watching your own wants. Study and reflect. The three steps of shravana, manana and nididhyasana (later Vedanta, built on Brihadaranyaka 2.4.5) turn knowledge of unity into experience. Give and be kind. Taittiriya 1.11 advises giving in faith and with sympathy.

Christian practice answers envy with gratitude, love and rejoicing with others. Rejoice with those who rejoice (Romans 12:15). Start by praying for the person you envy. Love. 1 Corinthians 13:4 says love "is not envious or boastful or arrogant." Practise the actions of love and the feeling often follows. Gratitude. 1 Thessalonians 5:18 and 1 Corinthians 4:7 point to what has been received. Trust God's generosity. Matthew 20:15 asks "Are you envious because I am generous?", and the answer is to accept grace given to others. Contentment. Philippians 4:11-13: "I have learned to be content with whatever I have." Different gifts. 1 Corinthians 12:14-26 says the body has many parts, and "If one member suffers, all suffer together with it; if one member is honored, all rejoice together with it." Confession. Naming the sin in confession or to a trusted person takes away its secrecy.

Buddhism trains the opposite of envy: mudita, sympathetic joy. Practise mudita. Bring to mind someone who is doing well and wish: "May your good fortune continue." Start with someone easy and move toward the person you envy. This is one of the four brahmaviharas (MN 7). Metta. Loving-kindness for all beings (Sn 1.8, Karaniya Metta Sutta) softens the aversion that envy grows from. Be content. Dhammapada 365 says do not despise what you have received or envy others' gains. Notice the eight winds. AN 8.6: gain and loss, praise and blame are not the measure of a life. Observe envy as it comes and goes. Dedicate merit. Rejoicing in others' good deeds (anumodana) is a standard practice in Buddhist communities. See not-self. SN 22.59 loosens the idea of a fixed "me" to be ranked.

Philosophy gives ways to turn comparison into proportion. Emulation, not envy. Aristotle (Rhetoric 2.11) separates envy from emulation: the emulous person is pained at not having the good thing and works to get it, rather than wanting the other to lose it. Ask the price. Epictetus (Enchiridion 25): has someone been honoured above you? Consider what they paid for it, and whether you would pay the same. Mind what is yours. The Stoic split between what is up to us and what is not (Enchiridion 1) puts others' success among the things we do not control. Look wider. Marcus Aurelius (Meditations 9.30) advises seeing life from a wide view in which rank means little. Duty of sympathy. Kant (Doctrine of Virtue 34) asks for sympathetic joy and sorrow as a duty to cultivate.

Note: This is an invented composite story, not a real case. It is built from patterns people commonly describe, so you can see how envy works and how people step out of it. Sara's story Sara and Meera joined the same design studio on the same day and became friends. Three years later Meera was made team lead. Sara said congratulations, went home and couldn't sleep. Over the next months she noticed herself checking Meera's posts, tallying her wins and finding flaws in her work. In meetings she held back ideas Meera might use. Once she let a small mistake in Meera's file go by without pointing it out. Meera noticed the distance and stopped asking Sara to lunch. The shift came when Sara caught herself enjoying a client's complaint about Meera. It felt ugly. She talked to a mentor, who asked: "What exactly do you want that she has?" After a long pause Sara said: "To be trusted with something big." What helped: She named it as envy, and what it pointed to (wanting responsibility). She asked for a stretch project and got one. She unfollowed Meera's work account on her phone for a month. She told Meera, "I've been jealous and it wasn't fair to you." Meera admitted she had been scared of leading her friend. She practised small, real congratulations and noticed the sting fade. The friendship came back, more honest than before. What it shows: Envy is often a map of what you want. Used as a map it can be a spur. Left alone it turns into spite.

Manthara and Kaikeyi In the Ramayana (Ayodhya Kanda), King Dasharatha decides to crown his eldest son Rama. All of Ayodhya celebrates, including Queen Kaikeyi, who loves Rama as her own son and rewards the servant who brings the news. That servant, Manthara, a hunchbacked maid who came with Kaikeyi from her father's house, cannot bear it. She sees only that Kausalya, Rama's mother, will rise, and that Kaikeyi and her son Bharata will be pushed aside. She hurries to Kaikeyi and works on her fears, step by step: Rama's mother will be queen mother, you will be her servant, and Bharata will be at Rama's mercy. At first Kaikeyi rejects her. Manthara persists, and reminds her of two boons the king once promised. Kaikeyi finally asks Dasharatha for them: Bharata to be crowned and Rama exiled for fourteen years. Dasharatha dies of grief, Rama goes to the forest, and Bharata, when he returns, rejects the throne and rebukes his mother. What it shows: One person's envy of another's good fortune can be passed on, like a spark. Kaikeyi's love was real, and envy still turned it.

A parable: the two birds The Mundaka Upanishad (3.1.1-2) and the Shvetashvatara Upanishad (4.6-7) use an image from the Rig Veda: two birds, close companions, sit on the same tree. One of them eats the sweet fruit of the tree. It hops from branch to branch, tastes, wants more, and sometimes finds bitter fruit. It feels lost and helpless and grieves. The other bird does not eat. It simply looks on, calm and bright. The text says that when the first bird, which has been caught up in the fruit, turns and sees the other, the Lord, and sees his greatness, its sorrow passes. What it shows: Envy lives in the bird that is busy comparing fruit. The teaching is not to find better fruit but to notice the witness that is already there, and is the same as you.

Joseph and his brothers Genesis 37 introduces Joseph, his father Jacob's favourite son. Jacob gives him a long robe, and the brothers "hated him, and could not speak peaceably to him." Joseph also tells them dreams in which they bow down to him, which makes it worse. Acts 7:9 says the patriarchs, "jealous of Joseph, sold him into Egypt." The brothers first plan to kill him, then sell him to traders for twenty pieces of silver, and tell their father an animal killed him. In Egypt, Joseph goes through slavery and prison and rises to rule under Pharaoh. Years later, famine brings the brothers to buy grain. They do not recognise him. After testing them, he tells them who he is (Genesis 45). They are afraid. He says, "Do not be distressed or angry with yourselves because you sold me here, for God sent me before you to preserve life." After their father dies, the brothers fear revenge. Joseph weeps and tells them: "Even though you intended to do harm to me, God intended it for good" (Genesis 50:20). What it shows: Envy led to a crime, but the story ends in forgiveness.

Devadatta Devadatta was the Buddha's cousin, and he joined the Sangha. Tradition says he developed psychic powers, but also a hunger for status and a growing envy of the Buddha's standing. The account is in the Vinaya (Cullavagga, chapter 7). At one point he asked the Buddha to hand over leadership of the Sangha, saying the Buddha was old. The Buddha refused, saying he would not even hand it to Sariputta and Moggallana, and certainly not to someone who has "swallowed spittle." Devadatta held a grudge. He is said to have won over Prince Ajatasattu, and then to have tried to have the Buddha killed, by hired men, by a rolling rock, and by a maddened elephant. He also tried to split the Sangha by pressing five strict rules, and some young monks followed him until Sariputta and Moggallana brought them back. Traditional accounts say Devadatta's end was grim, though they also hold that he can eventually be released. What it shows: Envy of status, even among those who have renounced the world, can grow into harm. It is why the tradition teaches mudita.

Aristides the Just Plutarch, in his Life of Aristides (chapter 7), tells of the Athenian statesman Aristides, known as "the Just." In the 480s BC, Athenians could vote to ostracise a citizen, sending him into exile for ten years, by writing his name on a piece of pottery. Aristides was a political rival of Themistocles. As the vote was held, says Plutarch, an illiterate farmer who did not know Aristides handed him his shard and asked him to write "Aristides" on it. Aristides asked whether the man had any grievance against him. The man said no: "I don't even know the fellow, but I am tired of hearing him everywhere called the Just" (Perrin translation). Aristides wrote his own name and gave it back. He was ostracised. Plutarch adds that when he left, he prayed that Athens would never need him back. What it shows: The man's only complaint was another's good name. It is envy in its plainest form: no harm done, only a reputation that stings.

Gluttony is over-indulgence: taking more than you need, or taking it in a way that is driven by craving instead of hunger. It is usually pictured as overeating, but it covers drink, and by extension any habit of consuming past the point of benefit, such as bingeing on screens or sweets. Aquinas listed five forms: eating too soon, too expensively, too much, too eagerly and too daintily. Modern research on hedonic eating (eating for pleasure when not hungry) and emotional eating fits the same picture. It is not the same as an eating disorder. Binge eating disorder and similar conditions are medical problems, and they call for care, not moral blame.

Hinduism has no single word equal to the Christian sin of gluttony. The closest ideas are lobha (greed), kama (craving) applied to taste, and the failure of sense-control (indriya-nigraha), with the tongue seen as the hardest sense to master. The Gita speaks to it directly. In 6.16-17, yoga is "not for one who eats too much or fasts too much", and it belongs to the one who is moderate in eating, recreation, work and sleep. In 17.8-10, it describes the food that each guna prefers: sattvic food is nourishing and pleasant, while rajasic food (very bitter, sour, salty, hot or dry) and tamasic food (stale, tasteless, impure) belong to the other two. This is related to gluttony and not identical to it: the focus is balance, not sin.

The Upanishads treat food as sacred and as something to be handled with care. The Taittiriya Upanishad describes food (anna) as the first sheath of the self (2.2) and, in the Bhrigu chapter, says food is Brahman (3.2). Its rules on food are: "Let him never abuse food, that is the rule" (3.7), "Let him never shun food" (3.8) and "Let him acquire much food" (3.9), in the Müller translation. The Chandogya Upanishad (7.26.2) links what one takes in to purity of mind: "When the intellectual aliment has been purified, the whole nature becomes purified" (Müller translation; traditional commentators differ on whether ahara means literal food or all that the senses take in). Gluttony in this view is the misuse of something holy: eating without awareness, or taking more than the body needs, or hoarding it from others. Taittiriya 3.10 also ties food to generosity, praising the one who gives food to others. This is related to gluttony and not identical to it: the texts speak of respect for food, not of a sin of overeating.

Christian tradition calls it gluttony (Latin gula): excessive eating or drinking, and the disordered love of food and drink behind it. The Catechism names temperance as the virtue that moderates the attraction of pleasures (CCC 1809) and warns against excess in food and drink (CCC 2290). The Bible warns against it often. Proverbs 23:20-21 says, "Do not be among winebibbers or among gluttonous eaters of meat; for the drunkard and the glutton will come to poverty." Philippians 3:19 speaks of those "their god is the belly." Luke 21:34 warns against "dissipation and drunkenness." Aquinas (ST II-II q.148) says the fault lies in the disordered desire, and that food itself is good. Gregory the Great (Moralia 30.60) described five ways of gluttony, which Aquinas took up.

Buddhism treats it as lack of moderation in eating (bhojane mattannuta, "knowing the right amount in eating"), a quality the Buddha taught monks and nuns, and a form of sensual craving (kama-tanha). The Maha-Assapura Sutta (MN 39) lists moderation in eating as part of training. The Kitagiri Sutta (MN 70) describes the Buddha giving up the evening meal and finding the benefits in health and ease. The Buddha also gave a lay example: in SN 3.13 (Doṇapāka Sutta) he advised King Pasenadi, who ate a large amount, to take a little less at each meal, and the king's health improved. For lay followers, the standard guidance is simply to avoid excess, and eight-precept days include not eating after noon. This is a training rule, not a sin in the Christian sense.

Greek philosophers treat gluttony as a failure of temperance (sophrosyne), the virtue about bodily pleasures. Aristotle. In the Nicomachean Ethics (3.10-11), temperance is the mean about the pleasures of touch and taste. The excess is licentiousness, and he says that gluttony is the person who takes pleasure in food and drink beyond what is right. He notes that "belly-gods" (gastrimargoi) fill themselves beyond what is natural. Plato. In the Republic (4, 430e-431d), temperance is a harmony in which the better part rules the appetites. In the Gorgias (493-494) appetite is likened to a leaky jar that can never be filled. Epicurus. In the Letter to Menoeceus, simple food gives as much pleasure as luxurious food, and the pleasure of eating is complete when hunger is gone.

Over-indulgence has several well-studied roots. Emotional regulation. People eat to soothe stress, boredom, loneliness or sadness. The food works for a few minutes, which trains the habit. Food environment. Cheap, highly palatable, calorie-dense food is everywhere, and large portions shift what feels normal. Reward and habit. Highly palatable foods engage reward circuits, and cues (a screen, a time of day) become triggers. Restriction. Strict dieting can make bingeing more likely in some people. Mindless eating. Distraction (TV, phone) reduces awareness of fullness. Sleep and stress. Poor sleep and high stress change hunger hormones.

Hindu thought traces over-indulgence of the senses to desire for pleasure and loss of mastery over the senses. The senses are strong. Gita 2.60 says the turbulent senses can carry off the mind of even a wise person who is striving. 2.67 compares the mind that follows the roving senses to a wind carrying away a boat. Dwelling on objects. Gita 2.62-63 gives the chain: thinking of sense objects leads to attachment, desire, anger, delusion, loss of memory and then ruin. The guna of rajas and tamas. Gita 17.9-10 ties craving for pungent or heavy foods to rajas and the taste for stale or leftover food to tamas. Craving the tongue's pleasure. Gita 2.59 says objects turn away from one who abstains, but the taste lingers, and falls away only on seeing the Highest.

The Upanishads place the source in outward-turned senses and the choice of the pleasant over the good. Senses turned outward. Katha 2.1.1 says the Self-existent pierced the senses outward, so people look to what is outside and do not see the inner Self. The chariot. Katha 1.3.3-6 compares the body to a chariot, the intellect to the driver and the mind to the reins. The senses are the horses. When the driver is untrained and the mind unsteady, the senses are like unruly horses. Pleasant versus good. Katha 1.2.1-2: the unwise choose preyas, the pleasant. Food shapes mind. Chandogya 6.5.4 says the mind is made of food, so what and how we eat shapes the mind.

Christian writers find the root in disordered appetite and the longing to fill a hunger that food cannot meet. Appetite over reason. Aquinas (ST II-II q.148) says the fault is in desire that goes against reason. Food is good, and the sin is in excess or in unruly desire. The belly as god. Philippians 3:19 describes those whose "god is the belly." Giving up what matters for pleasure. Esau trades his birthright for a bowl of stew (Genesis 25:29-34). The first temptation. Genesis 3:6 tells how the fruit looked "good for food." The tempting of Jesus in the desert begins with "turn these stones into bread" (Matthew 4:3). Deeper hunger. Matthew 4:4 answers, "One does not live by bread alone." Augustine's "our hearts are restless until they rest in You" (Confessions 1.1, Pilkington translation) names what food is sometimes asked to do.

Buddhism traces over-indulgence to craving, pleasure-seeking and inattention. Craving for sense pleasure. The first sermon (SN 56.11) names kama-tanha as one of three cravings that drive suffering. Lack of restraint of the senses. The standard training of "guarding the sense doors" (indriya-samvara, for example in MN 27) is taught because uncontrolled contact leads to desire. Not knowing "enough." Bhojane mattannuta is listed as a quality to cultivate, and its absence leads to heaviness and sloth. Eating to feel good. AN 3.39 (Sukhumala) shows how intoxication with comfort and health weakens restraint. Inattention. The Buddha describes mindful reflection on food (MN 2 and MN 39) so that eating is not driven by taste alone.

Philosophers locate it in appetite untrained by reason, and habit. Unruly appetite. Plato (Republic 4, 439d-441a) describes the appetitive part of the soul, which wants food, drink and sex, and which needs to be ruled by reason. In Phaedrus (253c-254e), appetite is the unruly horse of the soul. Habit. Aristotle (NE 2.1-3) says that we become temperate or intemperate through the pleasures we repeatedly choose. Pleasure as a trap. Aristotle (NE 3.10) says that people become intemperate because the pleasures of taste and touch are shared with animals and are easy to overdo. Empty desires. Epicurus separates natural and necessary desires, such as plain food, from empty ones that have no limit.

Chronic over-indulgence has costs for body, mind and life. Physical health. Habitual overeating is linked to weight gain and to higher risk of type 2 diabetes, heart disease and some cancers. Alcohol excess adds liver and other harms. Mood. Eating past comfort often brings guilt and shame, which can fuel the next episode. Energy and focus. Heavy meals and poor sleep go together with tiredness. Money and time. Food, drink and delivery costs add up, as do hours spent on it. Relationships. Shared meals and social life can be strained by secrecy or by drinking. Weight is shaped by genes, medicine, environment and income as well as by choices, so body size alone says nothing about someone's character.

The Hindu texts name the costs of indulging the senses. Loss of balance. Gita 6.16: yoga is not for one who eats too much or too little, sleeps too much or too little. Ruin of the mind. Gita 2.62-63 describes the downward chain from dwelling on objects to loss of reason. Disease and heaviness. Gita 17.10 notes that stale, tasteless and impure food belongs to tamas. 17.9 says that over-spicy and harsh food causes pain, grief and disease. Stirred senses. Gita 2.67: the mind drawn by one wandering sense carries off wisdom like wind a ship. Benefit of moderation. Gita 6.17: for the one moderate in food and recreation, yoga destroys sorrow.

The Upanishads connect eating with the quality of mind and of life. Mind follows food. Chandogya 6.5.4: the mind is made of food, and 7.26.2 adds, in Müller's rendering, that when the "aliment" is purified the whole nature is purified (commentators disagree on whether this means literal food). Misuse of food clouds the mind. Wasted gift. Taittiriya 3.7-8 instructs never to abuse or shun food, which suggests that both overindulgence and waste are a failure of respect. Wrong direction. Katha 1.2.2: the one who chooses the pleasant loses the aim. Unruly senses. Katha 1.3.4-5: the senses of the unsteady person are "like the wicked horses of a charioteer."

Scripture and tradition list the consequences. Poverty and drowsiness. Proverbs 23:21: "the drunkard and the glutton will come to poverty, and drowsiness will clothe them with rags." Dulled heart. Luke 21:34 warns that hearts can be "weighed down with dissipation and drunkenness." Lost birthright. Esau's stew costs him his inheritance (Genesis 25:34). Neglecting the poor. In Luke 16:19-31, the rich man "feasted sumptuously every day" while Lazarus lay hungry at his gate. Body as temple. 1 Corinthians 6:19-20 says the body is a temple of the Holy Spirit. Gregory the Great (Moralia 31.45) lists dullness of mind and excessive merriment among the effects of gluttony.

Excess in eating brings heaviness, sleepiness and distraction. Sloth and torpor. Overeating feeds thina-middha (sluggishness and drowsiness), one of the five hindrances to meditation. Health. In SN 3.13, King Pasenadi, who eats a large amount and is uncomfortable, is told that mindful moderation brings ease, and his health improves. Craving grows. Indulgence feeds kama-tanha, which the first sermon names as a source of suffering (SN 56.11). Distraction. The Buddha taught monks to eat only to maintain the body and support the holy life (MN 2), and not for fun or vanity. Benefits of restraint. MN 70 lists lightness, strength, health and comfort from eating less.

Philosophers describe the costs as lost freedom and lost pleasure. Slavery to appetite. Plato (Republic 9, 571-576) pictures the person ruled by appetite as inwardly enslaved. Self-defeat. Aristotle (NE 3.12) says the intemperate person's appetite grows with indulgence, and that he cannot be rid of it by reasoning in the moment. Reduced pleasure. Epicurus argues that luxury makes us dependent and anxious about losing it, while plain living gives security (Letter to Menoeceus, 130-131). Loss of reason. The Stoics (Seneca, Letters 95 and 122) describe heavy eating and drinking as dulling the mind. Harm to body. Seneca (Letters 95.15-18) writes that excess brings many illnesses, and that in earlier times "they enjoyed plain health. It took elaborate courses to produce elaborate diseases" (Gummere translation).

The aim is a calmer, more aware relationship with food and drink, not harsh dieting. Notice hunger and fullness. Rate hunger from 1 to 10 before you eat, and stop around comfortable. Eat without screens, slowly, and put the fork down between bites. Find your triggers. Track when and why you overeat for two weeks (stress, boredom, time of day). Meet the need. If it is stress, try a walk or a call. If it is tiredness, sleep. Shape the environment. Smaller plates, no stock of trigger foods at home, regular meals. Avoid all-or-nothing. Strict rules tend to backfire. After a slip, return to your next meal as planned. Get help when needed. A doctor, dietitian or therapist, especially if bingeing, purging or drinking is out of control.

Hindu practice answers it with moderation, sattvic food and fasting with purpose. Yukta-ahara. Gita 6.17: moderate in eating and recreation, in action and in rest. Sattvic food. Gita 17.8: foods that increase life, strength, health and cheer, and are tasty and nourishing. Offer the food. Gita 3.13 says those who eat what is left after offering are freed from sin, and that those who cook only for themselves eat sin. Giving thanks and sharing before eating is a standard practice (prasada). Fasting. Upavasa on set days (such as Ekadashi) trains self-control. It is traditionally done with a purpose, and the Gita (17.5-6) warns against severe, harmful austerity. Sense control. Gita 2.58 compares the sage to a tortoise drawing in its limbs.

The Upanishadic response is to treat food with respect and to train the "reins" of the mind. Honour food. Taittiriya 3.7-8: "Let him never abuse food... never shun food" (Müller translation). Eat with awareness and gratitude. Share it. Taittiriya 3.10 praises giving food: "If he gives food amply, food is given to him amply." Pure food, pure mind. Chandogya 7.26.2: "When the intellectual aliment has been purified, the whole nature becomes purified" (Müller translation). Traditional readings differ on whether ahara means literal food or all that the senses take in. Drive the chariot. Katha 1.3.3-9: the one who has a skilled driver (a steady intellect) and holds the reins (the mind) reaches the end of the road. Choose shreyas. Katha 1.2.1-2: choose the good over the merely pleasant.

Christian practice answers gluttony with temperance, thanksgiving and fasting. Temperance. Titus 2:12 and Galatians 5:23 name self-control as a fruit of the Spirit. Give thanks. 1 Timothy 4:4-5 says everything created is good if received with thanksgiving. Grace before meals is a habit of gratitude. Eat and drink for God's glory. 1 Corinthians 10:31. Fasting. Jesus assumes fasting as a normal practice (Matthew 6:16-18). The Church keeps seasons such as Lent. Fasting is meant to teach freedom, not to punish. Share the table. Luke 14:12-14 asks that feasts include the poor. Know your limit. Proverbs 25:16: "If you have found honey, eat only enough for you."

Buddhism offers specific training in eating. Reflect before you eat. MN 2 gives the monk's reflection: "Not for fun, indulgence, adornment, or decoration, but only to sustain this body, to avoid harm, and to support spiritual practice" (Sujato's translation). Know the right amount. Bhojane mattannuta: stop while still able to eat a little more. SN 3.13 shows the king counselled to take a little less each day. Mindfulness of eating. Notice taste, texture, hunger and satisfaction. Many teachers add eating slowly and in silence. Guard the sense doors. Indriya-samvara, as in MN 27. Eight precepts. On observance days, lay people refrain from food after noon, a temporary training and not a rule for everyone. Generosity. Offering food (dana) puts the focus on giving.

Philosophy offers training in measure. Hold to the mean. Aristotle (NE 3.11) says the temperate person desires what is right, as much as is right, and when it is right, and builds this by habit. Start small. Epicurus (Letter to Menoeceus, 130-131): plain fare gives full pleasure once hunger is gone, and brings health. Practise a little hardship. Seneca (Letters 18) suggests days of simple food, to know that one can do with little. Eat as a guest at a banquet. Epictetus (Enchiridion 15) says to take the dish as it comes, and to wait and not grab, as at a polite dinner. Reason rules appetite. Plato's Republic 4 describes temperance as harmony, with reason leading the appetites.

Note: This is an invented composite story, not a real case. It is built from patterns people commonly describe, so you can see how over-indulgence works and how people step out of it. Rohan's story Rohan, 31, worked long hours as an analyst and ate his dinner at 10 p.m. in front of the laptop. It began as a quick takeaway. It became a second takeaway, then dessert, then a bag of snacks while he watched something. He never felt hungry exactly. He felt wound up, then flat, and the food took the edge off both. He gained weight, felt sluggish, and hated the feeling of being stuffed. He would promise to "be good" on Monday, eat almost nothing all day, and by night eat twice as much. The turning point was a check-up. His doctor did not lecture. She asked him to describe a normal evening. Saying it aloud, he heard it. What helped: He kept a two-week log of what he ate and how he felt. The pattern was stress and the 10 p.m. hour, not hunger. He ate a real meal earlier, away from the screen. He added a 15-minute walk after work as his wind-down. He stopped the starve-and-binge cycle, with regular meals instead. He saw a dietitian and, later, a counsellor for the stress. He treated slips as data, not as proof he'd failed. It took months. He lost some weight, but the bigger change was that food stopped being his only way to unwind. What it shows: Over-eating is often about feelings, not food. Naming the trigger and meeting the need did more than willpower.

Kumbhakarna In the Ramayana, Kumbhakarna is the giant brother of the demon king Ravana. The tradition says that when he did severe penance, Brahma was about to grant him a boon, and the gods, fearing what he might ask, had the goddess Saraswati twist his tongue. Instead of nirdevatvam (a seat among the gods) he asked for nidravatvam (sleep). He was granted long sleep. He slept for months, and in the story, when he was woken, he ate vast amounts: buffaloes, deer and drink, in huge quantities, before he could think. When Ravana's war went badly, Kumbhakarna was woken and fed. He told Ravana plainly that he had been wrong to abduct Sita and should return her. But he said that as his brother he would fight. He did, and he died in battle against Rama. What it shows: The story is a vivid picture of appetite and sleep ruling a person's life. It is related to gluttony and sloth together, not identical to either, and the texts do not frame it as a sermon on eating.

Shvetaketu's fast In Chandogya Upanishad 6.7, the teacher Uddalaka Aruni wants to show his son Shvetaketu a point about food and the mind. He tells the boy to stay without eating for fifteen days, and to drink only water, since water is life-breath and will not be lost to a thirsty person. Shvetaketu does so, and then comes back to his father. Uddalaka asks him to recite the Vedas he has learned. The boy says nothing comes: "I do not remember, sir." Uddalaka explains with a fire. If a large fire is left with only a single ember the size of a firefly, it cannot burn much, but if you add straw it blazes up again. In the same way, of sixteen parts of the boy, only one is left, and with it he cannot recall the Vedas. "Eat," says his father. Shvetaketu eats, then recalls everything. The teacher concludes: "Mind is made of food, breath of water, speech of fire." What it shows: What and how we eat shape the mind. Starving is as unwise as overeating, and the aim is nourishment in right measure.

Esau's stew Genesis 25:19-34 tells of twin brothers, Esau and Jacob. Esau, born first, was entitled to the birthright: the family leadership and a double share of the inheritance. He was a hunter, and Jacob was a quiet man who stayed among the tents. One day Esau came in from the field, worn out. Jacob was cooking a red lentil stew. Esau said, "Let me eat some of that red stuff, for I am famished." Jacob answered, "First sell me your birthright." Esau said, "I am about to die; what use is a birthright to me?" Jacob made him swear, and Esau sold his birthright for bread and lentil stew. The text says, "he ate and drank, and rose and went his way. Thus Esau despised his birthright." Hebrews 12:16 later calls Esau "profane" for having sold his birthright "for a single meal." What it shows: Hunger is not the sin. The fault is in letting the demand of the moment outweigh what matters most. Esau's "I am about to die" shows how appetite can make a loss feel small.

King Pasenadi's meals The Donapaka Sutta (SN 3.13) tells of King Pasenadi of Kosala, a patron of the Buddha. The king used to eat boiled rice by the bucketful. After one such meal he went up to the Buddha, huffing and puffing. The Buddha, seeing this, spoke a verse: "When a man is always mindful, knowing moderation in eating, his discomfort fades, and he ages slowly, taking care of his life" (Sujato's translation). The king did not follow it on his own. He asked the student Sudassana, who was standing behind him, to memorise the verse and recite it whenever a meal was served, and offered him a daily allowance for doing so. The king gradually got used to having at most a cup of rice, and after some time his body slimmed right down. He then said: "In both ways the Buddha has sympathy for me: in the good of this life and the good of lives to come." What it shows: The Buddha did not shame him. A short verse, someone to remind him and small steps worked better than a rule or a vow.

Socrates and the shared dinner Xenophon's Memorabilia (3.14) records how Socrates dealt with a small problem at shared dinners. At such meals, some guests brought a small supply of food and others a large one. Socrates would tell the servants either to throw the small supplies into the common stock, or to give each guest an equal share all round. The result, Xenophon says, was that the guests with large supplies were ashamed not to share in the common stock, and also ashamed not to put their own in. So their supplies went in with the rest. Now being no better off than the small contributors, they soon stopped buying expensive delicacies. In the same chapter, at another supper, Socrates noticed a guest who had put aside the plain bread and was eating only the dainties (opson). He asked the company what makes a man a "dainty fellow" (opsophagos). They agreed that eating dainties with bread is not enough to earn the name, but that eating them with little or no plain food, only for pleasure, does. Elsewhere (Memorabilia 1.3.5-6) Xenophon says Socrates ate with an appetite that was itself the sauce, so he needed no special seasoning to enjoy his food. What it shows: Socrates used a quiet, practical move instead of a sermon. Moderation here is partly about fairness at the table, and partly about not needing luxury to enjoy food.

Wrath is uncontrolled anger: anger that turns into rage, resentment or the wish to get even. Anger itself is a normal emotion and can be useful, because it signals that something is wrong or unfair. The sin is anger that is out of proportion, holds on for too long, or leads to cruelty. Psychologists separate three things: Anger, the feeling. Hostility, a settled attitude of ill will and suspicion. Aggression, behaviour meant to harm. Wrath covers the second and third, and the first when it takes charge. Common signs are shouting or going cold and silent, replaying grievances, wanting someone to suffer, and saying things you later regret.

The Sanskrit word is krodha, anger, one of the six inner enemies (shadripu). It is closely tied to desire (kama): anger arises when desire is blocked. In the Gita, 3.37 names desire and anger, born of rajas, as the all-devouring enemy. In 16.21 they are two of the three gates to ruin. In 16.4, anger is listed among the traits of the asuri (demonic) nature. In contrast, the divine qualities of 16.1-3 include akrodha (freedom from anger), kshama (forgiveness), shanti (peace) and ahimsa (non-harm). The Yoga Sutras (2.35) add that where ahimsa is firmly established, hostility ceases in its presence.

The Upanishads rarely name anger directly. They describe the calm that is its opposite, and treat harshness as a sign of ignorance. Brihadaranyaka 4.4.23 describes the knower as shanta (calm), danta (self-controlled), uparata (withdrawn from distraction), titikshu (patient with hardship) and samahita (collected). Isha 6 says that the one who sees all beings in the Self, and the Self in all beings, does not hate (na vijugupsate). Brihadaranyaka 5.2.3 reports the thunder's advice to humans, gods and demons: da, da, da, which is read as self-control, giving and compassion. Katha 1.1.10 shows anger inside a family: Nachiketa asks that his father, who is angry at him, may calm down and be free of anger (vita-manyu). This is related to wrath and not identical to it: the texts describe calm and self-control and treat harshness as ignorance, rather than naming a sin of anger.

Christian tradition calls it wrath or anger (Latin ira): anger that seeks vengeance or turns to hatred. The Catechism says anger is a desire for revenge, and that it is gravely wrong to wish to harm one who must be punished, and a sin to desire to see a neighbour suffer (CCC 2302). The tradition distinguishes righteous anger at injustice from sinful anger. Ephesians 4:26 says, "Be angry but do not sin; do not let the sun go down on your anger." James 1:19-20 says to be "slow to anger, for your anger does not produce God's righteousness." In Matthew 5:21-22, Jesus links anger with murder at the level of the heart. Aquinas (ST II-II q.158) argues that anger is sinful when it goes against reason, in measure or in aim, and not when it is a proportionate response to wrong.

The Pali word is dosa, hatred or aversion, one of the three unwholesome roots with greed (lobha) and delusion (moha). Its forms include anger (kodha), ill will (vyapada), resentment (upanaha) and cruelty. The opening verses of the Dhammapada (3-5) describe people who keep thinking "He abused me, he struck me, he overpowered me, he robbed me" and so do not still their hatred. Verse 5 says: "Hatred is never appeased by hatred in this world. By non-hatred alone is hatred appeased. This is a law eternal" (Buddharakkhita translation). Ill will is also one of the five hindrances to meditation. Anger is not treated as a wrong to be hidden. It is to be seen clearly and let go.

Philosophers take anger seriously, and disagree about whether it can ever be good. Aristotle. In the Nicomachean Ethics (4.5) the virtue is mildness (praotes): being angry at the right things, with the right people, in the right way and for the right length of time. The vices are being too angry (irascibility) and never getting angry. In the Rhetoric (2.2) anger is a desire for revenge after an apparent slight. Seneca. In On Anger (1.1) he writes of anger as the passion that is, "above all others, hideous and wild" (Stewart translation), and argues it should not be used even for good ends. Plato. In the Republic (4) the spirited part (thumos) is the source of anger and should ally with reason. Kant. In the Doctrine of Virtue (sections 36-37, 40), he treats vengefulness as contrary to the duty to others.

Anger usually comes from how we read a situation, plus our state at the time. Perceived wrong or threat. Anger tends to follow the thought "that was unfair" or "they disrespected me." Blocked goals and stress. Tiredness, hunger, pain, noise, heat and overload lower the threshold. Hurt underneath. Anger often covers fear, shame, grief or feeling powerless, which are harder to admit. Rumination. Replaying a grievance keeps the feeling alive long after the event. Learned patterns. Many people copy the way anger was handled around them as children. Sense of entitlement and rigid "shoulds." Rules such as "people must treat me right" produce frequent anger. Substances such as alcohol reduce self-control.

Hindu thought traces anger to blocked desire and to the ego that feels wronged. The chain. Gita 2.62-63: dwelling on objects leads to attachment, attachment to desire, and "from desire comes anger" (kamat krodho 'bhijayate). Anger leads to delusion, loss of memory, loss of reason and ruin. Rajas. Gita 3.37 says that desire and anger are born of rajas. Ego and "mine." Gita 16.18 lists ahamkara (ego), power, arrogance, desire and anger together, as the traits that lead people to hate the Divine in themselves and others. Ignorance. Gita 16.4 ties anger to ajnana (ignorance). Karma and fate. Gita 18.60 says that one is bound by action born of one's own nature, and so acts even against one's wish.

The Upanishads place the root in separateness and unruly senses and mind. A second. Brihadaranyaka 1.4.2-3 says fear arose because there was a second. Where there is another, there can be conflict. Unruly horses. Katha 1.3.3-6 describes the senses as horses, which run wild when the driver (the intellect) is untrained and the reins (the mind) slack. Outward gaze. Katha 2.1.1 says the senses were turned outward, so people react to what happens outside and miss what is within. Ignorance of unity. Isha 6-7: the one who sees all as the Self has no hatred, so the one who does not see this is open to it.

Christian writers find anger's roots in pride, wounded self-love and unforgiveness. From pride. Gregory the Great (Moralia 31.45) lists anger as a child of pride. If I must be honoured, any slight enrages me. Desire for vengeance. Aquinas (ST II-II q.158) describes anger as a desire for retribution that goes beyond reason. Inner life. James 4:1-2 asks, "Those conflicts and disputes among you, where do they come from? Do they not come from your cravings that are at war within you?" Fall. Cain's anger follows the rejection of his offering (Genesis 4:5-7), and God warns him that "sin is lurking at the door." Unforgiveness. The parable of the unforgiving servant (Matthew 18:21-35) shows resentment as the refusal to give what one has received.

Buddhism traces anger to aversion, attachment to a self and wrong view. Aversion. Dosa is the root: pushing away what is unpleasant. Craving and aversion are two sides of the same grip (SN 56.11). Self-view. If there is a "me" to defend, every insult is an attack on it. SN 22.59 teaches that the aggregates are not self. Dwelling on grievances. Dhammapada 3-4 describes thoughts of "He abused me, he struck me" (Buddharakkhita translation), which keep hatred alive. Unwise attention. The suttas say that attending to the repulsive sign feeds ill will, as with the attractive sign for sensual desire (SN 46.51). Conditions of the body and mind. Pain, tiredness and hunger make irritation easier (MN 2 notes that discomfort and hardship are to be endured).

Philosophers see anger as arising from judgment about a wrong, plus bodily and social conditions. A judgment of slight. Aristotle (Rhetoric 2.2) says anger follows an apparent slight, belittlement or insult, and is mixed with the pleasure of hoped-for revenge. False opinion. The Stoics held that anger rests on a judgment that one has been wronged and that revenge is appropriate. Epictetus (Enchiridion 20) says it is not the person who insults you that harms you, but your belief that you are harmed. Weak character. Seneca (On Anger 1.20 and 2.19) says anger is more common in the soft, the sick and the over-indulged. Spirited part unruled. Plato (Republic 4, 439e-441c) shows anger as the spirited part, which needs to be trained by reason. Self-importance. Marcus Aurelius (Meditations 11.18) lists reminders that others act from ignorance, and that we too offend.

Unchecked anger costs health, relationships and judgment. Heart and body. A meta-analysis found that outbursts of anger were followed by a short-term rise in the risk of heart attack and stroke, though the absolute risk in any one episode is small. Relationships. Rage, contempt and silent treatment erode trust. Words said in anger are hard to take back. Work and legal. Angry outbursts can end careers and lead to violence or legal trouble. Judgment. Anger narrows attention and makes people more certain and less careful. Venting doesn't help. Experiments suggest that "letting it out" (for example hitting a pillow) tends to keep anger up, not reduce it. Children. Living with frequent rage can harm those around you, children especially.

The Gita describes how anger undoes a person. Ruin. Gita 2.63: from anger comes delusion, from delusion loss of memory, from loss of memory loss of reason, and from that destruction. Gate to hell. Gita 16.21 calls desire, anger and greed the three gates to self-destruction. Loss of peace. Gita 2.66 says that there is no peace for the unsteady mind. Harm to others. In the Mahabharata, Duryodhana's hatred, and Draupadi's vow of revenge after her humiliation, run through the whole war. The epic treats both the wrong done and the anger it raised as feeding the catastrophe. Freedom in the opposite. Gita 5.23 says the one who can resist the impulse of desire and anger before leaving the body is a yogi and is happy. 5.26 says those free of desire and anger find liberation.

In the Upanishads, anger belongs to the life of separateness, and its cost is sorrow and unrest. Fear and sorrow. Brihadaranyaka 1.4.2 links the sense of a second with fear, and Isha 7 says that for the one who sees unity there is no sorrow, so for the one who does not, there is. Wandering from death to death. Katha 2.1.10 says the one who sees multiplicity here goes from death to death. Broken households. Katha 1.1.10 shows the cost in a family: a son sent away in his father's anger, and the later wish for the father's anger to cool. No peace. Katha 2.2.13 gives peace only to those who perceive the one Self.

Scripture lists the damage anger does. Foolishness. Proverbs 14:29: "Whoever is slow to anger has great understanding, but one who has a hasty temper exalts folly." Ecclesiastes 7:9 says anger lodges in the bosom of fools. Strife. Proverbs 15:18: "Those who are hot-tempered stir up strife." Murder in the heart. Matthew 5:21-22 and 1 John 3:15 link hatred with killing. Giving the devil a foothold. Ephesians 4:26-27 warns that nursed anger gives the devil an opportunity. Unrighteousness. James 1:20: human anger does not produce God's righteousness. Cost to leaders. Moses, for striking the rock in anger, is not allowed to enter the promised land (Numbers 20:10-12).

Anger harms the angry person first. Hatred feeds on itself. Dhammapada 5: hatreds never cease through hatred. Burnt by one's own fire. The Buddha's image of "anger has a poisonous root and a sweet tip" (SN 1.71, Sujato's translation) shows that anger can feel good in the moment and bring suffering after. Ugly results. AN 7.64 (Kodhana Sutta) lists seven things that please an enemy about an angry person, including that they become ugly, sleep badly and lose wealth and friends. Karma. Harsh speech and harmful action from anger lead to suffering for oneself and others. Blocks meditation. Ill will is one of the five hindrances to concentration.

Philosophers describe anger as a kind of temporary madness. Loss of reason. Seneca (On Anger 1.1) calls anger "a short madness" (Stewart translation; he attributes the saying to "some of the wisest of men"), and says it makes people deaf to counsel and blind to what is useful. Harm without gain. Seneca (2.12) argues that anger is not useful even in war, because it gets in the way of calm judgment. Cruelty. Plutarch (On the Control of Anger) describes how anger leads people into acts they regret. Self-injury. Marcus Aurelius (Meditations 11.18) notes that the anger and grief that follow are worse than the thing that caused them. Disrespect for persons. Kant treats vengefulness as a violation of the respect owed to others.

The aim is not to never feel anger, but to respond without being run by it. Spot the early signs: tight jaw, heat, faster heartbeat. Pause. Step away, breathe slowly (longer out-breath), or count to ten. Wait until the peak has passed before you speak. Reappraise. Ask, "Is there another way to read this?" Research finds that reframing is more effective than suppressing. Find the feeling underneath (hurt, fear, shame) and say that instead of attacking. Say what you need, using "I" statements, calmly, once you are calm. Don't just vent. Exercise or a walk can help use up arousal. Hitting things tends to keep anger high. Look after the basics: sleep, food, alcohol, stress. Get help. Anger-management programmes and therapy work, especially if anger leads to violence or fear at home.

Hindu practice answers anger with forgiveness, equanimity and ahimsa. Kshama. Forgiveness is a divine quality (Gita 16.3). The Mahabharata (Udyoga Parva, Vidura's counsel) is often quoted: "conquer anger by freedom from anger" (akrodhena jayet krodham). Equal-mindedness. Gita 12.18-19: equal to friend and foe, in honour and dishonour, in cold and heat. Dear to Krishna. Gita 12.13-14: hating no being, friendly, compassionate, forgiving and content. Ahimsa. Yoga Sutras 2.35: in the presence of one firmly established in non-harm, hostility ceases. Practise non-harm in thought, word and deed. Pratipaksha-bhavana. Yoga Sutras 2.33: when harmful thoughts arise, cultivate the opposite. Mantra, prayer and breath practices to settle the mind.

The Upanishadic path to freedom from anger is the training of the self and the vision of unity. Da, da, da. Brihadaranyaka 5.2.3 reports the thunder's three teachings: damyata (control yourselves), datta (give), dayadhvam (be compassionate). Calm, controlled, patient. Brihadaranyaka 4.4.23: shanto danta uparatas titikshuh samahito. See the Self in all. Isha 6: one who sees all beings in the Self does not hate. Hold the reins. Katha 1.3.3-9: let the intellect be the driver and the mind the reins, and guide the senses. Ask for calm. Katha 1.1.10 shows a wish that a father's anger be calmed, a model of asking for peace. Study and meditate. Later Vedanta teaches reflection on unity as a way to weaken the grounds of enmity.

Christian practice answers anger with gentleness, forgiveness and love of enemies. Be slow to anger. James 1:19: "quick to listen, slow to speak, slow to anger." Answer softly. Proverbs 15:1: "A soft answer turns away wrath." Proverbs 16:32: "One who is slow to anger is better than the mighty." Settle things the same day. Ephesians 4:26-27, and Matthew 5:23-24 (be reconciled before bringing your gift). Forgive. Ephesians 4:32 and Colossians 3:13: forgive as you have been forgiven. In the Lord's Prayer: "forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors" (Matthew 6:12). Do not repay evil. Romans 12:17-21: "Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good." Love enemies and pray for them (Matthew 5:44). Confession and prayer, and where needed counsel.

Buddhism has detailed practice for anger. Non-hatred. Dhammapada 5 and 223: conquer anger by non-anger, the bad by good, the miser by giving, the liar by truth. Metta. Loving-kindness practice (Sn 1.8) wishes well for all beings, including those you resent. Start with yourself and a friend, and move toward the difficult person. The saw simile. The Kakacupama Sutta (MN 21) says that even if bandits were sawing you apart limb by limb, anyone who gave way to hatred would not be following the teaching. Five ways to remove resentment. AN 5.161: cultivate loving-kindness, compassion or equanimity toward the person, forget or ignore them, or reflect on karma as one's own. Patience. Khanti is called the highest austerity (Dhammapada 184). Notice and let go. Mindful attention to the feeling in the body without acting on it.

Philosophy offers practices for catching anger early. Delay. Seneca (On Anger 2.29): "The greatest remedy for anger is delay." Wait before you act. Examine the judgment. Epictetus (Enchiridion 20): the insult is in your opinion. Ask whether the claim is true, and if so, why be angry. Evening review. Seneca (On Anger 3.36) describes the custom of the philosopher Sextius, who asked his spirit each night, "What bad habit of yours have you cured to-day? what vice have you checked? in what respect are you better?" Seneca says he follows the practice himself. Assume ignorance. Marcus Aurelius (Meditations 2.1 and 11.18): people act from ignorance of good and evil, and we also offend. Remember we are all going to die soon. Aim at mildness. Aristotle (NE 4.5): train toward the right anger at the right time, which takes practice and judgment. Avoid the company of the irritable, and choose calm company (Seneca 3.8).

Note: This is an invented composite story, not a real case. It is built from patterns people commonly describe, so you can see how anger works and how people step out of it. Imran's story Imran, 42, ran a warehouse and was known as a man you didn't cross. A late truck, a mistake on a pick list, a driver cutting him off: each one set off a blast. At home it was quieter but worse. He would go silent for days if his wife disagreed with him, and he shouted at his 12-year-old son over homework. One evening he slammed his fist on the table so hard that the glasses jumped. His son flinched and ran from the room. Imran saw the fear on the boy's face, and recognised it, because it was how he used to look at his own father. The turning point was not the fear itself but his son's question later: "Are you always going to be angry?" What helped: He learned his early signs: a hot face and clenched hands. He built a pause. He walked out of the room and breathed slowly for a few minutes before answering. He asked "what's under this?" and found a lot of fear of failing and of losing control. He apologised properly to his son, without excuses, and said what he'd do next time. He joined an anger-management group and cut back on drinking. He used exercise, a daily walk and later swimming, to burn off stress. He still got angry. But the blasts became rarer and shorter, and he repaired them faster. What it shows: Anger is often covering fear or hurt. A pause, honest naming and repair made more difference than trying to never feel it.

Vishvamitra's anger In the Ramayana (Bala Kanda), Vishvamitra begins as a king. Out hunting with his army, he comes to the hermitage of the sage Vasishtha, who feeds the whole army with the help of his wish-granting cow, Shabala. Vishvamitra, dazzled, asks for the cow. Vasishtha refuses, and Vishvamitra tries to take her by force. His army is destroyed by beings that Shabala brings forth, and his hundred sons are burnt by Vasishtha's power. Humbled, Vishvamitra concludes that a kshatriya's strength is nothing against spiritual power, gives the kingdom to his one surviving son and goes to do austerities. Over a long time he gains great power, but he is also easily angered. In the story of Trishanku he curses, and at one point he curses Menaka's enticement of him. Each time he spends the merit he has gathered. In the end, the tradition says, he overcomes his anger. He is recognised by Vasishtha as a Brahmarshi, the highest rank of sage. What it shows: Power gained by austerity can be lost by anger. The story presents mastery of anger as the final step in Vishvamitra's journey, more than the power itself.

The thunder's three syllables Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 5.2 tells of Prajapati, the creator, and his three groups of children: gods (devas), humans and demons (asuras). Each lived for a time as a student of Prajapati. When they finished, the gods asked him, "Speak to us, sir." He answered with one syllable: "Da. Have you understood?" The gods said, "We have understood: you said damyata, control yourselves." "Yes," said Prajapati, "you have understood." Then the humans asked, and got the same Da. They said, "You said datta, give." "Yes." Then the demons asked, and heard Da again. They said, "You said dayadhvam, be compassionate." "Yes, you have understood." The text adds that the divine voice of thunder still repeats the same: Da, da, da. Therefore one should practise these three: self-control, giving and compassion. What it shows: The tradition reads each group's lack in the answer: gods lack restraint, humans lack generosity and demons lack compassion. The last is the one aimed at cruelty and rage.

Moses at the rock Numbers 20:1-13 tells of the people of Israel in the wilderness of Zin. There was no water, and the people quarrelled with Moses and Aaron, saying they had been brought out only to die. Moses and Aaron went to the tent of meeting and fell on their faces. God told Moses to take his staff, gather the people, and speak to the rock before their eyes so that it would give water. Moses took the staff and gathered the community. Then he said, "Listen, you rebels, shall we bring water for you out of this rock?" and struck the rock twice with his staff. Water came out in abundance, and the people and animals drank. But God said to Moses and Aaron, "Because you did not trust in me, to show my holiness before the eyes of the Israelites, therefore you shall not bring this assembly into the land that I have given them." Moses had led the people for forty years. He saw the promised land from a mountain but did not enter it (Deuteronomy 34:1-4). What it shows: After decades of patience, one moment of angry impatience cost Moses what he had worked for. The story shows how even a great leader's anger can undo good work.

The gift that was not accepted In the Akkosa Sutta (SN 7.2), the brahmin Bharadvaja "the Rude" hears that a brahmin of his clan has left home to follow the Buddha. Angry and displeased, he goes to the Buddha and abuses him with harsh and rude words. The Buddha waits until he has finished, then asks calmly: "What do you think, brahmin? Do friends and colleagues, relatives and kin, and guests still come to visit you?" "Sometimes they do." "Do you then serve them with fresh and cooked foods and savories?" "Sometimes I do." "But if they don't accept it, brahmin, who does it belong to?" "In that case it still belongs to me." "In the same way, brahmin," says the Buddha, "when you abuse, harass, and attack us who do not abuse, harass, and attack, we don't accept it. It still belongs to you, brahmin, it still belongs to you!"
