He adds that someone who answers abuse with abuse is said to "eat the food and have a reaction to it," and that "when you don't get angry at an angry person you win a battle hard to win" (Sujato's translation). Bharadvaja goes for refuge and asks for ordination. The sutta says that not long after, living alone and diligent, he became one of the perfected (an arahant). What it shows: The Buddha does not answer anger with more anger, and does not suppress it either. He shows that an insult only lands if it is accepted.

Plato and the raised hand Seneca, in On Anger (3.12), tells of Plato, who found that one of his slaves had done something wrong, and was angry. He raised his hand to strike, and then stopped, hand still in the air. A friend came in and asked what he was doing. Plato answered: "I am making an angry man expiate his crime." Seneca says he kept the posture of one about to give way to passion, as if struck by how degrading it was for a philosopher. On another occasion, being angry at a fault, Plato said, "Speusippus, will you please to correct that slave with stripes; for I am in a rage." He would not strike the slave himself: "I should beat him more than I ought," he said, and he would not let the slave fall "into the power of one who is not in his own power." Seneca asks whether anyone should give the power of revenge to an angry man when Plato himself gave up that right. The story, in his hands, is about not acting while angry. What it shows: The moment between anger and action is where freedom lies. Plato's pause made the difference.

Sloth is neglecting what matters, out of laziness, apathy or avoidance. It is not the same as resting. Rest restores you. Sloth is putting off or skipping the things you know you should do for yourself and others, until the neglect becomes a habit. Modern terms for the pieces are: Procrastination, delaying a task despite expecting to be worse off for it. Avoidance, steering away from things that cause discomfort. Apathy, a loss of care or motivation. Learned helplessness, giving up because past effort seemed pointless. Sloth also differs from depression, which is a medical condition that can look like laziness (low energy, no motivation) but is not a moral failing.

Hinduism has no single word equal to sloth, but the closest ideas are alasya (laziness) and tamas, the quality of inertia, dullness and heaviness, one of the three gunas. The Gita describes tamas in several places. In 14.8, it is born of ignorance and binds through heedlessness (pramada), laziness (alasya) and sleep (nidra). In 18.28, a tamasic doer is "unsteady, vulgar, stubborn, deceitful, malicious, lazy (alasa), despondent and procrastinating (dirgha-sutri)." And 18.39 describes a tamasic happiness that comes from sleep, laziness and heedlessness. Yoga Sutras 1.30 names alasya (laziness, heaviness of body and mind) among the nine obstacles to yoga. This is related to sloth and not identical to it: Hinduism sees it as a guna to be balanced, not as a sin.

The Upanishads do not list laziness as a sin. They treat it as the opposite of the effort the path demands, and as a form of the heedlessness (pramada) that keeps the seeker asleep. Wake up. Katha 1.3.14 says: "Arise, awake! Having obtained your boons, understand them. The path is sharp as a razor's edge, hard to cross, say the wise." Strength needed. Mundaka 3.2.4 says "This Self cannot be gained by one without strength, nor through heedlessness (pramada), nor by austerity without the right aim." Neglect of duty to learn and teach. Taittiriya 1.11 tells the graduate not to neglect study and teaching (svadhyaya-pravacanabhyam na pramaditavyam), nor truth, dharma, welfare, prosperity or duties to gods and ancestors. The theme is related to sloth and not identical to it: the texts speak of heedlessness, not of a sin of laziness.

Christian tradition calls it sloth (Latin acedia, from Greek akedia, "lack of care"). It began as a spiritual condition described by the desert monk Evagrius Ponticus as the "noonday demon": restlessness, boredom and distaste for one's work and prayer. Later it broadened to include laziness and neglect of duty. The Catechism (CCC 2733) describes acedia as a temptation to which presumption opens the gate: "a form of depression due to lax ascetical practice, decreasing vigilance, carelessness of heart." Aquinas (ST II-II q.35) defines it as sorrow about spiritual good: a sadness or weariness about doing what one ought. The Bible has plenty on idleness. Proverbs 6:6-11 tells the sluggard to learn from the ant. Proverbs 26:14 says "As a door turns on its hinges, so does a lazy person in bed." Romans 12:11 says, "Do not lag in zeal." 2 Thessalonians 3:10 says, "Anyone unwilling to work should not eat."

The Pali words are thina-middha, sloth and torpor, the third of the five hindrances to meditation, and kosajja, laziness, whose opposite is viriya, energy or effort. Thina is sluggishness of mind and middha is heaviness or drowsiness. They are described as a mental state, which can have causes such as heavy eating, and can be dealt with. The Buddha's last words, in the Mahaparinibbana Sutta (DN 16), were: "Conditions fall apart. Persist with diligence" (appamadena sampadetha, Sujato's translation, DN 16 at 6.7.3). Dhammapada 280 says that one who does not rise when it is time to rise, and who is young and strong but given to idleness, with a mind full of sluggish thoughts, will not find the way by wisdom.

Philosophers discuss sloth as a failure to act on what one knows is good, and as waste of the life one has. Aristotle. In the Nicomachean Ethics (7.1-10) he describes akrasia, weakness of will: knowing the better and doing otherwise. In the Politics and the Ethics he argues that happiness is an activity of the soul in line with virtue (NE 1.7), not a state of rest. Seneca. In On the Shortness of Life (1) he writes: "It is not that we have a short space of time, but that we waste much of it." Marcus Aurelius. In the Meditations (5.1) he scolds himself for lying in bed in the morning: "In the morning when thou risest unwillingly, let this thought be present: I am rising to the work of a human being" (Long translation). Kant. In the Groundwork (4:423), he argues that a rational being cannot will universal neglect of talents, so cultivating them is a duty to oneself.

Sloth rarely comes from simple "laziness". Common roots are: Avoiding discomfort. Tasks that cause anxiety, boredom or fear of failure get postponed to feel better now. Present bias. Humans tend to prefer immediate reward over later benefit, so future costs feel small. Perfectionism and fear of failure. If you might not do it well, not starting protects your self-image. Unclear or overwhelming goals. A big, vague task is hard to begin. Low energy. Poor sleep, inactivity, diet, and mental-health conditions such as depression reduce drive. Distraction. Phones and feeds offer instant, easy rewards. Learned helplessness. After repeated failure or lack of control, people stop trying.

Hindu thought traces sloth to tamas, the guna of inertia and ignorance. Born of ignorance. Gita 14.8 says that tamas arises from ignorance and deludes all embodied beings through heedlessness, laziness and sleep. Rising and falling gunas. Gita 14.10: sometimes sattva prevails over the other two, sometimes rajas, sometimes tamas. Habit and food, company and activity shift the balance. Food and environment. Gita 17.10 describes stale, tasteless, rotten and impure food as the food of tamas. Delusion about duty. Gita 18.32 says tamasic understanding sees wrong as right, covered in darkness. Gita 3.4-8 argues no one can avoid action, so refusing to act is itself self-deception. Fear and attachment. In Gita 1-2, Arjuna's despondency before the battle shows sloth as a failure of nerve.

The Upanishads place the cause in heedlessness (pramada) and ignorance. Heedlessness. Mundaka 3.2.4 names pramada as one of the ways the Self is missed. Ignorance as sleep. Katha 1.3.14 says "Arise, awake," which implies that ordinary life is a kind of sleep. Choosing the pleasant. Katha 1.2.1-2: the unwise choose the pleasant (preyas), which includes ease and comfort, over the good (shreyas). Not seeing the aim. Katha 1.2.5: living in ignorance, people go round like the blind led by the blind. Without a goal, there is nothing to rouse effort. Lack of strength. Mundaka 3.2.4 says the Self is not gained by one lacking strength (balahina), which links effort to inner vigour.

Christian writers find sloth's roots in weariness of spirit, loss of hope and misplaced love. Noonday demon. Evagrius describes acedia as a restlessness at midday that makes the day seem endless, the place unbearable and the work pointless. It arises from boredom and from the temptation to want to be elsewhere. Sorrow about the good. Aquinas (ST II-II q.35) says acedia is sorrow at spiritual good, because it demands effort. Discouragement. Galatians 6:9 urges, "Let us not grow weary in doing what is right," and Hebrews 12:3 says to consider Christ "so that you may not grow weary in your souls or lose heart." Love grown cold. Matthew 24:12 speaks of love growing cold. Revelation 3:15-16 criticises being "neither cold nor hot." Fear. In the parable of the talents (Matthew 25:24-25), the third servant says, "I was afraid, and I went and hid your talent in the ground."

Buddhism traces sloth and torpor to unwholesome conditions that can be changed. Heavy body and mind. The suttas list causes of the hindrance: discontent, sloth, yawning, sleepiness after eating and mental sluggishness, which "fuel the arising of dullness and drowsiness" (SN 46.51, Sujato's translation). Lack of energy and interest. Kosajja arises where there is no vision of the goal. The Buddha speaks of "unwise attention" feeding the hindrances. Over-comfort. AN 3.39 (Sukhumala) describes the intoxication of health and ease making people careless. Wrong view. Fatalist views that deny the point of effort were rejected by the Buddha (AN 3.61, the Sectarian Doctrines). Aversion to effort. Avoiding the discomfort of practice.

Philosophers find the cause of sloth in weak will, the pull of immediate pleasure and lack of purpose. Akrasia. Aristotle (NE 7.3) describes the person who knows the better course but is overcome by appetite or feeling. Habit. Aristotle (NE 2.1) says we become what we repeatedly do, so idleness grows by repetition. Pleasure of ease. Seneca (Letters 82) says that leisure without philosophy is a kind of death, and that comfort makes the mind soft. Wasted time. Seneca (On the Shortness of Life 9) sees people postponing the start of living: "postponement is the greatest waste of life." Fear of failure. Kant (Metaphysics of Morals, Doctrine of Virtue) treats neglect of one's natural powers as a failing in duty to oneself.

Chronic avoidance costs more than the task you put off. Stress and guilt. Procrastinators report higher stress and worse well-being on average, as the work and the worry build up. Health. Studies link procrastination with poorer sleep and delay in seeking medical care. Work and money. Missed deadlines, lower performance and late bills. Relationships. Others carry what you leave undone, which breeds resentment. Lost growth. Skills and goals stall, and regret about unlived years is common. Spiral. Shame about avoiding makes the next task feel worse, which feeds more avoidance.

The Gita describes where tamas leads. Darkness and delusion. Gita 14.13: when tamas prevails, there is darkness, inertia, heedlessness and delusion. Downward path. Gita 14.18: those in tamas go downward. 14.16-17 say that the fruit of tamas is ignorance, and that ignorance and delusion arise from it. Hollow happiness. Gita 18.39: the happiness of tamas deludes from beginning to end, arising from sleep, sloth and heedlessness. Duty undone. Gita 3.8 and 3.20 stress that action is better than inaction and that even keeping the body going depends on action. 3.16 says one who does not turn the wheel of action "lives in vain." Obstacle to yoga. Yoga Sutras 1.30-31: laziness is an obstacle that brings distress.

The Upanishads describe the cost of heedlessness as missing the goal. Missing the Self. Mundaka 3.2.4: the Self cannot be gained by the heedless or the weak. Staying asleep. Katha 1.3.14: "Arise, awake!" The cost of not waking is staying on the wrong path. Wandering. Katha 1.2.5-6: the ignorant go round and round, and the one who thinks "this world is all there is" falls under death's sway again and again. A wasted chance. Kena 2.5 says that if one knows here, then there is truth; if one does not know here, there is great loss. The human birth is the chance to know. Neglected duties. Taittiriya 1.11: do not be heedless about study, teaching, truth and dharma.

Scripture and tradition list sloth's costs. Poverty. Proverbs 6:9-11: "A little sleep, a little slumber... and poverty will come upon you like a robber." Proverbs 10:4: "A slack hand causes poverty, but the hand of the diligent makes rich." Unfinished work. Proverbs 12:24 says diligent hands will rule, while the lazy will be put to forced labour. A buried talent. In Matthew 25:24-30, the servant who hid his master's money out of fear loses what he had. Burden on others. 2 Thessalonians 3:10-12 asks those who live in idleness to earn their own bread. Despair. The desert fathers saw acedia as leading to despair and abandoning the call of one's life. Neglected love. Matthew 25:41-45 shows judgment on those who did nothing for the hungry, strangers and sick.

Sloth and laziness cost progress and bring regret. No path. Dhammapada 280: the idle one, young and strong but not rising, does not find the way by wisdom. Blocks meditation. Sloth and torpor cloud the mind and make concentration impossible. Lost opportunity. The Buddha's final advice was to strive on with diligence (DN 16). Life is short and the chance is rare. Slipping back. Dhammapada 168-169 urges one to rise up and not be heedless, and says the heedless suffer. Heedlessness is a path to death. Dhammapada 21: heedfulness (appamada) is the way to the deathless, and heedlessness the way to death.

Philosophers describe the cost as a life unlived. Wasted life. Seneca (On the Shortness of Life 1-3): life is long enough if you use it well, but it is wasted by those who put off and neglect it. Lost happiness. Aristotle (NE 1.7-8) argues that happiness lies in virtuous activity. A life of idle ease achieves none of it. Weakened will. Aristotle (NE 2.1): idleness repeated becomes character. Unrealised talents. Kant (Groundwork 4:423) says a rational being cannot will that talents be left to rust. Lost duty to others. Marcus Aurelius (Meditations 5.1) reminds himself that he is made for work, as bees are, and for the common good.

The aim is to make starting easy, and to be kind to yourself while you do. Rule out health causes. Check sleep, food, movement and mood. If low energy lasts for weeks, see a doctor, since depression is not laziness. Shrink the first step. Commit to five minutes. Starting is the hard part. Make the task clear. Break it into steps and write the very next action. Set a time and place ("after coffee, at the desk"), so you decide once. Remove distractions. Phone in another room, blockers on feeds. Reward progress with something small after you finish. Use self-compassion, not self-attack. Studies find that forgiving yourself for past procrastination makes it less likely next time. Add accountability. Tell a friend, or work alongside someone.

Hindu practice answers tamas by raising rajas and then sattva, and by acting without clinging to results. Act. Gita 3.8: "Perform your allotted duty, for action is better than inaction." Karma yoga. Gita 2.47-48: do your work without attachment to the result, and stay steady in success and failure. This frees you from the fear that stops many people starting. Lift yourself. Gita 6.5: "Let a person lift themselves by their own self; let them not degrade themselves." Moderation. Gita 6.16-17: not too much sleep or too little, not too much food or too little, with balanced effort. Sattvic food and routine. Gita 17.8 and the tradition of an early waking time (brahma-muhurta). Practice and detachment. Yoga Sutras 1.12-14: steady, long and devoted practice.

The Upanishadic call is to wake up and make effort. Arise, awake. Katha 1.3.14 is the classic call: get up, find a teacher and understand. Gather strength. Mundaka 3.2.4: the Self is not for the weak or the heedless. Cultivate vigour through discipline. Keep to study and duty. Taittiriya 1.11: do not neglect study and teaching, and do your duties. Choose the good. Katha 1.2.1-2: choose shreyas over preyas, which means doing the harder, worthwhile thing. Hold the reins. Katha 1.3.3-9: let the driver (intellect) hold the reins and the senses will follow. Seek the teacher. Mundaka 1.2.12 says to go to a teacher with fuel in hand, ready for service and study.

Christian practice answers sloth with work as service, perseverance and hope. Learn from the ant. Proverbs 6:6-8. Work as service. Colossians 3:23: "Whatever task you must do, work as if your soul depends on it, as for the Lord and not for humans." Do not grow weary. Galatians 6:9 and Hebrews 12:1-3: run with perseverance. Stay in your cell. The desert fathers advised, against the noonday demon, to stay and keep working and praying (Evagrius, Praktikos 12, and a saying attributed to Abba Moses that the cell itself will teach the monk everything; this saying was not checked against a specific edition of the Sayings of the Desert Fathers). Rhythm. Benedict's Rule gives a daily order of prayer and work (ora et labora). Rest too. Sabbath (Exodus 20:8-11) is built in, so diligence is not overwork. Ask for help. Philippians 4:13 and prayer.

Buddhism treats sloth as a hindrance with practical remedies. Cultivate energy (viriya). It is one of the five spiritual faculties and one of the seven factors of awakening, and the Buddha urged diligence (appamada) in his last words (DN 16). Specific remedies. The suttas and commentaries suggest: change posture, walk, splash water on the face, look at light, reflect on the Dhamma, and avoid overeating (as in AN 7.61, Pacalayamana Sutta, on the monk nodding). Right effort. The four efforts: prevent unwholesome states, abandon those that have arisen, develop wholesome states, maintain them (AN 4.13 and the eightfold path). Reflect on urgency. Death is certain and the time is unknown (AN 6.19-20, mindfulness of death). Friends. Good company (kalyana-mitta) is "the whole of the spiritual life" (SN 45.2, Sujato's translation).

Philosophy offers habits that make action easier. Remember why you are here. Marcus Aurelius (Meditations 5.1): when you struggle to get up in the morning, tell yourself, "I am rising to the work of a human being." Use your time. Seneca (On the Shortness of Life 3, 9): don't postpone, and live as if you will not have tomorrow. Build habits. Aristotle (NE 2.1-3): we become diligent by doing diligent things. Start with small repeated acts. Train will. Aristotle (NE 7.7-8) says the weak-willed can improve by foreseeing temptation and planning around it. Make it a duty. Kant (Groundwork 4:423) treats developing your talents as a duty to yourself. Daily review. Seneca (On Anger 3.36) and Epictetus (Discourses 3.10) recommend reviewing the day.

Note: This is an invented composite story, not a real case. It is built from patterns people commonly describe, so you can see how sloth works and how people step out of it. Nisha's story Nisha was in the last year of a master's degree with a thesis due in four months. She told herself she would start properly on Monday. Monday became next Monday. She tidied her desk, reorganised her notes, watched "one" video that turned into five, and told herself she worked better under pressure. The weeks passed. The thesis felt bigger each day, and the bigger it felt, the more she avoided it. She stopped replying to her supervisor. At night she lay awake feeling guilty, and the next day the guilt made her want to hide more. The turning point was an email from her supervisor, short and kind: "Send me anything, even a page, and we'll go from there." What helped: She checked her health. She was sleeping badly, and a doctor's visit confirmed she was low on energy and mood. She started treatment for it. She cut the task down. The goal for the day was one paragraph, written before opening any messages. She sent the supervisor a rough page, which was bad, and got useful comments. She set a fixed hour (9 to 10 a.m.) at the library, with the phone in her bag. She dropped the self-attack, and wrote down what she had done each day, not what she hadn't. She did not finish early, but she finished on time and the work was fine. What it shows: Sloth often hides fear and exhaustion. A small first step and some kindness did more than a strict resolve.

Arjuna's despondency The Bhagavad Gita begins on the battlefield of Kurukshetra, with two armies ready. Arjuna, the Pandava warrior, asks his charioteer Krishna to drive between the armies so he can see who he must fight. He sees teachers, uncles, cousins and friends on the other side. His limbs fail, his mouth goes dry, his body trembles and his bow slips from his hand (Gita 1.28-30). He says that he sees no good in killing his kin, and that he does not want victory or a kingdom. He sits down in the chariot, throws down his bow and, as the text says, "his mind overwhelmed with grief" (1.47). In chapter 2, Krishna's first words rebuke him: "Whence has this weakness (klaibya) come upon you in a time of crisis? Do not yield to it. It does not suit you. Give up this petty weakness of heart and arise" (2.2-3). The rest of the Gita is Krishna's teaching on duty, action without attachment and the Self. What it shows: Arjuna's refusal to act is not laziness in the usual sense, but it is the same inertia of tamas: freezing in front of what must be done. Krishna's answer is a call to arise and act with the right understanding.

Satyakama and the cattle In Chandogya Upanishad 4.4-9, a boy named Satyakama asks his mother Jabala who his father was, as he wishes to become a student. She tells him she does not know, as she was a servant who moved from house to house in her youth. "Tell the teacher your name is Satyakama Jabala," she says. He goes to the sage Gautama and says truthfully that he doesn't know his father. Gautama is struck by his honesty: "Only a true Brahmin could say that," and accepts him. Gautama gives him four hundred lean, weak cows and tells him to take them away and not come back until they are a thousand. Satyakama says, "I will not return until they number a thousand," and lives with them in the forest for years. When the herd reaches a thousand, a bull, then fire, a swan and a diving bird each speak to him in turn, teaching him a part of Brahman. When he returns, his teacher sees his face shine and says, "You shine like one who knows Brahman." The teacher then teaches him the rest. What it shows: This is the opposite of sloth: long, patient, unrewarded work done for a goal and a promise. Learning arrived through the effort.

Jonah runs away The Book of Jonah begins with God telling the prophet Jonah to go to Nineveh and preach against its wickedness. Nineveh was the capital of Assyria, a feared enemy. Jonah got up, but to run: he went to Joppa and boarded a ship for Tarshish, "away from the presence of the Lord" (Jonah 1:3). A great storm came, and the sailors were terrified and threw cargo overboard. And where was Jonah? "Jonah had gone down into the hold of the ship and had lain down and was fast asleep" (1:5). The captain woke him and told him to call on his God. Jonah told the sailors the storm was his fault and asked to be thrown overboard. They did so reluctantly, and the sea calmed. A large fish swallowed him, and in its belly, after three days, he prayed and was released. God told him again to go to Nineveh. This time he went and preached, and the city repented. Even so, Jonah was angry that God showed mercy (Jonah 4). What it shows: The first move of avoidance is to flee from what one is called to do, and sleep through the storm. The story shows that the call does not go away, and that the second try is possible.

Moggallana nods off The Pacalayamana Sutta (AN 7.61) tells how the Buddha's chief disciple in psychic powers, Maha Moggallana, was sitting in meditation near the village of Kallavalamutta in Magadha, and kept nodding with drowsiness. The Buddha saw this with his divine eye, appeared before him, and asked: "Are you nodding off, Moggallana? Are you nodding off?" "Yes, sir," said Moggallana. The Buddha then gave him a series of remedies, in order. If drowsiness comes while you are attending to a particular perception, don't give attention to it. If it persists, think over and examine the Dhamma you have learned. If that fails, recite it aloud. If that fails, pull your earlobes and rub your limbs. If that fails, get up and wash your eyes with water and look at the sky and stars. If that fails, attend to the perception of light, by day and by night. If that fails, walk back and forth, with senses turned inward. And finally, if that fails, lie down on the right side, mindful, focused on the time of getting up. On waking he should get up quickly, thinking that he will not live indulging in the pleasures of sleeping, lying down and drowsing. What it shows: Even a great disciple gets sleepy. The Buddha's answer is practical, a ladder of remedies, with no shame attached.

Heracles at the crossroads Xenophon's Memorabilia (2.1.21-34) records a story that Socrates says he heard from the sophist Prodicus. When the young Heracles was about to enter manhood, he went to a quiet place and sat wondering which road in life to take. Two tall women came toward him. One was Vice, plump and made-up, who called herself Happiness. She offered him an easy road to happiness without toil: "I will guide you by a short and easy road to happiness" (Dakyns translation). The other was Virtue, simply dressed, with a quiet face. She told him that "not one" of the lovely things has been given to mortals "apart from toil and pains": to win the favour of the gods he must serve them, to be loved by friends he must benefit them, and to have the earth yield fruit he must tend it (Dakyns translation). She said that Vice's pleasures were not satisfying, since those who take them before they are hungry or tired are never really content. Xenophon, as Socrates reports it, breaks off with Virtue's speech and does not record which road Heracles took. What it shows: Sloth is the first woman's offer: comfort now. Virtue's reply is that anything worth having is bought with effort.

Procrastination is putting off something you intend to do, even though you expect to be worse off for the delay. That last part matters. Doing a more urgent task first, or waiting for information you really need, is planning. Procrastination is delay you do not endorse and usually end up paying for. It tends to take a few forms: Avoiding a task that feels unpleasant, boring or frightening, such as a tax form, a hard email or a first draft. Substituting easier work, such as tidying, checking messages or "just a bit more research", so you feel busy without starting. Waiting to feel ready, motivated or in the right mood. Leaving everything to the last stretch and relying on deadline pressure. Researchers treat it as a problem of self-regulation, not of time management. Steel's 2007 review calls it "a prevalent and pernicious form of self-regulatory failure". It is related to sloth but not identical. Sloth is a wider neglect of what matters; procrastination is the specific habit of delay, and it is common among people who care a great deal and are far from lazy. Persistent trouble starting things can also have other causes, such as low mood, anxiety or attention difficulties, which a doctor or therapist can help to tell apart.

Hinduism has no sin called procrastination and no single word equal to it, but the Bhagavad Gita names the procrastinator directly. In 18.28, a performer of action "in the mode of ignorance" (tamas) is described as "undisciplined, vulgar, stubborn, deceitful, slothful, despondent, and a procrastinator". The Sanskrit word glossed "procrastinator" there is dirgha-sutri. Tamas is one of the three gunas, the qualities of inertia, dullness and heaviness. In 14.8 the Gita says it is born of ignorance and binds embodied beings through negligence (pramada), laziness (alasya) and sleep (nidra). This is related to procrastination and not identical to it. The Gita is describing a quality that shapes how a person acts, to be balanced and outgrown, and not a sin. See also sloth in Hinduism, which covers alasya more broadly.

The Upanishads have no word for procrastination, and their concern is wider than tasks and deadlines. The nearest idea is heedlessness and the habit of choosing what is pleasant now over what is good. In the Katha Upanishad, Death (Yama) tells Nachiketa: "The good is one thing, the pleasant another; these two, having different objects, chain a man." The wise person "prefers the good to the pleasant, but the fool chooses the pleasant through greed and avarice" (Katha 1.2.1-2). Delay is one way of choosing the pleasant. Katha 1.2.6 speaks of "the careless child, deluded by the delusion of wealth", for whom the Hereafter "never rises before the eyes". This is related to procrastination and not identical to it: the Upanishads are speaking of postponing the pursuit of knowledge of the Self, and of the pleasant over the good in general, and not of everyday tasks.

The Bible has no word for procrastination, but it describes the habit again and again in the figure of the sluggard, the person who always means to start later. Proverbs 6:9-11 asks: "How long will you lie there, O lazybones? When will you rise from your sleep? A little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to rest, and poverty will come upon you like a robber." Ecclesiastes 11:4 gives the excuse of waiting for the perfect moment: "Whoever observes the wind will not sow, and whoever regards the clouds will not reap." James 4:17 makes the link to conscience: "Anyone, then, who knows the right thing to do and fails to do it commits sin." Procrastination is related to the Christian idea of sloth (acedia) but not identical to it. The sluggard texts are about neglecting work and duty, and acedia is a deeper weariness of spirit; see sloth in Christianity.

Buddhist texts have no word for procrastination as such, but they speak about it in several ways: heedlessness (pamada) and its opposite heedfulness (appamada), laziness (kosajja) and the hindrance of sloth and torpor (thina-middha). See sloth in Buddhism. The Dhammapada says: "Heedfulness is the state free of death; heedlessness is the state of death. The heedful do not die, while the heedless are like the dead" (Dhp 21). The urgency of "now" is stated in the Bhaddekaratta Sutta (MN 131): "Today's the day to keenly work— who knows, tomorrow may bring death!" And Dhp 313 says: "If one is to do what should be done, one should staunchly strive." This is related to procrastination and not identical to it: the texts speak of heedlessness in practice and in livelihood, and not of tasks and deadlines in general.

Philosophers do not use the word procrastination, but they have long described acting against what you judge best. The Greek word is akrasia, weakness of will, and it is the closest philosophical idea. Hesiod is blunt about delay in Works and Days: "Do not put your work off till to-morrow and the day after; for a sluggish worker does not fill his barn, nor one who puts off his work: industry makes work go well, but a man who puts off work is always at hand-grips with ruin" (Evelyn-White's translation). Aristotle treats akrasia in Nicomachean Ethics 7. He notes that Socrates denied it could happen: "no one, he said, when he judges acts against what he judges best—people act so only by reason of ignorance." Aristotle says this "plainly contradicts the observed facts", and sets out to explain how a person can know the better and still not do it. Marcus Aurelius writes to himself: "Remember how long thou hast been putting off these things, and how often thou hast received an opportunity from the gods, and yet dost not use it" (Meditations 2, Long's translation). Akrasia is related to procrastination and not identical to it. It covers any case of acting against one's judgment of what is best, and procrastination is the form in which the action is delayed.

Research points to several causes that often work together. The task feels bad. In a meta-analysis of 691 correlations, the strong and consistent predictors of procrastination were task aversiveness, task delay, self-efficacy and impulsiveness, plus conscientiousness and its facets: self-control, distractibility, organisation and achievement motivation. Neuroticism, rebelliousness and sensation seeking showed only a weak connection. Now beats later. The authors explain these results with temporal motivation theory, which combines expectancy theory with hyperbolic discounting. In plain terms: a reward loses pull the further away it is, so the relief of avoiding a task today can outweigh a payoff that comes later. Mood repair. Sirois and Pychyl argue that procrastination has a great deal to do with short-term mood repair and emotion regulation: putting a task off makes an uncomfortable feeling go away for now. They add that the costs of delay fall mainly on the future self. Doubt about being able to do it. Low self-efficacy, the belief that you can carry the task out, is on the list above. Starting feels risky when you expect to do it badly.

The Gita traces the habit of putting things off to ignorance, attachment and the pull of comfort. Ignorance. Verse 14.8 says tamas is "born of ignorance". Verse 14.17 adds: "from the mode of ignorance arise negligence and delusion." Comfort mistaken for happiness. Verse 18.39 describes the happiness of tamas as the kind "derived from sleep, indolence, and negligence". It is pleasant now, which is the same pull that makes delay attractive. Fear of the outcome. Verse 2.47 says: "You have a right to perform your prescribed duties, but you are not entitled to the fruits of your actions. Never consider yourself to be the cause of the results of your activities, nor be attached to inaction." One reading is that worry about results can freeze a person into inaction, which is why the verse names both attachment to fruits and attachment to inaction. The mind as its own enemy. Verse 6.5 says the mind "can be the friend and also the enemy of the self".

The Upanishads place the root in the uncontrolled mind and in the pull of what pleases now. The pleasant over the good. Katha 1.2.2: "the wise prefers the good to the pleasant, but the fool chooses the pleasant through greed and avarice." Delusion by wealth and comfort. Katha 1.2.6: "The Hereafter never rises before the eyes of the careless child, deluded by the delusion of wealth. 'This is the world,' he thinks, 'there is no other.'" Reins that are not held. Katha 1.3.3-6 compares the self to a rider in a chariot: the body is the chariot, the intellect the charioteer, the mind the reins and the senses the horses. "He who has no understanding and whose mind (the reins) is never firmly held, his senses (horses) are unmanageable, like vicious horses of a charioteer."

Christian writers find the roots of delay in a divided will, in the force of habit, and in fear. A divided will. In Romans 7:15-19 Paul writes: "I do not understand my own actions. For I do not do what I want, but I do the very thing I hate... For I do not do the good I want, but the evil I do not want is what I do." The force of habit. Augustine describes how he kept putting off a change he knew he needed. In the Confessions (8.5) he says: "the law of sin is the violence of custom, whereby the mind is drawn and held, even against its will; deserving to be so held in that it so willingly falls into it." Waiting for perfect conditions. Ecclesiastes 11:4: "Whoever observes the wind will not sow, and whoever regards the clouds will not reap." Fear. In the parable of the talents, the third servant says: "I was afraid, and I went and hid your talent in the ground" (Matthew 25:25).

The Buddhist texts point to excuses, a sunken mind and a mind pulled away from the present. Excuses. In the Sigalovada Sutta (DN 31), the Buddha says of habitual laziness: "You don't get your work done because you think: 'It's too cold! It's too hot. It's too late! It's too early! I'm too hungry! I'm too full!'" A sunken, heavy mind. Dhp 280: "They don't get going when it's time to start; they're young and strong, but given to sloth. Their mind depressed in sunken thought, lazy and slothful, they can't discern the path." Heedlessness. Dhp 21 contrasts heedfulness with heedlessness, "the state of death". A mind that is elsewhere. MN 131 begins: "Don't run back to the past, don't anticipate the future. What's past is left behind, the future has not arrived; and any present phenomenon you clearly discern in every case." The advice implies that attention drifting to what was or will be keeps us from the work in front of us. That reading is ours.

The philosophers offer several explanations of why we know and still do not act. Ignorance (Socrates). In Aristotle's report, Socrates held that "no one... when he judges acts against what he judges best" and that people act so "only by reason of ignorance". On that view delay is a failure to see clearly what is best. Emotion overcoming a decision (Aristotle). Aristotle separates two kinds of incontinence: "impetuosity" and "weakness". In the second, "some men after deliberating fail, owing to their emotion, to stand by the conclusions of their deliberation". This is the one closest to the person who plans well and does not follow through. Carelessness (Seneca). In his first letter to Lucilius he writes: "The most disgraceful kind of loss, however, is that due to carelessness." Waiting for someone else (Epictetus). "What other master, then, do you wait for, to throw upon that the delay of reforming yourself?"

The costs usually arrive later than the relief. Stress and health. In two studies of students, Tice and Baumeister found that procrastinators reported less stress and less illness early in the semester, but more stress and more illness late in the term, and were sicker overall. They also received lower grades on all assignments. A loop. Avoiding a task brings quick relief, and the guilt and pressure come after. That is consistent with the mood-repair account in Root causes, where the cost is carried by the future self. Reading it as a loop is our inference, not a finding of these studies. A growing habit. Steel notes that the prevalence of procrastination appears to be growing. Everyday costs. Rushed work, late fees and strained trust with people who were waiting on you are common results, though these are general observations and not from the studies above. These studies were of students at one time and place, and they show association, not proof that delay caused the illness or the grades.

In the Gita the effects of tamas, the inertia behind procrastination, are described as a binding and a clouding. It binds. Verse 14.8 says tamas "binds" through negligence, laziness and sleep. It clouds judgment. Verse 14.17: "from the mode of ignorance arise negligence and delusion." It hides the self. Verse 18.39 says happiness derived from sleep, indolence and negligence "covers the nature of the self from beginning to end". It sits beside despair. In 18.28 the procrastinator is listed together with the "slothful" and the "despondent". Doing nothing is not an option. Verse 3.8 says "action is superior to inaction. By ceasing activity, even your bodily maintenance will not be possible." Taken at the extreme, putting everything off cannot be sustained.

The Upanishads describe the result of heedlessness as going round in circles, without arriving. Staggering in darkness. Katha 1.2.5: "Fools dwelling in darkness, wise in their own conceit, and puffed up with vain knowledge, go round and round, staggering to and fro, like blind men led by the blind." Falling under death's sway again and again. After the careless child thinks "there is no other" world, "thus he falls again and again under my sway" (Katha 1.2.6). The goal slips away. Mundaka 3.2.4: the Self is not gained "by one who is destitute of strength, or without earnestness, or without right meditation." The restless, uncontrolled mind never arrives. Katha 1.3.7: one "who has no understanding, who is unmindful and always impure, never reaches that place, but enters into the round of births."

Scripture describes delay as costing a person their harvest, and sometimes their chance. Poverty and loss. Proverbs 6:10-11: "A little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to rest, and poverty will come upon you like a robber, and want, like an armed warrior." A missed harvest. Proverbs 20:4: "The lazy person does not plow in season; harvest comes, and there is nothing to be found." Wanting without getting. Proverbs 13:4: "The appetite of the lazy craves and gets nothing, while the appetite of the diligent is richly supplied." An uncertain tomorrow. Proverbs 27:1: "Do not boast about tomorrow, for you do not know what a day may bring." James 4:14 adds: "you are a mist that appears for a little while and then vanishes." Delay that feels short and is not. Augustine writes that his answer to the call was only "Presently, lo, presently; Leave me a little while. But presently, presently, had no present; and my leave me a little while went on for a long while" (Confessions 8.5).

The Buddhist texts describe the effects as lost livelihood, a hard life and a wasted chance. Lost income. After the list of excuses, DN 31 says: "By dwelling on so many excuses for not working, you don't make any more money, and the money you already have runs out." The verses add: "When the young neglect their work like this, riches pass them by." A good deed left undone. Dhp 314: "A bad deed is better left undone, for it will plague you later on. A good deed is better done, one that does not plague you." A lax effort stirs up dust. Dhp 313 speaks of "the life gone forth when laxly led", which "just stirs up dust all the more". The verse is about the monastic life. No bargaining with time. MN 131: "who knows, tomorrow may bring death! For there is no bargain to be struck with Death and his mighty horde."

The philosophers describe the cost of delay as lost time, lost character and eventually a life half lived. Ruin. Hesiod: "a man who puts off work is always at hand-grips with ruin" (Works and Days, Evelyn-White). Time slips away. Seneca, Letter 1: "While we are postponing, life speeds by." And: "Nothing, Lucilius, is ours, except time." No progress, then no life. Epictetus warns that if you "always add procrastination to procrastination, purpose to purpose, and fix day after day in which you will attend to yourself, you will insensibly continue without proficiency, and, living and dying, persevere in being one of the vulgar" (Enchiridion, Higginson's translation). Opportunities pass. Marcus Aurelius: "how often thou hast received an opportunity from the gods, and yet dost not use it" (Meditations 2).

Most of what helps works on the feeling of starting, not on willpower. Name what you are avoiding. If a task feels bad, say how: boring, scary, unclear, or likely to show you a result you don't want. The mood-repair account suggests the delay is partly a way of escaping that feeling. Shrink the first step. Make it small enough that starting costs almost nothing: open the file, write one sentence, sort ten minutes of receipts. Decide when and where in advance. An implementation intention is an "if... then..." plan: "When I finish lunch, I will open the report and write for ten minutes." A meta-analysis of 94 tests found that forming such plans had a medium-to-large effect (d = .65) on reaching goals. Move the reward closer. Because distant rewards pull weakly, pair the task with something immediate: a fixed hour, a coffee, a person waiting. Cut the easy escapes. Put the phone in another room or close the tabs before you begin. Forgive the slip. In a study of first-year students, those who forgave themselves for procrastinating before a first exam tended to procrastinate less before the next one. Harsh self-attack adds more feeling to escape from. Check for other causes. If low mood, worry or poor sleep sits behind the delay, treating that comes first.

The Gita's answer is steady, unattached action, not waiting for the mood. Act. Verse 3.8: "action is superior to inaction." Do the work as duty, without clinging to results. Verse 3.19 begins: "Therefore, giving up attachment, perform actions as a matter of duty". This removes the fear of the outcome that feeds delay. Aim for the steady doer. Verse 18.26 describes the performer in the mode of goodness as one "free from egotism and attachment, endowed with enthusiasm and determination, and equipoised in success and failure." Lift yourself. Verse 6.5: "Elevate yourself through the power of your mind, and not degrade yourself." Keep the body regular. Verse 6.17 praises those "temperate in eating and recreation, balanced in work, and regulated in sleep". Arise. Krishna's first word to Arjuna in 2.3 is: "Give up such petty weakness of heart and arise."

The Upanishadic call is to wake up now and to strive with strength. Rise and awake. Katha 1.3.14: "Rise, awake! having obtained your boons, understand them! The sharp edge of a razor is difficult to pass over; thus the wise say the path (to the Self) is hard." The call to rise is made together with the warning that the way takes effort. Choose the good. Katha 1.2.1-2: distinguish the good from the pleasant and cling to the good. Take the reins. Katha 1.3.6: "he who has understanding and whose mind is always firmly held, his senses are under control, like good horses of a charioteer." Bring strength and earnestness. Mundaka 3.2.4 says the Self is gained by one who strives "by strength, earnestness, and right meditation".

The Christian answer joins urgency with grace. Make the most of the time. Ephesians 5:15-16: "Be careful, then, how you live, not as unwise people but as wise, making the most of the time." Now. 2 Corinthians 6:2: "Look, now is the acceptable time; look, now is the day of salvation!" Encourage one another daily. Hebrews 3:13: "But exhort one another every day, as long as it is called 'today'". Accountability is built into the text. Work with your might. Ecclesiastes 9:10: "Whatever your hand finds to do, do with your might". Do not tire of doing good. Galatians 6:9: "So let us not grow weary in doing what is right, for we will reap at harvest time, if we do not give up." Receive help and grace. After describing his divided will, Paul asks, "Who will rescue me from this body of death?" and answers, "Thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord!" (Romans 7:24-25). Romans 8:1 adds: "there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus." Failure does not end the path.

The Buddhist remedies are to begin now, with vigour, and to use the practical steps the Buddha gave. Begin today. MN 131: "Today's the day to keenly work— who knows, tomorrow may bring death!" Strive. Dhp 313: "If one is to do what should be done, one should staunchly strive." Stay with the present. MN 131: "Don't run back to the past, don't anticipate the future." Don't hide behind the weather. DN 31 praises the one "who considers heat and cold as no more than blades of grass", who does their duties, and "happiness never fails". Practise steadily. Dhp 23: "They who regularly meditate, always staunchly vigorous; the attentive realize extinguishment." Use a ladder of remedies. For drowsiness, the Buddha gave Moggallana a sequence from the lightest to the most active (AN 7.61): shift attention, think over the teaching, recite it aloud, rub the limbs, wash the eyes, walk about. The same idea applies to delay: try the smallest change first, then a bigger one. See A story in sloth.

The philosophers' remedies are to act now, to build the habit by acting, and to stop waiting for a better moment. Hold the hour. Seneca: "hold every hour in your grasp. Lay hold of to-day's task, and you will not need to depend so much upon to-morrow's." Begin as you are. Epictetus: "This instant, then, think yourself worthy of living as a man grown up, and a proficient." When pain or pleasure is set before you, "remember that now is the combat, now the Olympiad comes on, nor can it be put off." Become by doing. Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 2: "we learn by doing them, e.g. men become builders by building and lyreplayers by playing the lyre; so too we become just by doing just acts, temperate by doing temperate acts, brave by doing brave acts." Action builds the habit, and habit builds the character that acts. Answer the morning excuse. Marcus Aurelius's reply to himself when he does not want to get up is in A story.

Note: This is an invented composite story, not a real case. It is built from patterns people commonly describe, so you can see how procrastination works and how people step out of it. Dev's story Dev, a freelance designer, had a tax return due at the end of the month. The receipts were in three currencies and two email accounts. Each evening he opened the folder, saw the pile, and closed it. He answered client emails instead. That was useful work, and it felt like a good reason. The relief of closing the folder lasted about ten minutes. Then came a dull dread that followed him through dinner. He told himself he'd feel clearer on the weekend, and the weekend came and went. Two days before the deadline he sat up until three in the morning and filed. He found two mistakes later. The next year he tried something different. What helped: He named the feeling. It wasn't laziness. He was dreading finding out how much he owed. He shrank the first step. The goal was ten minutes of sorting receipts into piles, nothing more. He made an if-then plan. "When I finish lunch on Tuesday and Thursday, I will put the laptop on the kitchen table and sort receipts before opening email." He told his sister, who agreed to text him on Thursday evening: "Did you sort?" He forgave the slip. When he missed a Tuesday, he wrote "missed Tuesday, doing Thursday" and moved on, instead of deciding he was hopeless. The number at the end was no better than he feared, but it was no longer a secret. He filed a week early. What it shows: Procrastination often protects us from a feeling. A small first step, a plan fixed in advance and some kindness did more than a fresh resolve.

Arjuna puts down his bow The Bhagavad Gita opens on a battlefield. Arjuna, a warrior, sees his relatives and teachers on the other side and is overcome. In 1.47, "Arjun cast aside his bow and arrows, and sank into the seat of his chariot, his mind in distress and overwhelmed with grief." In 2.9 he tells Krishna, "Govind, I shall not fight," and falls silent. This is not procrastination in the narrow sense, since Arjuna is refusing, out of grief and fear, and not just putting off. It is related to it, though: a person who knows what duty asks of them and cannot begin. Krishna does not argue him into action at once. His first words in 2.3 are: "O Parth, it does not befit you to yield to this unmanliness. Give up such petty weakness of heart and arise, O vanquisher of enemies." Then comes the long teaching that follows, about duty, attachment to results and steadiness. At the end, in 18.73, Arjuna says: "by Your grace my illusion has been dispelled, and I am situated in knowledge. I am now free from doubts, and I shall act according to Your instructions." What it shows: Paralysis before a hard duty is treated as a state of confusion that can be lifted by understanding, and the answer is to rise and act, not to wait until the fear passes.

Nachiketa will not be put off In the Katha Upanishad, a boy named Nachiketa comes to the house of Death. Death offers him three wishes. For his third, Nachiketa asks what happens after death, a question that even the gods have doubted. Death tries to talk him out of it. He offers sons and grandsons who will live a hundred years, herds, elephants, gold, horses, a kingdom and long life, and says: "do not ask me about dying" (1.1.25). Nachiketa answers: "These things last till tomorrow, O Death, for they wear out this vigour of all the senses. Even the whole of life is short." And: "No man can be made happy by wealth." He asks only for the boon he chose (1.1.26-27), and keeps to it. Death's reply opens the second chapter with the choice of the good over the pleasant (1.2.1). This is a story of the opposite of procrastination: a boy who will not be distracted by the pleasant from the question that matters. What it shows: Each offer was a reason to put off the hard question, and he declined each. Knowing what matters most and refusing the easier substitute is the Upanishadic remedy.

Augustine in the garden In his Confessions, Augustine tells of years in which he knew he should change his life and put it off. He remembers praying: "Grant me chastity and continency, but not yet" (8.7). He was afraid, he says, that God would hear him too soon. The turning point comes in a garden in Milan (8.12). In tears, he cries out: "How long, how long? Tomorrow, and tomorrow? Why not now? Why is there not this hour an end to my uncleanness?" Then he hears a child's voice from a nearby house, repeating: "Take up and read; take up and read." He takes it as a command to open the book, picks up the volume of Paul's letters, and reads the first passage his eyes fall on, from Romans 13:13-14: "put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make not provision for the flesh, to fulfil the lusts thereof." He writes: "No further would I read, nor did I need; for instantly, as the sentence ended — by a light, as it were, of security infused into my heart — all the gloom of doubt vanished away." What it shows: Augustine's delay was over leaving a way of life he knew he should leave, and for years the hard part was not knowing what to do but starting. He describes it as a divided will and the force of habit, and what broke the pattern was one clear act of turning, not a stronger resolve to do it later.

Sigalaka and the six directions In the Sigalovada Sutta (DN 31), the Buddha is staying in the Bamboo Grove near Rajagaha. A young householder, Sigalaka, rises early and, with his clothes and hair wet, raises his cupped palms to revere the six directions: east, south, west, north, below and above. The Buddha sees him and asks why. Sigalaka says that on his deathbed his father told him: "My dear, please revere the quarters." He says he is honouring his father's words. The Buddha answers: "Householder's son, that's not how the six directions should be revered in the training of the Noble One." He then teaches what it really means: giving up corrupt deeds, avoiding six drains on wealth, telling fake friends from good-hearted ones, and so "covering" the six directions in daily conduct. One of those drains is habitual laziness. The Buddha says its drawback is that "You don't get your work done because you think: 'It's too cold! It's too hot. It's too late! It's too early! I'm too hungry! I'm too full!'" What it shows: The sutta is not about procrastination alone, but it names its excuses very exactly. The teaching also moves the young man from a ritual that costs nothing but a wet morning to the daily conduct that would change his life, which is a version of "stop performing, start doing".

Marcus Aurelius and the warm bed Marcus Aurelius was a Roman emperor and a Stoic. His Meditations are notes he wrote to himself, not a book written for readers, and in Book 5 he records an argument with himself about getting up in the morning. He begins: "In the morning when thou risest unwillingly, let this thought be present—I am rising to the work of a human being." He then puts his own excuse in the mouth of an objector and answers it: "Or have I been made for this, to lie in the bed-clothes and keep myself warm?—But this is more pleasant.—Dost thou exist then to take thy pleasure, and not at all for action or exertion? Dost thou not see the little plants, the little birds, the ants, the spiders, the bees working together to put in order their several parts of the universe?" He allows the objection that rest is necessary, and replies that nature "has fixed bounds to this too" (Long's translation). What it shows: The delay he describes is small and ordinary, a few more minutes in bed. His method is to say the excuse aloud, to answer it, and to remind himself what the day is for, and then to get up.

Overthinking is going over the same thoughts again and again without getting closer to a decision or to peace. Psychologists use more exact words for its forms: Rumination: repeatedly dwelling on distress, its causes and its consequences, usually about the past or the present. Worry: the same looping aimed at the future, rehearsing what might go wrong. Restlessness: an agitated mind that cannot settle, jumping from one thing to another. In a smartphone study of people's ongoing thoughts, Killingsworth and Gilbert found that people are thinking about what is not happening almost as often as they are thinking about what is. Repeated thinking is not harmful in itself. Watkins's review found that repetitive thought can be constructive, as in adaptive preparation, planning and recovery from upsetting events, or unconstructive, as in depression, anxiety and difficulties in physical health. The difference lies in how you think, not in how much. Overthinking is a different thing from depression or an anxiety disorder, though it can come with them. If the loops are constant or your mood is low, a doctor or therapist can help.

Hinduism has no single word for overthinking, but the Bhagavad Gita describes both the restless mind and a loop of dwelling that grows worse. Arjuna says in 6.34: "The mind is very restless, turbulent, strong and obstinate, O Krishna. It appears to me that it is more difficult to control than the wind." The Sanskrit words glossed there are chanchala (restless) and pramathi (turbulent). In 2.62-63, the Gita describes a chain that starts with dwelling: "While contemplating on the objects of the senses, one develops attachment to them. Attachment leads to desire, and from desire arises anger. Anger leads to clouding of judgment, which results in bewilderment of memory. When memory is bewildered, the intellect gets destroyed; and when the intellect is destroyed, one is ruined." This is related to overthinking and not identical to it. The Gita is speaking of dwelling on the objects of the senses and desire, and it does not use a word for brooding on the past or rehearsing the future.

The Upanishads have no word for overthinking. They speak of the unsteady mind and of grief that does not let go, and they set against these a still mind and a witness. In the Katha Upanishad, the self is compared to a rider in a chariot: the body is the chariot, the intellect the charioteer and the mind the reins (1.3.3-4). "He who has no understanding and whose mind (the reins) is never firmly held, his senses (horses) are unmanageable, like vicious horses of a charioteer" (1.3.5). The Mundaka Upanishad gives an image of two birds on one tree. "On the same tree man sits grieving, immersed, bewildered by his own impotence. But when he sees the other lord contented and knows his glory, then his grief passes away" (3.1.2). This is related to overthinking and not identical to it: the texts speak of the restless mind and of grief, within a path toward knowledge of the Self, and not of everyday loops of thought.

The Bible has no word for overthinking, but it names its relatives: worry, anxiety and a mind that is "disquieted within me". Jesus says: "do not worry about your life" (Matthew 6:25). To Martha he says: "you are worried and distracted by many things" (Luke 10:41). Proverbs 12:25 says: "Anxiety weighs down the human heart, but a good word cheers it up." The psalmist asks himself: "Why are you cast down, O my soul, and why are you disquieted within me?" (Psalm 42:5). The desert tradition calls tempting inner thoughts logismoi, "thoughts". Evagrius of Pontus writes: "Whether these thoughts are able to disturb the soul or not is not up to us; but whether they linger or not, and whether they arouse passions or not; that is up to us." This is related to overthinking and not identical to it. Scripture speaks of worry about life and provision, and Evagrius of the thoughts that tempt a monk, and neither describes a general habit of looping over the past and future.

Buddhist texts have no word for overthinking, but they describe its parts closely. Restlessness and remorse (uddhacca-kukkucca) is the fourth of the five hindrances to meditation (see sloth in Buddhism for the list). The mind itself is described as unsteady. Dhp 33 says: "The mind quivers and quakes, hard to guard, hard to curb." Dhp 35: "Hard to hold back, flighty, alighting where it will". The Buddha also describes how thinking feeds on itself. In MN 19 he says: "Whatever a mendicant frequently thinks about and considers becomes their heart's inclination." And in SN 36.6, the Sallatha Sutta, he describes the way thought adds suffering to pain: an unlearned person who feels a painful sensation sorrows and laments, and so "experiences two feelings: physical and mental. It's like a person who is struck with an arrow, only to be struck with a second arrow." This is related to overthinking and not identical to it. The texts speak of restlessness, remorse and the habits of thought in the context of meditation and suffering, and do not name overthinking as a category.

Philosophers describe overthinking as the mind disturbing itself, through judgments, anticipation and an inability to be still. Epictetus begins the Enchiridion by sorting what is up to us: "Some things are in our control and others not. Things in our control are opinion, pursuit, desire, aversion, and, in a word, whatever are our own actions." And in section 5: "Men are disturbed, not by things, but by the principles and notions which they form concerning things." Seneca writes to Lucilius about fear that runs ahead of events: "some things torment us more than they ought; some torment us before they ought; and some torment us when they ought not to torment us at all. We are in the habit of exaggerating, or imagining, or anticipating, sorrow" (Letter 13). Pascal names the restlessness behind it: "all the unhappiness of men arises from one single fact, that they cannot stay quietly in their own chamber" (Pensées, in the section on diversion). These are related to overthinking and not identical to it. The Stoics speak of judgments and fear, and Pascal of restlessness and distraction; none writes of rumination as a modern term.

Researchers describe overthinking as something that develops and is kept going by several factors working together. A habit that grows out of an unresolved goal. In their model of rumination, Watkins and Roberts say it results from "dwelling on problematic goals developing into a learnt habit". In plain terms, a problem you have not solved or let go of keeps pulling your thoughts back. Abstract thinking. The same model points to a tendency to process negative information in an abstract way (asking "why does this always happen to me?") and not concretely (asking "what exactly happened, and what is the next step?"). Watkins's earlier review identifies the level of construal, abstract against concrete, as one of the principles that explain whether repetitive thought is constructive or not. Weak mental control and negative bias. The model adds poor executive control, the ability to steer and switch attention, and a tendency to pick up negative information. Negative styles of thinking. Nolen-Hoeksema and colleagues report that rumination interacts with negative cognitive styles to predict how long depressive symptoms last.

The Gita traces the restless, circling mind to dwelling, desire and an undisciplined mind. Dwelling on what attracts. Verse 2.62: "While contemplating on the objects of the senses, one develops attachment to them. Attachment leads to desire, and from desire arises anger." The loop begins with attention that keeps returning. The nature of the mind. Arjuna in 6.34 calls it "restless, turbulent, strong and obstinate". The problem is a mind that moves, not a failing of character. Not being steady. Verse 2.66 says an undisciplined person "who has not controlled the mind and senses, can neither have a resolute intellect nor steady contemplation". Unmet desires pouring in. Verse 2.70 compares the sage to the ocean, unmoved "by the incessant flow of waters from rivers merging into it", and contrasts "the person who strives to satisfy desires".

The Upanishads locate the root in a mind that is not held, and in identifying with one's own helplessness. Reins not held. Katha 1.3.5: "He who has no understanding and whose mind (the reins) is never firmly held, his senses (horses) are unmanageable". The senses and thoughts run where they like. Being immersed in one's own distress. Mundaka 3.1.2: "On the same tree man sits grieving, immersed, bewildered by his own impotence." The man eats the fruit and is caught in it, while the other bird, in 3.1.1, "looks on without eating". Unmindfulness. Katha 1.3.7: "He who has no understanding, who is unmindful and always impure, never reaches that place, but enters into the round of births."

Scripture places the roots of a worried, circling mind in anxiety about life, in being pulled in too many directions, and in thoughts that are allowed to stay. Anxiety about provision and the future. Jesus names food, drink and clothing, and says: "Therefore do not worry, saying, 'What will we eat?' or 'What will we drink?' or 'What will we wear?'" He calls his hearers "you of little faith" (Matthew 6:30-31). Too many things at once. Luke 10:41: "you are worried and distracted by many things". A disquieted soul. Psalm 42:5: "Why are you cast down, O my soul, and why are you disquieted within me?" Thoughts allowed to linger. Evagrius: "whether they linger or not, and whether they arouse passions or not; that is up to us."

The Buddhist texts point to an unsettled mind, to resisting pain, and to the way habits of thought become inclinations. An unsettled mind, attended to unwisely. SN 46.51 asks what fuels restlessness and remorse: "There is the unsettled mind. Frequent irrational application of mind to that fuels the arising of restlessness and remorse, or, when they have arisen, makes them increase and grow." Resisting pain and reaching for relief. SN 36.6: when an unlearned person is touched by painful feeling "they resist it", and "look forward to enjoying sensual pleasures", because they "don't understand any escape from painful feeling apart from sensual pleasures." Habit. MN 19: "Whatever a mendicant frequently thinks about and considers becomes their heart's inclination." A mind that is hard to hold. Dhp 34 compares it to "a fish pulled from the sea and cast upon the shore", which "flounders about".

The philosophers find the roots in our judgments, in running ahead of events, and in not being able to be still. Judgments, not things. Epictetus, Enchiridion 5: "Men are disturbed, not by things, but by the principles and notions which they form concerning things." Marcus Aurelius says the same: "If thou art pained by any external thing, it is not this thing that disturbs thee, but thy own judgement about it" (Meditations 8). Exaggerating, imagining and anticipating. Seneca, Letter 13: "We are in the habit of exaggerating, or imagining, or anticipating, sorrow." He also says: "it is more often the case that we are troubled by our apprehensions". Striving over what is not in our control. Epictetus, Enchiridion 1: "Things not in our control are body, property, reputation, command, and, in one word, whatever are not our own actions." Being unable to be still. Pascal: unhappiness comes from the fact "that they cannot stay quietly in their own chamber."

Research links long, unproductive loops of thought with a range of costs. Mood. Nolen-Hoeksema and colleagues review evidence that rumination exacerbates depression, enhances negative thinking, impairs problem solving, interferes with instrumental behaviour (getting things done) and erodes social support. It appears to predict the onset of depression more consistently than its duration. A wider range of problems. The same review reports that rumination is associated with anxiety, binge eating, binge drinking and self-harm, as well as depression. A shared weak point. Watkins and Roberts describe rumination as a "transdiagnostic" vulnerability: it magnifies and prolongs negative mood, interferes with therapy, and is linked with anxiety, depression, psychosis, insomnia and impulsive behaviours. They also report that it exacerbates and maintains physiological stress responses. Unhappiness. Killingsworth and Gilbert found that thinking about what is not happening typically makes people unhappy. Most of this evidence shows association, and some is correlational, so it cannot show that thinking alone causes each problem. If you are thinking about harming yourself, please contact your local emergency number or a crisis line.

The Gita describes the effects of the unsteady, dwelling mind as a decline in judgment and loss of peace. A downward chain. Verse 2.63: "Anger leads to clouding of judgment, which results in bewilderment of memory. When memory is bewildered, the intellect gets destroyed; and when the intellect is destroyed, one is ruined." No peace. Verse 2.66: "For one who never unites the mind with God there is no peace; and how can one who lacks peace be happy?" A mind that overpowers. In 6.34 Arjuna says the mind is "turbulent", "strong and obstinate", harder to control than the wind. Giving up the path. In 6.33 Arjuna says the practice taught to him "appears impractical and unattainable to me, due to the restless mind."

The Upanishads describe the effects as grief, lack of control and going round without arriving. Grief. Mundaka 3.1.2: the man on the tree "sits grieving, immersed, bewildered". Unmanageable senses. Katha 1.3.5: when the mind is never firmly held, the senses are "unmanageable, like vicious horses of a charioteer". The round without end. Katha 1.3.7: the unmindful one "never reaches that place, but enters into the round of births". Here the cycle is the text's own word for the effect, and we read it as describing the going-round of an unquiet mind.

Scripture is plain that worry weighs on a person and gains nothing. It weighs. Proverbs 12:25: "Anxiety weighs down the human heart". It gains nothing. Matthew 6:27: "which of you by worrying can add a single hour to your span of life?" It crowds out what matters. Luke 10:40-42: Martha is "distracted by her many tasks", and says that her sister has left her to do the work. Jesus answers: "you are worried and distracted by many things, but few things are needed—indeed only one." It casts the soul down. Psalm 42:5: "Why are you cast down, O my soul?" The day's own trouble is enough. Matthew 6:34: "So do not worry about tomorrow, for tomorrow will bring worries of its own. Today's trouble is enough for today."

The Buddhist texts describe the effects as added suffering, a growing habit and a tired mind. A second arrow. SN 36.6: the unlearned person "sorrow[s] and wail[s] and lament[s], beating their breast and falling into confusion" and so feels both the physical pain and the mental pain, like being struck by a second arrow. Restlessness grows with attention. SN 46.51: frequent irrational attention to an unsettled mind "makes them increase and grow". The inclination deepens. MN 19: what a person frequently thinks about becomes the inclination of their mind. Even good thoughts can tire. In MN 19 the Buddha says of wholesome thoughts: "thinking and considering for too long would tire my body. And when the body is tired, the mind is stressed. And when the mind is stressed, it's far from immersion."

The philosophers describe the cost as needless suffering, a distorted view of events, and a restless search for distraction. Suffering before it is necessary. Seneca, Letter 98: "He suffers more than is necessary, who suffers before it is necessary." Imagined troubles. Seneca, Letter 13: "There are more things, Lucilius, likely to frighten us than there are to crush us; we suffer more often in imagination than in reality." Dangers that never arrive. In the same letter he says it may be "that the dangers before which you paled as if they were threatening you, will never come upon you; they certainly have not yet come." Terror from our own notion. Epictetus: "Death, for instance, is not terrible, else it would have appeared so to Socrates. But the terror consists in our notion of death that it is terrible." Flight into distraction. Pascal observes the "quarrels, passions, bold and often bad ventures" people expose themselves to, and traces them to the inability to stay quietly at home.

Most of what helps works on how you think, not on trying to stop thinking. Notice and name the loop. "I'm ruminating" or "I'm worrying" puts a little distance between you and the thought. Move from "why" to "what next". Watkins's work links abstract processing with unconstructive repetitive thought, so shift to concrete questions: what exactly happened, and what is one small step I can take? Reviews of treatments for rumination report that therapies aimed at these mechanisms look promising in preliminary trials. Talk to yourself as you would to someone else. Kross and colleagues found that people who used their own name or "you", instead of "I", while thinking about a stressful event enhanced self-distancing, performed better on a speech and a first-impression task, showed less distress and engaged in less maladaptive thinking afterwards. Interrupt with a pleasant or absorbing activity. The review by Nolen-Hoeksema and colleagues says dozens of experimental studies show positive distractions relieve depressed mood, though correlational studies are inconsistent. Treat it as relief for the moment, not a cure. Give the thinking a place and a limit. Some people set a short daily "thinking time" and park the rest. This is common advice, not drawn from the studies above. Act on what can be acted on. Write down what you can decide or do, do the first piece, and note what is out of your hands. Get help for persistent loops. If thoughts are constant or tied to low mood, anxiety or poor sleep, a doctor or therapist can help.

The Gita's answer is practice, detachment and returning again and again. Practice and detachment. Krishna replies to Arjuna in 6.35: "the mind is indeed very difficult to restrain. But by practice and detachment, it can be controlled." Bring it back. Verse 6.26: "Whenever and wherever the restless and unsteady mind wanders, one should bring it back and continually focus it on God." The instruction expects the mind to wander and says what to do when it does. In this translation the object is God; reading it as "your chosen object of attention" is our gloss. Be like the ocean. Verse 2.70: the sage remains undisturbed, as the ocean is by the rivers that flow into it, and attains peace. Lift yourself. Verse 6.5: "Elevate yourself through the power of your mind, and not degrade yourself, for the mind can be the friend and also the enemy of the self."

The Upanishadic answer is to still the mind, hold the reins, and become the witness. Still the mind. Katha 2.3.10-11: "When the five instruments of knowledge stand still together with the mind, and when the intellect does not move, that is called the highest state. This, the firm holding back of the senses, is what is called Yoga. He must be free from thoughtlessness then, for Yoga comes and goes." Hold the reins. Katha 1.3.6: "he who has understanding and whose mind is always firmly held, his senses are under control, like good horses of a charioteer." Be the onlooker. In the image of the two birds, grief passes when the man on the tree sees "the other lord contented and knows his glory" (Mundaka 3.1.2). The second bird "looks on without eating" (3.1.1). Wake up. Katha 1.3.14: "Rise, awake! having obtained your boons, understand them!" The last words of Katha 2.3.11, that "Yoga comes and goes", are an honest note that stillness is not permanent.

The Christian answer is to hand the worry over, to speak to the soul, and to guard the mind. Hand it over. Philippians 4:6-7: "Do not be anxious about anything, but in everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known to God. And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus." 1 Peter 5:7: "Cast all your anxiety on him, because he cares for you." Take one day at a time. Matthew 6:34: "Today's trouble is enough for today." Talk to your own soul. Psalm 42:5 answers its own question: "Hope in God, for I shall again praise him". Seek a good word. Proverbs 12:25: "a good word cheers it up". Other people can help. Take thoughts captive. 2 Corinthians 10:5: "we take every thought captive to obey Christ." Renew the mind. Romans 12:2: "be transformed by the renewing of the mind". Don't feed what lingers. Evagrius: whether thoughts linger "is up to us." Steadfast mind. Isaiah 26:3: "Those of steadfast mind you keep in peace".

The Buddhist remedies are to settle the mind, to sort thoughts, and to feel one arrow and not two. Starve what fuels it. SN 46.51: "There is the settled mind. Frequent rational application of mind to that starves the arising of restlessness and remorse, or, when they have arisen, starves their increase and growth." Sort your thoughts. In MN 19 the Buddha describes sorting thoughts into two classes: sensual, malicious and cruel thoughts in one, and thoughts of renunciation, good will and harmlessness in the other. When a harmful thought arose he reflected that it leads to hurting himself, others and both, and that it blocks wisdom, and "it went away". Guard the mind. Dhp 33: "The discerning straighten it out, like a fletcher an arrow." Dhp 36: "the discerning protect the mind, a guarded mind leads to bliss." Settle and still it. In MN 19 he says: "I stilled, settled, unified, and immersed my mind internally... So that my mind would not be stressed." Feel one arrow. SN 36.6: the learned disciple, touched by painful feeling, does not sorrow or wail, and "experiences one feeling: physical, not mental."

The philosophers' remedies are to test the thought, change the judgment, and focus on what is in your control. Change the judgment. Marcus Aurelius: "it is in thy power to wipe out this judgement now." Sort what is yours. Epictetus, Enchiridion 1: opinion, pursuit, desire and aversion are in our control; body, property and reputation are not. Spend effort on the first. Cross-examine the fear. Seneca, Letter 13: "Put the question voluntarily to yourself: 'Am I tormented without sufficient reason, am I morose, and do I convert what is not an evil into what is an evil?'" Test the evidence.
