Seneca's rule is to ask whether the trouble is present or only to come: "As to things present, the decision is easy... To-day there is nothing wrong with it." And for the future: "consider whether your proofs of future trouble are sure." Look for the thought behind the feeling. Epictetus, section 5: "When therefore we are hindered, or disturbed, or grieved, let us never attribute it to others, but to ourselves; that is, to our own principles."

Note: This is an invented composite story, not a real case. It is built from patterns people commonly describe, so you can see how overthinking works and how people step out of it. Anil's story In a team meeting, Anil disagreed with his manager's plan. His manager said, "Let's take that offline," and moved on. By midnight, Anil was lying awake replaying it. Had he sounded rude? Had the tone changed? Why does this always happen to me? What if it counted against him in the next review? Each pass through produced no new fact. It only produced more dread. The next day he was tired, short with a colleague, and could not focus on his own work. What helped: He named it. "This is rumination. I'm going round, not solving." He asked a concrete question. Instead of "why does this always happen?", he asked "what is one thing I can do?" The answer was to send his manager a two-line note: "Thanks for hearing me out. Happy to talk through the plan whenever suits." He changed the way he talked to himself. He tried, "Anil, you made a reasonable point. What would you tell a friend?" He gave the worry a limit. Ten minutes in the evening to think it through on paper, then a walk. He noticed that it was not getting better. After two weeks of poor sleep, he booked a visit with his doctor. His manager replied the next morning with a thumbs-up and a time for a chat. The loop did not vanish at once, but it got shorter each time. What it shows: Going round a problem feels like work and rarely is. A concrete next step, a kinder voice and a time limit moved Anil from replaying to doing.

Arjuna and the wind In chapter 6 of the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna has been teaching Arjuna how to steady the mind in meditation. Arjuna interrupts with an honest objection. In 6.33 he says: "The system of Yog that you have described, O Madhusudan, appears impractical and unattainable to me, due to the restless mind." He goes on in 6.34: "The mind is very restless, turbulent, strong and obstinate, O Krishna. It appears to me that it is more difficult to control than the wind." Krishna does not tell him he is wrong. In 6.35 he answers: "what you say is correct; the mind is indeed very difficult to restrain. But by practice and detachment, it can be controlled." And in 6.26 he adds what to do in practice: "Whenever and wherever the restless and unsteady mind wanders, one should bring it back". What it shows: The restless mind is treated as ordinary, even for the best warrior in the story. The remedy offered is not a one-time victory but steady returning, each time it wanders.

The two birds on one tree The Mundaka Upanishad tells a short parable. "Two birds, inseparable friends, cling to the same tree. One of them eats the sweet fruit, the other looks on without eating" (3.1.1). The first bird stands for the person caught up in life, tasting each fruit and being moved by it. The Upanishad says of this one: "On the same tree man sits grieving, immersed, bewildered by his own impotence" (3.1.2). The second bird only watches. And the verse turns on what happens when the first bird looks at it: "But when he sees the other lord contented and knows his glory, then his grief passes away." What it shows: The image says that the same person has two positions, one inside the thoughts and one watching them, and that grief eases when attention shifts from the first to the second. The teaching is that the watcher is already there.

Martha and Mary In Luke's Gospel, Jesus comes to a village where a woman named Martha welcomes him. Her sister Mary "sat at Jesus's feet and listened to what he was saying" (Luke 10:39). "But Martha was distracted by her many tasks, so she came to him and asked, 'Lord, do you not care that my sister has left me to do all the work by myself? Tell her, then, to help me.'" Jesus answers: "Martha, Martha, you are worried and distracted by many things, but few things are needed—indeed only one. Mary has chosen the better part, which will not be taken away from her" (10:40-42). Martha is not described as overthinking in so many words. The story shows a related state: a mind pulled in many directions, a rising resentment, and a sense that everything depends on her. What it shows: Jesus does not scold her for caring. He names the state ("worried and distracted by many things") and points to the one thing that matters. The way out is shown as choosing, not as thinking harder.

The Buddha sorts his thoughts In the Dvedhavitakka Sutta (MN 19), the Buddha tells his monks how he handled his own thoughts before his awakening. "Before my awakening—when I was still unawakened but intent on awakening—I thought: 'Why don't I meditate by continually dividing my thoughts into two classes?'" He put sensual, malicious and cruel thoughts in one class, and thoughts of renunciation, good will and harmlessness in the other. When a harmful thought arose, he did not fight it. He looked at where it led: "It leads to hurting myself, hurting others, and hurting both. It blocks wisdom, it's on the side of distress, and it doesn't lead to extinguishment." And then: "When I reflected that it leads to hurting myself, it went away." He compares this to a cowherd in the last month of the rains, when the crops stand close together: the cowherd keeps tapping and poking them with his staff, on this side and that, to keep them in check, because if the cattle wander into the crops he could be punished. Even with good thoughts, he adds, he did not go on without end: "thinking and considering for too long would tire my body. And when the body is tired, the mind is stressed." So he "stilled, settled, unified, and immersed" his mind. What it shows: The Buddha does not describe emptying the mind. He describes watching which thoughts arise, seeing where they lead, and then, when thinking has done its work, letting the mind rest.

Seneca's test for imagined troubles In Letter 13, Seneca writes to his friend Lucilius about fear. We do not know what Lucilius was afraid of, but Seneca's advice is a method anyone can follow. He observes how common the problem is: "There are more things, Lucilius, likely to frighten us than there are to crush us; we suffer more often in imagination than in reality." He tells Lucilius to ask himself directly: "Am I tormented without sufficient reason, am I morose, and do I convert what is not an evil into what is an evil?" Then comes the test. Lucilius might object: "How am I to know whether my sufferings are real or imaginary?" Seneca answers: "We are tormented either by things present, or by things to come, or by both." For the present, he says, the decision is easy: if you are free, healthy and uninjured, "To-day there is nothing wrong with it." For the future, he asks for proof: "consider whether your proofs of future trouble are sure." We are often troubled by our apprehensions, he says, and we agree too quickly with what we hear: "We do not put to the test those things which cause our fear; we do not examine into them." What it shows: Seneca does not tell Lucilius to stop thinking. He asks him to examine each fear, as a judge would look at evidence, and to separate what is happening now from what only might.

Perfectionism is holding yourself to standards so high, or so rigid, that anything short of flawless feels like failure. Psychologists do not treat it as one thing: Perfectionistic strivings: setting very high standards and working hard to meet them. Perfectionistic concerns: worry about mistakes and about how others will judge you. Three directions: the Multidimensional Perfectionism Scale (Hewitt and Flett, 1991) measures self-oriented perfectionism (demands on yourself), socially prescribed perfectionism (the sense that others demand perfection of you) and other-oriented perfectionism (demands on other people). High standards are not the problem in themselves. Stoeber and Otto's review found that perfectionistic strivings are associated with positive characteristics, and concluded that self-oriented strivings are positive "if perfectionists are not overly concerned about mistakes and negative evaluations by others". The trouble starts when the standard becomes a test of your worth. Perfectionism is not a diagnosis, and it can come with anxiety, depression or eating problems. If it is taking over your life, a doctor or therapist can help.

Hinduism has no single word for perfectionism, but the Bhagavad Gita speaks closely to its two sides: being tied to success and failure, and refusing to act unless the work can be flawless. On the first, Krishna says in 2.48: "Be steadfast in the performance of your duty, O Arjun, abandoning attachment to success and failure. Such equanimity is called Yog." On the second, 18.48 says: "One should not abandon duties born of one's nature, even if one sees defects in them, O son of Kunti. Indeed, all endeavors are veiled by some evil, as fire is by smoke." And 18.47 puts the standard in a different place: "It is better to do one's own dharma, even though imperfectly, than to do another's dharma, even though perfectly." This is related to perfectionism and not identical to it. The Gita is speaking of attachment to the results of action and of duty, and it does not describe the modern pattern of self-judgement over mistakes. The Gita also speaks of attaining "perfection" through one's duties (18.45), so the word there refers to spiritual fulfilment and not to flawless performance; that point is a reading of the verse, not checked against the Sanskrit.

The Upanishads do not discuss perfectionism, and no verse here is about it directly. What they do offer is a picture of what is whole and flawless, and it is not the person's performance. The Isha Upanishad describes the Self in verse 8: "He (the Self) encircled all, bright, incorporeal, scatheless, without muscles, pure, untouched by evil; a seer, wise, omnipresent, self-existent". Verse 2 says of work: "Though a man may wish to live a hundred years, performing works, it will be thus with him; but not in any other way: work will thus not cling to a man." Read together, the two verses suggest that what is untouched and complete is the Self, while work is something done that need not cling to us. That is a reading and not a statement in the text. Müller himself says in his introduction that this Upanishad is "one of the most difficult to understand properly" and that commentators have disputed verse 2. This is related to perfectionism and not identical to it. The Upanishad speaks of the Self and of action without clinging, not of standards or of fear of mistakes.

Christian texts do not name perfectionism, but the word "perfect" is in the New Testament, and some people take it as a demand for flawlessness. Jesus says in Matthew 5:48: "Be perfect, therefore, as your heavenly Father is perfect." The same texts also describe weakness and unfinished progress as the setting of faith. Paul writes in Philippians 3:12: "Not that I have already obtained this or have already reached the goal, but I press on to lay hold of that for which Christ has laid hold of me." And in 2 Corinthians 12:9 he reports the answer he was given: "My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness." Many readers take "perfect" in Matthew 5:48 to mean complete or mature and not faultless. That reading was not checked here against a Greek lexicon, so treat it as one common view. This is related to perfectionism and not identical to it. The verses speak of holiness, grace and weakness, and not of anxiety about mistakes.

Buddhist texts have no word for perfectionism, but one famous sutta describes over-striving closely. In AN 6.55, Venerable Soṇa thinks in private retreat: "I am one of the Buddha's most energetic disciples. Yet my mind is not freed from defilements by not grasping." He considers giving up the training and going back to a "lesser life". The Buddha asks him about the harp he played as a layman. Strings tuned too tight, or too slack, did not make it "resonant and playable". Then he says: "In the same way, Soṇa, when energy is too forceful it leads to restlessness. When energy is too slack it leads to laziness." Elsewhere the Buddha speaks of "two extremes" and a "middle way of practice" (SN 56.11); there the extremes are sensual indulgence and self-mortification. This is related to perfectionism and not identical to it. The sutta is about effort in meditation, and the texts do not discuss standards, mistakes or the fear of judgement as a pattern of its own.

The ancient philosophers did not name perfectionism, but they argued about how exact we should expect to be. Aristotle opens the Nicomachean Ethics with a point about precision: "Our discussion will be adequate if it has as much clearness as the subject-matter admits of, for precision is not to be sought for alike in all discussions". Later he describes virtue as a mean, "the mean relative to us", between excess and defect, which is not the same for everyone. Marcus Aurelius speaks to the person who fails to live up to his own principles: "Be not disgusted, nor discouraged, nor dissatisfied, if thou dost not succeed in doing everything according to right principles; but when thou hast failed, return back again, and be content if the greater part of what thou doest is consistent with man's nature." This is related to perfectionism and not identical to it. Aristotle is writing about method and about virtue, and Marcus about moral practice; neither describes the modern pattern of harsh self-judgement.

Researchers point to the culture people grow up in, and to how worth gets tied to performance. Rising demands. Curran and Hill pooled 164 samples and 41,641 college students in the United States, Canada and the United Kingdom, tested between 1989 and 2016. Self-oriented, socially prescribed and other-oriented perfectionism all rose over time, and young people "perceive that others are more demanding of them, are more demanding of others, and are more demanding of themselves." The authors suggest that competitive individualism, emphasised since the 1980s, is part of the reason. Worth tied to results. The "concerns" side of perfectionism is worry about mistakes and about being judged (Stoeber and Otto). When a mistake feels like a verdict on you, avoiding mistakes becomes the goal. Family and school. Early criticism, praise only for results and a fear of disappointing people are commonly given as roots. These are common explanations, not findings from the papers below.

The Gita finds the roots in attachment to results and in comparing one's own path with another's. Attachment to the fruit. Gita 2.47: "You have a right to perform your prescribed duties, but you are not entitled to the fruits of your actions. Never consider yourself to be the cause of the results of your activities, nor be attached to inaction." When the result is what the self depends on, anything less than a perfect result feels like a threat. Attachment to success and failure. 2.48 names "attachment to success and failure" as what equanimity gives up. Looking at another's path. 3.35: "It is far better to perform one's natural prescribed duty, though tinged with faults, than to perform another's prescribed duty, though perfectly." The pull to measure oneself against someone else's performance is the root in view here. Seeing only the defect. 18.48 says that people recoil from their duty when they see its defects, and states that "all endeavors are veiled by some evil, as fire is by smoke". This is related to perfectionism and not identical to it. The verses speak of attachment to results and of duty; the link to the modern pattern is ours.

The Upanishads do not analyse perfectionism, but two passages touch on its roots: wanting what belongs to someone else, and tying one's worth to learning and achievement. Covetousness. Isha 1 ends: "Do not covet the wealth of any man!" Measuring ourselves against another's accomplishment is a kind of covetousness, though the verse speaks of wealth. Worth through attainment. In the Chandogya Upanishad (6.1), Svetaketu returns from twelve years of study "having then studied all the Vedas,—conceited, considering himself well-read, and stern". His father asks: "have you ever asked for that instruction by which we hear what cannot be heard, by which we perceive what cannot be perceived, by which we know what cannot be known?" The story shows a person whose standing rests on achievement and who still lacks something. This is related to perfectionism and not identical to it. Neither passage speaks of fear of mistakes; they are read here for the root they share with perfectionism, which is worth that depends on what we have achieved. That connection is ours.

The Christian texts see the root in trying to earn one's standing, and in forgetting what we are. Earning acceptance. Ephesians 2:8-9: "For by grace you have been saved through faith, and this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God—not the result of works, so that no one may boast." The verse is answering the idea that standing before God has to be earned by flawless works. Forgetting what we are. Psalm 103:13-14: "As a father has compassion for his children, so the LORD has compassion for those who fear him. For he knows how we were made; he remembers that we are dust." A demand for perfection overlooks that. Pride in one's own record. The words "so that no one may boast" place the harm in a wish to stand on one's own achievement. This is related to perfectionism and not identical to it. The verses speak of grace, works and pride in theological terms, and do not describe anxiety about mistakes. Linking them to perfectionism is a reading.

The Buddhist texts have no account of the roots of perfectionism, but the story of Soṇa (AN 6.55) shows how over-striving starts. Effort measured against the result. Soṇa thinks: "I am one of the Buddha's most energetic disciples. Yet my mind is not freed from defilements by not grasping." He has put in the effort and the result is not there, so he decides the effort or the training must be wrong. Comparison. He compares himself with other disciples ("one of the Buddha's most energetic"). The sutta does not treat this as a fault; it is a fact about how he reasons. An all-or-nothing choice. His thought is to give up and return to "a lesser life", not to adjust his practice. This is related to perfectionism and not identical to it. The sutta does not use the language of standards or perfection, and the roots listed above are our reading of Soṇa's thought, not statements in the text.

The Stoics place the root in what we think we own and what we think we must achieve. Putting our worth in what we do not control. Epictetus, Enchiridion 1: "Things in our control are opinion, pursuit, desire, aversion, and, in a word, whatever are our own actions. Things not in our control are body, property, reputation, command, and, in one word, whatever are not our own actions." If a flawless result or other people's praise is what we need, we have put our peace in something we cannot command. The demand to succeed every time. Marcus Aurelius warns against being "disgusted, nor discouraged, nor dissatisfied, if thou dost not succeed in doing everything according to right principles". That he needs to say so suggests that failing to meet one's own principles was a real source of distress. This is related to perfectionism and not identical to it. Epictetus and Marcus are speaking of how to live well, not describing a pattern of harsh self-judgement; the link is ours.

The effects depend on which side of perfectionism is stronger. Strivings can help. Stoeber and Otto's review found that perfectionistic strivings are associated with positive characteristics, and that "healthy perfectionists" show higher levels of positive characteristics than "unhealthy perfectionists" and non-perfectionists. Worry about mistakes changes that. The same review concludes that strivings are positive only "if perfectionists are not overly concerned about mistakes and negative evaluations by others." Rising demands. Curran and Hill's results mean more young people report that others demand more of them and that they demand more of themselves, which makes the second pattern more common. Commonly reported costs. People describe putting work off for fear it will not be good enough (see procrastination), never calling a piece of work finished, sleeplessness and exhaustion. These are common descriptions, not findings from the papers cited here. If perfectionism comes with low mood, anxiety, an eating problem or constant exhaustion, a doctor or therapist can help.

The Gita links over-attachment to results with agitation, and the fear of defects with giving up. Loss of equanimity. Gita 2.48 asks for "abandoning attachment to success and failure", and calls the resulting "equanimity" Yog. By implication, attachment to the outcome costs us that evenness; the verse does not describe the cost directly. Abandoning the work. 18.48 says: "One should not abandon duties born of one's nature, even if one sees defects in them." The translator's commentary adds that people recoil from their duty when they see a defect in it. Holding out for flawless work can end in doing nothing. Skill is not lost by letting go. The commentary on 2.50 says that working without attachment to results "does not reduce the quality of our work; instead we become even more skillful than before". This is related to perfectionism and not identical to it. The verses speak of duty and attachment; the effects listed here are our reading of them.

The Upanishads do not list the effects of perfectionism. Two passages show what a life tied to achievement can lack, and what is said to ease it. Sternness and conceit. Svetaketu comes home from his studies "conceited, considering himself well-read, and stern" (Chandogya 6.1.2). His father's question shows that all his learning has left something out. Sorrow and its end. Isha 7: "When to a man who understands, the Self has become all things, what sorrow, what trouble can there be to him who once beheld that unity?" The Upanishad ties the end of sorrow to seeing unity, and says nothing here about performance or standards. This is related to perfectionism and not identical to it. Neither passage is about perfectionism, and the effects above are drawn by reading them for what they say about grief and attainment. That reading is ours.

The Bible warns that straining after righteousness or wisdom can harm a person, and shows Paul pressing on without claiming to have arrived. Self-destruction. Ecclesiastes 7:16: "Do not be too righteous, and do not act too wise; why should you destroy yourself?" The verse can be read as a warning against over-demanding standards, though commentators differ on what it means. Not yet there. Philippians 3:12-14: "Not that I have already obtained this or have already reached the goal, but I press on". Paul does not claim to be finished and does not stop either, "forgetting what lies behind and straining forward to what lies ahead". Strength in weakness. 2 Corinthians 12:9-10: "My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness. ... whenever I am weak, then I am strong." This is related to perfectionism and not identical to it. The verses speak of righteousness, pride and weakness, and applying them to perfectionism is a reading.

The harp image in AN 6.55 names the cost of driving too hard. Restlessness. The Buddha tells Soṇa: "when energy is too forceful it leads to restlessness. When energy is too slack it leads to laziness." Strain does not produce calm; it produces the agitation the practice is meant to settle. Wanting to quit. Soṇa, who has driven himself hard and not seen the result he wants, thinks of resigning the training and going back to "a lesser life". Over-striving that does not pay off can end in giving up. Two ways to miss. The harp is "not resonant and playable" if strung too tight or too slack, so the text says that too much effort is as much of a problem as too little. This is related to perfectionism and not identical to it. The sutta concerns effort in meditation, and the match to perfectionism is ours.

The philosophers describe what failing to meet a standard does to a person, and the cost of seeking more exactness than a matter allows. Disgust, discouragement and dissatisfaction. Marcus Aurelius names these three as the reaction to failing to do "everything according to right principles". He tells himself to "return back again" instead. Misplaced exactness. Aristotle (Nicomachean Ethics 1.3) says that "precision is not to be sought for alike in all discussions, any more than in all the products of the crafts", and that in subjects with "variety and fluctuation" we should "indicate the truth roughly and in outline". Demanding more precision than a matter allows is a mistake of method. Ignoring the person. Aristotle's mean is "the mean relative to us" (2.6): the right amount depends on the person, not on a single flawless standard. This is related to perfectionism and not identical to it. The effects are our reading of what each philosopher says about exactness and failure.

The aim is to keep high standards and loosen the grip of the fear behind them. Tell the two sides apart. Stoeber and Otto separate strivings (wanting to do well) from concerns (worry about mistakes and judgement). Ask which one is driving you today. Keep the first and work on the second. Choose where "good enough" will do. Aristotle's point that precision should match the subject is a useful rule: decide which tasks deserve your best and which only need to be finished. This is common advice, not a research finding. Set the finish line before you start. Decide what "done" looks like and a time limit, then stop when you reach either. Treat a mistake as information. Ask what you would learn from it, as you would for a friend. Self-talk in the third person helped in other studies on rumination (see Overthinking); that evidence is not about perfectionism. Try a small experiment. Hand in something at 80%, or leave a small flaw, and see what actually happens. This is a common step in cognitive behavioural therapy for perfectionism; no trial of it was read for this article. Expect a rising demand and name it. Curran and Hill found that young people report others as more demanding than before. Part of the pressure comes from outside, and it is worth asking whose standard you are meeting. Get help for persistent cases. If perfectionism comes with constant anxiety, low mood, an eating problem or exhaustion, a doctor or therapist can help.

The Gita's answer is to put the effort into the work and to let go of the result. Do the work, release the fruit. 2.47: "You have a right to perform your prescribed duties, but you are not entitled to the fruits of your actions." Standards stay; the demand on the result goes. Practise equanimity. 2.48: "Be steadfast in the performance of your duty, O Arjun, abandoning attachment to success and failure. Such equanimity is called Yog." Work skilfully. 2.50: "strive for Yog, which is the art of working skillfully (in proper consciousness)." The commentary says that working without attachment does not lower the quality of the work. Accept that no work is free of defect. 18.48: "all endeavors are veiled by some evil, as fire is by smoke". The point is to act anyway. Do your own work, even imperfectly. 18.47: "It is better to do one's own dharma, even though imperfectly, than to do another's dharma, even though perfectly." This is related to perfectionism and not identical to it. The Gita's guidance is about acting without attachment to results, and applying it to perfectionism is our reading.

The Isha Upanishad offers a short way of acting without clinging. Surrender the result. Verse 1: "All this, whatsoever moves on earth, is to be hidden in the Lord (the Self). When thou hast surrendered all this, then thou mayest enjoy." Keep acting. Verse 2: "Though a man may wish to live a hundred years, performing works, it will be thus with him; but not in any other way: work will thus not cling to a man." See the one Self in everything. Verses 6-7: "he never turns away from it", and "what sorrow, what trouble can there be to him who once beheld that unity?" Müller's note says the verse allows continued work "provided they are performed without any selfish motives, without any desire of reward". He also reports that Śaṅkara read verse 2 differently, so the meaning is disputed. This is related to perfectionism and not identical to it. The Upanishad does not discuss standards or fear of mistakes, and using it for perfectionism is a reading.

The Christian texts offer grace, honesty about weakness and balance. Receive grace. Ephesians 2:8-9: "For by grace you have been saved through faith, and this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God—not the result of works, so that no one may boast." Remember compassion. Psalm 103:13-14: "he knows how we were made; he remembers that we are dust." Admit weakness. 2 Corinthians 12:9: "My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness." Hold both. Ecclesiastes 7:16-18: "Do not be too righteous, and do not act too wise; why should you destroy yourself? ... It is good that you should take hold of the one without letting go of the other". The passage warns against both extremes. Press on without being finished. Philippians 3:13-14: "forgetting what lies behind and straining forward to what lies ahead, I press on toward the goal". This is related to perfectionism and not identical to it. Christian counsel for a person weighed down by guilt or anxiety also includes pastoral and medical help, which these verses do not discuss.

The advice of AN 6.55 is to tune the effort, as a harp is tuned. Neither too tight nor too slack. The Buddha asks Soṇa about strings "tuned neither too tight nor too slack, but fixed at an even tension" and whether the harp then sounded well. It did. Balance energy and serenity. "So, Soṇa, you should focus on energy and serenity, find a balance of the faculties, and learn the character of this situation." Look at the result. The sutta reports that Soṇa did this, and then, "living alone, withdrawn, diligent, keen, and resolute, soon realized the supreme culmination of the spiritual path". The effort stayed; the strain went. Avoid both extremes. SN 56.11 describes a "middle way of practice" that avoids "indulgence in sensual pleasures" and "indulgence in self-mortification". The extremes there are not about perfectionism, but the pattern of avoiding both is the same. This is related to perfectionism and not identical to it. The suttas give guidance for practice, and applying the harp to everyday standards is a reading.

The philosophers advise fitting the standard to the matter and returning after failing. Match the precision to the subject. Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 1.3: "Our discussion will be adequate if it has as much clearness as the subject-matter admits of". Find the mean for you. Virtue is "the mean relative to us", between excess and defect (2.6). Return without disgust. Marcus Aurelius: "when thou hast failed, return back again, and be content if the greater part of what thou doest is consistent with man's nature, and love this to which thou returnest". Keep it light. He adds: "do not return to philosophy as if she were a master, but act like those who have sore eyes and apply a bit of sponge and egg". Treat the practice as a remedy, not a taskmaster. Sort what you control. Epictetus, Enchiridion 1: opinion, pursuit, desire and aversion are in our control; "reputation" is not. This is related to perfectionism and not identical to it. These are rules for living and reasoning, and applying them to perfectionism is a reading.

Note: This is an invented composite story, not a real case. It is built from patterns people commonly describe, so you can see how perfectionism works and how people loosen its grip. Meera's story Meera, a junior designer, was asked to show a first draft of a new app screen to her team on Friday. By Wednesday she had redone the layout four times. On Thursday night she was still adjusting the spacing of one button, and she had told no one that the draft was not ready. On Friday she sent in a screen she called "not finished", and spent the meeting waiting for someone to say what was wrong with it. A colleague pointed to a real problem in the flow, which none of her polishing had touched. She went home feeling that the whole week had been wasted. What helped: She asked which side was driving. The wish to do well was fine. The dread of being seen to get it wrong was what had her redoing the layout. She set a finish line. For the next piece she wrote down what "done" meant (the flow works, the main screens exist) and a time limit of two days. She shared it early. She showed a rough version on day one. The first comments were about the flow, which was what mattered. She talked to herself as she would to a friend. "The draft has two problems. That is what a draft is for." She noticed the cost. After a month of poor sleep and constant dread before presentations, she spoke to her doctor, who helped her find a counsellor. The flow was fixed in a day. The dread eased over the following weeks, though it did not vanish. What it shows: Polishing felt like care, but it was a way of avoiding the one test that would help. A clear finish line, early sharing and a kinder voice moved Meera from guarding the work to improving it.

Krishna's lesson on defects and duty The Gita is a conversation between Krishna and Arjuna, who is hesitating over his duty on the eve of a battle. Near the end of the dialogue, Krishna speaks of the work each person is born to: "It is better to do one's own dharma, even though imperfectly, than to do another's dharma, even though perfectly" (18.47). He then answers the objection that the work has faults: "One should not abandon duties born of one's nature, even if one sees defects in them, O son of Kunti. Indeed, all endeavors are veiled by some evil, as fire is by smoke" (18.48). The verses are not addressed to perfectionism, but the image fits it: fire gives light and heat, and smoke is part of how it burns. What it shows: A flaw in the work is not a reason to put the work down. The image of fire and smoke says that every action comes with some imperfection, and the teaching is to act without attachment to a flawless result.

Svetaketu and the instruction not yet heard The Chandogya Upanishad tells of Svetaketu, whose father says to him: "go to school; for there is none belonging to our race, darling, who, not having studied (the Veda), is, as it were, a Brâhmana by birth only" (6.1.1). He begins at twelve and returns at twenty-four, "having then studied all the Vedas,—conceited, considering himself well-read, and stern" (6.1.2). His father asks: "have you ever asked for that instruction by which we hear what cannot be heard, by which we perceive what cannot be perceived, by which we know what cannot be known?" (6.1.3). Svetaketu does not know what it is, and the father explains with an image: "as by one clod of clay all that is made of clay is known" (6.1.4). Svetaketu answers: "Surely those venerable men (my teachers) did not know that. For if they had known it, why should they not have told it me? Do you, Sir, therefore tell me that" (6.1.7). He asks to be taught. What it shows: Svetaketu has done everything asked of him and is full of knowledge, yet his father shows him that something is still missing. The story does not mention mistakes or perfectionism; it shows a person whose standing rests on achievement, and who learns by asking.

Paul and the thorn In 2 Corinthians 12, Paul writes of a "thorn" he was given: "a thorn was given me in the flesh, a messenger of Satan to torment me, to keep me from being too elated." He says: "Three times I appealed to the Lord about this, that it would leave me" (12:7-8). The answer he reports: "My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness" (12:9). And he concludes: "Therefore I am content with weaknesses, insults, hardships, persecutions, and calamities for the sake of Christ, for whenever I am weak, then I am strong" (12:10). The text does not say what the thorn was, and readers have suggested many things. The story is not about perfectionism, but it shows a person asking for a flaw to be removed and being told that it stays, and that his standing does not depend on being rid of it. What it shows: A flaw can remain and the person can still be accepted and useful. The story does not say that effort is pointless; it says that a person's strength is not measured by the absence of weakness.

Soṇa and the harp Venerable Soṇa has been practising hard. In private retreat he thinks: "I am one of the Buddha's most energetic disciples. Yet my mind is not freed from defilements by not grasping. But my family has wealth. I could enjoy that wealth and make merit. Why don't I resign the training and return to a lesser life, so I can enjoy my wealth and make merit?" The Buddha knows his thought and appears in front of him. He asks: "When you were still a layman, weren't you a good player of the arched harp?" Soṇa says yes. "When your harp's strings were tuned too tight, was it resonant and playable?" "No, sir." The Buddha asks the same about strings tuned too slack. Then: "But when your harp's strings were tuned neither too tight nor too slack, but fixed at an even tension, was it resonant and playable?" The Buddha says: "In the same way, Soṇa, when energy is too forceful it leads to restlessness. When energy is too slack it leads to laziness. So, Soṇa, you should focus on energy and serenity, find a balance of the faculties, and learn the character of this situation." Soṇa does so, and "soon realized the supreme culmination of the spiritual path in this very life." What it shows: Soṇa was not lazy; he was straining, and he took the lack of a result to mean that he should quit. The Buddha does not tell him to try less or to try harder, but to tune the effort. The sutta is about meditation, and its use for perfectionism is a reading.

Marcus Aurelius and the sponge In the Meditations, the emperor Marcus Aurelius writes notes to himself. In one of them he considers what to do on days when he has not lived up to his own principles. He does not tell himself to try harder. He writes: "Be not disgusted, nor discouraged, nor dissatisfied, if thou dost not succeed in doing everything according to right principles; but when thou hast failed, return back again, and be content if the greater part of what thou doest is consistent with man's nature, and love this to which thou returnest." Then he adds an image: "do not return to philosophy as if she were a master, but act like those who have sore eyes and apply a bit of sponge and egg, or as another applies a plaster, or drenching with water." What it shows: Marcus treats philosophy as a remedy to be used, and failure as a reason to return to it without drama. The passage does not use the word perfectionism; it speaks to the habit of being disgusted with oneself, and offers a lighter way back.

Self-doubt is a lasting uncertainty about your ability or your worth. Its best-known form is impostor syndrome (also called the impostor phenomenon): feeling like a fraud, and expecting to be found out, despite evidence of competence. The idea goes back to a 1978 paper by Clance and Imes on high-achieving women. Two points from the research: It is common and hard to measure. A systematic review of 62 studies and 14,161 participants found that prevalence "varied widely from 9 to 82%", largely depending on the screening tool and cut-off used. It was common in men and women and across ages. It is not a diagnosis. The review describes it as often occurring with depression and anxiety, and notes that no published studies had evaluated treatments for it. Some self-doubt is healthy, because it keeps us checking our work and listening to others. The difficulty is doubt that does not respond to evidence. If it is constant, or comes with low mood or anxiety, a doctor or therapist can help.

Hinduism has no single word for self-doubt, but the Bhagavad Gita opens with a man in its grip. Arjuna says in 2.7: "I am confused about my duty, and am besieged with anxiety and faintheartedness. I am Your disciple, and am surrendered to You. Please instruct me for certain what is best for me." Krishna's first answer in 2.3 is: "O Parth, it does not befit you to yield to this unmanliness. Give up such petty weakness of heart and arise, O vanquisher of enemies." Later the Gita speaks of the mind as both ally and obstacle. 6.5: "Elevate yourself through the power of your mind, and not degrade yourself, for the mind can be the friend and also the enemy of the self." This is related to self-doubt and not identical to it. Arjuna's crisis is about duty and its cost, and the verses do not speak of competence or feeling like a fraud. The wording "unmanliness" in 2.3 is the translator's.

The Upanishads do not discuss self-doubt, but the Katha Upanishad begins with a boy who is unsure of what lies ahead and goes on anyway. Nachiketas, "still a boy", asks his father three times, "to whom wilt thou give me?" and is told "I shall give thee unto Death" (Katha 1.1.2-4). The Mundaka Upanishad speaks to those who feel unequal to the search: "That Self cannot be gained by the Veda, nor by understanding, nor by much learning. He whom the Self chooses, by him the Self can be gained" (3.2.3). And: "Nor is that Self to be gained by one who is destitute of strength, or without earnestness, or without right meditation" (3.2.4). This is related to self-doubt and not identical to it. The texts speak of strength, earnestness and the nature of the Self, and not of feeling like a fraud. Taking the first verse as a comfort to the doubtful (that learning is not the measure) is a reading and not stated in the text.

The Bible has no word for impostor syndrome, but it records several people who doubt that they are the right person for the task. Moses: "Who am I that I should go to Pharaoh and bring the Israelites out of Egypt?" (Exodus 3:11). Later: "I have never been eloquent... I am slow of speech and slow of tongue" (4:10). Gideon: "how can I deliver Israel? My clan is the weakest in Manasseh, and I am the least in my family" (Judges 6:15). Jeremiah: "Truly I do not know how to speak, for I am only a boy" (Jeremiah 1:6). In each case the answer is the same: "I will be with you" (Exodus 3:12; Judges 6:16; see also Jeremiah 1:8). This is related to self-doubt and not identical to it. These people doubt their fitness for a calling, and the texts do not describe a general feeling of being a fraud.

Buddhist texts have no word for self-doubt as we use it. Doubt (vicikiccha) is the fifth of the five hindrances, but it is doubt about the teaching and the path, so it is related to self-doubt and not identical to it (see sloth in Buddhism for the list). SN 46.51 describes how doubt feeds: "And what fuels the arising of doubt, or, when it has arisen, makes it increase and grow? There are things that are grounds for doubt." The Dhammapada has a chapter on the self that speaks to the other side. Dhp 157: "If you knew your self as beloved, you'd look after it so well." Dhp 160: "One is indeed the lord of oneself, for who else would be one's lord?"

The Greek philosophers had a name for the opposite fault to vanity: being too modest about one's own worth. Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 4.3: "The man who thinks himself worthy of less than he is really worthy of is unduly humble, whether his deserts be great or moderate". Self-doubt that sets one's worth below the facts fits this description. Marcus Aurelius addresses a related reluctance: "In the morning when thou risest unwillingly, let this thought be present: I am rising to the work of a human being." This is related to self-doubt and not identical to it. Aristotle is describing a trait of character, and Marcus a reluctance to get up and work, and neither describes the feeling of being a fraud.

Research on impostor feelings is still uneven, so the roots below are the ones commonly proposed, with the little the sources say. Where it shows up. Bravata and colleagues found impostor feelings "particularly high among ethnic minority groups" and common across ages, from adolescents to late-stage professionals. The abstract does not explain why. Measurement. Prevalence ranged from 9 to 82% depending on the tool and cut-off, so part of what looks like a cause may be how it is counted. Link with other states. The review reports that impostor syndrome is often comorbid with depression and anxiety. The abstract does not say which comes first. Commonly proposed roots. Early messages that worth depends on achievement, high standards (see Perfectionism), being the first or only one of your group in a setting, and attributing success to luck are all frequently given. These are common explanations and not findings from the paper read here.

The Gita traces Arjuna's collapse to confusion about duty and to the mind turned against its owner. Confusion and anxiety. Arjuna's own account in 2.7: "I am confused about my duty, and am besieged with anxiety and faintheartedness." The mind as enemy. 6.6: "For those who have conquered the mind, it is their friend. For those who have failed to do so, the mind works like an enemy." A mind that argues against us is the root in view. Doubt without faith or knowledge. 4.40 says that "persons who possess neither faith nor knowledge, and who are of a doubting nature, suffer a downfall". The doubt is about the teaching, and the verse is not about self-doubt. This is related to self-doubt and not identical to it. The verses speak of duty, the mind and faith, and the roots listed are our reading.

The Upanishads do not describe where self-doubt comes from. Two passages suggest a root: measuring ourselves by learning, and forgetting what the Self is. Measuring by learning. Mundaka 3.2.3: "That Self cannot be gained by the Veda, nor by understanding, nor by much learning." If we treat knowledge or cleverness as the measure of a person, we will always find ourselves short. Lacking strength and earnestness. 3.2.4 names "destitute of strength, or without earnestness, or without right meditation" as the causes of failure to reach the Self. Doubt is not named, but a person who gives up through feeling unfit lacks strength in this sense. That is a reading. Standing on achievement. In the Chandogya (6.1.2), Svetaketu comes home "conceited, considering himself well-read", and his father shows him what he lacks. Standing built on attainment is exposed when someone asks a question we cannot answer. This is related to self-doubt and not identical to it. These passages are read for the roots they point to and are not about impostor feelings.

The Bible places the root in looking at oneself alone, and says what the doubters of the Bible were told to look at instead. Comparing self with task. Moses asks "Who am I?" (Exodus 3:11), Gideon says "I am the least in my family" (Judges 6:15), and Jeremiah says "I am only a boy" (Jeremiah 1:6). Each measures themselves against the task and finds themselves short. Where adequacy comes from. Paul writes: "Not that we are qualified of ourselves to claim anything as coming from us; our qualification is from God" (2 Corinthians 3:5). The text is saying that the standard of being qualified of ourselves is not the right one. Grace. "By the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace toward me has not been in vain" (1 Corinthians 15:10). This is related to self-doubt and not identical to it. The passages are about calling and grace, and reading them for the roots of self-doubt is ours.

The Buddhist texts do not trace self-doubt itself, but SN 46.51 says how doubt in general is fed. Grounds for doubt. "And what fuels the arising of doubt, or, when it has arisen, makes it increase and grow? There are things that are grounds for doubt." Doubt grows on what we give it to grow on. Not knowing the self. Dhp 157: "If you knew your self as beloved, you'd look after it so well." The verse implies that failing to care for the self comes from not knowing it as dear, and that is a reading. This is related to self-doubt and not identical to it. The hindrance of doubt is mainly about the teaching and the path, and the roots here are our reading.

The philosophers find the root in a mistaken judgement of one's own worth, and in resting that worth on things outside us. A false estimate. Aristotle's "unduly humble" person thinks himself "worthy of less than he is really worthy of" (Nicomachean Ethics 4.3). The fault is a wrong measurement. Worth in what is not ours. Epictetus, Enchiridion 1: "Things not in our control are body, property, reputation, command, and, in one word, whatever are not our own actions." If our sense of worth rests on reputation or on others' approval, any slight shakes it. Reluctance at the start. Marcus Aurelius notes the pull of the bed in the morning ("when thou risest unwillingly", Meditations 5). He treats it as a reluctance to be answered, and not as a verdict on himself. This is related to self-doubt and not identical to it. These are accounts of character and judgement; the link to impostor feelings is ours.

Bravata and colleagues' review links impostor syndrome with several costs. It is "often comorbid with depression and anxiety and is associated with impaired job performance, job satisfaction, and burnout among various employee populations including clinicians". The authors add that studies were heterogeneous and that publication bias may be present, and the abstract gives no cause and effect. Commonly described effects, which are not findings from that review: Holding back. Not applying, not speaking up, or turning down a chance because you expect to be found out. Over-working to hide the gap. Preparing far past the point of use, which feeds the cycle (see Perfectionism). Discounting praise. Success is put down to luck, so it never raises confidence. If self-doubt comes with low mood, constant anxiety or exhaustion, a doctor or therapist can help.

The Gita shows the effects at the moment of collapse and in the verses that follow. Paralysis. Arjuna cannot act: he is "besieged with anxiety and faintheartedness" and asks to be told what is best (2.7). Yielding. Krishna's first words name the pull: "it does not befit you to yield to this unmanliness" (2.3). A doubting nature. 4.40: "persons who possess neither faith nor knowledge, and who are of a doubting nature, suffer a downfall. For the skeptical souls, there is no happiness either in this world or the next." This verse is about doubt of the teaching, not self-doubt, and is quoted for what the Gita says doubt costs. This is related to self-doubt and not identical to it.

The Upanishads do not list effects of self-doubt. The Mundaka says what stops a seeker: "Nor is that Self to be gained by one who is destitute of strength, or without earnestness, or without right meditation" (3.2.4). A person who gives up before starting has, in this sense, lost strength and earnestness. The Katha shows the opposite effect in Nachiketas. Death offers him sons, cattle, gold and long life if he will stop asking his question, and he answers: "These things last till tomorrow, O Death, for they wear out this vigour of all the senses" (1.1.26). He does not give up the question. This is related to self-doubt and not identical to it. The first passage is about the seeker's strength, and the second about steadiness in the face of temptation. Setting them against self-doubt is a reading.

The Bible shows hesitation, fear and a plea for someone else, and it shows the answer. Hesitation. Moses objects "I am slow of speech and slow of tongue" (Exodus 4:10), and Jeremiah says "Truly I do not know how to speak, for I am only a boy" (Jeremiah 1:6). Fear. The reply to Jeremiah is "Do not be afraid of them, for I am with you to deliver you" (1:8), and Isaiah 41:10 says "do not fear, for I am with you". Strength. Paul writes: "I can do all things through him who strengthens me" (Philippians 4:13). This is related to self-doubt and not identical to it. The people in these texts hesitate over a calling, and the texts do not describe impostor feelings or their effects on work.

The Buddhist texts do not describe the effects of self-doubt. SN 46.51 says how doubt in general behaves: it can "increase and grow" once it has arisen. That is what many people report of self-doubt, that it feeds on itself. Dhp 160 points to what is lost: "One is indeed the lord of oneself, for who else would be one's lord?" A person who hands the verdict to a doubting voice has, in this sense, given up being the lord of themselves. That is a reading. This is related to self-doubt and not identical to it.

Aristotle describes what the unduly humble person loses. In Nicomachean Ethics 4.3 he says such a person "robs himself of what he deserves", and that "these people stand back even from noble actions and undertakings, deeming themselves unworthy". He adds that they are "not thought to be fools, but rather unduly retiring", and that the reputation makes them worse. Marcus Aurelius names a quieter effect, the loss of purpose in the morning: "Why then am I dissatisfied if I am going to do the things for which I exist and for which I was brought into the world?" (Meditations 5). This is related to self-doubt and not identical to it. Aristotle writes about a trait of character and Marcus about reluctance; neither describes impostor feelings.

The review of impostor syndrome found no published studies of treatment, so what follows is common advice and not evidence of what works. Name it. "This is the impostor feeling" separates the feeling from the facts. Keep a record of what you did. Write down tasks completed, feedback received and problems solved, and read it when the doubt is loud. Doubt that does not respond to evidence needs evidence in front of it. Check the story against the facts. Ask what you would say to a friend with the same record. Talk to someone. A mentor, colleague or friend often says they feel the same, which matters because the review found impostor feelings common across ages and groups. Learn the skill you doubt. Self-doubt about a real gap is useful information; fill the gap. Act before you feel ready. Confidence often follows action. This is common advice, not a finding here. Get help if it takes over. The review reports that impostor syndrome often goes with depression and anxiety. If doubt is constant or your mood is low, a doctor or therapist can help.

The Gita's answer to Arjuna runs from a firm word to a steadying view of the mind. Rise. 2.3: "Give up such petty weakness of heart and arise." The translator's commentary says the path requires "high spirits and morale". Ask for guidance. Arjuna's own step in 2.7: "I am Your disciple... Please instruct me for certain what is best for me." Admitting the confusion is where the teaching begins. Make the mind a friend. 6.5: "Elevate yourself through the power of your mind, and not degrade yourself, for the mind can be the friend and also the enemy of the self." Train it. 6.6: "For those who have conquered the mind, it is their friend." This is related to self-doubt and not identical to it. A firm word like 2.3 suits some people and not others, and nothing here replaces help from a doctor or therapist where doubt is severe.

The Upanishads point to strength, earnestness and steadiness. Do not rest worth on learning. Mundaka 3.2.3: "That Self cannot be gained by the Veda, nor by understanding, nor by much learning." Not knowing enough is not the measure. Bring strength and earnestness. 3.2.4: the Self is not gained by one "destitute of strength, or without earnestness, or without right meditation. But if a wise man strives after it by those means... then his Self enters the home of Brahman." Stay with the question. Nachiketas keeps asking when offered wealth and long life instead: "These things last till tomorrow, O Death" (Katha 1.1.26). This is related to self-doubt and not identical to it. The Upanishads give no method for doubt of one's competence, and these passages are read for the steadiness they show.

The Bible's answer to the doubters is presence and a different measure. Remember you are not alone. To Moses and Gideon: "I will be with you" (Exodus 3:12; Judges 6:16). To Jeremiah: "Do not be afraid of them, for I am with you" (1:8). Change the measure. 2 Corinthians 3:5: "our qualification is from God". Say what you are. 1 Corinthians 15:10: "by the grace of God I am what I am". Ask for strength. Philippians 4:13: "I can do all things through him who strengthens me." Take it step by step. In Exodus 4:12 the instruction is only "now go, and I will be with your mouth and teach you what you are to speak". This is related to self-doubt and not identical to it. These verses address calling and faith, and pastoral and medical help is also part of Christian care for constant doubt.

The Dhammapada's chapter on the self gives the Buddhist direction. Treat yourself as someone dear. Dhp 157: "If you knew your self as beloved, you'd look after it so well." Be your own lord. Dhp 160: "One is indeed the lord of oneself, for who else would be one's lord? By means of a well-tamed self, one gains a lord that's rare indeed." Do not feed the doubt. SN 46.51 says that doubt arises, grows and is starved by what is given to it. The sutta says there are "things that are grounds for doubt" and, separately, what "starves" its growth. Seeing which is which is the practice, though what the sutta lists was not read here. This is related to self-doubt and not identical to it. The suttas are about the path, and nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist where doubt is severe.

The philosophers advise measuring accurately and then acting. Measure yourself correctly. Aristotle's fault is "worthy of less than he is really worthy of" (Nicomachean Ethics 4.3). The remedy is an honest estimate, neither above nor below the facts. Act for what you are for. Marcus Aurelius: "I am rising to the work of a human being. Why then am I dissatisfied if I am going to do the things for which I exist and for which I was brought into the world?" Rest worth on what is yours. Epictetus, Enchiridion 1: opinion, pursuit, desire and aversion are in our control, "reputation" is not. Judging your own conduct is yours; others' approval is not. This is related to self-doubt and not identical to it. These are rules for living and judging, and applying them to impostor feelings is a reading.

Note: This is an invented composite story, not a real case. It is built from patterns people commonly describe, so you can see how self-doubt works and how people loosen its grip. Rohan's story Rohan was promoted to team lead after two years as an engineer. His manager said he had earned it. Rohan thought they had made a mistake. He stayed late to double-check everything, avoided asking questions in case they showed what he did not know, and put off giving feedback to a colleague because he felt he had no right to. When the team praised the release, he told himself that the others had done the hard parts. What helped: He named it. A colleague mentioned "impostor feelings" in passing, and Rohan recognised the pattern. He kept a list. Each Friday he wrote down three things he had done that week and one piece of feedback he had received. After a month the list was hard to argue with. He asked a friend. The friend, a manager at another company, said she had felt the same for years. He asked his questions. The first two turned out to be questions others had been afraid to ask. He noticed it was not lifting. After a few months of poor sleep and dread on Sunday evenings, he spoke to his doctor. The doubt did not disappear. It got quieter, and he stopped letting it make decisions. What it shows: Rohan did not argue himself out of the feeling. He put evidence beside it, spoke about it and acted before he felt ready.

Arjuna lays down his courage The Gita is a conversation between Krishna and Arjuna on the eve of a battle. Arjuna, a skilled warrior, stops. His own account is in 2.7: "I am confused about my duty, and am besieged with anxiety and faintheartedness. I am Your disciple, and am surrendered to You. Please instruct me for certain what is best for me." Krishna's first words (2.3) are blunt: "O Parth, it does not befit you to yield to this unmanliness. Give up such petty weakness of heart and arise, O vanquisher of enemies." The rest of the Gita is the teaching that follows. Later Krishna says of the mind: "For those who have conquered the mind, it is their friend. For those who have failed to do so, the mind works like an enemy" (6.6). What it shows: A capable person can freeze, and the first step out is to say so and ask for guidance. Arjuna is not an impostor in the poem, and his crisis is over duty, not over feeling like a fraud; the story is read here for how it shows doubt and the way through.

Nachiketas and the third boon The Katha Upanishad begins with a boy. His father has promised to give away all he owns, and "faith entered into the heart of Nachiketas, who was still a boy" (1.1.2). He asks, "Dear father, to whom wilt thou give me?" three times, and the angry father says, "I shall give thee unto Death" (1.1.4). Nachiketas goes to the house of Death, waits, and is granted three boons. For the third he asks what happens after death: "There is that doubt, when a man is dead, - some saying, he is; others, he is not. This I should like to know, taught by thee" (1.1.20). Death tries to put him off: "On this point even the gods have doubted formerly; it is not easy to understand. ... do not press me" (1.1.21). He offers sons, cattle, gold and long life. Nachiketas answers: "These things last till tomorrow, O Death, for they wear out this vigour of all the senses" (1.1.26). What it shows: A boy with no standing, facing the one who has the power to refuse him, keeps to his question. The story is about the seeker's resolve, and not about self-doubt as such; it shows steadiness against being told that the question is too hard.

Gideon, "the least in my family" In the Book of Judges, the Lord turns to Gideon and says: "Go in this might of yours and deliver Israel from the hand of Midian; I hereby commission you" (6:14). Gideon answers: "But sir, how can I deliver Israel? My clan is the weakest in Manasseh, and I am the least in my family" (6:15). The reply does not argue with him about his clan or his place. It says: "But I will be with you, and you shall strike down the Midianites, every one of them" (6:16). What it shows: Gideon's doubt is stated plainly, and the answer moves the question from what he is to who is with him. The passage is about a calling and not about impostor feelings; it is read here because it shows doubt named openly and answered.

The chapter on the self The Dhammapada is a collection of verses and has no single story of self-doubt. The twelfth chapter, on the self, comes closest to speaking to it. It begins: "If you knew your self as beloved, you'd look after it so well" (Dhp 157). And then: "One is indeed the lord of oneself, for who else would be one's lord? By means of a well-tamed self, one gains a lord that's rare indeed" (Dhp 160). Traditional commentaries attach narratives to these verses. They were not read for this article, so none is retold here. What it shows: The verses do not say that doubt is wrong. They say that the person is the one who has to look after and govern their own mind, and that doing it well is rare and worth doing. This is not about self-doubt directly, and the reading is ours.

Marcus Aurelius gets out of bed In the Meditations, the emperor Marcus Aurelius writes notes to himself. In one of them he describes a morning when he does not want to rise. "In the morning when thou risest unwillingly, let this thought be present: I am rising to the work of a human being. Why then am I dissatisfied if I am going to do the things for which I exist and for which I was brought into the world? Or have I been made for this, to lie in the bed-clothes and keep myself warm?" An objector answers: "But this is more pleasant." He replies: "Dost thou exist then to take thy pleasure, and not at all for action or exertion?" He goes on to point to the little plants, the little birds, the ants, the spiders and the bees, each doing its own work. What it shows: Marcus does not wait for the feeling to pass. He reminds himself what he is for and gets up. The passage is about reluctance, and not about self-doubt as such; it shows acting before the mood is right.

Self-criticism is a harsh inner voice that judges and punishes you for mistakes and shortcomings, when it could be helping you improve. It is not the same as honest self-assessment: noticing an error and asking how to fix it is one thing, and attacking yourself for it is another. Researchers often study its opposite. Zessin and colleagues describe self-compassion as "a positive and caring attitude of a person toward her- or himself in the face of failures and individual shortcomings". Neff's 2003 paper presents self-compassion as "a healthy attitude toward oneself", and Gilbert and Procter's 2006 pilot study of a group therapy approach was designed for "people with high shame and self-criticism". Self-criticism is close to perfectionism and often comes with shame. It is not a diagnosis, but it can go with low mood and anxiety. If the voice is relentless, a doctor or therapist can help.

Hinduism has no single word for the inner critic, but the Bhagavad Gita describes the mind that turns on its owner. 6.5: "Elevate yourself through the power of your mind, and not degrade yourself, for the mind can be the friend and also the enemy of the self." And 6.6: "For those who have conquered the mind, it is their friend. For those who have failed to do so, the mind works like an enemy." The translator's commentary on 6.5 adds: "We are responsible for our own elevation or debasement." This is related to self-criticism and not identical to it. The Gita is speaking of the undisciplined mind in general, and does not describe a harsh voice of self-judgement. Reading 6.5-6.6 as speaking to the inner critic is ours.

The Upanishads do not name an inner critic. They speak of grief, and of a self that is not touched by what the mind says about it. The Mundaka Upanishad (3.1.2) describes a person who "sits grieving, immersed, bewildered by his own impotence", and says that when he sees the other, "then his grief passes away". Katha 1.2.22 says: "The wise who knows the Self as bodiless within the bodies, as unchanging among changing things, as great and omnipresent, does never grieve." This is related to self-criticism and not identical to it. The passages are about grief and the nature of the Self, and not about harsh self-judgement. Reading them as speaking to the inner critic is ours.

Christian texts do not speak of an inner critic, but they speak of the heart that condemns. 1 John 3:19-20: "And by this we will know that we are from the truth and will reassure our hearts before him whenever our hearts condemn us, for God is greater than our hearts, and he knows everything." And Romans 8:1: "Therefore there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus." This is related to self-criticism and not identical to it. The verses are about conscience and standing before God, and not about a pattern of harsh self-talk. Reading them as speaking to the inner critic is ours.

Buddhist texts have no term for the inner critic, but SN 3.4 speaks of treating oneself as an enemy. King Pasenadi says: "Those who do bad things by way of body, speech, and mind don't love themselves... It's because they treat themselves like an enemy." And those who do good "treat themselves like a loved one". The Buddha agrees with him. Here the point is about conduct, not self-talk. Dhp 159 turns to how we treat ourselves: "If one were to treat oneself as one instructs another, the well-tamed indeed would tame: for the self, it seems, is hard to tame." This is related to self-criticism and not identical to it. Pasenadi means that harmful action is how a person treats themselves badly, and the texts do not describe a harsh inner voice. Reading Dhp 159 as speaking to it is ours.

The Stoics separate blaming others, blaming ourselves and blaming no one. Epictetus, Enchiridion 5: "When therefore we are hindered, or disturbed, or grieved, let us never attribute it to others, but to ourselves; that is, to our own principles. An uninstructed person will lay the fault of his own bad condition upon others. Someone just starting instruction will lay the fault on himself. Some who is perfectly instructed will place blame neither on others nor on himself." So even blaming oneself, which can look like the humble course, is placed below not blaming at all. This is related to self-criticism and not identical to it. Epictetus is speaking of blame for our disturbance, and does not describe a harsh inner voice.

None of the sources read for this article explains where the inner critic comes from, so what follows is common explanation, not finding. Learned from others. A harsh voice is often described as an internalised version of critical parents, teachers or peers. A belief that harshness works. Many people feel that going easy on themselves would let them slip, so the critic is kept as a motivator. Protection. Criticising yourself first can feel like a way of getting ahead of other people's judgement. Shame and perfectionism. Gilbert and Procter's approach was designed for people with "high shame and self-criticism" (title), which suggests the two often go together; see also Perfectionism.

The Gita locates the root in an untrained mind. The mind as enemy. 6.6: "For those who have failed to do so, the mind works like an enemy." Without training, the mind's habits run against us. Responsibility. The commentary on 6.5 says we are responsible for our own elevation or debasement, so the mind's verdicts are not final. Sorrow over what does not warrant it. In 2.11 Krishna tells Arjuna: "you are mourning for that which is not worthy of grief." The verse is about grief for others, but it shows a mind spending sorrow where it does not belong. This is related to self-criticism and not identical to it. The Gita does not describe the roots of a harsh voice; these verses are read for the idea of an untrained mind.

The Upanishads do not give a root for self-criticism. The Mundaka's image of the grieving bird points to one: identification with the experiencer. Immersion. "On the same tree man sits grieving, immersed, bewildered by his own impotence" (Mundaka 3.1.2). The person who is fully taken up in what happens to them feels every blow. Not seeing the other. The verse goes on: "But when he sees the other lord contented and knows his glory, then his grief passes away." The root is that the watching self is overlooked. This is related to self-criticism and not identical to it. The verse is about grief, and its use here for the inner critic is ours.

The Bible shows the root in a person who judges himself by his own record and by what he has lost. In the parable of the prodigal son (Luke 15:17-24), the young man who has wasted his inheritance plans what to say: "Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you; I am no longer worthy to be called your son; treat me like one of your hired hands." His own verdict is that he has forfeited his place. The father has not said so. Matthew 7:3-5 shows a related habit, a standard held up to others and missed in oneself: "Why do you see the speck in your neighbor's eye but do not notice the log in your own eye?" This is related to self-criticism and not identical to it. The parable is about repentance and the second passage about judging others, and reading them for the roots of the inner critic is ours.

SN 36.6, the Arrow Sutta, describes how suffering is added to. When an unlearned person experiences painful physical feelings, they "sorrow and wail and lament, beating their breast and falling into confusion. They experience two feelings: physical and mental. It's like a person who is struck with an arrow, only to be struck with a second arrow." The second arrow is the reaction. The sutta is speaking of physical pain, but it names the pattern the inner critic follows: a first hurt, then the extra hurt of what we do with it. SN 3.4 adds that treating oneself "like an enemy" is how a person fails to love themselves. This is related to self-criticism and not identical to it. The sutta is about physical pain, and the use here for self-attack is ours.

The philosophers find the root in our own principles and judgements, not in the event. Epictetus, Enchiridion 5: "Men are disturbed, not by things, but by the principles and notions which they form concerning things." The disturbance of self-blame, on this view, comes from the rule we apply: that every mistake should be punished. Aristotle describes how a person's relation to themselves breaks down. In Nicomachean Ethics 9.4, bad men, "having nothing lovable in them", and "their soul is rent by faction", and "bad men are laden with repentance". For Aristotle this follows from wickedness. Applying it to people who are only hard on themselves would go beyond his text. This is related to self-criticism and not identical to it.

The research read here is on the caring opposite of self-criticism, and it is mostly correlational. Mental health. MacBeth and Gumley pooled 20 samples from 14 studies, all using Neff's Self-Compassion Scale, and found a large association between self-compassion and psychopathology, r = -0.54: people higher in self-compassion reported fewer symptoms. Well-being. Zessin and colleagues combined 79 samples (N = 16,416) and found a relationship of r = .47 between self-compassion and well-being, "a subsample of studies indicated a causal effect". What this does not show. Correlations do not show that harsh self-criticism causes symptoms, and neither abstract measures self-criticism as such. Commonly described effects, not findings from these papers: dread of mistakes, avoiding tasks you might do badly, poor sleep and low mood. If these are constant, a doctor or therapist can help.

The Gita names the cost of a mind that turns on itself. 6.5 warns against the mind that makes us "degrade yourself", and 6.6 says that for those who have not conquered it "the mind works like an enemy". The cost is that the thing we have to work with is working against us. The Gita also names what freedom looks like. After the teaching, Arjuna says: "by Your grace my illusion has been dispelled, and I am situated in knowledge. I am now free from doubts, and I shall act according to Your instructions" (18.73). This is related to self-criticism and not identical to it. The verses are about the untrained mind and about doubt, and the effects of a harsh inner voice are not described.

The Mundaka names the effect as grief: the person "sits grieving, immersed, bewildered by his own impotence" (3.1.2). The Katha adds a caution, so that the point is not read as ignoring wrongdoing. Verse 1.2.24 says that he "who has not first turned away from his wickedness, who is not tranquil, and subdued, or whose mind is not at rest" cannot obtain the Self even by knowledge. Turning away from what is wrong is part of the path, while grief that goes round and round is not. This is related to self-criticism and not identical to it. Both passages are about the seeker and the Self, and the effects of a harsh inner voice are not described. The balance drawn here between the two is ours.

The Bible shows both the weight of self-condemnation and what lifts it. The condemning heart. 1 John 3:20 names it: "whenever our hearts condemn us". Removal. Psalm 103:10-12: "He does not deal with us according to our sins nor repay us according to our iniquities... as far as the east is from the west, so far he removes our transgressions from us." Welcome. The father in the parable runs to his son, "filled with compassion", and says "this son of mine was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found!" (Luke 15:20, 24). The son's own sentence ("I am no longer worthy") is not what the father carries out. This is related to self-criticism and not identical to it. The texts speak of sin and forgiveness, and do not describe the toll of a harsh inner voice.

SN 3.4 says what treating oneself badly leads to: "happiness is not easy to find by someone who does bad deeds". The sutta is about harmful action, not self-talk. Dhp 161 describes the weight of one's own wrongdoing: "For the evil that is done by oneself, born and produced in oneself, grinds down a simpleton, as diamond grinds a lesser gem." SN 36.6 shows the added suffering of the second arrow. It says the learned disciple, "they don't sorrow or wail or lament": the pain is the same, and the second arrow is missing. This is related to self-criticism and not identical to it. The texts speak of wrongdoing, pain and the response to it, and not of a harsh inner voice.

The Stoics see the cost in lost time and in a mind at war with itself. Marcus Aurelius names the reaction to failing: "Be not disgusted, nor discouraged, nor dissatisfied, if thou dost not succeed in doing everything according to right principles" (Meditations 5). Disgust at oneself, discouragement and dissatisfaction are the effects he wants to avoid, and he tells himself instead to "return back again". Aristotle (Nicomachean Ethics 9.4) says that people who are at odds with themselves are "laden with repentance" and "their soul is rent by faction". He means bad men, so the application to people who are simply hard on themselves is ours. This is related to self-criticism and not identical to it.

The aim is to keep honest self-assessment and drop the contempt. Notice the voice. Give it a name or a tone ("the critic") so it is something you hear and not simply who you are. Ask whether it is useful. "Is this telling me something I can fix, or just attacking me?" Keep the first kind of message and let the second go. Speak to yourself as to a friend. Zessin and colleagues describe self-compassion as a "caring attitude... in the face of failures and individual shortcomings". Ask what you would say to a friend with the same slip. Try distance in your self-talk. Kross and colleagues found that using non-first-person language and your own name during introspection enhanced self-distancing and lowered distress in stressful social tasks. That evidence is about social stress, not about self-criticism. Expect help to exist. Gilbert and Procter piloted a group therapy approach, compassionate mind training, for people with high shame and self-criticism. A pilot study is not proof it works, and it was not read in full. Do not use the critic as your only motivator. Whether kindness motivates as well as harshness was not tested in the sources read here. Get help if it is relentless.
