A doctor or therapist can help with constant self-attack, low mood or anxiety.

The Gita's way is to make the mind a friend through discipline, and then to put down the weight. Elevate, do not degrade. 6.5: "Elevate yourself through the power of your mind, and not degrade yourself, for the mind can be the friend and also the enemy of the self." Train the mind. 6.6: "For those who have conquered the mind, it is their friend." Do not fear. 18.66: "Abandon all varieties of dharmas and simply surrender unto Me alone. I shall liberate you from all sinful reactions; do not fear." Trust the resolve. 9.30-31: even "the vilest sinners" who worship with exclusive devotion "are to be considered righteous because they have made the proper resolve", and "no devotee of Mine is ever lost". This is related to self-criticism and not identical to it. The verses are about devotion and the mind, and nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist for relentless self-attack.

The Upanishads point to shifting from the one who suffers to the one who watches. See the other bird. Mundaka 3.1.2: "when he sees the other lord contented and knows his glory, then his grief passes away." Shake off the verdicts. 3.1.3: "then he is wise, and shaking off good and evil, he reaches the highest oneness, free from passions". Know the Self. Katha 1.2.22: "The wise who knows the Self as bodiless within the bodies, as unchanging among changing things, as great and omnipresent, does never grieve." Do not skip the turning. Katha 1.2.24 says that one who "has not first turned away from his wickedness" cannot obtain the Self. Changing what is wrong still matters. This is related to self-criticism and not identical to it. The passages describe a path of knowledge, and applying them to a harsh inner voice is ours.

The Bible's answer to the condemning heart is to point to a greater one. Remember who is greater. 1 John 3:20: "whenever our hearts condemn us, for God is greater than our hearts, and he knows everything." Receive the verdict. Romans 8:1: "there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus." Remember how far. Psalm 103:12: "as far as the east is from the west, so far he removes our transgressions from us." Go home. In Luke 15, the son gets up and returns, though his words are about unworthiness. The father is already running to meet him (15:20). Look at your own eye first, kindly. Matthew 7:5 asks for honesty about oneself before judging others; it is not a call for self-attack. This is related to self-criticism and not identical to it. Christian care for a person weighed down by guilt also includes pastoral and medical help, which these verses do not discuss.

The Buddhist texts point to treating oneself as one would treat someone dear, and to not adding the second arrow. Know yourself as beloved. Dhp 157: "If you knew your self as beloved, you'd look after it so well." Treat yourself as you instruct another. Dhp 159: "If one were to treat oneself as one instructs another, the well-tamed indeed would tame: for the self, it seems, is hard to tame." Do not treat yourself as an enemy. SN 3.4: those who treat themselves "like a loved one" are those who love themselves. Feel the first arrow only. SN 36.6: the learned disciple feels the pain but they "don't sorrow or wail or lament". The practice is to notice the second arrow and put it down. This is related to self-criticism and not identical to it. SN 3.4 and SN 36.6 are not about harsh self-talk, and nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist for relentless self-attack.

The philosophers advise moving from blame to understanding, and returning without disgust. Look to your principles. Epictetus, Enchiridion 5: "Men are disturbed, not by things, but by the principles and notions which they form concerning things." Ask which rule you are punishing yourself under. Move up the ladder of blame. In the same chapter the uninstructed blame others, the beginner blames himself, and the "perfectly instructed" blame "neither on others nor on himself". Return. Marcus Aurelius: "when thou hast failed, return back again, and be content if the greater part of what thou doest is consistent with man's nature, and love this to which thou returnest." Treat the practice as a remedy. "Do not return to philosophy as if she were a master", but as one who applies "a bit of sponge and egg" to sore eyes. This is related to self-criticism and not identical to it. These are rules for living, and applying them to a harsh inner voice is a reading.

Note: This is an invented composite story, not a real case. It is built from patterns people commonly describe, so you can see how self-criticism works and how people loosen its grip. Leila's story Leila, a nurse, gave the wrong time on a handover note. A colleague caught it within minutes and no harm was done. On the drive home the voice started: "You're careless. You always do this. They'll stop trusting you." By bedtime she had gone through the whole shift, picking out every small slip. She slept badly, and the next day she double-checked everything twice and was slower than usual. What helped: She noticed the voice. A friend asked, "Would you say that to a new nurse?" Leila realised she would not. She sorted the message. Useful: check times against the chart before writing. Not useful: "you're careless". She spoke to herself by name. "Leila, that was a slip. The fix is to check the chart." She wrote down one fix and stopped. The fix went on a sticky note, and the rest of the evening was hers. She noticed it was not lifting. After weeks of poor sleep and dread before shifts, she spoke to her doctor and was referred to a counsellor. The voice did not go. It became shorter, and it started to say something she could use. What it shows: The mistake needed a fix, not a sentence. Sorting the message, using a kinder voice and stopping at one fix changed what the critic was for.

Arjuna, freed from doubt The Gita begins with Arjuna overwhelmed and ends with him steady. The setting is a conversation with Krishna before a battle. Along the way Krishna names the mind as friend or enemy: "For those who have conquered the mind, it is their friend. For those who have failed to do so, the mind works like an enemy" (6.6). And near the end he gives his last instruction: "Abandon all varieties of dharmas and simply surrender unto Me alone. I shall liberate you from all sinful reactions; do not fear" (18.66). Arjuna answers: "O Infallible One, by Your grace my illusion has been dispelled, and I am situated in knowledge. I am now free from doubts, and I shall act according to Your instructions" (18.73). What it shows: The poem moves a person from being stuck to acting. It is not about an inner critic, and Arjuna's crisis is about duty; the story is read here for the move from fear to steadiness.

Yama on grief and the Self The Katha Upanishad is a conversation between a boy, Nachiketas, and Death (Yama), who teaches him about the Self. It has no narrative of self-criticism, so this is a short passage from the teaching, not a tale. Yama says: "The wise who knows the Self as bodiless within the bodies, as unchanging among changing things, as great and omnipresent, does never grieve" (1.2.22). He also says that the Self is not reached through learning alone: "That Self cannot be gained by the Veda, nor by understanding, nor by much learning" (1.2.23). And then he adds the condition: "But he who has not first turned away from his wickedness, who is not tranquil, and subdued, or whose mind is not at rest, he can never obtain the Self (even) by knowledge" (1.2.24). What it shows: The teaching has two sides. One is a Self that does not grieve, and the other is a call to turn away from what is wrong. It is not about an inner critic, and the link is ours: turning away from a fault is asked for, and grieving over and over is not.

The son who rehearsed his sentence In Luke 15, a younger son asks for his share of the property, spends it and is left hungry. "When he came to his senses" he plans his return: "Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you; I am no longer worthy to be called your son; treat me like one of your hired hands" (15:17-19). He sets off. "But while he was still far off, his father saw him and was filled with compassion; he ran and put his arms around him and kissed him" (15:20). The son begins his speech ("I am no longer worthy to be called your son"). The father does not let him finish it. He says: "Quickly, bring out a robe—the best one—and put it on him; put a ring on his finger and sandals on his feet... for this son of mine was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found!" (15:22-24). What it shows: The son has already passed sentence on himself, and the father does not agree with it. The parable is about repentance and welcome and not about the inner critic as such; it shows a self-verdict set aside.

King Pasenadi asks who loves themselves In SN 3.4, King Pasenadi tells the Buddha of a thought he had in private retreat: "Who are those who love themselves? And who are those who don't love themselves?" His answer: "Those who do bad things by way of body, speech, and mind don't love themselves. Even though they may say: 'I love myself', they don't really. Why is that? It's because they treat themselves like an enemy." And those who do good do love themselves, "even though they may say: 'I don't love myself'", because "they treat themselves like a loved one". The Buddha says: "That's so true, Great King! That's so true!" and repeats the king's words, adding verses that begin: "If you knew your self as beloved, you'd not yoke yourself to wickedness. For happiness is not easy to find by someone who does bad deeds." What it shows: Caring for yourself is shown in what you do, more than in what you say about yourself. The sutta is about conduct and not self-talk, so it speaks to the inner critic only indirectly: harshness in words is not the same as care.

Epictetus's three kinds of person In the Enchiridion, Epictetus says that disturbance comes from our own judgements. "Men are disturbed, not by things, but by the principles and notions which they form concerning things. Death, for instance, is not terrible, else it would have appeared so to Socrates." Then he sorts people into three kinds: "An uninstructed person will lay the fault of his own bad condition upon others. Someone just starting instruction will lay the fault on himself. Some who is perfectly instructed will place blame neither on others nor on himself." He is not saying that faults do not matter. He is saying that the one who has learned stops treating blame as the answer, and looks at the principle behind the disturbance. What it shows: Self-blame is a step up from blaming everyone else, and Epictetus puts it in the middle. The passage is about disturbance and not about an inner critic; the point for self-criticism is that the aim is to see the principle, not to find the culprit.

Jealousy is the fear, and the hurt, of losing something you value to a rival, who may be real or imagined. Most often it is someone's love or attention. It is different from envy, which is wanting what another person has: envy involves two people, jealousy three. Jealousy shows up in romantic relationships, and also between friends, siblings and colleagues. Smith and Kim, reviewing the research on envy, define it as "an unpleasant, often painful emotion characterized by feelings of inferiority, hostility, and resentment caused by an awareness of a desired attribute enjoyed by another person or group of persons". Parrott and Smith's 1993 paper is titled "Distinguishing the experiences of envy and jealousy", so researchers treat the two as separate experiences. Everyday signs, as people commonly describe them and not as findings from these papers: A drop in the stomach when your partner laughs at someone else's message. Asking "who were you with?" and not quite believing the answer. Checking a phone, a profile or a location. Feeling replaced when a friend makes a new friend. Jealousy is not a diagnosis. If it is constant, or leads you to check, follow or control someone, a doctor or therapist can help.

Hinduism has no single word in the Bhagavad Gita for jealousy as the fear of losing someone to a rival, but the Gita describes the person who is free of its roots. Gita 12.13-14: "Those devotees are very dear to Me who are free from malice toward all living beings, who are friendly, and compassionate. They are free from attachment to possessions and egotism, equipoised in happiness and distress, and ever-forgiving." The translator's commentary on these verses says of such devotees: "If they harbor envy toward others, it is tantamount to harboring envy toward God Himself." This is related to jealousy and not identical to it. The verses speak of malice, envy and attachment to possessions, and do not describe the fear of losing someone to a rival. Reading them as speaking to jealousy is ours.

The Upanishads do not name jealousy, and the closest they come is a warning against grasping at what belongs to another. Isha Upanishad 1: "All this, whatsoever moves on earth, is to be hidden in the Lord (the Self). When thou hast surrendered all this, then thou mayest enjoy. Do not covet the wealth of any man!" The verse says to give up the sense of owning and then enjoy. It does not say to stop loving. This is related to jealousy and not identical to it. The verse is about coveting wealth, which is closer to greed and envy than to the fear of losing someone to a rival. Reading it as speaking to jealousy is ours.

Christian texts speak of jealousy as a force that is hard to stand against. Proverbs 27:4: "Wrath is cruel, anger is overwhelming, but who is able to stand before jealousy?" The Song of Solomon links it with love. In the King James Version, 8:6 reads: "love is strong as death; jealousy is cruel as the grave". The NRSV renders the same line "passion fierce as the grave". The Bible also calls God "a jealous God" (Exodus 20:5). That is a statement about God's claim on his people, and this article is about human jealousy, so it is not treated here. This is related to jealousy and not identical to it. Proverbs and the Song of Solomon speak of jealousy as a power, and do not define it as the fear of losing someone to a rival.

In the Buddhist texts jealousy is joined with stinginess, the clinging to what is one's own. In the Dhammapada (209) the Buddha describes a person who forgets their goal and "cling[s] to what you hold dear, jealous of those devoted to their heart's goal". In the Sakka sutta (DN 21), the god Sakka asks what binds beings who wish to be at peace, and the Buddha answers: "the fetters of jealousy and stinginess bind the gods, humans, titans, dragons, centaurs—and any of the other diverse creatures—so that, though they wish to be free of enmity, violence, hostility, and hate, they still have enmity, violence, hostility, and hate." This is related to jealousy and not identical to it. The translation renders the Pali as "jealousy", but the word is generally described as envy, and the fear of losing a loved one to a rival is not the sutta's topic.

Spinoza gives one of the clearest definitions of jealousy in philosophy. In the Ethics (Part III, Proposition 35): "If anyone conceives, that an object of his love joins itself to another with closer bonds of friendship than he himself has attained to, he will be affected with hatred towards the loved object and with envy towards his rival." In the note that follows he names it: "This hatred towards an object of love joined with envy is called Jealousy, which accordingly is nothing else but a wavering of the disposition arising from combined love and hatred, accompanied by the idea of some rival who is envied." Spinoza names jealousy directly, so no "related, not identical" caveat is needed. His account is one philosopher's definition of the emotion and not the view of philosophy as a whole, and it says nothing about what to do about it.

The sources read for this article do not give a full account of where jealousy comes from, so most of what follows is common explanation and not finding. Fear of losing something that matters. Jealousy needs something valued and a sense that it is at risk, whether or not the risk is real. Insecurity. A shaky sense of your own worth makes a rival's presence feel like proof that you will be left. Past hurt. Being betrayed or left before can make later ambiguity feel like a repeat. Attachment style. A 2025 study of 265 people in Chile and Spain measured digital jealousy and found "anxious attachment and closeness were significant predictors of jealousy, explaining nearly 30% of its variance". Sharpsteen and Kirkpatrick's 1997 paper is titled "Romantic jealousy and adult romantic attachment", which points the same way. Feeling loved. In the Chilean part of that sample, "feeling loved negatively predicted jealousy": people who felt more loved reported less. These are associations in questionnaire samples. They do not show that anxious attachment causes jealousy, and the study measured jealousy about online behaviour, not jealousy in general.

The Gita describes how a mind slides from attachment to anger. Gita 2.62: "While contemplating on the objects of the senses, one develops attachment to them. Attachment leads to desire, and from desire arises anger." Gita 2.63 follows the slide: "Anger leads to clouding of judgment, which results in bewilderment of memory. When memory is bewildered, the intellect gets destroyed; and when the intellect is destroyed, one is ruined." Gita 2.71 names what stands opposite: "That person, who gives up all material desires and lives free from a sense of greed, proprietorship, and egoism, attains perfect peace." This is related to jealousy and not identical to it. The verses are about attachment to the objects of the senses in general. Reading the sense of "mine" over a person as one case of that chain is ours.

The Katha Upanishad names seeing difference as the thing that keeps a person circling. Katha 2.1.10: "What is here (visible in the world), the same is there (invisible in Brahman); and what is there, the same is here. He who sees any difference here (between Brahman and the world), goes from death to death." And 2.1.11: "Even by the mind this (Brahman) is to be obtained, and then there is no difference whatsoever. He goes from death to death who sees any difference here." This is related to jealousy and not identical to it. The verses are about the difference between Brahman and the world, not between two people. Reading "difference" as the sense of a rival who is other than me is ours.

The Bible does not give a theory of where jealousy comes from, but two passages touch the roots. The first is fear. 1 John 4:18: "There is no fear in love, but perfect love casts out fear; for fear has to do with punishment, and whoever fears has not reached perfection in love." The second is the feeling of being overlooked. In the parable of the two sons, the elder son says to his father: "For all these years I have been working like a slave for you, and I have never disobeyed your command, yet you have never given me even a young goat so that I might celebrate with my friends" (Luke 15:29). This is related to jealousy and not identical to it. 1 John 4:18 is about love and fear of punishment, and the elder son's complaint is a grievance and not a fear of loss. Reading them as roots of jealousy is ours.

DN 21 traces jealousy back through a chain. Sakka asks about the source of jealousy and stinginess, and the Buddha says: "The liked and the disliked, lord of gods, are the source of jealousy and stinginess." Then, question by question: "Desire is the source of what is liked and disliked." "Thought is the source of desire." "Judgments driven by the proliferation of perceptions are the source of thoughts." The Sutta Nipata (4.11) gives a similar line: "Quarrels and disputes come from what we hold dear". Asked where what we hold dear comes from, it answers: "What we hold dear in the world spring from desire". This is related to jealousy and not identical to it. The suttas speak of jealousy, stinginess and quarrels together, and not of the fear of losing a person to a rival. Reading the chain as the roots of that fear is ours.

Epictetus puts the root in treating things that belong to others as our own. Enchiridion 1: "Remember, then, that if you suppose that things which are slavish by nature are also free, and that what belongs to others is your own, then you will be hindered." And in 14: "If you wish your children, and your wife, and your friends to live for ever, you are stupid; for you wish to be in control of things which you cannot, you wish for things that belong to others to be your own." Spinoza adds the other half. The lover will "endeavour, as far as he can, to imagine the loved object as most closely bound to him", and this endeavour is "checked by the image of the loved object in conjunction with the image of him whom the loved object has joined to itself" (Ethics III.35, proof). This is related to jealousy and not identical to it. Epictetus is speaking of things outside our control in general, and Spinoza of the structure of the emotion. Reading Epictetus's point as the root of jealousy is ours.

The research read here is small and mostly correlational, and it shows jealousy and relationship trouble travelling together. Checking and dissatisfaction. Elphinston and Noller studied undergraduates in romantic relationships and found that "Facebook intrusion was linked to relationship dissatisfaction, via jealous cognitions and surveillance behaviors". Jealous thoughts and checking sat on the path between heavy social-media use and unhappiness with the relationship. Control. De Sousa and colleagues studied 279 adolescent couples and found that "higher jealousy in both partners was associated with increased self- and partner-reported domination victimization". Controlling behaviour is a form of dating violence, and these researchers conclude that prevention should address "maladaptive expressions of jealousy". What this does not show. These are questionnaire associations in particular groups. They do not show that jealousy causes control or dissatisfaction, and they say nothing about every jealous person. Commonly described effects, not findings from these papers: arguments, pushing away the person you fear losing, poor sleep, and a mind that will not rest. If jealousy leads you to control a partner, or a partner's jealousy frightens or isolates you, a doctor, a therapist or a domestic abuse service can help.

The Gita traces where an unchecked mind ends. Gita 2.63: "Anger leads to clouding of judgment, which results in bewilderment of memory. When memory is bewildered, the intellect gets destroyed; and when the intellect is destroyed, one is ruined." The translator's commentary on 6.6 says of the enemies of the mind: "the demons sitting within our own mind have the ability to make us live in constant wretchedness". It lists "lust, anger, greed, envy, illusion" among them. By contrast, Gita 12.15 describes the one who is "not a source of annoyance to anyone and who in turn are not agitated by anyone". This is related to jealousy and not identical to it. The verses do not mention jealousy, and the commentary names envy and not jealousy. Reading the chain as the toll of jealousy is ours.

The Upanishads do not describe the effects of jealousy, but they describe grief as the lot of a person caught up in the world. The Mundaka Upanishad (3.1.2) says that a person "sits grieving, immersed, bewildered by his own impotence", and that when he sees the other, "then his grief passes away". Katha 2.1.10 gives the longer reach of the same blindness: "He who sees any difference here (between Brahman and the world), goes from death to death." This is related to jealousy and not identical to it. The passages are about grief and the cycle of death, and do not mention jealousy. Reading them as its toll is ours.

The Bible shows what jealousy does to people and to the places they live. It is hard to stand against. Proverbs 27:4: "Wrath is cruel, anger is overwhelming, but who is able to stand before jealousy?" It breaks things. Galatians 5:19-21 lists "enmities, strife, jealousy, anger, quarrels, dissensions, factions, envy" among "the works of the flesh". It wears the body. Proverbs 14:30: "A tranquil mind gives life to the flesh, but jealousy makes the bones rot." (See also Envy.) This is related to jealousy and not identical to it. The Galatians list sets jealousy beside envy and other vices, and Proverbs 14:30 is also used in the Envy articles, and which of the two the Hebrew word means was not checked. They name its effects and not the fear of losing a rival.

The Buddhist texts name sorrow, fear and conflict as what comes from holding things dear. Sorrow and fear. Dhp 212: "Sorrow springs from what we hold dear, fear springs from what we hold dear; one free from holding anything dear has no sorrow, let alone fear." Quarrels. Snp 4.11: "Quarrels and disputes come from what we hold dear, as do lamentation and sorrow, stinginess, conceit and arrogance." Enmity. DN 21: beings bound by jealousy and stinginess "still have enmity, violence, hostility, and hate", though they wish to be free of them. This is related to jealousy and not identical to it. The verses are about clinging in general, and do not describe a jealous person in particular. Reading them as the toll of jealousy is ours.

The philosophers describe the disturbance jealousy causes in the mind and in the relationship. Lament and disturbance. Epictetus, Enchiridion 1: if you take what belongs to others as your own, "You will lament, you will be disturbed, and you will find fault both with gods and men." A divided mind. Spinoza calls jealousy "a wavering of the disposition arising from combined love and hatred". Pain on both sides. Spinoza adds that "a jealous man is not greeted by his beloved with the same joyful countenance as before, and this also gives him pain as a lover". The jealous person's behaviour changes how they are met. This is related to jealousy and not identical to it. Epictetus is speaking of disturbance in general, and Spinoza describes the emotion as he understood it. Neither is a study of what jealousy does to a particular person or relationship.

The aim is to feel the fear without letting it run your behaviour. Name the fear under the jealousy. "I am afraid I will be left" is truer, and easier to work with, than "I know something is going on". Separate what you know from what you imagine. Write down what happened and what you have added to it. Say the feeling, not the accusation. "I felt left out tonight" invites a conversation; "who were you with?" invites a defence. Cut back the checking. Elphinston and Noller linked jealous thoughts and "surveillance behaviors" with relationship dissatisfaction. That is an association, but checking also keeps the worry alive, which is a common observation and not a finding here. Ask for reassurance, but not on a loop. A 2025 study found that in the Chilean sample "feeling loved negatively predicted jealousy", which suggests feeling secure matters. It was not a test of treatment, and asking again and again is not the same as feeling loved. Build your own footing. Friends, work and interests that do not depend on one person make a rival less of a threat. Do not use jealousy to control. Where it leads to isolating or dominating someone, De Sousa and colleagues point to addressing "maladaptive expressions of jealousy". Stop, and get help. Get help if it is constant. A doctor or therapist can help with jealousy that fills your days, and a domestic abuse service can help if you are the one who is afraid.

The Gita points to a loosening of possessiveness, and to goodwill toward others, held together by a steady mind. Loosen the sense of "mine". Gita 2.71: "That person, who gives up all material desires and lives free from a sense of greed, proprietorship, and egoism, attains perfect peace." Practise goodwill toward the rival too. Gita 12.13-14 describes the devotees who are "free from malice toward all living beings, who are friendly, and compassionate", and "free from attachment to possessions and egotism". Stay level in loss and gain. The same verses say "equipoised in happiness and distress". Make the mind a friend. Gita 6.5: "Elevate yourself through the power of your mind, and not degrade yourself, for the mind can be the friend and also the enemy of the self." This is related to jealousy and not identical to it. The verses are about detachment and goodwill in general, and nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist for constant jealousy, or for jealousy that leads to controlling someone. Taking "proprietorship" to mean the sense of owning a person is ours.

The Upanishads point to seeing the same Self in everyone, so that a rival is no longer wholly other. See beings in the Self. Isha 6: "And he who beholds all beings in the Self, and the Self in all beings, he never turns away from it." Look at the unity. Isha 7: "When to a man who understands, the Self has become all things, what sorrow, what trouble can there be to him who once beheld that unity?" Drop the sense of difference. Katha 2.1.11: "Even by the mind this (Brahman) is to be obtained, and then there is no difference whatsoever." Hold what you have lightly. Isha 1: "Do not covet the wealth of any man!" This is related to jealousy and not identical to it. The verses are about the Self and unity, and nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist for constant jealousy, or for jealousy that leads to controlling someone. Applying them to a rival is ours.

The Bible points to love that is secure enough not to grasp. Let love push out fear. 1 John 4:18: "There is no fear in love, but perfect love casts out fear." Practise the kind of love that is not envious. 1 Corinthians 13:4-5: "Love is patient; love is kind; love is not envious or boastful or arrogant or rude. It does not insist on its own way." Grow what the Spirit grows. Galatians 5:22-23: "the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, generosity, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control." Hear the reassurance. In the parable, the father says to the elder son: "Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours" (Luke 15:31). This is related to jealousy and not identical to it. These verses are about love, fear and the fruit of the Spirit in general, and nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist for constant jealousy, or for jealousy that leads to controlling someone.

The Buddhist texts point to loosening the clinging that jealousy grows from. See the chain. Dhp 213-216 trace sorrow and fear back through attachment, relishing, desire and craving. Dhp 215: "Sorrow springs from desire, fear springs from desire; one free from desire has no sorrow, let alone fear." Ask what a feeling grows. DN 21 says of happiness: "should you know of a happiness: 'When I cultivate this kind of happiness, unskillful qualities grow, and skillful qualities decline.' You should not cultivate that kind of happiness." The sutta says the same of sadness and equanimity. Applying the test to jealous thoughts is ours. Understand what the states depend on. Snp 4.11: "Knowing that these states are dependent, and knowing what they depend on, the inquiring sage, having understood, is freed, and enters no dispute." This is related to jealousy and not identical to it. The passages are about desire and clinging in general, and nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist for constant jealousy, or for jealousy that leads to controlling someone. The Dhammapada's counsel is read here as about clinging, which is a reading and not a claim about loving less.

Epictetus's advice is to know what kind of thing you hold, and to hold it as a loan. Remember what you are fond of. Enchiridion 3: "If you kiss your child, or your wife, say that you only kiss things which are human, and thus you will not be disturbed if either of them dies." Say "returned", not "lost". Enchiridion 11: "Never say of anything, 'I have lost it'; but, 'I have returned it.'" And: "While he gives it to you to possess, take care of it; but don't view it as your own, just as travelers view a hotel." Stop wishing for control that you do not have. Enchiridion 14: "you wish to be in control of things which you cannot". Work on what is yours. Enchiridion 14: "if you wish to have your desires undisappointed, this is in your own control." This is related to jealousy and not identical to it. Epictetus is speaking of loss and of what is outside our control, and nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist for constant jealousy. Other people are not things to be returned, and the point taken here is only that another person's choices and life are not ours to own, which is ours.

Note: This is an invented composite story, not a real case. It is built from patterns people commonly describe, so you can see how jealousy works and how people loosen its grip. Tomas's story Tomas's partner, Priya, moved to a new team. She came home talking about a colleague who had made her laugh. Tomas smiled, then spent the evening running the sentence over in his head. Within a week he was reading her messages when she was in the shower. He asked about her lunches. When she stopped answering, he said she was hiding something. Priya, who had hidden nothing, began to stay quiet. What helped: He named the fear. A friend asked what he was afraid of. "That she will find someone better and I will not see it coming." He sorted what he knew from what he imagined. He knew she had a new job and a colleague who was funny. The rest was a story. He said the feeling. "I have felt insecure since you changed teams. I do not think you have done anything. I wanted to tell you instead of checking." He stopped checking. The first fortnight was the hardest, and he went for a walk when the urge came. He noticed it was not lifting. After weeks of poor sleep and a mind that would not rest, he spoke to his doctor and was referred to a counsellor. The fear did not vanish. It got smaller, and it stopped giving the orders. What it shows: The jealousy was about a fear of loss, not about anything Priya did. Naming it and saying it aloud did what checking could not.

Two roads in one chapter The Gita has no story of jealousy, so this is a passage from Krishna's teaching and not a tale. In Chapter 2 Krishna describes a road down and a road back. The road down begins in attachment: "While contemplating on the objects of the senses, one develops attachment to them. Attachment leads to desire, and from desire arises anger" (2.62). The road back is described a few verses on: "But one who controls the mind, and is free from attachment and aversion, even while using the objects of the senses, attains the Grace of God" (2.64). Then: "By divine grace comes the peace in which all sorrows end" (2.65). Krishna gives a picture of that peace: "Just as the ocean remains undisturbed by the incessant flow of waters from rivers merging into it, likewise the sage who is unmoved despite the flow of desirable objects all around him attains peace, and not the person who strives to satisfy desires" (2.70). What it shows: Attachment is not the same as having things or loving people, and the Gita's point is that peace comes from not being driven by them. It is not about jealousy, and the link is ours: the fear of losing someone belongs to the road down.

The bees and the honey In the Chandogya Upanishad a father, Uddalaka, teaches his son Svetaketu in parables. The ninth section begins: "As the bees, my son, make honey by collecting the juices of distant trees, and reduce the juice into one form, And as these juices have no discrimination, so that they might say, I am the juice of this tree or that, in the same manner, my son, all these creatures, when they have become merged in the True (either in deep sleep or in death), know not that they are merged in the True." The next section gives a second picture, the rivers: "as those rivers, when they are in the sea, do not know, I am this or that river". After each, the father says: "It is the Self, and thou, O Svetaketu, art it." What it shows: The parable pictures separate things that are one in the end. It is not about jealousy, and the link is ours: jealousy depends on telling "mine" from "theirs", and the parable shows juices that cannot say whose tree they came from.

The elder son at the door In Luke 15 the younger son has come home and his father has held a feast. The elder son was in the field: "as he came and approached the house, he heard music and dancing." A slave tells him: "Your brother has come, and your father has killed the fatted calf because he has got him back safe and sound" (15:25-27). "Then he became angry and refused to go in. His father came out and began to plead with him" (15:28). The elder son answers with his record of service and a complaint: "when this son of yours came back, who has devoured your assets with prostitutes, you killed the fatted calf for him!" (15:30). The father replies: "Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours. But we had to celebrate and rejoice, because this brother of yours was dead and has come to life; he was lost and has been found" (15:31-32). What it shows: The elder son stands outside his own father's house because he thinks his place has been taken. The parable is about welcome and repentance and not about jealousy as such; it shows the father going out to him and telling him that all the father has is his. The parable ends there, and the text does not say whether he went in.

Sakka asks what binds the world In DN 21, Sakka, the king of the gods, comes to the Buddha with questions. The first is: "Good fellow, what fetters bind the gods, humans, titans, dragons, centaurs—and any of the other diverse creatures—so that, though they wish to be free of enmity, violence, hostility, and hate, they still have enmity, violence, hostility, and hate?" The Buddha answers: "Lord of gods, the fetters of jealousy and stinginess bind" them. Sakka asks where jealousy and stinginess come from, and the Buddha says: "The liked and the disliked, lord of gods, are the source of jealousy and stinginess. When the liked and the disliked exist there is jealousy and stinginess. When the liked and the disliked don't exist there is no jealousy and stinginess." Sakka replies to the first answer: "That's so true, Blessed One! That's so true, Holy One! Hearing the Buddha's answer, I've gone beyond doubt and got rid of indecision." What it shows: Even the king of the gods is asking how to be free of enmity. The sutta traces jealousy to likes and dislikes and then on to desire. It is about jealousy and stinginess in general and not about the fear of losing a person.

Epictetus and the ship In Enchiridion 7 Epictetus gives a picture. "Consider when, on a voyage, your ship is anchored; if you go on shore to get water you may along the way amuse yourself with picking up a shellfish, or an onion. However, your thoughts and continual attention ought to be bent towards the ship, waiting for the captain to call on board." Then he turns it to life: "So it is with life. If, instead of an onion or a shellfish, you are given a wife or child, that is fine. But if the captain calls, you must run to the ship, leaving them, and regarding none of them." His advice is to enjoy what you are given, and to keep your attention on the ship. What it shows: Epictetus asks us to hold even our dearest people as given and not owned, which takes away the thing a rival could steal. It is a hard saying and it is about loss, not about jealousy; the link is ours. It does not say to love less, and it says nothing about how to treat a partner.

Fear is the alarm that goes off at a threat, and anxiety is the same alarm sounding about a threat that may come. Fear is usually tied to something in front of you; anxiety tends to look ahead and can be vague ("what if...?"). Some fear and anxiety is normal and useful. It becomes a problem when it is out of proportion or will not switch off. The World Health Organization says: "Everyone can feel anxious sometimes, but people with anxiety disorders often experience fear and worry that is both intense and excessive." These feelings, it adds, "are difficult to control, cause significant distress and can last a long time if untreated". Of people with an anxiety disorder it says: "Usually they avoid the situations that make them anxious." It is common. The WHO estimates that "5.8% of the global population currently experience an anxiety disorder", and that in 2023 "470 million people in the world had an anxiety disorder, making anxiety disorders the most common of all mental disorders". Everyday signs, as people commonly describe them and not as findings from the WHO page: a racing heart before a talk, a mind that rehearses disasters, putting off a phone call, lying awake with "what if". Worry that loops on one subject overlaps with overthinking. Feeling anxious is not a failing, and an anxiety disorder is a health condition that can be treated. If your fear or anxiety is intense, constant or getting in the way of daily life, please talk to a doctor or therapist.

Hinduism has no single word in the Bhagavad Gita for anxiety as the modern lens describes it, but the Gita speaks of fear and of its absence. Gita 2.56: "One whose mind remains undisturbed amidst misery, who does not crave for pleasure, and who is free from attachment, fear, and anger, is called a sage of steady wisdom." Gita 16.1-3 begins its list of "saintly virtues of those endowed with a divine nature" with "fearlessness". And Gita 18.30 speaks of the intellect that understands "what is to be feared and what is not to be feared". This is related to fear and anxiety and not identical to them. The Gita is describing a steady mind and its qualities, and it does not describe anxiety as a condition. Reading these verses as speaking to it is ours.

The Upanishads do not name anxiety, and they speak of fear mostly by its absence. In the Katha Upanishad, the boy Nachiketas says of the world of heaven: "In the heaven-world there is no fear; thou art not there, O Death, and no one is afraid on account of old age" (1.1.12). Katha 2.1.12 describes the person who knows the Self: "The person (purusha), of the size of a thumb, stands in the middle of the Self (body ?), as lord of the past and the future, and henceforward fears no more." This is related to fear and anxiety and not identical to them. The passages are about death and knowledge of the Self, and do not describe anxiety as a condition. Reading them as speaking to it is ours.

The Bible does not hide fear and anxiety. Psalm 56:3-4: "when I am afraid, I put my trust in you. In God, whose word I praise, in God I trust; I am not afraid; what can flesh do to me?" Proverbs 12:25 names anxiety: "Anxiety weighs down the human heart, but a good word cheers it up." And Psalm 94:19: "When the cares of my heart are many, your consolations cheer my soul." This is related to fear and anxiety as the modern lens describes them, and not identical to them. The texts are prayers and proverbs about trust and care, and do not describe anxiety as a condition or tell anyone to stop feeling it. An anxious person is not asked to hide it.

The Buddhist texts treat fear as something that can be met and trained. Dhp 39 describes a person with a steady mind: "One whose mind is not festering, whose heart is undamaged, who's given up right and wrong, alert, has nothing to fear." In the Fear and Dread sutta (MN 4) the Buddha says that some people who go to remote places "summon unskillful fear and dread because of these defects in their conduct". Fear here is something the mind brings to the place. This is related to fear and anxiety and not identical to them. Dhp 39 describes the end of fear in an awakened person, and MN 4 describes fear in the wilderness; neither describes anxiety as a condition.

Aristotle gives a definition of fear. In the Rhetoric (2.5): "Fear may be defined as a pain or disturbance due to a mental picture of some destructive or painful evil in the future." In the Nicomachean Ethics (3.6) he says people "even define fear as expectation of evil", and that not all fear is wrong: "to fear some things is even right and noble, and it is base not to fear them". This fits the philosophical lens closely, since Aristotle's definition is of fear directly. It is a definition of fear in general and not of anxiety as a disorder, and it says nothing about what to do about it.

The WHO says that "Anxiety disorders, like other mental health conditions, result from a complex interaction of social, psychological and biological factors." It adds that "people who have lived through abuse, severe losses or other adverse experiences are more likely to develop one", and that anxiety disorders "are closely related to and affected by physical health". Craske and colleagues, writing about exposure therapy, say that "anxious individuals show deficits in the mechanisms believed to underlie exposure therapy, such as inhibitory learning". In plain terms, learning that a feared thing turns out to be safe may be harder for some anxious people. The abstract does not say this is what causes anxiety. Common explanations, not findings from these sources: A cautious alarm. Some people's threat alarm fires early and often. Avoidance. Steering clear of what scares you brings relief, which can teach the alarm that it was right. Uncertainty. Not knowing how something will turn out leaves room for the mind to fill in the worst. No single cause is established by these sources, and having anxiety is not a sign of weakness or of having done something wrong.

The Gita pairs fear with attachment. Gita 2.56 describes the sage as "free from attachment, fear, and anger", and Gita 4.10 speaks of those "free from attachment, fear, and anger, becoming fully absorbed in Me, and taking refuge in Me". Gita 18.30 adds judgement: the intellect in the mode of goodness understands "what is to be feared and what is not to be feared". Reading this as meaning that fear grows from mistaking what is to be feared is ours. The verses do not say that attachment causes fear. They list the two together, and the link between them is the reader's inference. This is related to fear and anxiety and not identical to them. The Gita is speaking of the steady mind in general, and not of an anxious one.

The Katha Upanishad puts fear of death at the centre of the human situation, and speaks to it. Katha 1.2.18: "The knowing (Self) is not born, it dies not; it sprang from nothing, nothing sprang from it. The Ancient is unborn, eternal, everlasting; he is not killed, though the body is killed." And 1.2.19: "If the killer thinks that he kills, if the killed thinks that he is killed, they do not understand; for this one does not kill, nor is that one killed." This is related to fear and anxiety and not identical to them. The verses are about the Self and death, and say nothing of anxiety or of where it comes from. Reading them as naming the fear of death as a root of fear is ours.

The Bible touches several roots of fear. Fear of other people. Proverbs 29:25: "The fear of others lays a snare, but one who trusts in the Lord is secure." Fear of punishment. 1 John 4:18: "There is no fear in love, but perfect love casts out fear; for fear has to do with punishment, and whoever fears has not reached perfection in love." A sense of being left alone. In the storm, the disciples wake Jesus with: "Teacher, do you not care that we are perishing?" (Mark 4:38). This is related to fear and anxiety and not identical to them. These texts speak of fear of others, of punishment and of danger, and not of anxiety as a condition. Reading them as roots of anxiety is ours, and 1 John 4:18 should not be read as saying that being afraid is a failing of love.

MN 4 names causes of unskillful fear in those who go to the wilderness: faults in conduct, in livelihood, and a lack of understanding. Each time the wording is the same: they "summon unskillful fear and dread because of the defects of witlessness and stupidity", or of their conduct or livelihood. The Dart (Snp 3.8) points to a deeper root: mortality. "Unforeseen and unknown is the extent of this mortal life— hard and short and bound to pain. There is no way that those born will not die." Dhp 212 links fear to what we hold dear: "fear springs from what we hold dear". This is related to fear and anxiety and not identical to them. MN 4 is about fear in the forest, Snp 3.8 about death, and Dhp 212 about attachment. Reading them together as roots of anxiety is ours.

The Stoics place the root of fear in how we judge things, and in imagining what has not happened. Epictetus, Enchiridion 5: "Men are disturbed, not by things, but by the principles and notions which they form concerning things." Seneca, Letters 13.4: "There are more things, Lucilius, likely to frighten us than there are to crush us; we suffer more often in imagination than in reality." And 13.8: "it is more often the case that we are troubled by our apprehensions". This is related to fear and anxiety and not identical to them. The Stoics are speaking of fear and judgement in general, and not of anxiety as a condition. They do not say that anxious people are imagining danger that is not there, and some dangers are real.

The WHO page describes what anxiety disorders do to daily life and health. Everyday life. "Anxiety disorders interfere with daily activities and can impair a person's family, social and school or working life." Other conditions. "Anxiety disorders increase the risk for depression and substance use disorders as well as the risk of suicidal thoughts and behaviours." Physical health. "Many of the impacts of anxiety (such as physical tension, nervous system hyperactivity or harmful use of alcohol) are also known risk factors for diseases such as cardiovascular disease." Getting help. Only "about 1 in 4 people in need (27.6%) receive any treatment", although "highly effective treatments for anxiety disorders exist". These describe anxiety disorders, not the ordinary worry everyone has. Commonly described effects, not findings from the WHO page: avoiding places and tasks, poor sleep, irritability and exhaustion from being on guard. If you are thinking of harming yourself, contact your local emergency services or a crisis line now. For anxiety that is intense or constant, a doctor or therapist can help.

At the start of the Gita, Arjuna shows what fear does to the body and mind. Gita 1.28: "my limbs are giving way and my mouth is drying up." Gita 1.29-31: "My whole body shudders; my hair is standing on end. My bow, the Gāṇḍīv, is slipping from my hand, and my skin is burning all over. My mind is in quandary and whirling in confusion; I am unable to hold myself steady any longer." This is related to fear and anxiety and not identical to them. Arjuna's distress comes from the sight of his kinsmen across the battlefield, and the text describes grief and confusion as well as fear. Reading it as showing the toll of fear and anxiety is ours.

The Upanishads do not describe the effects of fear. They describe grief and bewilderment, and what lifts them. The Mundaka Upanishad (3.1.2) says that a person "sits grieving, immersed, bewildered by his own impotence", and that when he sees the other, "then his grief passes away". Katha 1.2.20 says: "A man who is free from desires and free from grief, sees the majesty of the Self by the grace of the Creator." And 1.2.22: "The wise who knows the Self as bodiless within the bodies, as unchanging among changing things, as great and omnipresent, does never grieve." This is related to fear and anxiety and not identical to them. The passages are about grief and the Self, and do not mention fear except where it is said to end. Reading them as the toll of fear is ours.

The Bible shows fear and anxiety weighing on people. Weight on the heart. Proverbs 12:25: "Anxiety weighs down the human heart". Terror. When the disciples see Jesus walking on the sea: "they were terrified, saying, 'It is a ghost!' And they cried out in fear" (Matthew 14:26). Sinking. Peter steps onto the water, but "when he noticed the strong wind, he became frightened, and, beginning to sink, he cried out, 'Lord, save me!'" (Matthew 14:30). This is related to fear and anxiety and not identical to them. These are scenes of fear in danger, and a proverb about the heart, and not a description of anxiety as a condition. Reading them as its toll is ours.

The Buddhist texts describe fear as heavy and shared by everyone. Grief at death. Snp 3.8 shows people wailing as "mortals are led away one by one, like a cow to the slaughter". It says "the attentive do not grieve, for they understand the way of the world". Lament that does not help. The same sutta says: "For one whose path you do not know—not whence they came nor where they went—you lament in vain, seeing neither end." Sorrow and fear together. Dhp 212: "Sorrow springs from what we hold dear, fear springs from what we hold dear". This is related to fear and anxiety and not identical to them. The Dart is about death and grief, and Dhp 212 about attachment. They do not describe the toll of anxiety, and reading them as doing so is ours.

The philosophers describe what fear does to the mind. It sets us thinking. Aristotle, Rhetoric 2.5: "fear sets us thinking what can be done, which of course nobody does when things are hopeless". Fear, on his account, can prompt action. It runs ahead of events. Seneca, Letters 13.10: "It is likely that some troubles will befall us; but it is not a present fact. How often has the unexpected happened! How often has the expected never come to pass! And even though it is ordained to be, what does it avail to run out to meet your suffering?" It is more than the thing itself. Marcus Aurelius, Meditations 8.36: "neither the future nor the past pains thee, but only the present". This is related to fear and anxiety and not identical to them. These are reflections on fear in general, and none is a study of anxiety. Seneca's and Marcus's remarks do not claim that the future is never painful.

The WHO says plainly: "There are several effective treatments for anxiety disorders. People with symptoms of anxiety should seek care." What the sources read here say works: Talk therapy. "The psychological interventions with the most evidence for treating a range of anxiety disorders are those based on principles of cognitive-behavioural therapy. These include exposure therapy, during which people learn to face their fears." A review of meta-analyses found "the strongest support exists for CBT of anxiety disorders, somatoform disorders, bulimia, anger control problems, and general stress". Facing fears gradually. Craske and colleagues call exposure therapy "an effective approach for treating anxiety disorders", though "a substantial number of individuals fail to benefit or experience a return of fear after treatment". It works best with a therapist. Calming skills. "Learning stress management skills, such as relaxation skills and mindfulness skills, can help reduce symptoms of anxiety disorders." Exercise. "Exercise programmes can also be effective in preventing anxiety disorders in adults." Medicine is for a doctor to decide. The WHO says antidepressants "can also be useful in treating adults with anxiety disorders", and that benzodiazepines "are generally not recommended" for anxiety disorders. Common advice, not tied to a source here: name the feeling ("this is anxiety"), do the thing in small steps instead of avoiding it, and write down a worry and a next step so it is not only in your head. If you are thinking of harming yourself, contact your local emergency services or a crisis line now.

The Gita points to a steady mind that can stay level, and to taking refuge. Make the mind a friend. Gita 6.5: "Elevate yourself through the power of your mind, and not degrade yourself, for the mind can be the friend and also the enemy of the self." Stay undisturbed in misery. Gita 2.56 describes a sage "whose mind remains undisturbed amidst misery". Be like the ocean. Gita 2.70: "Just as the ocean remains undisturbed by the incessant flow of waters from rivers merging into it, likewise the sage who is unmoved despite the flow of desirable objects all around him attains peace". Take refuge. Gita 4.10 speaks of those "free from attachment, fear, and anger, becoming fully absorbed in Me, and taking refuge in Me". Hear the reassurance. Gita 11.49: "Be neither afraid nor bewildered on seeing this terrible form of Mine. Be free from fear and with a cheerful heart". This is related to fear and anxiety and not identical to them. These verses speak of steadiness and devotion in general, and nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist for intense or constant anxiety.

The Katha Upanishad gives the picture of a charioteer who holds the reins, and it points to a "fearless shore". Hold the reins. Katha 1.3.3: "Know the Self to be sitting in the chariot, the body to be the chariot, the intellect (buddhi) the charioteer, and the mind the reins." Do not let the horses run. Katha 1.3.5-6: "He who has no understanding and whose mind (the reins) is never firmly held, his senses (horses) are unmanageable, like vicious horses of a charioteer. But he who has understanding and whose mind is always firmly held, his senses are under control, like good horses of a charioteer." Aim for the fearless shore. Katha 1.3.2 speaks of "the highest, imperishable Brahman for those who wish to cross over to the fearless shore". This is related to fear and anxiety and not identical to them. The passages are about self-mastery and the Self, and nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist for intense or constant anxiety. Reading the charioteer as a picture of steadying an anxious mind is ours.

The Bible's answer to fear is presence and courage, not being told to feel nothing. Remember you are not alone. Psalm 23:4: "Even though I walk through the darkest valley, I fear no evil, for you are with me; your rod and your staff, they comfort me." Be courageous with company. Joshua 1:9: "Be strong and courageous; do not be frightened or dismayed, for the Lord your God is with you wherever you go." Remember the spirit you were given. 2 Timothy 1:7: "for God did not give us a spirit of cowardice but rather a spirit of power and of love and of self-discipline." Let love push out fear. 1 John 4:18: "There is no fear in love, but perfect love casts out fear". Take your cares somewhere. Psalm 94:19: "When the cares of my heart are many, your consolations cheer my soul." (See also Philippians 4:6-7 in Overthinking.) This is related to fear and anxiety and not identical to them. These verses are about trust and courage in general, and nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist for intense or constant anxiety. They are not a command to stop feeling afraid.

The Buddhist texts teach staying with the present and facing fear directly. Do not run back or ahead. MN 131: "Don't run back to the past, don't anticipate the future. What's past is left behind, the future has not arrived; and any present phenomenon you clearly discern in every case." Meet fear as it comes. In MN 4 the Buddha says: "Why don't I get rid of that fear and dread just as it comes, while remaining just as I am?" (see the story). Fortify the mind. Dhp 40: "fortifying the mind like a citadel". Be alert. Dhp 39: "alert, has nothing to fear". This is related to fear and anxiety and not identical to them. The passages are about meditation and awakening, and nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist for intense or constant anxiety. Reading MN 131 as speaking to anxiety about the future is ours.

The Stoics' advice is to test the fear, to stay with the present, and to act on what is yours. Test the proofs. Seneca, Letters 13.8: "consider whether your proofs of future trouble are sure." And: "We do not put to the test those things which cause our fear; we do not examine into them". Do not meet trouble early. Seneca, 13.10: "what does it avail to run out to meet your suffering? You will suffer soon enough, when it arrives". Take one thing at a time. Marcus Aurelius, Meditations 8.36: "Do not disturb thyself by thinking of the whole of thy life. Let not thy thoughts at once embrace all the various troubles which thou mayest expect to befall thee". Ask what is unbearable. Marcus, 8.36: "on every occasion ask thyself, What is there in this which is intolerable and past bearing?" This is related to fear and anxiety and not identical to them. These are practices for fear in general, and nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist for intense or constant anxiety.

Note: This is an invented composite story, not a real case. It is built from patterns people commonly describe, so you can see how anxiety works and how people loosen its grip. Amira's story Amira was asked to present her team's results at a meeting of forty people. Her stomach dropped. Over the next week she rehearsed the ways it could go wrong: her voice shaking, a question she could not answer, everyone's faces. She considered telling her manager she was ill. Each time she thought of backing out she felt a wave of relief, and then, an hour later, a heavier dread about the next time. What helped: She named it. "This is anxiety. It is loud, and it is not a forecast." She stopped treating avoidance as the answer. The relief from backing out was short, and the dread came back bigger. She went in small steps. She presented to two colleagues, then to her team of eight, before the big meeting. She slowed her breathing for a minute before she began, and kept one page of notes. She noticed it was not lifting. Weeks of poor sleep and dread before any meeting led her to her doctor, who referred her to a therapist. The anxiety did not vanish. It got smaller, and she presented. What it shows: Avoiding the thing taught her alarm that it was right. Small, planned steps, and help when the dread would not ease, did more than waiting to feel ready.

Arjuna sees the universal form In Chapter 11 of the Gita, Arjuna asks to see Krishna's universal form, and Krishna grants it. Arjuna is overwhelmed: "Having seen Your universal form that I had never seen before, I feel great joy. And yet, my mind trembles with fear. Please have mercy on me and again show me Your pleasing form" (11.45). He asks to see Krishna in the form he knows: "I wish to see You in Your four-armed form, carrying the mace and disc, and wearing the crown" (11.46). Krishna answers: "Be neither afraid nor bewildered on seeing this terrible form of Mine. Be free from fear and with a cheerful heart, behold Me once again in My personal form" (11.49). Sanjay then reports that Krishna "further consoled the frightened Arjun by assuming His gentle (two-armed) form" (11.50). What it shows: Fear and joy arrive together in Arjuna, and the answer is reassurance and a form he can bear. The chapter is about the vision of the cosmic form and not about anxiety as such; the story is read here for how fear is met.

Nachiketas goes to Death The Katha Upanishad opens with a boy and a rash word. Nachiketas's father is giving away his possessions at a sacrifice. The boy asks: "Dear father, to whom wilt thou give me?" He says it a second and a third time. "Then the father replied (angrily): 'I shall give thee unto Death'" (1.1.4). Nachiketas goes. He says: "I go as the first, at the head of many (who have still to die); I go in the midst of many (who are now dying)" (1.1.5). And: "A mortal ripens like corn, like corn he springs up again" (1.1.6). Yama, Death, is away for three nights, and the boy is not received. When Yama returns he offers three boons. Nachiketas asks first that his father be "pacified, kind, and free from anger towards me" (1.1.10), and then speaks of the heaven-world: "there is no fear" (1.1.12). What it shows: The boy faces what most people fear, and does not run from it. He asks for his father's peace before anything for himself. The story is about death and knowledge, and not about anxiety; its link to fear is ours.

Peter on the water In Matthew 14 the disciples are in a boat "battered by the waves", with the wind against them. Jesus comes toward them walking on the sea. They are terrified and think he is a ghost, and he says: "Take heart, it is I; do not be afraid" (14:24-27). Peter answers: "Lord, if it is you, command me to come to you on the water." Jesus says, "Come." Peter gets out of the boat and walks toward Jesus. "But when he noticed the strong wind, he became frightened, and, beginning to sink, he cried out, 'Lord, save me!'" (14:28-30). "Jesus immediately reached out his hand and caught him, saying to him, 'You of little faith, why did you doubt?'" (14:31). When they got into the boat, the wind ceased. What it shows: Peter walks while he is looking at Jesus, and sinks when he notices the wind, and in both cases the help is a hand held out at once. The story is about faith and not about anxiety as a condition. It does not blame him for being afraid; it shows fear arriving and a hand reaching out.

The Buddha waits for fear In MN 4 the Buddha tells a brahmin how he faced fear and dread in remote forest lodgings before his awakening. He recalls: "As I was staying there a deer came by, or a peacock snapped a twig, or the wind rustled the leaves. Then I thought, 'Is this that fear and dread coming?'" He then reasons: "Why do I always meditate expecting that fear to come? Why don't I get rid of that fear and dread just as it comes, while remaining just as I am?" So he does. "Then that fear and dread came upon me as I was walking. I didn't stand still or sit down or lie down until I had got rid of that fear and dread while walking." He does the same standing, sitting and lying down. What it shows: The Buddha does not wait for fear in a safe posture, and he does not run from it; he faces it where he is. The sutta is about fear in the wilderness and not about anxiety as a condition. It shows what facing fear can look like, and it is not advice to do this alone.

Socrates on the fear of death In Plato's Apology, Socrates is on trial for his life. He tells the jury he will not abandon his post because of fear: "if I who, when I was ordered by the generals whom you chose to command me at Potidaea and Amphipolis and Delium, remained where they placed me, like any other man, facing death; if, I say, now... I were to desert my post through fear of death, or any other fear; that would indeed be strange". Then he questions the fear itself: "For this fear of death is indeed the pretence of wisdom, and not real wisdom, being the appearance of knowing the unknown; since no one knows whether death, which they in their fear apprehend to be the greatest evil, may not be the greatest good." What it shows: Socrates does not say there is nothing to fear. He says that the fear of death claims to know what no one knows. The speech is about death and about duty and not about anxiety as a condition; its link to fear in general is that he questions what the fear assumes.

Fear of failure is dread of not succeeding, and of what that would cost you or say about you. Fear of success is less obvious: it means associating success with negative consequences, such as more pressure, envy or change. Both can lead to the same place, which is staying out of the attempt. Researchers have studied both. Kosakowska-Berezecka and colleagues asked students to complete scales measuring "their associations with success (fear of success) and tendency for self-promotion", and note that avoiding self-promotion "is also potentially related to associating success with negative consequences". Fear of failure is not only harmful. Boileau and colleagues developed a scale because existing measures "typically overlook" its motivational role "in favor of its negative effects". Teevan and McGhee's 1972 paper, "Childhood development of fear of failure motivation", is an early study of how it forms. Everyday signs, as people commonly describe them and not as findings from these papers: putting off an application, starting many things and finishing few, turning down the promotion, or undermining your own work the night before it is due. See also perfectionism and procrastination. This is not a diagnosis. If the fear comes with constant anxiety or low mood, a doctor or therapist can help.

Hinduism has no single word in the Bhagavad Gita for fear of failure or of success, but the Gita speaks of treating them alike. Gita 2.38: "Fight for the sake of duty, treating alike happiness and distress, loss and gain, victory and defeat." Gita 4.22 describes the person "content with whatever gain comes of its own accord, and free from envy", who is "equipoised in success and failure" and so "not bound by their actions, even while performing all kinds of activities". This is related to fear of failure and success and not identical to it. The Gita is describing equanimity toward results, and it does not describe the dread of the attempt. Reading it as speaking to that dread is ours.

The Upanishads do not name fear of failure or of success, and the closest they come is the idea of acting without clinging to the result. Isha Upanishad 2: "Though a man may wish to live a hundred years, performing works, it will be thus with him; but not in any other way: work will thus not cling to a man." The verse follows the instruction to give up the sense of ownership (Isha 1) and then to act: work does not cling to the one who acts in this way. This is related to fear of failure and success and not identical to it. The verse is about action and non-attachment, and does not describe fear of the attempt. Reading it as speaking to that fear is ours.

The Bible does not name fear of failure, but it speaks of falling and rising. Proverbs 24:16: "for though they fall seven times, they will rise again, but the wicked are overthrown by calamity." And Paul writes of weakness: "My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness" (2 Corinthians 12:9). This is related to fear of failure and success and not identical to it. The verses speak of falling and of weakness, and not of the dread that stops a person trying. Reading them as speaking to that dread is ours.

The Buddhist texts do not name fear of failure, but they name the pairs that success and failure belong to. AN 8.6: "the eight worldly conditions revolve around the world, and the world revolves around the eight worldly conditions. What eight? Gain and loss, fame and disgrace, blame and praise, pleasure and pain." The sutta says everyone meets them: "An unlearned ordinary person encounters gain and loss, fame and disgrace, blame and praise, and pleasure and pain. And so does a learned noble disciple." This is related to fear of failure and success and not identical to it. The sutta is about how we meet gain and loss, praise and blame, and not about dread of the attempt. Reading success and failure as gain and loss is ours.

Aristotle names a version of fear of success: claiming less than you deserve. In the Nicomachean Ethics (4.3): "The man who thinks himself worthy of worthy of less than he is really worthy of is unduly humble, whether his deserts be great or moderate". He adds: "And the man whose deserts are great would seem most unduly humble; for what would he have done if they had been less?" This is related to fear of failure and success and not identical to it. Aristotle is speaking of honour and of rating oneself rightly, and not of fear. Reading undue humility as one face of fear of success is ours.

The sources read for this article touch two possible roots, and neither is a full account. A controlling environment. Moreno-Murcia and colleagues studied 340 athletes and found "a significant and positive relationship between coaches' controlling style and athletes' fear of failure whereas coach autonomy support was associated with reduced fear of failure". Hu and colleagues, with 252 athletes, describe a controlling coaching style as "a key predictor of athletes' fear of failure". These are questionnaire associations in athletes and do not show cause. Expecting success to cost something. Kosakowska-Berezecka and colleagues found that, among university students, "in comparison to men, women expect lower salaries in the future, anticipate lower test performance and associate success with more negative consequences". Among younger pupils "girls and boys in high school do not differ with regard to fear of success". The authors' model suggests that women "insufficiently self-promote because they fear backlash for behavior which is incongruent with traditional gender roles". Common explanations, not findings from these papers: shame after an earlier failure, praise that depends on results, and a belief that your worth is measured by what you achieve.

The Gita places the root in being tied to results. Gita 2.47: "You have a right to perform your prescribed duties, but you are not entitled to the fruits of your actions. Never consider yourself to be the cause of the results of your activities, nor be attached to inaction." Gita 2.49 goes further: "discard reward-seeking actions that are certainly inferior to works performed with the intellect established in divine knowledge. Miserly are those who seek to enjoy the fruits of their works." This is related to fear of failure and success and not identical to it. The Gita is speaking of attachment to the fruits of action in general. Reading that attachment as the root of the fear of failing, or of succeeding, is ours.

The Katha Upanishad separates the good from the pleasant. Death says to Nachiketas (1.2.1): "The good is one thing, the pleasant another; these two, having different objects, chain a man." And (1.2.2): "The good and the pleasant approach man: the wise goes round about them and distinguishes them. Yea, the wise prefers the good to the pleasant, but the fool chooses the pleasant through greed and avarice." This is related to fear of failure and success and not identical to it. The passage is about choosing between the good and the pleasant, and not about fear. Reading the pull toward the safe and comfortable as one form of "the pleasant" is ours.

In the parable of the talents the servant who hid his money gives a reason. Matthew 25:24-25: "Master, I knew that you were a harsh man, reaping where you did not sow and gathering where you did not scatter, so I was afraid, and I went and hid your talent in the ground. Here you have what is yours." His fear rests on a picture of the one he serves, as harsh and sure to punish a loss. The master's reply begins: "You knew, did you, that I reap where I did not sow and gather where I did not scatter?" (25:26). This is related to fear of failure and success and not identical to it. The parable is about stewardship, and the servant's fear is of his master. Reading it as a picture of how fear of failure grows is ours, and the master's picture of himself may differ from the servant's.

AN 8.6 places the root in how the unlearned person meets gain and loss. They do not reflect: "'I've encountered this gain. It's impermanent, suffering, and perishable.' They don't truly understand it." And so they take sides: "They favor gain and oppose loss. They favor fame and oppose disgrace. They favor praise and oppose blame. They favor pleasure and oppose pain." This is related to fear of failure and success and not identical to it. The sutta is about favouring and opposing in general. Reading the opposing of loss and disgrace as the root of fear of failure is ours.

Epictetus puts the root in tying our worth to things we do not control. Enchiridion 1: "Things in our control are opinion, pursuit, desire, aversion, and, in a word, whatever are our own actions. Things not in our control are body, property, reputation, command, and, in one word, whatever are not our own actions." And in 19, on how people look to us: "When, therefore, you see anyone eminent in honors, or power, or in high esteem on any other account, take heed not to be hurried away with the appearance, and to pronounce him happy". This is related to fear of failure and success and not identical to it. Epictetus is speaking of what is and is not up to us, and he does not describe fear of the attempt. Reading reputation as the thing that fear of failure protects is ours.

The research read here is small, mostly in athletes and students, and correlational. Burnout. Yıldırım and colleagues studied 335 young athletes and found that "fear of failure had significant predictive effects on resilience, extrinsic motivation, and burnout". Resilience and extrinsic motivation "partially mediated" the link, and the authors suggest that the harm "can be mitigated by cultivating resilience and hindering extrinsic motivation". Lower expectations. In Kosakowska-Berezecka and colleagues' student sample, "Both tendency for self-promotion and fear of success are related to anticipation of success in test performance and expectations concerning future earnings". Not only harm. Boileau and colleagues argue that fear of failure also has "positive influences on goal pursuit and achievement". These are self-reported questionnaires in particular groups. They do not show that the fear causes burnout or lower expectations. Commonly described effects, not findings from these papers: avoiding chances, self-sabotage, putting things off, and relief that is followed by regret. If the fear comes with constant anxiety or low mood, a doctor or therapist can help.

The Gita shows what follows when a person stops. Arjuna, facing the battle, says "Govind, I shall not fight," and "became silent" (2.9). Gita 18.8 names a related pattern: "To give up prescribed duties because they are troublesome or cause bodily discomfort is renunciation in the mode of passion. Such renunciation is never beneficial or elevating." This is related to fear of failure and success and not identical to it. Arjuna's refusal comes from grief at the sight of his kinsmen, and 18.8 names trouble and discomfort and does not mention fear. Reading them as the effect of fear of failure is ours.

The Katha Upanishad says what choosing the pleasant costs. Katha 1.2.1: "It is well with him who clings to the good; he who chooses the pleasant, misses his end." And 1.2.4: "Wide apart and leading to different points are these two, ignorance, and what is known as wisdom." This is related to fear of failure and success and not identical to it. The verses speak of the end of human life and the two roads to it, and do not mention fear, avoidance or achievement. Reading them as the effect of staying with the safe choice is ours.

The parable of the talents shows what the fear costs. The two servants who traded with their money are told: "Well done, good and trustworthy slave; you have been trustworthy in a few things; I will put you in charge of many things; enter into the joy of your master" (Matthew 25:21, 23). The servant who buried his talent returns it unchanged, and the master says: "So take the talent from him, and give it to the one with the ten talents" (25:28). This is related to fear of failure and success and not identical to it. The parable's judgement on the third servant is severe, and it should not be read as a threat to anyone who is afraid. It shows a talent that gained nothing because it was hidden, and that reading is ours.
