This is related to resentment and not identical to it. The verses are about forgiveness and impartiality in general, and nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist for serious hurt. They are not a call to stay near someone who harms you.

The Upanishads point to seeing the same Self in everyone, and to the end of difference. See beings in the Self. Isha 6: "And he who beholds all beings in the Self, and the Self in all beings, he never turns away from it." Look at the unity. Isha 7: "When to a man who understands, the Self has become all things, what sorrow, what trouble can there be to him who once beheld that unity?" Drop the sense of difference. Katha 2.1.11: "Even by the mind this (Brahman) is to be obtained, and then there is no difference whatsoever." This is related to resentment and not identical to it. These verses are about the Self and unity, and nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist for serious hurt. They are not a call to stay near someone who harms you.

The Bible's counsel is to deal with anger quickly, to forgive, and to leave vengeance alone. Do not let it settle. Ephesians 4:26: "do not let the sun go down on your anger". Put it away and forgive. Ephesians 4:31-32: "Be kind to one another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, as God in Christ has forgiven you." Bear with each other. Colossians 3:13: "Bear with one another and, if anyone has a complaint against another, forgive each other". Leave vengeance. Romans 12:19: "Beloved, never avenge yourselves, but leave room for the wrath of God". And 12:21: "Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good." Keep forgiving. Peter asks how often to forgive, "As many as seven times?" and Jesus answers: "Not seven times, but, I tell you, seventy-seven times" (Matthew 18:21-22). This is related to resentment and not identical to it. These verses are about forgiveness in general, and nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist for serious hurt. Romans 12:18 adds "so far as it depends on you, live peaceably with all", and none of these verses asks anyone to stay in danger.

The Buddhist texts teach answering hatred with its opposite, five ways of getting rid of resentment, and a heart of love without secret hate. Answer hatred with love. Dhp 5: "For never is hatred laid to rest by hate, it's laid to rest by love: this is an ancient teaching." Use the five ways. AN 5.161: "You should develop love for an individual you resent." Then compassion, equanimity, "disregard an individual you resent, paying no attention to them", and "focus on the ownership of deeds regarding that individual". Train the heart. MN 21: "'My mind will not degenerate. I will blurt out no bad words. I will remain full of sympathy, with a heart of love and no secret hate.'" This is related to resentment and not identical to it. These passages are about hatred and resentment in general, and nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist for serious hurt. "Disregard" in AN 5.161 is a method, and none of the passages asks anyone to stay near someone who harms them.

The Stoics' advice is to read the other person generously, to pick the right handle, and not to become like the wrongdoer. Read the motive. Epictetus, Enchiridion 42: "if he judges from a wrong appearance, he is the person hurt, since he too is the person deceived." So "you will meekly bear a person who reviles you, for you will say upon every occasion, 'It seemed so to him.'" Pick the handle. Enchiridion 43: "Everything has two handles, the one by which it may be carried, the other by which it cannot. If your brother acts unjustly, don't lay hold on the action by the handle of his injustice, for by that it cannot be carried; but by the opposite, that he is your brother". Do not copy the wrong. Marcus Aurelius, Meditations 6: "The best way of avenging thyself is not to become like the wrong doer." This is related to resentment and not identical to it. These are practices for how we meet harm in general, and nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist for serious hurt. They do not say that a wrong did not happen or ask anyone to stay near someone who harms them.

Note: This is an invented composite story, not a real case. It is built from patterns people commonly describe, so you can see how resentment works and how people loosen its grip. Nadia's story When their mother was ill, Nadia did most of the caring. Her brother Karim visited twice, and at the funeral he said, in front of relatives, that she had "made a fuss". They stopped speaking. Two years later Nadia could still recite what he had said. She replayed it on her commute. When his name came up at a family dinner she went quiet and left early. What helped: She named the wrong. She wrote down what happened and what it had cost her, including the years of care nobody had thanked her for. She wrote a letter she did not send. It said all of it, and writing it let her see what she wanted: to be acknowledged. She decided what she would ask for. She told Karim, by message, that the funeral remark had hurt her and that she needed him to know how much the caring had been. She stopped waiting for the apology. He answered briefly and without saying sorry. She decided she would not keep the tally open. She separated forgiving from reconciling. She kept her distance from him, and stopped spending her commute rehearsing the quarrel. She noticed it was not lifting. The replaying eased but the grief behind it did not, and she spoke to her doctor, who referred her to a counsellor. The memory did not vanish. It stopped running her days. What it shows: Nadia did not have to pretend nothing had happened, and she did not have to get an apology. Saying what she needed and putting down the tally did what replaying could not.

Friend and foe alike The Gita has no story of a grudge, so this is a portrait from Krishna's teaching and not a tale. In Chapter 12 Krishna describes the person who is dear to him: "Those, who are alike to friend and foe, equipoised in honor and dishonor, cold and heat, joy and sorrow, and are free from all unfavorable association; those who take praise and reproach alike, who are given to silent contemplation, content with what comes their way, without attachment to the place of residence, whose intellect is firmly fixed in Me, and who are full of devotion to Me, such persons are very dear to Me" (12.18-19). What it shows: The portrait is of a person who does not keep a tally of honour and dishonour, friend and foe. It is about devotion and not about resentment; the link is ours, and the passage should not be read as asking anyone to ignore harm done to them.

Nachiketas and his father's anger In the Katha Upanishad, the boy Nachiketas asks his father, who is giving away his possessions, "Dear father, to whom wilt thou give me?" He asks a second and a third time. "Then the father replied (angrily): 'I shall give thee unto Death'" (1.1.4). Nachiketas goes to Death. When Death offers him three boons, the first thing he asks for is about his father: "that Gautama, my father, be pacified, kind, and free from anger towards me; and that he may know me and greet me, when I shall have been dismissed by thee" (1.1.10). Death answers: "Through my favour Auddâlaki Âru n i, thy father, will know thee, and be again towards thee as he was before. He shall sleep peacefully through the night, and free from anger, after having seen thee freed from the mouth of death" (1.1.11). What it shows: The first thing Nachiketas asks for is not for himself, but for his father's anger to end. The story is about death and knowledge and not about resentment; it shows a son who has every reason to be hurt, asking that his father be at peace with him.

Joseph and his brothers In Genesis 37 Joseph's brothers hated him "and could not speak peaceably to him" because their father loved him more. They sold him, and years later he became powerful in Egypt. After their father's death they are afraid: "What if Joseph still bears a grudge against us and pays us back in full for all the wrong that we did to him?" (50:15). They send word that their father asked him to forgive, and they come to him, saying, "We are here as your slaves" (50:16-18). "Joseph wept when they spoke to him." Joseph answers: "Do not be afraid! Am I in the place of God? Even though you intended to do harm to me, God intended it for good, in order to preserve a numerous people, as he is doing today. So have no fear; I myself will provide for you and your little ones" (50:19-21). What it shows: Joseph has the power to take revenge, and he does not. The story is about providence and a family and not a model for every situation; Joseph does not say that what they did was acceptable, and the text records what he says and not what it cost him.

Vedehikā and her maid In MN 21 the Buddha tells of a housewife in Sāvatthī, Vedehikā, who "had this good reputation: 'The housewife Vedehikā is gentle, placid, and calm.'" Her maid Kāḷī wonders: "does she actually have anger in her and just not show it? Or does she have no anger?" She decides to test her mistress. Kāḷī gets up late in the day, then later, then later still. Each time Vedehikā grows angrier, first scowling, then blurting out angry words, and the third time she "grabbed a door-pin and hit Kāḷī on the head, cracking it open." Kāḷī denounces her to the neighbours, and "Vedehikā got this bad reputation: 'The housewife Vedehikā is fierce, ill-tempered, and not calm at all.'" The Buddha applies it: "a mendicant may be the gentlest of the gentle, the most placid of the placid, the calmest of the calm, so long as they don't encounter any disagreeable criticism. But it's when they encounter disagreeable criticism that you'll know whether they're really gentle, placid, and calm." What it shows: Anger that is kept out of sight is still there, and it shows when it is tested. The sutta is about anger and criticism and not about resentment as such; the link is ours. The story includes violence, and it is not a model for how to treat anyone.

Marcus Aurelius meets the difficult people Marcus Aurelius is not telling a story in Meditations 2, but the opening is a scene of a morning. "Begin the morning by saying to thyself, I shall meet with the busy-body, the ungrateful, arrogant, deceitful, envious, unsocial. All these things happen to them by reason of their ignorance of what is good and evil." He then says what he will do about it. He knows "the nature of him who does wrong, that it is akin to me", so "I can neither be injured by any of them, for no one can fix on me what is ugly, nor can I be angry with my kinsman, nor hate him". He explains: "we are made for co-operation, like feet, like hands, like eyelids, like the rows of the upper and lower teeth." What it shows: Marcus prepares for the difficult people before they arrive, and decides in advance not to hate them. The passage is about the Stoic view of other people and not about resentment as such; the link is ours, and it is one philosopher's discipline, which does not say what to do when someone has really harmed you.

The need for validation is relying on other people's approval, praise or admiration to feel that you are worth something. "Ego" is used loosely here: the self you display and defend. Wanting to be liked is ordinary; the trouble starts when your sense of worth rises and falls with the response you get. Crocker and Park describe it as a goal: "in domains in which their self-worth is invested, people adopt the goal to validate their abilities and qualities, and hence their self-worth." They propose that "the importance of self-esteem lies more in how people strive for it rather than whether it is high or low." Neff and Vonk compared self-esteem with self-compassion in 2,187 people and found that self-compassion "predicted more stable feelings of self-worth than self-esteem and was less contingent on particular outcomes." Everyday signs, as people commonly describe them and not as findings from these papers: checking how a post is doing, rehearsing a remark that was not praised, shaping an opinion to the room, and a day that feels ruined by one cool reply. It overlaps with self-criticism and self-doubt. This is not a diagnosis. If the need for approval is wearing you down, a doctor or therapist can help.

Hinduism has no single word in the Bhagavad Gita for needing approval, but it names the ego-sense behind it. Gita 3.27: "All activities are carried out by the three modes of material nature. But in ignorance, the soul, deluded by false identification with the body, thinks of itself as the doer." The page's word-by-word gloss renders the compound for "deluded" as "those who are bewildered by the ego". A self that believes it is the doer will also want credit for what is done. This is related to the need for validation and not identical to it. The verse is about doership and false identification, and does not mention praise. The step from doer to wanting credit is ours.

The Upanishads do not speak of validation, and the nearest picture is the two birds. Mundaka 3.1.1: "Two birds, inseparable friends, cling to the same tree. One of them eats the sweet fruit, the other looks on without eating." Mundaka 3.1.2: "On the same tree man sits grieving, immersed, bewildered by his own impotence." This is related to the need for validation and not identical to it. The verses are about the individual self and the other lord, and do not mention approval. Reading the bird that eats as the self that feeds on praise is ours.

The Gospel of Matthew names the habit of doing good in order to be seen. Matthew 6:1: "Beware of practicing your righteousness before others in order to be seen by them, for then you have no reward from your Father in heaven." John 12:43 says of leaders who would not confess their belief: "they loved human glory more than the glory that comes from God." Galatians 1:10 asks: "Am I now seeking human approval or God's approval? Or am I trying to please people?" This is related to the need for validation and not identical to it. These verses are about righteousness and faith, and nothing here says that wanting any approval is wrong.

In Buddhist texts the nearest term is conceit, the sense of "I am". In SN 22.89 the mendicant Khemaka says he does not regard anything in the five grasping aggregates as self, and adds: "I'm not rid of the conceit 'I am'. But I don't regard anything as 'I am this'." AN 8.6 names the pull of approval among the eight worldly conditions: "Gain and loss, fame and disgrace, blame and praise, pleasure and pain." And of the ordinary person: "They favor praise and oppose blame." This is related to the need for validation and not identical to it. SN 22.89 is about a subtle sense of self and AN 8.6 is about eight conditions, so reading them as the same thing is ours.

Aristotle asks whether honour could be the good for a person and decides it is too thin. Nicomachean Ethics 1.5: "it seems too superficial to be what we are looking for, since it is thought to depend on those who bestow honour rather than on him who receives it, but the good we divine to be something proper to a man and not easily taken from him." For Aristotle the point is where the good lives: in us or in others' hands. If your worth depends on others' response, someone else holds it. This is related to the need for validation and not identical to it. Aristotle is asking about the highest good for a person, and does not describe a habit of seeking approval. Applying it so is ours.

The sources read here point to how approval can come to steer us more than to one origin. Worth that is staked on a domain. Crocker and Park argue that "in domains in which their self-worth is invested, people adopt the goal to validate their abilities and qualities, and hence their self-worth", and they consider "cultural roots of the pursuit of self-esteem". This is a review of research, and the abstract does not say what those roots are. Peer endorsement. Sherman and colleagues scanned adolescents while they viewed photos ostensibly posted to Instagram. They "were more likely to like photos depicted with many likes than photos with few likes", and viewing photos with many likes "was associated with greater activity in neural regions implicated in reward processing, social cognition, imitation, and attention." This was a laboratory simulation with adolescents, and it does not show that likes cause a need for approval. Common explanations, not findings from these papers: being praised for results more than for effort, growing up where love felt conditional, and social media that shows other people's response as a number.

The Gita's root is the ego that sets itself above others. In 16.13-15 Krishna describes people who think, "I am like God Himself, I am the enjoyer, I am perfect, I am powerful, and I am happy. I am wealthy and I have highly placed relatives. Who else is equal to me?" The verses end: "In this way, they are deluded by ignorance." Verse 16.4 lists "hypocrisy, arrogance, conceit, anger, harshness, and ignorance" among the qualities of a demoniac nature. This is related to the need for validation and not identical to it. The Gita describes pride and self-importance, and not a craving to be admired. Reading the first as a root of the second is ours.

In the Katha Upanishad Death names a root: choosing what pleases over what is good. Katha 1.2.1: "The good is one thing, the pleasant another; these two, having different objects, chain a man." And 1.2.5: "Fools dwelling in darkness, wise in their own conceit, and puffed up with vain knowledge, go round and round, staggering to and fro, like blind men led by the blind." This is related to the need for validation and not identical to it. The verses are about the good and the pleasant and about conceit in knowledge, and do not mention approval. Taking applause as one of the pleasant things is ours.

The Gospels name the roots as trust in oneself and love of human glory. Luke 18:9 introduces a parable "to some who trusted in themselves that they were righteous and regarded others with contempt". John 12:42-43: "Nevertheless many, even of the authorities, believed in him. But because of the Pharisees they did not confess it, for fear that they would be put out of the synagogue, for they loved human glory more than the glory that comes from God." This is related to the need for validation and not identical to it. The verses are about faith, self-righteousness and fear of expulsion, and the text does not describe what the authorities felt inside. Taking their fear of losing standing as a form of the need for approval is ours.

The Buddhist root is craving for status and the grasping of "I am". Dhp 74 describes the fool who wants to be the one in charge: "Let both layfolk and renunciants think the work was done by me alone. In anything at all that's to be done, let them fall under my sway alone." The verse ends: "So thinks the fool, their greed and pride only growing." AN 8.6 names what keeps the pull alive: "So gain and loss, fame and disgrace, blame and praise, and pleasure and pain occupy their mind." This is related to the need for validation and not identical to it. Dhp 74 is about wanting authority and recognition, and AN 8.6 is about eight worldly conditions. Reading both as roots of needing approval is ours.

Marcus Aurelius notices a strange imbalance. Meditations 12.4: "I have often wondered how it is that every man loves himself more than all the rest of men, but yet sets less value on his own opinion of himself than on the opinion of others." Aristotle gives a reason for seeking honour. Nicomachean Ethics 1.5: "men seem to pursue honour in order that they may be assured of their goodness". He adds that they seek to be honoured "by men of practical wisdom" and "among those who know them, and on the ground of their virtue". This is related to the need for validation and not identical to it. Marcus is describing a habit, and Aristotle is describing why people value honour. Putting them together as roots is ours, and this passage does not say whether wanting honour is a fault.

The research read here suggests costs when worth depends on approval, and its limits matter. Long-run costs. Crocker and Park write that "when people have self-validation goals, they react to threats in these domains in ways that undermine learning; relatedness; autonomy and self-regulation; and over time, mental and physical health." They conclude that "the short-term emotional benefits of pursuing self-esteem are often outweighed by long-term costs." This is a review that proposes an account, and it is not one experiment. Narcissism. In Neff and Vonk's first study (N = 2,187) "self-esteem (but not self-compassion) was positively associated with narcissism." This is a correlation in self-report data, and it does not show that high self-esteem leads to narcissism. Less stable worth. The same study found that self-compassion "predicted more stable feelings of self-worth than self-esteem and was less contingent on particular outcomes." Commonly described effects, not findings from these papers: saying yes to avoid disapproval, hiding opinions, being hurt by neutral feedback, and feeling empty after praise fades. If this is wearing you down, a doctor or therapist can help.

The Gita says what ego-driven action costs. Gita 17.18: "Austerity that is performed with ostentation for the sake of gaining honor, respect, and adoration is in the mode of passion. Its benefits are unstable and transitory." Krishna also warns Arjuna: "But if, due to pride, you do not listen to My advice, you will perish" (18.58). This is related to the need for validation and not identical to it. 17.18 is about one kind of austerity, and 18.58 is a warning to one person about pride. Reading them as the cost of seeking approval is ours.

The Upanishads name the cost of choosing the pleasant. Katha 1.2.1: "It is well with him who clings to the good; he who chooses the pleasant, misses his end." Mundaka 3.1.2 describes the grief: "On the same tree man sits grieving, immersed, bewildered by his own impotence." This is related to the need for validation and not identical to it. The verses are about the good and the pleasant and about the self and the other lord, and do not mention approval. Reading them as the toll of living on applause is ours.

The Gospels say that praise sought from people is all the reward there is. Matthew 6:2: "So whenever you give alms, do not sound a trumpet before you, as the hypocrites do in the synagogues and in the streets, so that they may be praised by others. Truly I tell you, they have received their reward." Matthew 23:5-7 describes the habit: "They do all their deeds to be seen by others... They love to have the place of honor at banquets and the best seats in the synagogues and to be greeted with respect in the marketplaces and to have people call them rabbi." And Luke 6:26: "Woe to you when all speak well of you, for that is how their ancestors treated the false prophets." This is related to the need for validation and not identical to it. These verses are about giving, religious leaders and prophets. Reading them as the cost of living on approval is ours.

The Buddhist texts say what chasing praise costs. AN 8.6: "Being so full of favoring and opposing, they're not freed from rebirth, old age, and death, from sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress." The phrase comes after "They favor praise and oppose blame." Dhp 75 puts the choice: "For the means to profit and the path to quenching are two quite different things. A mendicant disciple of the Buddha, understanding what this really means, would never delight in honors, but rather would foster seclusion." This is related to the need for validation and not identical to it. AN 8.6 is about eight worldly conditions and Dhp 75 is addressed to a mendicant. Reading them as the cost of needing approval is ours, and the texts are not describing everyday social life.

Epictetus says what it costs to live for others' approval. Enchiridion 23: "If you ever happen to turn your attention to externals, so as to wish to please anyone, be assured that you have ruined your scheme of life." Marcus Aurelius turns to the wish to be remembered. Meditations 4: "He who has a vehement desire for posthumous fame does not consider that every one of those who remember him will himself also die very soon". The passage goes on to ask what even immortal remembrance would be "to thee". This is related to the need for validation and not identical to it. Epictetus is writing about a philosopher's life and Marcus about fame after death. Reading them as the cost of needing approval is ours.

The research read here suggests that how you relate to yourself matters, and says little about method. The rest is common advice. Notice what you are checking. Count how often in a day you look for a reaction, such as a like, a reply or a nod. That is common advice. Ask whose approval you want. Crocker and Park say the pursuit works through "domains in which their self-worth is invested". Naming the domain, such as looks, work or being liked, shows where you are exposed. Naming it is our suggestion, not their method. Treat yourself the way you would a friend. Neff and Vonk found that self-compassion "predicted more stable feelings of self-worth than self-esteem and was less contingent on particular outcomes." It entails "treating oneself with kindness, recognizing one's shared humanity, and being mindful when considering negative aspects of oneself." This was a correlation, and the abstract does not test a fix. Do some things unseen. Write, practise or help without telling anyone. That is common advice. Keep some approval. Wanting to be valued is normal, and these papers do not say otherwise. Talk to someone. If your sense of worth feels wholly dependent on others, a doctor or therapist can help. That is common advice.

The Gita's counsel is to see through the doer and to hold praise and blame alike. See that you are not the sole doer. Gita 3.27: "All activities are carried out by the three modes of material nature. But in ignorance, the soul, deluded by false identification with the body, thinks of itself as the doer." Let go of egoism. Gita 2.71: "That person, who gives up all material desires and lives free from a sense of greed, proprietorship, and egoism, attains perfect peace." Meet honour and dishonour evenly. Gita 12.18-19 describes those "equipoised in honor and dishonor... who take praise and reproach alike". And 14.24-25: "who accept both blame and praise with equanimity; who remain the same in honor and dishonor". Cultivate humility. Gita 13.8 begins its list with "Humbleness; freedom from hypocrisy" and includes "absence of egotism". This is related to the need for validation and not identical to it. These verses are about doership, devotion and equanimity, and the Gita sets them within its own path. Reading them as a way through the need for approval is ours.

The Upanishads point to the witness and to the good over the pleasant. Choose the good over the pleasant. Katha 1.2.1: "It is well with him who clings to the good; he who chooses the pleasant, misses his end." Look to the other lord. Mundaka 3.1.2: when man sees "the other lord" "contented and knows his glory, then his grief passes away." Be unmoved by what is offered. In the Katha, Death offers Nachiketas long life, wealth and pleasures, and he answers: "These things last till tomorrow, O Death, for they wear out this vigour of all the senses" (1.1.26). And: "No man can be made happy by wealth" (1.1.27). This is related to the need for validation and not identical to it. These verses are about the Self, the good and the pleasant, and wealth. Reading them as a way through the need for approval is ours, and nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist.

The Bible's counsel is to do good quietly and to look to a different judge. Give in secret. Matthew 6:3-4: "But when you give alms, do not let your left hand know what your right hand is doing, so that your alms may be done in secret, and your Father who sees in secret will reward you." Pray unseen. Matthew 6:6: "But whenever you pray, go into your room and shut the door and pray to your Father who is in secret". Serve. Matthew 23:11-12: "The greatest among you will be your servant. All who exalt themselves will be humbled, and all who humble themselves will be exalted." Ask whom you are trying to please. Galatians 1:10: "Am I now seeking human approval or God's approval? Or am I trying to please people? If I were still pleasing people, I would not be a servant of Christ." This is related to the need for validation and not identical to it. These verses are about giving, prayer and service, and they do not tell anyone to avoid all company or praise. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist.

The Buddhist texts counsel seeing every condition as passing. Reflect on each condition. AN 8.6: "A learned noble disciple encounters gain. They reflect: 'I've encountered this gain. It's impermanent, suffering, and perishable.' They truly understand it." The same is said of praise and blame. Stop favouring and opposing. AN 8.6: "They don't favor praise or oppose blame." Remember nobody is all one thing. Dhp 228: "There never was, nor will be, nor is there today, someone who is wholly praised or wholly blamed." Be steady like a rock. Dhp 81: "As the wind cannot stir a solid mass of rock, so too blame and praise do not affect the wise." Watch the "I am" rise and fall. SN 22.89 says the lingering residue is removed as the noble disciple meditates "observing rise and fall in the five grasping aggregates." This is related to the need for validation and not identical to it. These passages are about the eight worldly conditions and the grasping aggregates, and they sit within the Buddhist path. Reading them as a way through the need for approval is ours, and nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist.

The philosophers' counsel is to judge by your own standard. Be your own audience first. Epictetus, Enchiridion 23: "Be contented, then, in everything with being a philosopher; and, if you wish to be thought so likewise by anyone, appear so to yourself, and it will suffice you." Accept being laughed at. Enchiridion 22: "prepare yourself from the very first to be laughed at, to be sneered by the multitude". Count dishonour fairly. Enchiridion 24: "if dishonor is an evil, you can no more be involved in any evil by the means of another, than be engaged in anything base." Ask whose opinion you weigh. Marcus Aurelius, Meditations 12: "So much more respect have we to what our neighbours shall think of us than to what we shall think of ourselves." This is related to the need for validation and not identical to it. These passages are written for a philosopher's life and are one school's discipline, not a rule for everyone. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist.

Note: This is an invented composite story, not a real case. It is built from patterns people commonly describe, so you can see how the need for validation works and how people loosen its grip. Tomas's story Tomas designs posters and posts one each week. For a year he checked how it was doing every few minutes. A good number lifted his whole day, and a quiet one sent him back to the file to change things that were fine. He noticed it when a friend said the poster looked great and he found himself waiting for more. What helped: He noticed what he was checking. He kept a tally for a week and was shocked by how long it ran. He named the domain. His worth was tied to being seen as talented, and he saw how exposed that made him. He did some work unseen. He made a poster each week that he did not post, only to see what he liked. He spoke to himself as to a friend. After a flat week he said what he would have said to a colleague, not what he would have said to himself. He kept some approval. He still liked a kind word. He stopped steering his week by the count. He asked for help. The urge to refresh stayed strong, and he talked to his doctor, who suggested a counsellor. The wish to be liked did not vanish. It stopped deciding his mood. What it shows: Tomas did not have to stop caring what anyone thought. Putting some of his worth somewhere that no count could reach did what checking never could.

Arjuna and the pride that decides The Gita has no tale of a person who needs praise, so this is a moment in the dialogue and not a story of validation. Near the end Krishna warns Arjuna: "If you always remember Me, by My grace you shall overcome all obstacles and difficulties. But if, due to pride, you do not listen to My advice, you will perish." And: "If, motivated by pride, you think, 'I shall not fight,' your decision will be in vain. Your own nature will compel you to fight" (18.58-59). He goes on: "that action which out of delusion you do not wish to do, you will be driven to do it by your own inclination, born of your own material nature" (18.60). Arjuna answers in 18.73: "O Infallible One, by Your grace my illusion has been dispelled, and I am situated in knowledge. I am now free from doubts, and I shall act according to Your instructions." What it shows: A pride that decides for you can be set down, and Arjuna says so himself. The passage is about pride, duty and fighting and not about approval; the link is ours, and Arjuna's reply is about the whole teaching and not only about pride.

Nachiketas and the things on offer In the Katha Upanishad the boy Nachiketas is offered all that people want. Death says: "Choose sons and grandsons who shall live a hundred years, herds of cattle, elephants, gold, and horses." He also says "choose wealth, and long life", and "I make thee the enjoyer of all desires" (1.1.23-24). Nachiketas does not take it: "These things last till tomorrow, O Death, for they wear out this vigour of all the senses. Even the whole of life is short. Keep thou thy horses, keep dance and song for thyself" (1.1.26). He adds: "No man can be made happy by wealth" (1.1.27), and returns to his question about what lies beyond death. What it shows: Nachiketas is not bought by what is offered. The story is about death and knowledge and not about validation; the link is ours, and the text names wealth, long life and pleasures and not praise.

The Pharisee and the tax collector In Luke 18 Jesus tells a parable "to some who trusted in themselves that they were righteous and regarded others with contempt". Two men go to the temple to pray. The Pharisee prays "standing by himself", thanking God "that I am not like other people: thieves, rogues, adulterers, or even like this tax collector. I fast twice a week; I give a tenth of all my income" (18:11-12). The tax collector, "standing far off, would not even lift up his eyes to heaven but was beating his breast and saying, 'God, be merciful to me, a sinner!'" (18:13). Jesus says: "I tell you, this man went down to his home justified rather than the other, for all who exalt themselves will be humbled, but all who humble themselves will be exalted" (18:14). What it shows: The Pharisee needs a lesser man beside him to feel good about himself. The parable is about prayer and justification and not about approval as such; the link is ours, and it does not say that every Pharisee was like this one.

Khemaka and the scent of the flower In SN 22.89 senior mendicants ask the sick Khemaka whether he regards anything in the five grasping aggregates as self. He answers: "I do not regard anything among these five grasping aggregates as self or as belonging to self." They say that makes him a perfected one, but he replies: "I am not a perfected one, with defilements ended. For when it comes to the five grasping aggregates I'm not rid of the conceit 'I am'. But I don't regard anything as 'I am this'." When they press him on what "I am" refers to, he says: "It's like the scent of a blue water lily, or a pink or white lotus. Would it be right to say that the scent belongs to the petals or the stalk or the pistil?" "No, reverend." "It would be right to say that the scent belongs to the flower." He tells them that a noble disciple, though they have given up the five lower fetters, "still have a lingering residue of the conceit 'I am'", and that it is removed as they meditate "observing rise and fall in the five grasping aggregates." At the end, "the minds of sixty senior mendicants and of Venerable Khemaka were freed from defilements by not grasping." What it shows: A subtle sense of "I am" can remain after the coarser views are gone, and it fades by watching. The sutta is about the sense of self and not about validation as such; the link is ours.

Epictetus and the laughing crowd Epictetus is not telling a story in Enchiridion 22, but he pictures a scene. "If you have an earnest desire of attaining to philosophy, prepare yourself from the very first to be laughed at, to be sneered by the multitude, to hear them say, 'He is returned to us a philosopher all at once,' and 'Whence this supercilious look?'" He says what to do: "don't have a supercilious look indeed; but keep steadily to those things which appear best to you as one appointed by God to this station." He adds: "if you adhere to the same point, those very persons who at first ridiculed will afterwards admire you. But if you are conquered by them, you will incur a double ridicule." What it shows: Epictetus says to expect mockery and to keep to what you think best, whatever the crowd says. The passage is about taking up philosophy and not about the need for approval; the link is ours, and it is one Stoic's advice.

Denial is refusing to accept a fact that is plain to others, and self-deception is believing what you would prefer to be true. Cognitive dissonance is the discomfort of holding two things that do not fit, such as "I am an honest person" and "I just did something dishonest", and the urge to explain it away. These are standard definitions and not taken from the papers below. Researchers have studied the last step. Egan, Santos and Bloom describe "decision rationalization": after a choice between two equally liked options, children and monkeys later treated the option they had not chosen as less valuable. Chance and colleagues ran four experiments on people who "go beyond merely explaining away their misconduct to actively deceiving themselves", and found that people who exploited chances to cheat on tests inferred "that their elevated performance is a sign of intelligence." Everyday signs, as people commonly describe them and not as findings from these papers: "it's not that bad", changing the subject when a worry comes up, finding a reason after the fact for something you already did, and being sure of a version of events that others do not recognise. It overlaps with overthinking, where a mind can rehearse reasons for hours. Denial is not a diagnosis, and it is not always a fault: people sometimes need time before they can face bad news. If it keeps you from facing a health problem, a harmful habit, or a danger to you or someone else, a doctor or therapist can help.

Hinduism has no single word in the Bhagavad Gita for denial, but it describes the self-deceiver. Gita 3.6: "Those who restrain the external organs of action, while continuing to dwell on sense objects in the mind, certainly delude themselves and are to be called hypocrites." And 18.32 describes an intellect "shrouded in darkness, imagining irreligion to be religion, and perceiving untruth to be the truth". This is related to denial and not identical to it. 3.6 is about restraint of the senses and 18.32 about a darkened intellect, and neither speaks of a refusal to face facts. Reading them as portraits of self-deception is ours.

The Upanishads describe the one who does not look past the visible. Katha 1.2.6: "The Hereafter never rises before the eyes of the careless child, deluded by the delusion of wealth. 'This is the world,' he thinks, 'there is no other;' — thus he falls again and again under my sway." This is related to denial and not identical to it. The verse is about the Hereafter and a child deluded by wealth, and does not describe the refusal of an uncomfortable fact. Reading it as a picture of closing the eyes is ours.

The Bible says plainly that we can deceive ourselves. 1 John 1:8: "If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us." Jeremiah 17:9: "The heart is devious above all else; it is perverse— who can understand it?" This is related to denial and not identical to it. 1 John 1:8 is about sin and Jeremiah about the heart, and neither describes a refusal to face every kind of fact. The wording of Jeremiah 17:9 differs in other translations, and the NRSVUE page was the only one read.

In Buddhist texts the closest idea is delusion and the perversions of view. Dhp 63: "The fool who thinks they're a fool is wise at least to that extent. But the true fool is said to be one who imagines that they are wise." AN 4.49 names four perversions of perception, thought and view: "Taking impermanence as permanence. Taking suffering as happiness. Taking not-self as self. Taking ugliness as beauty." This is related to denial and not identical to it. Dhp 63 is about thinking oneself wise, and AN 4.49 is about four mistaken views. Reading both as self-deception is ours.

Socrates describes meeting someone who is wrong about himself. Plato's Apology: "he was not really wise, although he was thought wise by many, and wiser still by himself". And: "for he knows nothing, and thinks that he knows. I neither know nor think that I know." This is related to denial and not identical to it. Socrates is speaking of false wisdom, and not of refusing to face facts. Reading it as a picture of self-deception is ours.

The sources read here offer accounts of why we do it, and they are still debated. Reducing discomfort. Egan and colleagues found "decision rationalization" in preschoolers and capuchin monkeys, and suggest that "the mechanisms underlying cognitive-dissonance reduction in human adults may have originated both developmentally and evolutionarily earlier than previously thought." The task was a choice between two stickers or two sweets. An evolutionary account. von Hippel and Trivers "argue that self-deception evolved to facilitate interpersonal deception by allowing people to avoid the cues to conscious deception that might reveal deceptive intent." They add that it "eliminates the costly cognitive load that is typically associated with deceiving". This is an argument, and the abstract is of a target article followed by commentary, so it does not show the account is settled. A benefit in the moment. Chance and colleagues found that "this short-term psychological benefit of self-deception" can come with longer-term costs. Common explanations, not findings from these papers: protecting a picture of oneself as good, avoiding a painful truth, fear of the consequences of admitting it, and the pull of what we hope is true.

The Gita's root is ignorance that covers knowledge. Gita 5.15: "The living entities are deluded because their inner knowledge is covered by ignorance." And 7.13: "Deluded by the three modes of Maya, people in this world are unable to know Me, the imperishable and eternal." This is related to denial and not identical to it. These verses are about ignorance and illusion in general, and do not mention looking away from a fact. Reading them as roots of self-deception is ours.

The Upanishads name conceit and the lure of wealth. Mundaka 1.2.8: "Fools dwelling in darkness, wise in their own conceit, and puffed up with vain knowledge, go round and round staggering to and fro, like blind men led by the blind." Katha 1.2.6 gives the cause of the child's blindness: "deluded by the delusion of wealth." This is related to denial and not identical to it. The verses are about conceit and wealth, and do not speak of avoiding an uncomfortable fact. Taking them as roots of self-deception is ours. Mundaka 1.2.8 repeats the words of Katha 1.2.5, which are used in Ego and validation.

The Bible's root is that we judge ourselves by our own eyes. Proverbs 16:2: "All one's ways may be pure in one's own eyes, but the Lord weighs the spirit." Galatians 6:3: "For if those who are nothing think they are something, they deceive themselves." This is related to denial and not identical to it. These verses are about self-assessment and about thinking too well of oneself, and do not speak of refusing to face a fact. Taking them as roots of self-deception is ours.

The Buddhist root is that we see others' faults more easily than our own. Dhp 252: "It's easy to see the faults of others, hard to see one's own. For the faults of others are tossed high like hay, while one's own are hidden, as a cheat hides a bad hand." AN 4.49 puts the root in a deeper error: "Yoked by Māra's yoke, these people find no sanctuary from the yoke." This is related to denial and not identical to it. Dhp 252 is about noticing faults in oneself and others, and AN 4.49 is about wrong view. Reading them as roots of self-deception is ours.

Seneca says that some people turn their faults into virtues. Letters 28: "Some boast of their faults. Do you think that the man has any thought of mending his ways who counts over his vices as if they were virtues?" Socrates describes how the politician was "wiser still by himself" than others thought him (Plato, Apology). This is related to denial and not identical to it. Seneca is writing about boasting of faults and Plato about false wisdom. Reading them as roots of self-deception is ours.

The research read here suggests that self-deception can feel good now and cost later, and its limits matter. A cost over time. Chance and colleagues found that people who cheated on tests inferred "that their elevated performance is a sign of intelligence". When predicting future performance, "participants expect to perform equally well-a lack of awareness that persists even when these inflated expectations prove costly." Not foreseen. The authors write that "although people expect to cheat, they do not foresee self-deception". What this does not show. These were laboratory experiments on cheating at tests. They do not show what denial does about illness, grief or a relationship. Commonly described effects, not findings from these papers: problems that grow because they are left alone, repeated mistakes, strained trust with people who see what you do not, and a nagging unease under the calm. If denial is keeping you from facing a health problem, a harmful habit or a danger, a doctor or therapist can help.

The Gita says what a clouded mind leads to. Gita 2.63: "Anger leads to clouding of judgment, which results in bewilderment of memory. When memory is bewildered, the intellect gets destroyed; and when the intellect is destroyed, one is ruined." And 18.32 describes the intellect that perceives "untruth to be the truth" as being "of the nature of ignorance". This is related to denial and not identical to it. 2.63 is about the chain that starts with anger, and 18.32 about a darkened intellect. Reading them as the cost of self-deception is ours. The same verse is used in Resentment.

The Upanishads say what the deluded face. Katha 1.2.6: "'This is the world,' he thinks, 'there is no other;' — thus he falls again and again under my sway." Mundaka 1.2.8 describes the going round: "go round and round staggering to and fro, like blind men led by the blind." This is related to denial and not identical to it. The verses are about the Hereafter and about conceit, and do not mention a refusal to face a fact. Reading them as the cost of self-deception is ours.

The Bible says what self-deception costs. Proverbs 14:12: "There is a way that seems right to a person, but its end is the way to death." Proverbs 28:13: "No one who conceals transgressions will prosper, but one who confesses and forsakes them will obtain mercy." James 1:23-24 gives a picture: hearers who do not act "are like those who look at themselves in a mirror; for they look at themselves and, on going away, immediately forget what they were like." This is related to denial and not identical to it. These verses are about right and wrong ways, hidden wrongdoing and hearing without doing. Reading them as the cost of self-deception is ours, and "death" in Proverbs 14:12 is not explained in the page read.

The Buddhist texts say what looking only at others' faults does. Dhp 253: "When you look for the flaws of others, always finding fault, your defilements only grow, you're far from ending defilements." MN 61 says what happens once lying is easy: "when someone is not ashamed to tell a deliberate lie, there is no bad deed they would not do, I say." This is related to denial and not identical to it. Dhp 253 is about fault-finding, and MN 61 is about lying to others. Reading them as the cost of self-deception is ours.

Seneca says what comes of not knowing one's fault. Letters 28: "he who does not know that he has sinned does not desire correction; you must discover yourself in the wrong before you can reform yourself." Socrates names the stakes. Plato, Apology: "the life which is unexamined is not worth living". This is related to denial and not identical to it. Seneca is writing about knowing one's faults and Socrates about examining one's life. Reading them as the cost of self-deception is ours.

The research read here describes self-deception and its costs and tests no remedy. The rest is common advice. Notice the discomfort. A sudden urge to explain, change the subject or defend is a common sign that something is being pushed away. That is common advice. Write down the facts. Put on paper what happened, what you did and what the evidence is, apart from how you feel about it. That is common advice. Ask someone you trust. Choose a person who will tell you the truth kindly, and listen before you answer. That is common advice. Look ahead. Chance and colleagues found that people "expect to cheat" but "do not foresee self-deception", and that inflated expectations "prove costly". A fair question to put to yourself is how the story you are telling will look in a year. That use of the finding is ours, and the study did not test it. Go slowly if it hurts. People sometimes need time before they can face bad news, and a counsellor can go at your pace. Get help for what is at stake. If denial is keeping you from facing a health problem, a harmful habit or a danger to you or someone else, a doctor or therapist can help. That is common advice.

The Gita's counsel is to seek knowledge, and to use the mind as a friend and not an enemy. Ask a teacher. Gita 4.34: "Learn the Truth by approaching a spiritual master. Inquire from him with reverence and render service unto him." Value knowledge. Gita 4.38: "In this world, there is nothing as purifying as divine knowledge." Make the mind a friend. Gita 6.5: "Elevate yourself through the power of your mind, and not degrade yourself, for the mind can be the friend and also the enemy of the self." Check the match between act and thought. Gita 3.6 warns of those who restrain action "while continuing to dwell on sense objects in the mind", and "certainly delude themselves". This is related to denial and not identical to it. These verses are about knowledge, a teacher and the mind, and the Gita sets them within its own path. Reading them as a way through self-deception is ours, and nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist.

The Upanishads call for waking up and for asking. Wake. Katha 1.3.14: "Rise, awake! having obtained your boons, understand them! The sharp edge of a razor is difficult to pass over; thus the wise say the path (to the Self) is hard." Ask the question you have not asked. In Chandogya 6.1.3 a father asks his conceited son: "have you ever asked for that instruction by which we hear what cannot be heard, by which we perceive what cannot be perceived, by which we know what cannot be known?" Admit what you did not know. The son answers in 6.1.7: "Surely those venerable men (my teachers) did not know that. For if they had known it, why should they not have told it me?" This is related to denial and not identical to it. These verses are about the Self and about a student's learning, and they do not describe facing an uncomfortable fact. Reading them as a way through self-deception is ours, and nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist.

The Bible's counsel is to ask to be searched, to confess and to look at your own log first. Ask to be searched. Psalm 139:23-24: "Search me, O God, and know my heart; test me and know my thoughts. See if there is any wicked way in me, and lead me in the way everlasting." Confess. 1 John 1:9: "If we confess our sins, he who is faithful and just will forgive us our sins and cleanse us from all unrighteousness." And Proverbs 28:13: "one who confesses and forsakes them will obtain mercy." Look at your own first. Matthew 7:5: "You hypocrite, first take the log out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to take the speck out of your neighbor's eye." Test your own work. Galatians 6:4: "All must test their own work". This is related to denial and not identical to it. These verses are about sin, confession and judging others, and they sit within the Christian life. Reading them as a way through self-deception is ours, and nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist.

The Buddhist texts counsel checking, as one checks a mirror, and telling a trusted friend. Use a mirror. In MN 61 the Buddha asks Rāhula: "What is the purpose of a mirror?" "It's for checking your reflection, sir." "In the same way, deeds of body, speech, and mind should be done only after repeated checking." Check before, during and after. He teaches Rāhula to ask: "Does this act with the body that I want to do lead to hurting myself, hurting others, or hurting both?" Confess to a friend. "Then, Rāhula, you should confess, reveal, and clarify such a deed to the Teacher or a sensible spiritual companion." Take the correction. AN 4.49: "When a wise person hears them, they get their mind back." This is related to denial and not identical to it. MN 61 is advice to a young monastic on honesty and action, and AN 4.49 is about wrong view. Reading them as a way through self-deception is ours, and nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist.

The philosophers' counsel is to examine yourself, and to be your own accuser first. Examine your life. Plato's Apology: "the life which is unexamined is not worth living". Be your own accuser. Seneca, Letters 28: "prove yourself guilty, hunt up charges against yourself; play the part, first of accuser, then of judge, last of intercessor. At times be harsh with yourself." Start with what you do not know. Socrates: "I neither know nor think that I know." This is related to denial and not identical to it. These are one school's disciplines, and Seneca's advice to be harsh with yourself should be read beside Self-criticism, which describes how a harsh inner voice can do harm. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist.

Note: This is an invented composite story, not a real case. It is built from patterns people commonly describe, so you can see how denial works and how people loosen its grip. Anil's story Anil opened a small shop with his savings. For two years it lost money. Each month he said it was a slow season, then that the street was being dug up, then that the next festival would fix it. When his sister asked how it was going he said "fine" and changed the subject. He knew, when he looked at the accounts, and he often did not look. What helped: He noticed the discomfort. The tightness in his chest when his sister asked was the sign that something was being pushed away. He wrote down the facts. Rent, sales and what he had put in, for each month, with no commentary. He asked someone he trusted. His sister said what she had seen, without blame, and he listened before answering. He looked ahead. He asked what the story would sound like in a year if nothing changed. He went at his own pace. He took a month to decide, and spoke to an adviser about the debts. He kept his dignity. He closed the shop and kept the lessons, and told people honestly why. The disappointment was real. The two years of "next month" had cost more than the truth did. What it shows: Anil did not have to be harsh with himself. Looking at the accounts, and letting someone else look with him, did what a good story had not.

Arjuna admits it The Gita opens with a man who says plainly what is wrong with him. In 2.7 Arjuna tells Krishna: "I am confused about my duty, and am besieged with anxiety and faintheartedness. I am Your disciple, and am surrendered to You. Please instruct me for certain what is best for me." In 2.8 he adds: "I can find no means of driving away this anguish that is drying up my senses. Even if I win a prosperous and unrivalled kingdom on the earth, or gain sovereignty like the celestial gods, I will be unable to dispel this grief." What it shows: The teaching begins when Arjuna stops pretending he is fine and says that he is confused and grieving. The Gita has no tale of denial, so this is a moment in the dialogue and not a story of self-deception; the link is ours, and Arjuna's words are about his duty in the war.

The careless child and the call to wake The Upanishads have no tale of self-deception, so this is a picture from the Katha. Death describes "the careless child, deluded by the delusion of wealth", who thinks "'This is the world... there is no other;'" and "thus he falls again and again under my sway" (1.2.6). Later the text calls: "Rise, awake! having obtained your boons, understand them! The sharp edge of a razor is difficult to pass over; thus the wise say the path (to the Self) is hard" (1.3.14). What it shows: The text sets the sleeper beside the call to wake, and says the path is hard. The passage is about the Self and the Hereafter and not about denial; the link is ours.

Nathan and David In 2 Samuel 12 the prophet Nathan comes to King David with a story. A rich man with "very many flocks and herds" takes a poor man's one little ewe lamb to feed a guest. "David's anger was greatly kindled against the man. He said to Nathan, 'As the Lord lives, the man who has done this deserves to die; he shall restore the lamb fourfold because he did this thing and because he had no pity.'" Nathan says: "You are the man!" He names what David has done: "You have struck down Uriah the Hittite with the sword and have taken his wife to be your wife and have killed him with the sword of the Ammonites" (12:7-9). David answers: "I have sinned against the Lord" (12:13). What it shows: David can see the wrong clearly in someone else's story, and not in his own. The account of what David did to Uriah is in the chapters before this one, and it involves adultery and a killing. The story is about justice and a king's wrongdoing and not about self-deception as such; the link is ours.

Rāhula and the water pot In MN 61 the Buddha visits his son Rāhula, who sets out water for his feet. The Buddha leaves "a little water in the pot" and asks: "Rāhula, do you see this little bit of water left in the pot?" "Yes, sir." "That's how little of the ascetic's nature is left in those who are not ashamed to tell a deliberate lie." He throws the water away: "That's how the ascetic's nature is discarded in those who are not ashamed to tell a deliberate lie." He turns the pot upside down, then upright and empty: "That's how vacant and hollow the ascetic's nature is in those who are not ashamed to tell a deliberate lie." Then he asks: "What is the purpose of a mirror?" "It's for checking your reflection, sir." "In the same way, deeds of body, speech, and mind should be done only after repeated checking." What it shows: The Buddha moves from a pot to a mirror, from the cost of lying to the habit of looking at one's own acts. The sutta is about lying and the checking of deeds and not about self-deception as such; the link is ours.

Socrates and the man who thought himself wise In Plato's Apology Socrates tells the jury why he has enemies. An oracle called him the wisest of men, and he went to test it. He went "to one who had the reputation of wisdom", a politician: "I could not help thinking that he was not really wise, although he was thought wise by many, and wiser still by himself; and I went and tried to explain to him that he thought himself wise, but was not really wise; and the consequence was that he hated me". He left reflecting: "I am better off than he is - for he knows nothing, and thinks that he knows. I neither know nor think that I know." What it shows: The man was not told what he did not want to hear, and he took it badly. The passage is about wisdom and the examination of others and not about denial as such; the link is ours, and it is Socrates' own account of events, told at his trial.

"The true self" is an idea from religion and philosophy: that beneath our roles, moods and habits there is a deeper self, and that we are mostly mistaken about it. Psychology has not established that such a self exists. What it can say is how hard it is to know ourselves, and what people believe about their "true" selves. Wilson and Dunn review the research and begin: "Because of personal motives and the architecture of the mind, it may be difficult for people to know themselves." Strohminger, Knobe and Newman describe a recent line of work in which, "even among characteristics that are internal to the self, people pick out a subset as belonging to the true self." These are "judged as making people who they really are, deep down", and they find that the true self "is perceived as positive and moral". That is a finding about what people believe, and it does not show that a true self exists. Everyday signs, as people commonly describe them and not as findings from these papers: feeling empty when a role or job ends, being surprised by your own reaction, and feeling that the person others see is not quite you. It overlaps with ego and validation and denial. This is not a diagnosis. If you feel unreal, lost or detached, or that you do not know who you are, a doctor or therapist can help.

In the Bhagavad Gita delusion is taking the changing body for the self. Gita 2.13: "Just as the embodied soul continuously passes from childhood to youth to old age, similarly, at the time of death, the soul passes into another body. The wise are not deluded by this." And 2.20: "The soul is neither born, nor does it ever die; nor having once existed, does it ever cease to be. The soul is without birth, eternal, immortal, and ageless. It is not destroyed when the body is destroyed." This is related to the idea of the true self and not identical to it. The Gita speaks of the soul and of delusion in its own terms. The page for 7.27 renders words from the root moha as "illusion" and "delusion", and the Sanskrit was otherwise not examined.

The Upanishads name ignorance and place it against wisdom. Katha 1.2.4: "Wide apart and leading to different points are these two, ignorance, and what is known as wisdom." And Chandogya 6.8.7, a father to his son: "Now that which is that subtile essence (the root of all), in it all that exists has its self. It is the True. It is the Self, and thou ... art it." This is related to the idea of the true self and not identical to it. The Katha verse sets ignorance against wisdom, and the Chandogya verse is a teaching to one student about the Self.

The New Testament speaks of an old self and a new self. Ephesians 4:22-24: "to put away your former way of life, your old self, corrupt and deluded by its lusts, and to be renewed in the spirit of your minds, and to clothe yourselves with the new self, created according to the likeness of God in true righteousness and holiness." 1 John 3:2 adds that identity is not yet fully seen: "Beloved, we are God's children now; what we will be has not yet been revealed." This is related to the idea of the true self and not identical to it. These verses are about a way of life and about being God's children, and do not describe a hidden self to be discovered by looking within. Reading them as speaking of the true self is ours.

The Buddhist texts do not teach a true self, and the topic's title does not fit them. They name the mistake of taking the changing parts of a person to be a self. SN 22.59: "But if it's impermanent, suffering, and perishable, is it fit to be regarded thus: 'This is mine, I am this, this is my self'?" "No, sir." AN 4.49 names it among four perversions: "Taking not-self as self." This is related to the idea of the true self and not identical to it. The texts speak of not-self, and this article reads delusion (moha) and ignorance (avijjā) here only as mistaking what the self is. Whether the Buddha affirmed any self is outside what was read.

Plato pictures people who mistake shadows for the real. In the Republic Socrates asks us to behold "human beings living in a underground den", chained from childhood, who "can only see before them". When Glaucon says they are strange, Socrates answers: "Like ourselves... they see only their own shadows". And: "To them... the truth would be literally nothing but the shadows of the images." This is related to the idea of the true self and not identical to it. The cave is a picture of ignorance of reality, and the passage is not mainly about the self. Reading it as a picture of mistaking oneself is ours.

The sources read here point to why knowing ourselves is hard, and they say little about a hidden "true" self. Motives and the structure of the mind. Wilson and Dunn write that "people often attempt to block out unwanted thoughts and feelings through conscious suppression and perhaps through unconscious repression, though whether such attempts are successful is controversial." They add: "A more common source of self-knowledge failure is the inaccessibility of much of the mind to consciousness". This is a review of research, and its abstract is a summary. A flattering picture. Strohminger and colleagues find that the true self "is perceived as positive and moral". That suggests we may imagine our true self to be better than we are, and the abstract does not say so itself. Common explanations, not findings from these papers: being defined by others' expectations early on, taking on roles that fit a family or a job, and living busily enough that there is little time to look inward.

The Gita's root is illusion that arises from the modes of nature. Gita 7.27: "O descendant of Bharat, the dualities of desire and aversion arise from illusion. O conqueror of enemies, all living beings in the material realm are deluded by these." Gita 14.8: "tamo guṇa, which is born of ignorance, is the cause of illusion for the embodied souls. It deludes all living beings through negligence, laziness, and sleep." This is related to the idea of the true self and not identical to it. These verses are about illusion, desire and the mode of ignorance, and do not speak of a self to be found. Reading them as roots of ignorance of the self is ours.

The Katha Upanishad names the root as taking the Self for the body and its doings. Katha 1.2.19: "If the killer thinks that he kills, if the killed thinks that he is killed, they do not understand; for this one does not kill, nor is that one killed." And in the chariot picture, 1.3.4: "When he (the Highest Self) is in union with the body, the senses, and the mind, then wise people call him the Enjoyer." This is related to the idea of the true self and not identical to it. The first verse is about the Self that neither kills nor is killed, and the second about the Self joined to body, senses and mind. Reading them as roots of ignorance of the Self is ours.

The New Testament names ignorance and a hardened heart. Ephesians 4:17-18: "you must no longer walk as the gentiles walk, in the futility of their minds; they are darkened in their understanding, alienated from the life of God because of their ignorance and hardness of heart." This is related to the idea of the true self and not identical to it. The passage is about darkened understanding and a way of life, and does not speak of ignorance of the self. The wording in the page's footnote on "gentiles" was not read. Reading the verses as a root of ignorance of oneself is ours.

The Buddhist texts put ignorance at the start of the chain that ends in suffering. SN 12.1: "Ignorance is a requirement for choices. Choices are a requirement for consciousness." The sutta continues through craving and grasping to its end: "That is how this entire mass of suffering originates." This is related to the idea of the true self and not identical to it. SN 12.1 is about dependent origination, and the ignorance it names is the sutta's own term, which this article does not claim is ignorance of a true self. This topic's title does not fit the Buddhist texts, which teach not-self.

Plato's root is a life lived facing the wall. Republic 7: the prisoners have been in the den "from their childhood", with "their legs and necks chained so that they cannot move, and can only see before them, being prevented by the chains from turning round their heads." Hume offers a different view, and a puzzle for any theory of a true self. Treatise 1.4.6: "when I enter most intimately into what I call myself, I always stumble on some particular perception or other, of heat or cold, light or shade, love or hatred, pain or pleasure. I never can catch myself at any time without a perception, and never can observe any thing but the perception." This is related to the idea of the true self and not identical to it. Plato's passage is about a life of illusion, and Hume's is his report of looking inward. They do not agree, and this site does not take a side. The reading of Plato as a root of ignorance of oneself is ours.

The sources read here say little about effects, and what they say is cautious. Self-knowledge has value, with limits. Wilson and Dunn write: "It is not always advantageous to hold self-perceptions that correspond perfectly with reality, but increasing awareness of nonconscious motives and personality is generally beneficial." The abstract does not list what the benefits are. What this does not show. Neither abstract tests what happens to a person who holds a mistaken view of who they are, and neither shows that a "true self" exists. Commonly described effects, not findings from these papers: decisions that do not fit your values, being thrown by a change of job or role, and a gap between how you act and how you feel. If you feel lost or unreal, a doctor or therapist can help.

The Gita says what the illusion costs. Gita 7.27: "the dualities of desire and aversion arise from illusion." And at the start of the teaching, Krishna says: "While you speak words of wisdom, you are mourning for that which is not worthy of grief" (2.11). This is related to the idea of the true self and not identical to it. 7.27 is about desire and aversion, and 2.11 is addressed to Arjuna in a battlefield. Reading them as the cost of ignorance of the self is ours.

The Katha Upanishad says what unmastered senses do. Katha 1.3.5: "He who has no understanding and whose mind (the reins) is never firmly held, his senses (horses) are unmanageable, like vicious horses of a charioteer." It gives the opposite in 1.2.22: "The wise who knows the Self as bodiless within the bodies, as unchanging among changing things, as great and omnipresent, does never grieve." This is related to the idea of the true self and not identical to it. The first verse is about understanding and the senses, and the second about the wise who knows the Self. Reading the first as the cost of ignorance of the Self is ours.

The Gospels say what it costs to lose one's life by holding it too tightly. Matthew 16:25-26: "For those who want to save their life will lose it, and those who lose their life for my sake will find it. For what will it profit them if they gain the whole world but forfeit their life?" Paul names a limit of sight. 1 Corinthians 13:12: "For now we see only a reflection, as in a mirror, but then we will see face to face. Now I know only in part; then I will know fully, even as I have been fully known." This is related to the idea of the true self and not identical to it. Matthew 16 is about following Jesus at a cost, and 1 Corinthians 13 about partial knowledge. Reading them as the cost of ignorance of the self is ours.

The Buddhist texts say what taking the changing for a self brings. SN 22.59: "But because form is not-self, it leads to affliction. And you can't compel form: 'May my form be like this! May it not be like that!'" SN 12.1 gives the whole chain: "Rebirth is a requirement for old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress to come to be." This is related to the idea of the true self and not identical to it. SN 22.59 is about the five aggregates and SN 12.1 about dependent origination, and both speak of not-self and not of a true self. Reading them as the cost of mistaking what the self is is ours.

Plato says seeing the truth first hurts. Republic 7: when a prisoner is freed and made to look towards the light, "he will suffer sharp pains; the glare will distress him, and he will be unable to see the realities of which in his former state he had seen the shadows". Marcus Aurelius reduces what we take ourselves to be. Meditations 4: "Thou art a little soul bearing about a corpse, as Epictetus used to say." This is related to the idea of the true self and not identical to it. Plato is describing the pain of leaving illusion, and Marcus is repeating a saying of Epictetus about the body. Reading them as the cost of ignorance of the self is ours.

The research read here suggests ways to know yourself better, and it says that obstacles are large. The rest is common advice. Expect to be partly wrong about yourself. Wilson and Dunn: "it may be difficult for people to know themselves." Use other people's eyes. They list "looking at ourselves through the eyes of others and observing our own behavior" as ways of increasing self-knowledge, and add that "major obstacles exist". Be careful with introspection. "Introspection cannot provide a direct pipeline to these mental processes, though some types of introspection may help people construct beneficial personal narratives." Looking inward is not a clear window. Notice what you imagine your "true self" to be. Strohminger and colleagues find people see it as "positive and moral". Ask whether that picture is a hope more than an observation. That use of the finding is ours, and the study did not test it. Check roles against values. Write down the roles you hold and ask which you chose. That is common advice. Get help if you feel lost. If you feel unreal, detached or that you do not know who you are, a doctor or therapist can help. That is common advice.

The Gita's counsel is to see what changes and what does not, and to see all beings alike. See the body change. Gita 2.22: "As a person sheds worn-out garments and wears new ones, likewise, at the time of death, the soul casts off its worn-out body and enters a new one." Know what does not change. Gita 2.20: "The soul is neither born, nor does it ever die". Look with an equal eye. Gita 6.29: "The true yogis, uniting their consciousness with God, see with equal eye, all living beings in God and God in all living beings." Use the mind as a friend. Gita 6.5: "Elevate yourself through the power of your mind, and not degrade yourself, for the mind can be the friend and also the enemy of the self." This is related to the idea of the true self and not identical to it. These verses are about the soul, yoga and the mind, and the Gita sets them within its own path. Reading them as a way through ignorance of the self is ours, and nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist.

The Upanishads point to knowing the Self, and to guiding the chariot. Know the Self in the chariot. Katha 1.3.3: "Know the Self to be sitting in the chariot, the body to be the chariot, the intellect (buddhi) the charioteer, and the mind the reins." Hold the reins. Katha 1.3.9: "But he who has understanding for his charioteer, and who holds the reins of the mind, he reaches the end of his journey". Hear the teaching. Chandogya 6.8.7: "It is the True. It is the Self, and thou ... art it." Do not grieve. Katha 1.2.22: "The wise who knows the Self as bodiless within the bodies, as unchanging among changing things, as great and omnipresent, does never grieve." This is related to the idea of the true self and not identical to it. These verses are about the Self, the chariot and a teaching to a student. Reading them as a way through ignorance of the self is ours, and nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist.

The New Testament's counsel is to renew the mind and to find one's life in Christ. Be transformed. Romans 12:2: "Do not be conformed to this age, but be transformed by the renewing of the mind". Put on the new self. Ephesians 4:23-24: "to be renewed in the spirit of your minds, and to clothe yourselves with the new self, created according to the likeness of God in true righteousness and holiness." Take your life as given. Galatians 2:20: "it is no longer I who live, but it is Christ who lives in me." Know where your life is. Colossians 3:3: "for you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God." This is related to the idea of the true self and not identical to it. These verses are about renewal and life in Christ, and they sit within the Christian life. Reading them as a way through ignorance of the self is ours, and nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist.

The Buddhist texts counsel seeing the five aggregates for what they are. Ask the question. SN 22.59: "is it fit to be regarded thus: 'This is mine, I am this, this is my self'?" "No, sir." See with right understanding. SN 22.59: "This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self." See it with wisdom. Dhp 279: "All things are not-self—when this is seen with wisdom, one grows disillusioned with suffering: this is the path to purity." Let ignorance fade. SN 12.1: "When ignorance fades away and ceases no residue left behind, choices cease." This is related to the idea of the true self and not identical to it. These passages are about the five aggregates and not-self, and they sit within the Buddhist path. The texts do not say that a person does not matter, and nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist.

The philosophers' counsel is to turn towards the light and to retire into oneself. Turn towards the light. Plato, Republic 7: the freed prisoner is "compelled suddenly to stand up and turn his neck round and walk and look towards the light". Retire into yourself. Marcus Aurelius, Meditations 4: "it is in thy power whenever thou shalt choose to retire into thyself." Order the mind. Marcus: "tranquility is nothing else than the good ordering of the mind." Renew yourself. Marcus: "Constantly then give to thyself this retreat, and renew thyself". This is related to the idea of the true self and not identical to it. These passages are one school's discipline and a picture, and Hume's report in root causes shows that philosophers do not agree on what is found when we look inward. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist.

Note: This is an invented composite story, not a real case. It is built from patterns people commonly describe, so you can see how a narrow picture of oneself works and how people widen it.
