Haroon's story For thirty years Haroon was "the one who runs the department". When it restructured and his post went, he found that he did not know what to do with a Tuesday. He said "I'm nothing without the job" so often that his family stopped answering. What helped: He expected to be partly wrong. The sentence "I'm nothing" felt like a fact. He began to treat it as one view among others. He asked other people. A former colleague said what he had been like to work with. A neighbour said what he was like at home. Neither was the picture he had of himself. He did not trust looking inward alone. Sitting and thinking led in circles, so he wrote down what he did in a week and looked at that. He questioned the flattering picture. He had imagined his real self as the manager. He noticed he also liked teaching a younger neighbour to repair things. He checked roles against values. He listed the roles he had and asked which he had chosen and which had simply happened. He asked for help. The flat feeling did not lift, and he spoke to his doctor, who referred him to a counsellor. The old role did not stop mattering. It stopped being the whole of him. What it shows: Haroon did not find a hidden self. He found that the picture he had was narrower than the life he was living, and he widened it with the help of other people.

Krishna begins the teaching The Gita has no tale of delusion about the self, so this is the opening of Krishna's teaching and not a story. Arjuna has told Krishna that he is confused and grieving (2.7-2.8). Krishna answers: "While you speak words of wisdom, you are mourning for that which is not worthy of grief. The wise lament neither for the living nor for the dead" (2.11). He goes on: "Never was there a time when I did not exist, nor you, nor all these kings; nor in the future shall any of us cease to be" (2.12). And: "The soul is neither born, nor does it ever die" (2.20). What it shows: The teaching starts by telling Arjuna that what he mourns is not the whole of who he and the others are. The passage is about grief on a battlefield and the soul, and not about delusion as a habit; the link is ours.

Svetaketu and the salt In the Chandogya Upanishad a father asks his son to do something simple: "Place this salt in water, and then wait on me in the morning." In the morning he says: "Bring me the salt, which you placed in the water last night." The son looks for it, "found it not, for, of course, it was melted." The father says: "Taste it from the surface of the water. How is it?" "It is salt." "Taste it from the middle." "It is salt." "Taste it from the bottom." "It is salt." Then: "Here also, in this body, forsooth, you do not perceive the True (Sat), my son; but there indeed it is." He ends: "That which is the subtile essence, in it all that exists has its self. It is the True. It is the Self, and thou ... art it" (6.13.1-3). What it shows: What cannot be seen is still there, and it can be known by taste. The teaching is about the Self and the True, and the story is told to one student; reading it as a lesson about ignorance of oneself is ours.

Saul on the road to Damascus In Acts 9 Saul is "still breathing threats and murder against the disciples of the Lord", on his way to Damascus to bring any who belong to the Way "bound to Jerusalem". "Suddenly a light from heaven flashed around him. He fell to the ground and heard a voice saying to him, 'Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?'" (9:3-4). "Saul got up from the ground, and though his eyes were open, he could see nothing" (9:8). For three days he is without sight. Then Ananias comes to him: "Brother Saul, the Lord Jesus, who appeared to you on your way here, has sent me so that you may regain your sight". And "immediately something like scales fell from his eyes, and his sight was restored" (9:17-18). What it shows: Saul is sure of what he is doing, and the text describes his being stopped and then seeing again. The story is about a conversion and not about the true self as such; the link is ours, and it has a long history of interpretation that was not read.

The Buddha and the group of five In SN 22.59 the Buddha addresses the group of five mendicants at Isipatana. He says: "form is not-self. For if form were self, it wouldn't lead to affliction. And you could compel form: 'May my form be like this! May it not be like that!'" He asks whether form is permanent, and they answer that it is impermanent, then: "But if it's impermanent, suffering, and perishable, is it fit to be regarded thus: 'This is mine, I am this, this is my self'?" "No, sir." The same is asked of feeling, perception, choices and consciousness. He concludes: "So you should truly see any kind of form at all ... with right understanding: 'This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.'" At the end, "the minds of the group of five mendicants were freed from defilements by not grasping." What it shows: The Buddha does not tell them what the self is. He asks, of each part of a person, whether it is fit to be called "my self". The sutta teaches not-self and does not speak of a true self; this topic's title does not fit it.

Plato's cave In Book 7 of the Republic Socrates asks Glaucon to picture "human beings living in a underground den", chained from childhood so that they can see only the wall in front of them. Behind them a fire burns, and people carry objects along a raised way. The prisoners see only shadows. Glaucon says: "You have shown me a strange image, and they are strange prisoners." Socrates answers: "Like ourselves". If one is freed, "he will suffer sharp pains; the glare will distress him". He comes slowly to see reflections, then things, then the sun. Remembering the den, "do you not suppose that he would felicitate himself on the change, and pity them?" What it shows: The prisoners take the shadows for the real, and Socrates says they are "like ourselves". The cave is a picture of ignorance and education and not of the self as such; the link is ours, and it is one philosopher's image.

Guilt is the painful sense of having done something wrong. Shame is the painful sense of being wrong, of being bad or small as a person. A common way to put it is that guilt says "I did something bad" and shame says "I am bad". That is a standard summary and not a quotation from the papers below. Researchers treat them as two "moral emotions". Tangney, Stuewig and Mashek's review covers "the distinction between shame and guilt, and the relative advantages and disadvantages of these two moral emotions." In two studies of undergraduates, Tangney, Wagner and Gramzow found that "Shame-proneness was strongly related to psychological maladjustment in general", while "Guilt-proneness was only moderately related to psychopathology." Those are correlations from questionnaires and do not show that shame causes distress. Everyday signs, as people commonly describe them and not as findings from these papers: wanting to hide or disappear, replaying a moment, going quiet around the person involved. Guilt often points toward repair, and it can be a fitting response to real harm. It overlaps with self-criticism, where the harsh voice turns a deed into a verdict on the person. Neither is a diagnosis. If shame is heavy or long-lasting, is tied to abuse, or comes with thoughts of harming yourself, please talk to a doctor or therapist, and in an emergency contact your local emergency services.

Hinduism has no single word in the Bhagavad Gita for the pair of shame and guilt, but it names an inner check on wrongdoing as a virtue. Gita 16.1-3 lists qualities of "those endowed with a divine nature", among them "fearlessness", "compassion toward all living beings", "forgiveness" and "modesty". The Sanskrit word behind "modesty" is hrīḥ, and the translator's commentary explains it as a "sense of guilt in performing actions contrary to the injunctions of scriptures and society." It says the saintly nature "is imbued with a ruthless inner conscience". In this reading a sense of having done wrong is counted among the good qualities and not as a flaw. This is related to shame and guilt and not identical to them. The verse itself says "modesty", and the meaning of guilt comes from the commentary. It speaks of a check before and during action and not of the long ache after a wrong, and it says nothing of judging oneself to be bad. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist, and shame that is heavy or lasting is worth telling someone about.

The Upanishads speak of the same distress without using a word for shame. Taittiriya Upanishad 2.9 says of the one who knows the bliss of Brahman: "He does not distress himself with the thought, Why did I not do what is good? Why did I do what is bad? He who thus knows these two (good and bad), frees himself." The verse names the habit of tormenting oneself over the good left undone and the bad done, and says that knowledge frees a person from it. This is related to shame and guilt and not identical to them. The verse describes a person who has already realised Brahman, and it does not say that wrongs do not matter or what to do about harm caused. How the knowledge acts on the deeds is not explained in the passage read. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist, and shame that is heavy or lasting is worth telling someone about.

Christianity has words for both. Guilt is the awareness of a wrong done, and the Bible also shows the urge to hide. In Genesis 3 the man and woman "knew that they were naked", and "hid themselves from the presence of the Lord God among the trees of the garden." Asked where he is, the man says: "I heard the sound of you in the garden, and I was afraid, because I was naked, and I hid myself." Psalm 51:3 shows the other side: "For I know my transgressions, and my sin is ever before me." In verse 4 the speaker says: "Against you, you alone, have I sinned and done what is evil in your sight." This is related to shame and guilt and not identical to it. Reading Genesis 3:7-10 as an account of shame, and Psalm 51 as guilt, is ours. The verses read do not use the words "shame" or "guilt" of the man and woman, and the Psalm is about sin before God and not a general feeling. What both show is a person who knows something is wrong and is aware of being seen. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist, and shame that is heavy or lasting is worth telling someone about.

The Buddhist texts treat a sense of wrongdoing as a protection. AN 2.9: "These two bright things, mendicants, protect the world. What two? Conscience and prudence." Without them, "the world would become dissolute, like goats and sheep, chickens and pigs, and hounds and jackals." The sutta says these two qualities are bright, and that without them there would be no recognition of the status of mother, aunts, or wives and partners of tutors and respected people. This is related to shame and guilt and not identical to them. Bhikkhu Sujato renders the pair as "conscience and prudence", and the root text reads "Hirī ca ottappañca". They are commonly explained as a sense of moral shame and a wariness of doing wrong, but that explanation was not checked here. Nothing in the passage read speaks of shame as a verdict on oneself. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist, and shame that is heavy or lasting is worth telling someone about.

Aristotle gives shame a place, and says what it is not. In the Nicomachean Ethics (4.9): "Shame should not be described as a virtue; for it is more like a feeling than a state of character. It is defined, at any rate, as a kind of fear of dishonour, and produces an effect similar to that produced by fear of danger; for people who feel disgraced blush, and those who fear death turn pale." For him it is a bodily feeling about disgrace in the eyes of others, and not a settled quality of character. This is related to shame as people use the word now and not identical to it. The translator's "shame", "disgrace" and "dishonour" point at how one appears to others, and the passage says nothing of shame as a belief that one is bad. The Greek was not examined. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist, and shame that is heavy or lasting is worth telling someone about.

The sources read here point to a few causes, and say little about how they work. Early harm. The abstract of the Tangney review lists research on "the link between childhood abuse and later proneness to shame", and on "styles of coping with shame". It does not give the strength of the link or its mechanism. Doing harm. Guilt follows an act: breaking a rule you hold, or hurting someone. That is a standard account and not drawn from the papers. High standards and harsh judging. Many people describe the same pattern as in perfectionism and self-criticism: a standard set too high, then a verdict on the self when it is missed. That is common description, not a finding here. Secrecy. What is hidden tends to grow, as people commonly describe it. Shame that began in childhood harm is not a personal failing, and a therapist can help with it.

The Gita shows distress rising from fear of wrongdoing and from attachment. In Arjuna's first speech he says: "Even though they may be aggressors, sin will certainly come upon us if we slay them" (1.36). Before that he says: "my limbs are giving way and my mouth is drying up" (1.28). The translator's commentary on 1.28 gives a cause: "He was filled with remorse and fearful of performing his duty of fighting this war. The cause for these sentiments was his attachment towards his bodily relatives." This is related to shame and guilt and not identical to them. Arjuna dreads a wrong he has not yet done, and the cause named is attachment and forgetting that he "was not just the body", in the commentary's words. Krishna's answer comes in the chapters after and was not read here. Reading Arjuna's anguish as a root of guilt is ours. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist, and shame that is heavy or lasting is worth telling someone about.

The Upanishads place the root of grief in not knowing the Self. In Chandogya 7.1 Narada comes to Sanatkumara knowing the Vedas and many sciences and says: "with all this I know the Mantras only, the sacred books, I do not know the Self. I have heard from men like you, that he who knows the Self overcomes grief. I am in grief." Sanatkumara answers: "Whatever you have read, is only a name." This is related to shame and guilt and not identical to them. Narada's grief is not named as guilt or shame, and the root given is not knowing the Self. Reading it as a source of those feelings is ours. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist, and shame that is heavy or lasting is worth telling someone about.

In Genesis 3 the hiding is followed by passing the blame. God asks: "Who told you that you were naked? Have you eaten from the tree of which I commanded you not to eat?" The man says: "The woman whom you gave to be with me, she gave me fruit from the tree, and I ate." The woman says: "The serpent tricked me, and I ate." The text shows fear, hiding and blame running together after a wrong. 1 John 3:19-20 speaks of the heart's own verdict: "whenever our hearts condemn us, for God is greater than our hearts, and he knows everything." This is related to shame and guilt and not identical to it. The causes in these verses are an act and the fear that follows it. The sentence "this is how guilt and shame begin" is ours, since the passages do not say it. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist, and shame that is heavy or lasting is worth telling someone about.

The Buddhist texts trace remorse to the deed, and the deed to heedlessness. Dhp 15: "Here they grieve, hereafter they grieve, an evildoer grieves in both places. They grieve and fret, seeing their own corrupt deeds." In MN 86 the former bandit Aṅgulimāla says: "He who once was heedless, but turned to heedfulness, shines upon this world, like the moon freed from clouds." This is related to shame and guilt and not identical to them. Dhp 15 speaks of grief at one's own deeds, and the Aṅgulimāla verse sets heedlessness before and heedfulness after, and neither describes shame as a feeling about the self. Reading them as roots of those feelings is ours. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist, and shame that is heavy or lasting is worth telling someone about.

The Stoics place the root in our judgments. Epictetus, Enchiridion 5: "Men are disturbed, not by things, but by the principles and notions which they form concerning things." He goes on: "When therefore we are hindered, or disturbed, or grieved, let us never attribute it to others, but to ourselves; that is, to our own principles." This is related to shame and guilt and not identical to them. The passage is about being disturbed in general. Applying it to shame is ours, and it should not be read as saying that remorse for real harm is a mistake in judgment. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist, and shame that is heavy or lasting is worth telling someone about.

The research read here describes costs and benefits, and mostly for shame. In two studies of undergraduates, Tangney, Wagner and Gramzow report that "Shame-proneness was strongly related to psychological maladjustment in general" and that "shame accounted for substantial variance in depression, above and beyond attributional style." Guilt-proneness was "only moderately related to psychopathology", and the correlations "were ascribable entirely to the shared variance between shame and guilt." These are correlations from questionnaires. The review by Tangney, Stuewig and Mashek weighs "the relative advantages and disadvantages" of the two emotions, and the abstract does not give its conclusions. Common effects, as people describe them and not findings from these papers: hiding from people, snapping at them, over-apologising, a tight chest, and sometimes, with guilt, repair and a changed course. Heavy shame can feed low mood. If shame is heavy or long-lasting, is tied to abuse, or comes with thoughts of harming yourself, please talk to a doctor or therapist, and in an emergency contact your local emergency services.

The Gita shows what distress does to a body. Arjuna says: "My whole body shudders; my hair is standing on end. My bow, the Gāṇḍīv, is slipping from my hand, and my skin is burning all over. My mind is in quandary and whirling in confusion; I am unable to hold myself steady any longer." The same chapter lists the other side. Among the divine qualities of 16.1-3 is hrīḥ, translated "modesty", which the commentary explains as "sense of guilt in performing actions contrary to the injunctions of scriptures and society". An inner check is counted as a gain. This is related to shame and guilt and not identical to them. Arjuna's distress is about killing his kinsmen, and the commentary calls it remorse and fear. Reading it as an effect of guilt is ours. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist, and shame that is heavy or lasting is worth telling someone about.

The Upanishads name self-torment as a cost, and freedom from it as a result of knowledge. Taittiriya 2.9: "He does not distress himself with the thought, Why did I not do what is good? Why did I do what is bad?" The sentence that follows says: "He who knows both, frees himself." In Chandogya 7.1.3 Narada puts the cost plainly: "I am in grief. Do, Sir, help me over this grief of mine." This is related to shame and guilt and not identical to them. The Taittiriya verse is about the knower, and Narada's grief has no named cause. Reading these as effects of guilt or shame is ours. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist, and shame that is heavy or lasting is worth telling someone about.

Psalm 32 describes what hidden guilt does to a body: "While I kept silent, my body wasted away through my groaning all day long. For day and night your hand was heavy upon me; my strength was dried up as by the heat of summer." Then it turns: "Then I acknowledged my sin to you, and I did not hide my iniquity; I said, 'I will confess my transgressions to the Lord,' and you forgave the guilt of my sin." Genesis 3:8 shows the hiding that comes with it: the man and woman "hid themselves from the presence of the Lord God". This is related to shame and guilt and not identical to them. The Psalm connects silence with wasting and confession with forgiveness. It does not claim that every ache of conscience has this cause, and a footnote on the page says the Hebrew of verse 4 is uncertain. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist, and shame that is heavy or lasting is worth telling someone about.

The Buddhist texts set grief and joy side by side. Dhp 15-16: "Here they grieve, hereafter they grieve, an evildoer grieves in both places." and "Here they rejoice, hereafter they rejoice, one who does good rejoices in both places." AN 10.1 gives a chain of effects that starts with conduct: "having no regrets is the goal and benefit of skillful ethics" and "Joy is the goal and benefit of having no regrets." This is related to shame and guilt and not identical to them. Dhp 15 is about the grief of an evildoer, and AN 10.1 is about the benefit of ethical conduct, one step of which is having no regrets. Neither describes shame as a feeling about the self, and reading them as effects of guilt is ours. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist, and shame that is heavy or lasting is worth telling someone about.

Aristotle describes what shame does. It "produces an effect similar to that produced by fear of danger; for people who feel disgraced blush, and those who fear death turn pale." It is a bodily condition, and so "characteristic of feeling rather than of a state of character." He also names a use: "young people should be prone to the feeling of shame because they live by feeling and therefore commit many errors, but are restrained by shame". And a limit: "the sense of disgrace is not even characteristic of a good man, since it is consequent on bad actions". This is related to shame as people use the word now and not identical to it. Aristotle is describing disgrace before others, not shame as a belief about the self, and he says nothing of long-term effects. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist, and shame that is heavy or lasting is worth telling someone about.

The research read here describes shame and guilt and tests no remedy. The rest is common advice. Say which it is. Try the sentence "I did something I regret" before "I am bad". The first points at what can be repaired. That is common advice. Repair what you can. If you hurt someone, say plainly what you did and apologise without excuses, where it is safe to. That is common advice. Tell someone you trust. Shame tends to want hiding, and saying it aloud to a kind person often loosens it. That is common advice. Speak to yourself as to a friend. A harsh verdict on yourself repairs nothing; see self-criticism. That is common advice. Let guilt do its job, then put it down. Once you have understood and repaired what you can, the feeling has done its work. That is common advice. Get help. If shame is heavy or long-lasting, is tied to abuse, or comes with thoughts of harming yourself, please talk to a doctor or therapist, and in an emergency contact your local emergency services.

The Gita offers comfort for those who feel they have fallen. Gita 9.30-31: "Even if the vilest sinners worship Me with exclusive devotion, they are to be considered righteous because they have made the proper resolve. Quickly they become virtuous, and attain lasting peace." 4.36: "Even those who are considered the most immoral of all sinners can cross over this ocean of material existence by seating themselves in the boat of divine knowledge." 18.66: "Abandon all varieties of dharmas and simply surrender unto Me alone. I shall liberate you from all sinful reactions; do not fear." This is related to shame and guilt and not identical to them. These verses are about devotion and knowledge and not about the feeling of shame, and they do not speak of making amends to people harmed. Reading them as comfort for guilt is ours. How the three verses fit with each other was not checked. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist, and shame that is heavy or lasting is worth telling someone about.

The Upanishads answer with knowledge, and not with a technique. Taittiriya 2.9: "He who thus knows these two (good and bad), frees himself. He who knows both, frees himself." In Chandogya 7.1.3 Narada asks: "Do, Sir, help me over this grief of mine." The first reply is: "Whatever you have read, is only a name." This is related to shame and guilt and not identical to them. Neither passage turns into steps, and the teaching that follows Sanatkumara's reply was not read here. The site makes no claim about how to practise it, and nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist.

The Christian texts counsel confession and receiving forgiveness. Name it. Psalm 51:3: "For I know my transgressions, and my sin is ever before me." Ask for a fresh start. Psalm 51:10: "Create in me a clean heart, O God, and put a new and right spirit within me." Confess. 1 John 1:9: "If we confess our sins, he who is faithful and just will forgive us our sins and cleanse us from all unrighteousness." Hear the verdict that follows. Romans 8:1: "Therefore there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus." Answer a heart that condemns. 1 John 3:19-20: "whenever our hearts condemn us, for God is greater than our hearts, and he knows everything." This is related to shame and guilt and not identical to it. These verses are about sin and forgiveness before God, and they do not describe amends to people harmed, which other texts of the tradition may discuss. Reading them as a way through shame and guilt is ours, and nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist.

The Buddhist texts counsel recognising a mistake, and turning to good. Recognise it. AN 2.21: "There are two who are astute. What two? One who recognizes when they've made a mistake. And one who properly accepts the confession of someone who's made a mistake." Turn to heedfulness. Dhp 173: "Someone whose bad deed is supplanted by the good, shines upon this world, like the moon freed from clouds." Build conduct that leaves no regret. AN 10.1: "having no regrets is the goal and benefit of skillful ethics." This is related to shame and guilt and not identical to them. AN 2.21 is about the wise and the foolish and says nothing of making amends, and Dhp 173 is about good done after a bad deed and does not describe a feeling. Reading them as a way through shame and guilt is ours, and nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist.

The philosophers' counsel is to look at your judgments, and to be accurate about blame. Check the judgment. Epictetus, Enchiridion 5: "Men are disturbed, not by things, but by the principles and notions which they form concerning things." Be accurate about blame. Same section: "An uninstructed person will lay the fault of his own bad condition upon others. Someone just starting instruction will lay the fault on himself. Some who is perfectly instructed will place blame neither on others nor on himself." Aim at not needing the feeling. Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 4.9: "the good man will never voluntarily do bad actions." This is related to shame and guilt and not identical to them. Epictetus is writing about being disturbed in general, and Aristotle is saying shame is not a virtue, so neither gives a method for the feeling. Step 3 is a standard that does not help once something has gone wrong, and it should be read beside Self-criticism. Reading these as a way through shame and guilt is ours, and nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist.

Note: This is an invented composite story, not a real case. It is built from patterns people commonly describe, so you can see how shame and guilt work and how people ease them. Rohan's story At a dinner, Rohan made a joke about his friend Leela's failed business, and the table laughed. Leela went quiet. For the next week he rehearsed it each night and did not answer her messages. The sentence he kept telling himself was "I am a terrible friend". What helped: He split the sentence. "I said something cruel" was about what he did, and could be dealt with. "I am terrible" was a verdict, and it kept him hiding. He repaired what he could. He rang Leela, said what he had said and that it was unkind, and did not ask her to say it was fine. He told someone. His brother listened and did not rush to excuse him. He spoke to himself as to a friend. He asked what he would say to a friend who had done the same. He let it do its work. The guilt had pointed him to Leela. Once he had called, he let it go. He asked for more help. The "terrible person" thought stayed for weeks, and he spoke to a counsellor. Leela took time to answer, and the friendship did not snap back at once. What it shows: Rohan did not need to feel nothing. Separating the deed from the verdict let him act, and the repair did more than the hiding had.

Arjuna on the battlefield In Gita 1.28-30 Arjuna sees his own kinsmen arrayed for battle. "O Krishna, seeing my own kinsmen arrayed for battle here and intent on killing each other, my limbs are giving way and my mouth is drying up." "My whole body shudders; my hair is standing on end. My bow, the Gāṇḍīv, is slipping from my hand, and my skin is burning all over." He reasons that "sin will certainly come upon us if we slay them" (1.36). The teaching of the rest of the Gita answers this distress, and the last verse read here is 18.66: "I shall liberate you from all sinful reactions; do not fear." What it shows: Arjuna is overwhelmed by the thought of a wrong not yet done, and what he is given is not a rule but a teaching. This is a moment in a dialogue and not a tale of shame, and linking it to shame and guilt is ours. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist, and shame that is heavy or lasting is worth telling someone about.

Narada and Sanatkumara In Chandogya 7.1 Narada comes to Sanatkumara and says: "Teach me, Sir!" Sanatkumara asks what he already knows. Narada lists the four Vedas and many sciences, then says: "with all this I know the Mantras only, the sacred books, I do not know the Self. I have heard from men like you, that he who knows the Self overcomes grief. I am in grief. Do, Sir, help me over this grief of mine." Sanatkumara's first reply is: "Whatever you have read, is only a name." A long teaching follows in the chapter. What it shows: Narada does not cover his grief with what he knows. He names it and asks for help. This is a moment in a dialogue and not a tale of shame or guilt, and linking it to them is ours. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist, and shame that is heavy or lasting is worth telling someone about.

The son who came to his senses In Luke 15 a younger son takes his share of the wealth, travels to "a distant region" and "squandered his wealth in dissolute living." A famine comes, and he feeds pigs and "would gladly have filled his stomach with the pods that the pigs were eating". Then: "when he came to his senses he said, 'How many of my father's hired hands have bread enough and to spare, but here I am dying of hunger! I will get up and go to my father, and I will say to him, "Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you; I am no longer worthy to be called your son."'" "While he was still far off, his father saw him and was filled with compassion; he ran and put his arms around him and kissed him." The father orders a robe, a ring and sandals, and says: "this son of mine was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found!" What it shows: The son's sense of unworthiness leads him to go home and say what he did, and the father does not wait for the speech to be finished. The story is about a father's welcome and not about shame as such; the link is ours. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist, and shame that is heavy or lasting is worth telling someone about.

Aṅgulimāla In MN 86 Aṅgulimāla, a former bandit who has become a monk, says of himself: "I have intentionally killed many living creatures." He is sent to a woman in a difficult labour with words that begin "Ever since I was born in the noble birth" and end: "By this truth, may both you and your baby be safe." She and the baby are safe. Later someone throws a stone, a stick and gravel at him. he goes to the Buddha "with cracked head, bleeding, his bowl broken, and his outer robe torn". The Buddha says: "Endure it, brahmin! Endure it, brahmin! You're experiencing in this very life the result of deeds that might have caused you to be tormented in hell for many years". He then speaks verses: "I used to be a bandit, the notorious Aṅgulimāla." "My name is 'Harmless', though I used to be harmful." And: "Someone whose bad deed is supplanted by the good, shines upon this world, like the moon freed from clouds." What it shows: Aṅgulimāla does not deny what he did, and does not stay defined by it. The sutta is about a murderer who becomes a monk and is not a tale of shame as such; the link is ours. It involves killing and harm to a body, and may be hard to read. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist, and shame that is heavy or lasting is worth telling someone about.

Alcibiades and Socrates In Plato's Symposium Alcibiades praises Socrates in a speech. He says that Socrates "makes me confess that I ought not to live as I do, neglecting the wants of my own soul, and busying myself with the concerns of the Athenians; therefore I hold my ears and tear myself away from him." Then: "he is the only person who ever made me ashamed, which you might think not to be in my nature". He cannot answer Socrates, and "when I leave his presence the love of popularity gets the better of me. And therefore I run away and fly from him, and when I see him I am ashamed of what I have confessed to him." What it shows: Alcibiades' shame shows him what he is neglecting, and he runs from it. The scene is a speech of praise and not an account of a remedy, and reading it as a picture of shame is ours. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist, and shame that is heavy or lasting is worth telling someone about.

Hopelessness is the belief that things will not get better and that nothing you do will change that. Despair is the deeper, heavier form. That is a standard definition and not taken from the papers below. Researchers have studied it as part of depression. Abela's study of third- and seventh-grade children tests "the hopelessness theory of depression", which names cognitive styles as "vulnerability factors". Maier and Seligman describe the older idea of learned helplessness: "Seligman and Maier (1967) theorized that animals learned that outcomes were independent of their responses-that nothing they did mattered", and then report that "the original theory got it backward". That work is on animals given shocks, and the abstract only speculates about what it means for people. Everyday signs, as people commonly describe them and not as findings from these papers: the future looks closed, effort feels pointless, and the thought "nothing will change" feels like a plain fact and not a thought. It overlaps with procrastination and fear and anxiety. Hopelessness can be a sign of depression, and it is nothing to be ashamed of. If it lasts or keeps coming back, please talk to a doctor, therapist or someone you trust. If you are thinking of ending your life or harming yourself, tell someone today, and if you may act on those thoughts contact your local emergency services now. The International Association for Suicide Prevention points to a directory of verified helplines in over 150 countries.

Hinduism has no single word in the Bhagavad Gita for hopelessness, but it shows the collapse. In Gita 1.47 Arjuna, "his mind in distress and overwhelmed with grief", "cast aside his bow and arrows, and sank into the seat of his chariot." Krishna answers: "how has this delusion overcome you in this hour of peril?" (2.2) and "it does not befit you to yield to this unmanliness. Give up such petty weakness of heart and arise" (2.3). This is related to hopelessness and not identical to it. Arjuna's despondency is about a battle and a duty, and Krishna's first words are a rebuke. They should not be read as "snap out of it" for someone whose low mood is an illness. The long teaching that follows was not read here. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist. If you are thinking of ending your life or harming yourself, please tell someone today and contact your local emergency services if you may act on it.

The Upanishads describe hope as a force, which shows by contrast what is missing in hopelessness. In Chandogya 7.14 Sanatkumara tells Narada: "Hope (āśā) is better than memory. Fired by hope does memory read the sacred hymns, perform sacrifices, desire sons and cattle, desire this world and the other." He adds that for one who meditates on hope as Brahman, "all his desires are fulfilled by hope, his prayers are not in vain". Narada asks: "Sir, is there something better than hope?" and the answer is: "Yes, there is something better than hope." This is related to hopelessness and not identical to it. The passage does not name despair, and reading hope's absence as despair is ours. It also ranks hope below something higher, which the next section names as breath. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist. If you are thinking of ending your life or harming yourself, please tell someone today and contact your local emergency services if you may act on it.

Christianity names despair openly. In Lamentations 3 the speaker says: "my soul is bereft of peace; I have forgotten what happiness is; so I say, 'Gone is my glory and all that I had hoped for from the Lord.'" Paul's letter to the Corinthians says: "afflicted in every way but not crushed, perplexed but not driven to despair" (2 Corinthians 4:8). The Psalms give the question: "How long, O Lord? Will you forget me forever? How long will you hide your face from me? How long must I bear pain in my soul and have sorrow in my heart all day long?" (13:1-2). This is related to hopelessness and not identical to it. These passages describe the state and do not offer a definition. Reading them together as an account of hopelessness is ours, and how the tradition treats despair as a doctrine was not checked. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist. If you are thinking of ending your life or harming yourself, please tell someone today and contact your local emergency services if you may act on it.

The Buddhist texts begin with suffering and hold out an end to it. In SN 56.11, the first teaching, the Buddha says: "Rebirth is suffering; old age is suffering; illness is suffering; death is suffering; being coupled with the disliked is suffering; separation from the liked is suffering; not getting what you wish for is suffering." Then: "Now this is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering. It's the fading away and cessation of that very same craving no residue left behind; giving it away, letting it go, releasing it, and not clinging to it." This is related to hopelessness and not identical to it. The sutta does not name hopelessness, and its subject is suffering in general. What it shows is the claim that suffering has an end, and the claim is the opposite of the belief that nothing can change. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist. If you are thinking of ending your life or harming yourself, please tell someone today and contact your local emergency services if you may act on it.

Boethius wrote the Consolation of Philosophy in prison, and it opens with his complaint: "Now perforce in tears and sadness / Learn a mournful strain to raise." Then Philosophy appears and names what she sees: "thou art pining with regretful longing for thy former fortune." She adds: "all sudden changes of circumstances bring inevitably a certain commotion of spirit. Thus it hath come to pass that thou also for awhile hast been parted from thy mind's tranquillity." This is related to hopelessness and not identical to it. Boethius' grief follows a loss of fortune, and Philosophy treats it as a sickness of the mind that she can address. Later lines of his opening song long for death and are not quoted here; the pages of the work were read only in part. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist. If you are thinking of ending your life or harming yourself, please tell someone today and contact your local emergency services if you may act on it.

The sources read here point to a few causes, and are limited. A way of explaining bad events. Abela's study found that "A depressogenic attributional style interacted with negative events to predict increases in depressive symptoms in seventh-grade children but not in third-grade children." It also reports that "None of these interactions were mediated by hopelessness", so that study did not find hopelessness to be the route. It followed children for six weekly assessments. Prolonged hard events. Maier and Seligman report that "Passivity in response to shock is not learned. It is the default, unlearned response to prolonged aversive events", and that it "can be overcome by learning control". This is work on animals. Depression itself. Common description, not from these papers: low mood makes the future look bleak, and the bleakness then feels like evidence. Loss, illness, isolation and long strain. Also common description, not from these papers. Hopelessness is not a character flaw. Hopelessness can be a sign of depression, and it is nothing to be ashamed of. If it lasts or keeps coming back, please talk to a doctor, therapist or someone you trust. If you are thinking of ending your life or harming yourself, tell someone today, and if you may act on those thoughts contact your local emergency services now. The International Association for Suicide Prevention points to a directory of verified helplines in over 150 countries.

The Gita's account of Arjuna's collapse names attachment and delusion. The translator's commentary on 1.47 says: "He had now surrendered to his grief and slumped into deep dejection. His condition was the creation of his own material attachments". After the teaching Arjuna says: "by Your grace my illusion has been dispelled, and I am situated in knowledge. I am now free from doubts" (18.73), and Krishna had asked at the start: "how has this delusion overcome you in this hour of peril?" (2.2). This is related to hopelessness and not identical to it. The cause given is attachment and illusion, in one man's situation, and the commentary's wording is blunt. It should not be read as saying that people who feel hopeless have brought it on themselves, and low mood can have other causes. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist. If you are thinking of ending your life or harming yourself, please tell someone today and contact your local emergency services if you may act on it.

Chandogya 7 builds a ladder of "better than", and at its end it puts the root of acting in a condition of the self. In 7.19-7.22 Sanatkumara says: "When one believes, then one perceives." "When one attends on a tutor (spiritual guide), then one believes." "When one performs all sacred duties, then one attends really on a tutor." And: "When one obtains bliss (in oneself), then one performs duties. One who does not obtain bliss, does not perform duties." The chain runs from bliss back to the self's condition, and says that where it is lacking, nothing follows. This is related to hopelessness and not identical to it. The passage is about the order in which knowledge arises, and says nothing of depression or despair. Reading it as a root of hopelessness is ours, and it should not be used to blame anyone who finds it hard to act. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist. If you are thinking of ending your life or harming yourself, please tell someone today and contact your local emergency services if you may act on it.

Lamentations 3 shows how brooding feeds despair: "The thought of my affliction and my homelessness is wormwood and gall! My soul continually thinks of it and is bowed down within me." In 1 Kings 19 the prophet Elijah, after a threat, is afraid: "he got up and fled for his life". In the wilderness he "came and sat down under a solitary broom tree. He asked that he might die, 'It is enough; now, O Lord, take away my life, for I am no better than my ancestors.'" This is related to hopelessness and not identical to it. The causes named are affliction, fear and a sense of failure. The text does not give a single cause, and reading these as roots of hopelessness is ours. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist. If you are thinking of ending your life or harming yourself, please tell someone today and contact your local emergency services if you may act on it.

The Buddhist texts name craving as the origin of suffering. SN 56.11: "Now this is the noble truth of the origin of suffering. It's the craving that leads to future lives, mixed up with relishing and greed, taking pleasure there wherever it alights. That is, craving for sensual pleasures, craving for continued existence, and craving for nonexistence." The Buddha also lists, among kinds of suffering, "not getting what you wish for". This is related to hopelessness and not identical to it. The sutta explains suffering in general, and the origin it names is craving, which does not match the usual causes of a depressed mood. It should not be read as saying that people who feel hopeless have caused it by wanting. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist. If you are thinking of ending your life or harming yourself, please tell someone today and contact your local emergency services if you may act on it.

Seneca locates the trouble in looking ahead. Letters 5: "hope and fear, dissimilar as they are, keep step together; fear follows hope." And: "the chief cause of both these ills is that we do not adapt ourselves to the present, but send our thoughts a long way ahead." Boethius' Philosophy gives a second cause: "all sudden changes of circumstances bring inevitably a certain commotion of spirit." This is related to hopelessness and not identical to it. Seneca is writing about hope and fear and does not recommend giving up hope; the same letter quotes Hecato: "Cease to hope," he says, "and you will cease to fear", which is about calming desire and is not advice to despair. Reading the passages as causes of hopelessness is ours. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist. If you are thinking of ending your life or harming yourself, please tell someone today and contact your local emergency services if you may act on it.

The research read here describes effects on mood, and on risk. Abela's study reports that a depressogenic way of explaining events predicted "increases in depressive symptoms". Maier and Seligman describe passivity: in their animals it is mediated by an area of the brain that "in turn inhibits escape", and "can be overcome by learning control". A meta-analysis by Ribeiro and colleagues looked at depression and hopelessness as risk factors for suicidal thoughts and behaviours. It found that "Overall prediction was weaker than anticipated, with weighted mean odds ratios of 1.96 (1.81-2.13) for ideation, 1.63 (1.55-1.72) for attempt and 1.33 (1.18-1.49) for death". In plain terms, these factors went with higher odds, yet the authors call the prediction "weaker than anticipated", so hopelessness alone does not tell anyone what a person will do, and the abstract adds that methodological limits were prominent. Common effects, as people describe them and not findings from these papers: pulling away from people, doing less, sleep and appetite changing, and the future shrinking to the next hour. Hopelessness is a good reason to reach out, and not a reason to wait. Hopelessness can be a sign of depression, and it is nothing to be ashamed of. If it lasts or keeps coming back, please talk to a doctor, therapist or someone you trust. If you are thinking of ending your life or harming yourself, tell someone today, and if you may act on those thoughts contact your local emergency services now. The International Association for Suicide Prevention points to a directory of verified helplines in over 150 countries.

The Gita shows what hopelessness does to action. Arjuna "cast aside his bow and arrows, and sank into the seat of his chariot" (1.47). The commentary says: "Arjun's reluctance to fight the war had now reached its climax. He had now surrendered to his grief and slumped into deep dejection." The other side is the end of the teaching, in 18.73: "I am now free from doubts, and I shall act according to Your instructions." This is related to hopelessness and not identical to it. The effect shown is stopping, and the recovery comes through a long teaching, not a quick fix. The text shows that dejection can end, and does not say how long it takes. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist. If you are thinking of ending your life or harming yourself, please tell someone today and contact your local emergency services if you may act on it.

The Upanishads link hope and action. Chandogya 7.14: "Fired by hope does memory read the sacred hymns, perform sacrifices, desire sons and cattle, desire this world and the other." In 7.22: "When one obtains bliss (in oneself), then one performs duties. One who does not obtain bliss, does not perform duties." The effect named is that without the inner condition, action does not follow. This is related to hopelessness and not identical to it. Neither passage speaks of despair, and the second is about knowledge and not about mood. Reading them as effects of hopelessness is ours. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist. Psalm 88 describes the effects without softening them: "You have caused my companions to shun me; you have made me a thing of horror to them. I am shut in so that I cannot escape; my eye grows dim through sorrow." It ends without relief: "You have caused friend and neighbor to shun me; my companions are in darkness." Lamentations 3 adds the loss of happiness: "I have forgotten what happiness is". This is related to hopelessness and not identical to it. The Bible keeps a prayer that does not resolve, and does not say it should. Reading it as a description of hopelessness is ours. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist. If you are thinking of ending your life or harming yourself, please tell someone today and contact your local emergency services if you may act on it.

The Buddhist texts show what loss does. In the verses of Kisāgotamī (Thig 10.1) she says: "I was on the road, near to giving birth, when I saw my husband dead. I gave birth there on the road before I'd reached my own house. My two children have died, and on the road my husband lies dead". The teacher answers: "Oh woe is you whose family is lost, the suffering you have undergone has no measure". The poem includes lines about women harming themselves, which are left out here. This is related to hopelessness and not identical to it. The poem is about grief after death and does not name hopelessness, and reading it as an effect of despair is ours. It involves the deaths of children and may be hard to read. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist. Boethius describes what grief did to him: "Old? Ah yes; swift, ere I knew it, / By these sorrows on me pressed / Age hath come; lo, Grief hath bid me / Wear the garb that fits her best." And: "And the skin hangs loose and shrivelled / On this sorrow-shrunken frame." Philosophy names a further effect: "thou also for awhile hast been parted from thy mind's tranquillity." This is related to hopelessness and not identical to it. The song is a poet's description of grief, and the lines that follow it, which long for death, are not quoted. Reading the passage as an effect of hopelessness is ours. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist. If you are thinking of ending your life or harming yourself, please tell someone today and contact your local emergency services if you may act on it.

The research read here describes the problem and mostly tests no remedy. Maier and Seligman report, in animals, that passivity "can be overcome by learning control", and their abstract only speculates about "how to treat depression". The rest is common advice. Say what it is. "I feel hopeless" is a report about now. "Nothing will ever change" is a prediction, and low mood makes poor predictions. That is common advice. Tell someone. A friend, family member, doctor or therapist. Hopelessness tends to want silence, and saying it aloud often loosens it. That is common advice. Get treatment. Doctors and therapists treat low mood and hopelessness, and persistent low mood may be depression. That is a standard statement, not tied to a study read here. Make one small thing. A short walk, a message, a meal. Maier and Seligman's animal work is about control, and linking it to small acts is the site's own idea and is untested here. Look after the basics. Sleep, food, daylight, company. That is common advice. Keep safe. Hopelessness can be a sign of depression, and it is nothing to be ashamed of. If it lasts or keeps coming back, please talk to a doctor, therapist or someone you trust. The Gita offers self-effort and patience, and it should be read with care. Rise. 2.3: "Give up such petty weakness of heart and arise". This is said to a healthy warrior, and for someone who is ill it is not an instruction to try harder. Use the mind as an ally. 6.5: "Elevate yourself through the power of your mind, and not degrade yourself, for the mind can be the friend and also the enemy of the self." Practise. 6.35: "the mind is indeed very difficult to restrain. But by practice and detachment, it can be controlled." This is related to hopelessness and not identical to it. These verses are about the disciplined life and do not speak of depression, and Krishna in 6.35 agrees that the mind is hard to restrain. Reading them as a way through hopelessness is ours, and they do not replace a doctor or therapist. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist. If you are thinking of ending your life or harming yourself, please tell someone today and contact your local emergency services if you may act on it.

The Upanishads answer with strength, steadiness and knowledge, and not with a technique. Note: This is an invented composite story, not a real case. It is built from patterns people commonly describe, so you can see how hopelessness works and how people find a way through it. Priya's story After a redundancy and months of searching for work, Priya stopped applying. "Nothing is going to change" had stopped feeling like a thought and had started feeling like a fact. She slept late, let messages pile up, and told her sister she was fine. What helped: She said what it was. "I feel hopeless" was about now. "Nothing will change" was a prediction made by a tired mind. She told someone. Her sister came round and did not try to fix it, only stayed. She saw a doctor. She said that some nights she did not want to be here. It was the hardest sentence she had said, and the doctor took it seriously and arranged treatment and a follow-up. She made one small thing. A ten-minute walk, then one email a day. She looked after the basics. She went to bed at a fixed time, and kept the curtains open. She kept someone close. She and her sister spoke every evening for a month. It took months and it was not a straight line, and some days she did only the walk. What it shows: Priya did not argue herself out of hopelessness. Telling people, and getting treatment, gave her a future to act in again.

Arjuna sinks, and rises In Gita 1.47 Arjuna, "his mind in distress and overwhelmed with grief", "cast aside his bow and arrows, and sank into the seat of his chariot." Krishna answers: "it does not befit you to yield to this unmanliness. Give up such petty weakness of heart and arise" (2.3). Later, answering a remark about how hard the mind is to hold, Krishna says: "what you say is correct; the mind is indeed very difficult to restrain. But by practice and detachment, it can be controlled" (6.35). At the end Arjuna says: "by Your grace my illusion has been dispelled, and I am situated in knowledge. I am now free from doubts, and I shall act according to Your instructions" (18.73). What it shows: The man who sat down gets up again, and the way between is a long conversation. This is a moment in a dialogue and not a tale of despair, and linking it to hopelessness is ours. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist. Boethius in prison Boethius writes his Consolation in prison. He begins: "Now perforce in tears and sadness / Learn a mournful strain to raise." Then a woman appears above his head, "of a countenance exceeding venerable", and she is Philosophy. She tells him: "thou art pining with regretful longing for thy former fortune." She does not scold. "What is it, then, poor mortal, that hath cast thee into lamentation and mourning?" And she begins gently: "it is time for thee to take and drain a draught, soft and pleasant to the taste, which, as it penetrates within, may prepare the way for stronger potions." What it shows: The first help Boethius is given is attention and a gentle remedy, and stronger medicine comes later. The scene opens a long argument and is not a tale of hopelessness as such; the link is ours, and the rest of the work was not read. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist. Loneliness is the painful gap between the connection you want and the connection you have. Social isolation is having few contacts. You can have either without the other, which is a standard distinction and not taken from the papers below. Researchers describe it as "perceived social isolation (i.e. loneliness)". Cacioppo and Hawkley report research that links it to "heightened sensitivity to social threats, a confirmatory bias in social cognition that is self-protective and paradoxically self-defeating". That is one way of describing the pull to withdraw while wanting company. Holt-Lunstad and colleagues write that "Actual and perceived social isolation are both associated with increased risk for early mortality." Everyday signs, as people commonly describe them and not as findings from these papers: staying in when invitations come, reading a short reply as a rejection, feeling alone in a crowd, and wanting someone but not knowing whom to ask. It overlaps with shame and guilt and self-doubt. Loneliness is common and nothing to be ashamed of. If it is heavy or lasts, or comes with hopeless thoughts, please talk to a doctor, therapist or someone you trust. If you are thinking of ending your life or harming yourself, tell someone today, and if you may act on those thoughts contact your local emergency services now. Hinduism has no single word in the Bhagavad Gita for loneliness, but it treats both company and solitude. Gita 6.10 says: "Those who seek the state of Yog should reside in seclusion, constantly engaged in meditation with a controlled mind and body". That is solitude chosen for practice. On the other side, 5.29 describes the Lord as "the selfless friend of all living beings": "Having realized Me as the enjoyer of all sacrifices and austerities, the Supreme Lord of all the worlds and the selfless friend of all living beings, My devotee attains peace." This is related to loneliness and not identical to it. 6.10 is about a discipline of seclusion and not about the ache of being alone, and 5.29 speaks of peace and not of human company. Reading them together as an account of loneliness is ours. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist, and loneliness that is heavy or lasting is worth telling someone about.

The Upanishads describe separateness as a kind of small seeing. Isha 6-7: "he who beholds all beings in the Self, and the Self in all beings, he never turns away from it. When to a man who understands, the Self has become all things, what sorrow, what trouble can there be to him who once beheld that unity?" Chandogya 7.24 draws the line: "Where one sees nothing else, hears nothing else, understands nothing else, that is the Infinite. Where one sees something else, hears something else, understands something else, that is the finite." This is related to loneliness and not identical to it. Both passages are about seeing the Self in all things and say nothing of lacking company, so reading them as an account of loneliness is ours. They do not say the lonely person has failed to see anything. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist, and loneliness that is heavy or lasting is worth telling someone about.

Christianity says aloneness is a lack. In Genesis 2:18: "It is not good that the man should be alone; I will make him a helper as his partner." The Psalms give the voice of the lonely: "Turn to me and be gracious to me, for I am lonely and afflicted" (25:16). And the answer: "Father of orphans and protector of widows is God in his holy habitation. God gives the desolate a home to live in" (68:5-6). This is related to loneliness and not identical to it. These passages name the want of company and a promise of a home. They do not define loneliness, and reading them together as an account of it is ours. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist, and loneliness that is heavy or lasting is worth telling someone about.

The Buddhist texts praise good company, and they also praise solitude. In SN 45.2 Ānanda says: "Sir, good friends, companions, and associates are half the spiritual life." The Buddha answers: "Not so, Ānanda! Not so, Ānanda! Good friends, companions, and associates are the whole of the spiritual life." Dhp 328-329 gives both: "If you find an alert companion, an attentive friend to live happily together, then, overcoming all adversities, wander with them, joyful and mindful." "If you find no alert companion, no attentive friend to live happily together, then, like a king who flees his conquered realm, wander alone like a tusker in the wilds." Epictetus separates being alone from being lonely. Discourses 3.13: "Solitude is a certain condition of a helpless man. For because a man is alone, he is not for that reason also solitary; just as though a man is among numbers, he is not therefore not solitary." And: "it is not the sight of a human creature which removes us from solitude, but the sight of one who is faithful and modest and helpful to us." Aristotle says why we feel it: "without friends no one would choose to live, though he had all other goods" (Nicomachean Ethics 8.1). This is related to loneliness and not identical to it. Epictetus' word, translated "solitude" and "solitary", means being left helpless and without anyone to trust, and the passage goes on to argue for being sufficient to oneself. Aristotle is writing about friendship. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist, and loneliness that is heavy or lasting is worth telling someone about.

The sources read here point to a few causes, and are limited. Trends. Masi and colleagues note that "Social and demographic trends are placing an increasing number of adults at risk for loneliness". A threat-watching mind. Cacioppo and Hawkley report "heightened sensitivity to social threats" and "a confirmatory bias in social cognition that is self-protective and paradoxically self-defeating". A lonely mind may read cold signals into ordinary events, and avoid people, which keeps it lonely. The abstract says research indicates this and does not say which comes first. Social thinking that has gone wrong. Masi and colleagues say the most successful interventions "addressed maladaptive social cognition", "consistent with current theories regarding loneliness and its etiology". Everyday causes. Common description, not from these papers: moving, losing someone, a change of job or life stage, illness, shyness, and shame about being alone. Loneliness is not a character flaw. Loneliness is common and nothing to be ashamed of. If it is heavy or lasts, or comes with hopeless thoughts, please talk to a doctor, therapist or someone you trust. They are free from attachment to possessions and egotism, equipoised in happiness and distress, and ever-forgiving." By implication, malice, attachment and egotism are what stand between a person and others. This is related to loneliness and not identical to it. The Buddhist texts count separation as suffering. SN 56.11: "being coupled with the disliked is suffering; separation from the liked is suffering; not getting what you wish for is suffering." Aristotle and Epictetus both root it in our nature. Aristotle, Politics 1.2: "man is by nature a political animal." And: "the individual, when isolated, is not self-sufficing; and therefore he is like a part in relation to the whole." Epictetus: people feel it because "they set out from a certain natural principle, from the natural desire of community and mutual love and from the pleasure of conversation among men." This is related to loneliness and not identical to it. Aristotle is describing the state and the individual, and "political animal" is about life in a community and not only about feelings. Both passages say the wish for company is natural, and that is not a fault. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist, and loneliness that is heavy or lasting is worth telling someone about.

The research read here describes effects, mostly as statistical associations. Holt-Lunstad and colleagues (2015) report that "social isolation odds ratio (OR) = 1.29, loneliness OR = 1.26, and living alone OR = 1.32, corresponding to an average of 29%, 26%, and 32% increased likelihood of mortality, respectively", and that "initial health status has an influence on the findings". Holt-Lunstad, Smith and Layton (2010), across "148 studies (308,849 participants)", report a "50% increased likelihood of survival for participants with stronger social relationships". These are group averages from observational studies and say nothing certain about any one person. Cacioppo and Hawkley report that perceived social isolation "is a risk factor for, and may contribute to, poorer overall cognitive performance, faster cognitive decline, poorer executive functioning, increased negativity and depressive cognition". Common effects, as people describe them and not findings from these papers: poor sleep, low mood, pulling further away, and doing less. None of this is a reason for alarm. It is a reason to ask for company. Loneliness is common and nothing to be ashamed of.
