Note: This is an invented composite story, not a real case. It is built from patterns people commonly describe, so you can see how loneliness works and how people ease it. Tomás's story Tomás moved to a new city for work. The evenings were long and the flat was quiet. A colleague invited him for a drink and he said he was busy, because he assumed the invitation was politeness. A few weeks later he noticed he had stopped checking his phone. What helped: He named it. "I am lonely" was about now. It did not mean something was wrong with him. He checked the story. He asked what else the invitation could have been, and decided it might simply have been an invitation. He added small contacts. A weekly call with his brother, and a Thursday walk with the colleague. He found a shared task. He joined a five-a-side game, where there was something to do besides talk. He reached out first. He asked two people from the game to dinner. He asked for more help. Some evenings were still heavy, so he told his doctor, who suggested a counsellor. It took months, and some weeks he still cancelled. What it shows: Tomás did not need a crowd. A few regular contacts, and a different reading of one invitation, were enough to start.

A seat in seclusion, and a friend of all Two verses of the Gita put solitude and company side by side. In 6.10: "Those who seek the state of Yog should reside in seclusion, constantly engaged in meditation with a controlled mind and body, getting rid of desires and possessions for enjoyment." In 5.29 the Lord is described as "the selfless friend of all living beings": "My devotee attains peace." What it shows: The yogi alone in seclusion is not described as abandoned, since the same text names a friend of all beings. This is a picture drawn from two verses and not a tale of a lonely person, and linking it to loneliness is ours. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist, and loneliness that is heavy or lasting is worth telling someone about.

Seeing all beings in the Self In Isha 6-7 a teacher says: "he who beholds all beings in the Self, and the Self in all beings, he never turns away from it. When to a man who understands, the Self has become all things, what sorrow, what trouble can there be to him who once beheld that unity?" What it shows: The verse holds up a person for whom nothing is other, and so nothing left out. It is a picture and not a tale, and linking it to loneliness is ours. It should not be read as saying that a lonely person is missing something. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist, and loneliness that is heavy or lasting is worth telling someone about.

Ruth and Naomi In Ruth 1 Naomi, widowed and with both sons dead, sets out for home. She urges her daughters-in-law to turn back, and one does. Ruth does not: "Do not press me to leave you, to turn back from following you! Where you go, I will go; where you lodge, I will lodge; your people shall be my people and your God my God. Where you die, I will die, and there will I be buried." At Bethlehem the women ask: "Is this Naomi?" She says: "Call me no longer Naomi; call me Mara, for the Almighty has dealt bitterly with me. I went away full, but the Lord has brought me back empty". What it shows: Naomi arrives home with a companion, though she does not feel it yet. The story is about loyalty and loss and not about loneliness as such; the link is ours. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist, and loneliness that is heavy or lasting is worth telling someone about.

The Buddha and the bull elephant In Ud 4.5 the Buddha is "crowded by monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen; by rulers and their chief ministers, and monastics of other religions and their disciples." He thinks: "Why don't I live alone, withdrawn from the group?" He sets out "to go wandering alone toward Pārileyyaka, with no companion." A bull elephant, "crowded by other males, females, younglings, and cubs", has had the same thought: "Why don't I live alone, withdrawn from the herd?" He comes to the Buddha and attends on him, "clearing the vegetation from the place where the Buddha stayed, and using his trunk to set out water for drinking and washing." The Buddha says: "The giant elephant, with tusks like draft-poles, agrees heart to heart with the spiritual giant, since each finds joy in the woods alone." What it shows: This is solitude chosen and enjoyed, and not loneliness. The elephant who is also alone becomes a companion, and the text counts that as joy. The link to loneliness is ours. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist, and loneliness that is heavy or lasting is worth telling someone about.

Zeus alone, and the children with shells Epictetus takes the case of Zeus alone: "if being alone is enough to make solitude, you may say that even Zeus is solitary in the conflagration and bewails himself saying, 'Unhappy that I am who have neither Hera, nor Athena, nor Apollo, nor brother, nor son, nor descendant nor kinsman.'" But he answers: "as Zeus dwells with himself, and is tranquil by himself, and thinks of his own administration and of its nature, and is employed in thoughts suitable to himself; so ought we also to be able to talk with ourselves". And of children left alone: "They take up shells and ashes, and they build something, then pull it down, and build something else, and so they never want the means of passing the time." What it shows: Epictetus argues that company does not prove one is not lonely, and that being alone does not prove one is. It is an argument and not a tale, and linking it to loneliness is ours. For many people being alone with their thoughts is not easy, so this should not be read as advice that a lonely person should simply be content. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist, and loneliness that is heavy or lasting is worth telling someone about.

Addiction is a repeated pull toward a substance or an activity, such as alcohol, drugs, gambling, a phone or pornography, that goes on despite a wish to stop and despite the harm. Compulsion is the sense that the act is driven and not chosen. Those are standard descriptions and not taken from the papers below. Researchers disagree about what to call it. Leshner writes that "drug addiction is a chronic, relapsing disease that results from the prolonged effects of drugs on the brain", with "behavioral and social-context aspects" that "are important parts of the disorder itself". Lewis describes Heyman's view differently: "Rather than view addiction as a disease, Heyman sees it as a choice-one that works like other choices, whereby immediate rewards outshine long-term gains." Lewis himself argues that "the disease-versus-choice debate creates a false dichotomy". These abstracts are about drugs and alcohol, and do not cover phones or gambling. Everyday signs, as people commonly describe them and not as findings from these papers: doing more than you meant, failed attempts to cut down, hiding it, and craving when a cue appears. It overlaps with impulsivity and distraction. Struggling to stop is common, and it is nothing to be ashamed of. If you are finding it hard, please talk to a doctor, therapist or a local support service. Stopping some substances suddenly, including alcohol and certain medicines, can be dangerous, so ask a doctor before stopping on your own (a standard safety point, not drawn from the papers below). If you are in danger, or thinking of harming yourself, contact your local emergency services now; the International Association for Suicide Prevention points to a directory of verified helplines in over 150 countries.

Hinduism has no single word in the Bhagavad Gita for addiction, but it describes the pull. Gita 2.60: "The senses are so strong and turbulent, O son of Kunti, that they can forcibly carry away the mind even of a person endowed with discrimination who practices self-control." And 3.34: "The senses naturally experience attachment and aversion to the sense objects, but do not be controlled by them, for they are way-layers and foes." This is related to addiction and not identical to it. The verses are about the senses and the mind in general, and do not describe a medical condition. Reading them as an account of compulsion is ours. They say that even a disciplined person can be carried away, which is a reason to see the pull as common and not shameful. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist, and a doctor can help with stopping safely.

The Upanishads name the same pull as the choice of the pleasant over the good. Katha 1.2.1: "The good is one thing, the pleasant another; these two, having different objects, chain a man. It is well with him who clings to the good; he who chooses the pleasant, misses his end." And 1.3.5: "He who has no understanding and whose mind (the reins) is never firmly held, his senses (horses) are unmanageable, like vicious horses of a charioteer." This is related to addiction and not identical to it. The Katha describes a choice made by a person with understanding or without it, and does not describe a condition that takes the choice away. Reading it as an account of compulsion is ours. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist, and a doctor can help with stopping safely.

Paul describes what it is like to act against your own wish. Romans 7:15: "I do not understand my own actions. For I do not do what I want, but I do the very thing I hate." And 7:19: "For I do not do the good I want, but the evil I do not want is what I do." This is related to addiction and not identical to it. Paul is writing about sin and the law, and the verses are not about substances or behaviours. Reading them as an account of compulsion is ours. The tradition's word for what he describes is not applied to people who struggle with addiction here, and the site does not treat addiction as a sin. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist, and a doctor can help with stopping safely.

The Buddhist texts name the pull as craving. SN 56.11, the first teaching: "Now this is the noble truth of the origin of suffering. It's the craving that leads to future lives, mixed up with relishing and greed, taking pleasure there wherever it alights." Dhp 334: "When a man lives heedlessly, craving grows in them like a camel's foot creeper. They jump from one thing to the next, like a langur greedy for fruit in a forest grove." This is related to addiction and not identical to it. The Pali word for craving is broader than addiction, and the texts describe it as part of ordinary suffering. Reading them as an account of compulsion is ours. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist, and a doctor can help with stopping safely.

Aristotle describes acting against what you know. Nicomachean Ethics 7.1: "the incontinent man, knowing that what he does is bad, does it as a result of passion, while the continent man, knowing that his appetites are bad, refuses on account of his rational principle to follow them". Plato gives the picture. Phaedrus: "the human charioteer drives his in a pair; and one of them is noble and of noble breed, and the other is ignoble and of ignoble breed; and the driving of them of necessity gives a great deal of trouble to him." This is related to addiction and not identical to it. Aristotle's "incontinence" (the Greek word is akrasia, weakness of will) is about acting against one's judgment and not about a medical condition, and Plato's image is of the soul in general. Reading them as an account of addiction is ours. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist, and a doctor can help with stopping safely.

The sources read here offer accounts of why it happens, and they disagree. The brain's response to repeated use. Leshner: addiction "results from the prolonged effects of drugs on the brain". Lewis: "the salience of drug-related cues is enhanced by dopamine activity in the ventral striatum, orbitofrontal cortex, and amygdala, due to the intense hedonic impact of repeated drug experiences", and "dopamine-based craving peaks when drug (or alcohol or gambling) rewards become available, in the moment, and this rapid increase in attractiveness preempts rational judgment." Choice, with the odds tilted. Lewis calls addiction "a recurrent series of choices that permit negotiation, and sometimes cooperation, between immediate and long-range goals." A challenge to the dopamine account. Heyman writes that "there is more to the biology of addiction than dopamine", and cites an experiment in which "rats readily gave up cocaine for saccharin, even when they had been consuming massive amounts of the drug for weeks." Common causes, as people describe them and not findings from these abstracts: stress, trauma, loneliness, easy access, and family history. None of this makes anyone to blame. Struggling to stop is common, and it is nothing to be ashamed of. If you are finding it hard, please talk to a doctor, therapist or a local support service. Stopping some substances suddenly, including alcohol and certain medicines, can be dangerous, so ask a doctor before stopping on your own (a standard safety point, not drawn from the papers below). If you are in danger, or thinking of harming yourself, contact your local emergency services now; the International Association for Suicide Prevention points to a directory of verified helplines in over 150 countries.

The Gita describes a chain that starts with dwelling on the object. 2.62: "While contemplating on the objects of the senses, one develops attachment to them. Attachment leads to desire, and from desire arises anger." 2.63 continues: "Anger leads to clouding of judgment, which results in bewilderment of memory. When memory is bewildered, the intellect gets destroyed; and when the intellect is destroyed, one is ruined." This is related to addiction and not identical to it. The chain is a general account of how desire grows and ends in anger and confusion, and it does not mention substances or a medical cause. Reading it as a root of compulsion is ours. The word "ruined" is the translator's, and it should not be taken as a verdict on a person. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist, and a doctor can help with stopping safely.

The Katha puts the cause in who is holding the reins. 1.3.3-4: "Know the Self to be sitting in the chariot, the body to be the chariot, the intellect (buddhi) the charioteer, and the mind the reins. The senses they call the horses, the objects of the senses their roads." 1.3.5: "He who has no understanding and whose mind (the reins) is never firmly held, his senses (horses) are unmanageable, like vicious horses of a charioteer." This is related to addiction and not identical to it. The image is of the person as a whole and is not an account of the causes of a condition. Reading it as a root of compulsion is ours, and it should not be used to say that people who struggle lack understanding. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist, and a doctor can help with stopping safely.

Paul describes a split between wanting and doing. Romans 7:18-19: "For I know that the good does not dwell within me, that is, in my flesh. For the desire to do the good lies close at hand, but not the ability." And 7:23: "but I see in my members another law at war with the law of my mind, making me captive to the law of sin that dwells in my members." In 1 Corinthians 6:12: "'All things are permitted for me,' but I will not be dominated by anything." This is related to addiction and not identical to it. The passages are about sin and the flesh, and the cause they name is a divided self. Reading them as roots of compulsion is ours, and the site does not treat addiction as a sin. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist, and a doctor can help with stopping safely.

The Buddhist texts name craving as the origin. SN 56.11: "It's the craving that leads to future lives, mixed up with relishing and greed, taking pleasure there wherever it alights. That is, craving for sensual pleasures, craving for continued existence, and craving for nonexistence." Dhp 334 adds heedlessness: "When a man lives heedlessly, craving grows in them like a camel's foot creeper." This is related to addiction and not identical to it. Craving here is the root of suffering for everyone, and the texts do not discuss addiction as a condition. Reading them as a root of compulsion is ours, and it should not be read as saying that people with an addiction have caused it by wanting. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist, and a doctor can help with stopping safely.

Plato locates the trouble in the mixed nature of the soul. Phaedrus: "the human charioteer drives his in a pair; and one of them is noble and of noble breed, and the other is ignoble and of ignoble breed; and the driving of them of necessity gives a great deal of trouble to him." Aristotle says who is most at risk of acting before thinking: "It is keen and excitable people that suffer especially from the impetuous form of incontinence; for the former by reason of their quickness and the latter by reason of the violence of their passions do not await the argument, because they are apt to follow their imagination." This is related to addiction and not identical to it. Plato's image is of the soul and Aristotle's of weakness of will, and neither is about dependence on a substance. Reading them as roots of addiction is ours. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist, and a doctor can help with stopping safely.

The research read here describes costs mostly for alcohol and drugs. Kelly and colleagues write that "Alcohol and other drug (AOD) problems confer a global, prodigious burden of disease, disability, and premature mortality." The Cochrane review adds that alcohol use disorder "confers a prodigious burden of disease, disability, premature mortality, and high economic costs from lost productivity, accidents, violence, incarceration, and increased healthcare utilization." Leshner points to "the health and social costs associated with drug abuse and addiction". These abstracts are about alcohol and other drugs, and do not cover phones, gambling or pornography. Common effects, as people describe them and not findings from these papers: secrecy, money trouble, strained relationships, poor sleep, and a growing distance from what you used to enjoy. Shame often follows, and it tends to feed the pattern; see shame and guilt. Struggling to stop is common, and it is nothing to be ashamed of. If you are finding it hard, please talk to a doctor, therapist or a local support service. Stopping some substances suddenly, including alcohol and certain medicines, can be dangerous, so ask a doctor before stopping on your own (a standard safety point, not drawn from the papers below). If you are in danger, or thinking of harming yourself, contact your local emergency services now; the International Association for Suicide Prevention points to a directory of verified helplines in over 150 countries.

The Gita names where the chain ends. 2.63: "Anger leads to clouding of judgment, which results in bewilderment of memory. When memory is bewildered, the intellect gets destroyed; and when the intellect is destroyed, one is ruined." And 3.37 names the enemy: "It is lust alone, which is born of contact with the mode of passion, and later transformed into anger. Know this as the sinful, all-devouring enemy in the world." The commentary on 3.37 says the Vedas use the word for lust "not only for sexual desires but also to include all desires for material enjoyment". This is related to addiction and not identical to it. The verses describe what unchecked desire does, and the harsh words ("ruined", "sinful", "enemy") are the translator's and should not be taken as a verdict on a person. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist, and a doctor can help with stopping safely.

The Katha names the cost of the pleasant. 1.2.1: "he who chooses the pleasant, misses his end." And 1.3.7: "He who has no understanding, who is unmindful and always impure, never reaches that place, but enters into the round of births." This is related to addiction and not identical to it. The passages are about what a life spent on the pleasant misses, and are not about the effects of a condition. Reading them as effects of addiction is ours, and the harsh verdict of 1.3.7 should not be taken as a verdict on anyone who struggles. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist, and a doctor can help with stopping safely.

Proverbs describes the effects of drinking without softening them: "Who has woe? Who has sorrow? Who has strife? Who has complaining? Who has wounds without cause? Who has redness of eyes? Those who linger late over wine". It ends with the voice of the one who cannot stop: "'They struck me,' you will say, 'but I was not hurt; they beat me, but I did not feel it. When shall I awake? I will seek another drink.'" Romans 7:24 gives the cry: "Wretched person that I am! Who will rescue me from this body of death?" This is related to addiction and not identical to it. Proverbs is wisdom writing about wine, and Romans 7:24 is about sin. Reading them together as effects of addiction is ours. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist, and a doctor can help with stopping safely.

The Buddhist texts set sorrow and its falling away side by side. Dhp 335: "Whoever is beaten by this wretched craving, this attachment to the world, their sorrow grows, like grass in the rain." Dhp 336: "But whoever prevails over this wretched craving, so hard to get over in the world, their sorrows fall from them, like a drop from a lotus-leaf." This is related to addiction and not identical to it. The verses are about craving in general and say it is "so hard to get over", which is a gentle word for the difficulty. Reading them as effects of addiction is ours. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist, and a doctor can help with stopping safely.

Aristotle describes what follows the act. Nicomachean Ethics 7.8: "incontinent man is likely to repent." He draws a contrast with the self-indulgent man, who "stands by his choice". He also says: "the incontinent man curable". Plato's picture gives the cost of the struggle: "the driving of them of necessity gives a great deal of trouble to him." This is related to addiction and not identical to it. Aristotle's "curable" is about weakness of will and not a medical claim, and the passage compares the two kinds of person in terms the site does not adopt. Reading these as effects of addiction is ours. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist, and a doctor can help with stopping safely.

The research read here finds that recovery is common and that help takes several forms. Kelly and colleagues, in a survey of US adults, found a "Weighted prevalence of problem resolution" of 9.1%, concluding that "Tens of millions of Americans have successfully resolved an AOD problem using a variety of traditional and non-traditional means", and that 53.9% reported "assisted" pathways, with mutual help most used (45.1%), then treatment (27.6%). Those are self-reports. The Cochrane review, for alcohol use disorder, found "high quality evidence that manualized AA/TSF interventions are more effective than other established treatments, such as CBT, for increasing abstinence", and that "Non-manualized AA/TSF may perform as well". The steps below are common advice. Tell someone. Secrecy helps the pattern. That is common advice. See a doctor. A doctor can assess what is going on, advise on stopping safely, and discuss treatment, including medicines where they are suitable. That is a standard statement, not drawn from the papers. Use support. Mutual-help groups, counselling and treatment are the main routes in Kelly and colleagues' survey, and no one route is right for everyone. Change the setting. Remove or block what triggers the habit, and tell people who can help. That is common advice; see impulsivity. Ride out urges. Urges rise and fall; a delay, a walk or a call can get you past one. That is common advice. Treat a slip as information. A slip is a reason to adjust the plan and not to give up, and shame does not help. That is common advice. Keep safe. Struggling to stop is common, and it is nothing to be ashamed of. If you are finding it hard, please talk to a doctor, therapist or a local support service. Stopping some substances suddenly, including alcohol and certain medicines, can be dangerous, so ask a doctor before stopping on your own (a standard safety point, not drawn from the papers below). If you are in danger, or thinking of harming yourself, contact your local emergency services now; the International Association for Suicide Prevention points to a directory of verified helplines in over 150 countries.

The Gita counsels moderation, practice and not being ruled by the senses. Do not be controlled. 3.34: "The senses naturally experience attachment and aversion to the sense objects, but do not be controlled by them". Keep a steady rhythm. 6.17: "those who are temperate in eating and recreation, balanced in work, and regulated in sleep, can mitigate all sorrows by practicing Yog." Practise, and let go. 6.35: "the mind is indeed very difficult to restrain. But by practice and detachment, it can be controlled." It is also honest about relapse. 2.59: "Aspirants may restrain the senses from their objects of enjoyment, but the taste for the sense objects remains." This is related to addiction and not identical to it. These verses are about the disciplined life and not about treatment. Reading them as a way through addiction is ours, and nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist, and a doctor can help with stopping safely.

The Katha counsels telling the good from the pleasant, and taking the reins. Tell them apart. 1.2.2: "The good and the pleasant approach man: the wise goes round about them and distinguishes them." Take the reins. 1.3.6: "But he who has understanding and whose mind is always firmly held, his senses are under control, like good horses of a charioteer." This is related to addiction and not identical to it. The passages are about wisdom and understanding, and the image of holding reins should not be read as "just control it". The site makes no claim about how to practise this, and nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist, and a doctor can help with stopping safely.

The Christian texts counsel not being alone in the struggle, asking to be rescued, and standing firm. You are not alone in this. 1 Corinthians 10:13: "No testing has overtaken you that is not common to everyone." Look for the way out. The same verse: "God is faithful, and he will not let you be tested beyond your strength, but with the testing he will also provide the way out so that you may be able to endure it." Ask to be rescued. Romans 7:24-25: "Wretched person that I am! Who will rescue me from this body of death? Thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord!" Stand firm. Galatians 5:1: "For freedom Christ has set us free. Stand firm, therefore, and do not submit again to a yoke of slavery." This is related to addiction and not identical to it. The verses should not be read as saying that someone who slips lacked faith. Reading them as a way through addiction is ours, and nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist, and a doctor can help with stopping safely.

The Buddhist texts counsel digging up the root, and trying again. Go to the root. Dhp 337: "dig up the root of craving, as you'd dig up grass in search of roots." Let it go. SN 56.11: "the fading away and cessation of that very same craving no residue left behind; giving it away, letting it go, releasing it, and not clinging to it." Do not be broken by a slip. Dhp 337: "Don't let Māra break you again and again, like a stream breaking a reed." Know it can fall away. Dhp 336: "their sorrows fall from them, like a drop from a lotus-leaf." This is related to addiction and not identical to it. The texts speak of craving in general and of a path of practice, and do not describe treatment. Reading them as a way through addiction is ours, and nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist, and a doctor can help with stopping safely.

The philosophers' counsel is to know which horse is pulling, and to decide before the pull. Name the pull. Plato, Phaedrus: "one of them is noble and of noble breed, and the other is ignoble and of ignoble breed". Decide before the moment. Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 7.7: the impetuous "do not await the argument, because they are apt to follow their imagination." So the argument is best made early. Let regret lead somewhere. Nicomachean Ethics 7.8: "incontinent man is likely to repent." This is related to addiction and not identical to it. Aristotle is writing about weakness of will, and step 2 is the site's own reading of his remark about those who do not wait for the argument. Plato's "ignoble" horse is an image in the text, and neither should be read as calling a person ignoble. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist, and a doctor can help with stopping safely.

Note: This is an invented composite story, not a real case. It is built from patterns people commonly describe, so you can see how a compulsion works and how people loosen it. Dev's story Dev started betting on his phone for fun. Within a year he was betting most evenings, chasing losses, and moving money between accounts so his partner would not see. Each time he said it would be the last. What helped: He told someone. After a bad night he told his sister everything. She did not shout, and she stayed on the phone. He saw a doctor. The doctor asked about his sleep, mood and money, and put him in touch with a counsellor and a local support group. He used support. The group met weekly, and it helped to hear that others had slipped and kept going. He changed the setting. He blocked the betting sites, handed his partner a say over his accounts, and deleted the apps. He rode out urges. When the urge rose, he rang someone or went for a walk, and noticed it passing. He treated a slip as information. In the fourth month he placed a bet, and told his counsellor the next day. They worked out what had set it off. It took many months, and the habit did not vanish all at once. What it shows: Dev did not beat it by willpower alone. Telling people, getting support and changing the setting made the urge easier to ride out, and a slip became something to learn from and not a reason to hide.

The taste that remains Gita 2.59 speaks of someone who has restrained the senses: "Aspirants may restrain the senses from their objects of enjoyment, but the taste for the sense objects remains. However, even this taste ceases for those who realize the Supreme." The commentary explains: "When one gives up eating, as in a fast, the desires of the senses become feeble. Similarly, in sickness one loses interest toward the objects of enjoyment. These states of dispassion are temporary, for the seed of desire remains within the mind." What it shows: The text expects the taste to remain after the act is stopped, and does not treat that as failure. This is a picture drawn from one verse and its commentary and not a tale of a person, and linking it to addiction is ours. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist, and a doctor can help with stopping safely.

Nachiketa and Death In the Katha Upanishad the boy Nachiketa asks Death a question about what lies beyond. Death tries to turn him aside: "Choose sons and grandsons who shall live a hundred years, herds of cattle, elephants, gold, and horses." "Whatever desires are difficult to attain among mortals, ask for them according to thy wish". Nachiketa answers: "These things last till tomorrow, O Death, for they wear out this vigour of all the senses. Even the whole of life is short. Keep thou thy horses, keep dance and song for thyself." "No man can be made happy by wealth." Death then says: "The good is one thing, the pleasant another; these two, having different objects, chain a man." And of Nachiketa: "Thou, O Nachiketas, after pondering all pleasures that are or seem delightful, hast dismissed them all." What it shows: Nachiketa is offered the pleasant in full, and turns it down for what he asked. He is a boy making a choice in a teaching and not a person with an addiction, and linking the two is ours. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist, and a doctor can help with stopping safely.

The one who seeks another drink Proverbs 23 gives a picture and not a tale: "Who has woe? Who has sorrow? Who has strife? Who has complaining? Who has wounds without cause? Who has redness of eyes? Those who linger late over wine". The last verse gives the voice: "'They struck me,' you will say, 'but I was not hurt; they beat me, but I did not feel it. When shall I awake? I will seek another drink.'" Paul's cry in Romans 7 answers it from another side: "Wretched person that I am! Who will rescue me from this body of death? Thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord!" What it shows: The proverb shows how the pull sounds from inside, and the second text shows a cry for help that is answered with thanks. They are two texts about different things, and linking them to addiction is ours. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist, and a doctor can help with stopping safely.

The creeper, the langur and the reed Dhp 334-337 gives three pictures of craving. Heedlessness grows it "like a camel's foot creeper", and they "jump from one thing to the next, like a langur greedy for fruit in a forest grove." The sorrow it brings grows "like grass in the rain" (335), and when someone prevails, "their sorrows fall from them, like a drop from a lotus-leaf" (336). The teacher then says: "dig up the root of craving, as you'd dig up grass in search of roots. Don't let Māra break you again and again, like a stream breaking a reed." (337) What it shows: Craving is pictured as growing, jumping and returning, and the way out as digging at the root, and the verse expects the stream to break against the reed more than once. These are similes and not a tale of a person, and linking them to addiction is ours. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist, and a doctor can help with stopping safely.

The charioteer and the two horses In Plato's Phaedrus Socrates gives a picture of the soul: "a pair of winged horses and a charioteer." The gods' horses "are all of them noble and of noble descent, but those of other races are mixed; the human charioteer drives his in a pair; and one of them is noble and of noble breed, and the other is ignoble and of ignoble breed; and the driving of them of necessity gives a great deal of trouble to him." What it shows: The struggle is built into the picture of being human, and the charioteer's trouble is not a sign of failure. It is an image in a dialogue and not a tale of a person, and linking it to addiction is ours. "Ignoble" is the text's word for one horse and should not be read as a word for any person. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist, and a doctor can help with stopping safely.

Burnout is exhaustion from long strain that has left you drained, distant and doubting your own use. Apathy is the flatness that can come with it: little interest in what once mattered. Those are standard descriptions and not taken from the sources below, and apathy is not defined in them. Maslach, Schaufeli and Leiter write that "Burnout is a prolonged response to chronic emotional and interpersonal stressors on the job, and is defined by the three dimensions of exhaustion, cynicism, and inefficacy." The World Health Organization's ICD-11 describes it as "a syndrome conceptualized as resulting from chronic workplace stress that has not been successfully managed", with three dimensions: "feelings of energy depletion or exhaustion; increased mental distance from one's job, or feelings of negativism or cynicism related to one's job; and reduced professional efficacy." The WHO says burn-out "is not classified as a medical condition", and "should not be applied to describe experiences in other areas of life." Everyday signs, as people commonly describe them and not as findings from these sources: waking tired, dreading what you used to manage, snapping, and feeling nothing about things that used to matter. It is a cousin of sloth, and it is not laziness. Burnout is not laziness, and it is nothing to be ashamed of. If exhaustion or flatness lasts, or comes with low mood, hopelessness or thoughts of harming yourself, please talk to a doctor, therapist or someone you trust; a doctor can also check whether something else, such as illness or depression, is involved (a standard statement, not drawn from the sources below). If you may harm yourself, contact your local emergency services now; the International Association for Suicide Prevention points to a directory of verified helplines in over 150 countries.

Hinduism has no single word in the Bhagavad Gita for burnout, but it names both ends of a strained life. Gita 6.16: "those who eat too much or too little, sleep too much or too little, cannot attain success in Yog." On the other side, 2.47: "You have a right to perform your prescribed duties, but you are not entitled to the fruits of your actions. Never consider yourself to be the cause of the results of your activities, nor be attached to inaction." This is related to burnout and not identical to it. 6.16 is advice on the discipline of yoga and 2.47 is about working without clinging to results, and neither describes exhaustion as a state. Reading them as an account of burnout is ours. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist, and exhaustion that is heavy or lasting is worth telling someone about.

The Upanishads show depletion in their ladder of "better than". Chandogya 7.9: "Food (anna) is better than power. Therefore if a man abstain from food for ten days, though he live, he would be unable to see, hear, perceive, think, act, and understand." And 7.8: "Power (bala) is better than understanding. One powerful man shakes a hundred men of understanding. If a man is powerful, he becomes a rising man." This is related to burnout and not identical to it. The passage is about food and power as steps in a teaching, and does not speak of work or exhaustion. Reading it as an account of burnout is ours. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist, and exhaustion that is heavy or lasting is worth telling someone about.

The Bible names being worn out. Jethro says to Moses: "What you are doing is not good. You will surely wear yourself out, both you and these people with you, for the task is too heavy for you; you cannot do it alone" (Exodus 18:17-18). Isaiah 40:30: "Even youths will faint and be weary, and the young will fall exhausted". And Psalm 127:2: "It is in vain that you rise up early and go late to rest, eating the bread of anxious toil, for he gives sleep to his beloved." This is related to burnout and not identical to it. These passages describe the state and its cause without a name for it. The tradition's own word for a weariness of spirit, acedia, is not read here and is discussed in Sloth. Reading the passages as an account of burnout is ours. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist, and exhaustion that is heavy or lasting is worth telling someone about.

The Buddhist texts name dullness as one of the five hindrances. SN 46.51 says what fuels "dullness and drowsiness": "There is discontent, sloth, yawning, sleepiness after eating, and mental sluggishness." AN 6.55 names the two ways energy goes wrong: "when energy is too forceful it leads to restlessness. When energy is too slack it leads to laziness." This is related to burnout and not identical to it. The texts are about practice and not about work, and "sloth" and "laziness" are the translator's words for states that are not the same as exhaustion from strain. Reading them as an account of burnout is ours. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist, and exhaustion that is heavy or lasting is worth telling someone about.

Aristotle says we cannot work without stopping. Nicomachean Ethics 10.6: "amusement is a sort of relaxation, and we need relaxation because we cannot work continuously." Seneca names what unbroken work does: "continuous toil produces a sort of numbness and sluggishness." This is related to burnout and not identical to it. Aristotle is explaining why we amuse ourselves, and Seneca is writing about the mind's need for rest. Neither describes a syndrome. Reading them as an account of burnout is ours. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist, and exhaustion that is heavy or lasting is worth telling someone about.

The sources read here place the cause in work and its setting, as well as in the person. Chronic strain. The WHO's description: "chronic workplace stress that has not been successfully managed." The organisation. Maslach and colleagues say research "places the individual stress experience within a larger organizational context of people's relation to their work." Panagioti and colleagues conclude: "This finding provides support for the view that burnout is a problem of the whole health care organization, rather than individuals." Long strain without recovery. Common description, not from these sources: overload, little control, little reward, unfair treatment, a team that has broken apart, and work that clashes with your values. Other causes of flatness. Also common description: apathy can come from illness, grief or depression, and not only from work. Burnout is not a character flaw. Burnout is not laziness, and it is nothing to be ashamed of. If exhaustion or flatness lasts, or comes with low mood, hopelessness or thoughts of harming yourself, please talk to a doctor, therapist or someone you trust; a doctor can also check whether something else, such as illness or depression, is involved (a standard statement, not drawn from the sources below). If you may harm yourself, contact your local emergency services now; the International Association for Suicide Prevention points to a directory of verified helplines in over 150 countries.

The Gita names attachment to results as a cause of strain. 2.47: "You have a right to perform your prescribed duties, but you are not entitled to the fruits of your actions. Never consider yourself to be the cause of the results of your activities". 2.48: "Be steadfast in the performance of your duty, O Arjun, abandoning attachment to success and failure. Such equanimity is called Yog." This is related to burnout and not identical to it. The verses are about the mind's relation to results, and burnout often comes from overload and an unfair setting, which are not mentioned. Reading them as a root of burnout is ours, and they should not be used to tell an overworked person that the fault is their attachment. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist, and exhaustion that is heavy or lasting is worth telling someone about.

The Upanishads place the basis of effort in what feeds the body. Chandogya 7.9: "Food (anna) is better than power. Therefore if a man abstain from food for ten days, though he live, he would be unable to see, hear, perceive, think, act, and understand. But when he obtains food, he is able to see, hear, perceive, think, act, and understand." Chandogya 7.8 puts power before the rest: "If a man is powerful, he becomes a rising man." This is related to burnout and not identical to it. The passage is about food and power in a teaching, and it does not speak of work. Reading it as a root of burnout is ours. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist, and exhaustion that is heavy or lasting is worth telling someone about.

Exodus shows how a good task wears a person out. Jethro asks Moses: "Why do you sit alone, while all the people stand around you from morning until evening?" He answers his own question: "the task is too heavy for you; you cannot do it alone." Mark 6:31 describes the apostles' day: "they had no leisure even to eat." Psalm 127:2 names the strain: "the bread of anxious toil". This is related to burnout and not identical to it. The causes shown are too much, alone, and without breaks. Reading these as roots of burnout is ours, and how commentators read them was not checked. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist, and exhaustion that is heavy or lasting is worth telling someone about.

The Buddhist texts name tension and slackness in energy, and the way attention feeds them. AN 6.55: "when energy is too forceful it leads to restlessness. When energy is too slack it leads to laziness." SN 46.51 says what fuels dullness: "There is discontent, sloth, yawning, sleepiness after eating, and mental sluggishness. Frequent irrational application of mind to that fuels the arising of dullness and drowsiness". This is related to burnout and not identical to it. The texts are about a monk's practice, and "irrational application of mind" is the translator's phrase for a way of attending. Reading them as roots of burnout is ours, and they should not be read as saying that burnout is a failure of attention. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist, and exhaustion that is heavy or lasting is worth telling someone about.

Seneca places the cause in unbroken labour. Of Peace of Mind: "Neither ought we always to keep the mind strained to the same pitch, but it ought sometimes to be relaxed by amusement." And: "the liveliness of our minds will be destroyed by unceasing labour". Aristotle gives the reason: "we need relaxation because we cannot work continuously." This is related to burnout and not identical to it. Both are arguments for rest and not accounts of a syndrome, and neither speaks of unfair or overloaded work. Reading them as roots of burnout is ours. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist, and exhaustion that is heavy or lasting is worth telling someone about.

The research read here describes effects on health and work. Salvagioni and colleagues reviewed prospective studies and report that "Burnout was a significant predictor of the following physical consequences: hypercholesterolemia, type 2 diabetes, coronary heart disease, hospitalization due to cardiovascular disorder, musculoskeletal pain, changes in pain experiences, prolonged fatigue, headaches, gastrointestinal issues, respiratory problems, severe injuries and mortality below the age of 45 years." The psychological effects were "insomnia, depressive symptoms, use of psychotropic and antidepressant medications, hospitalization for mental disorders and psychological ill-health symptoms." They also note: "Conflicting findings were observed." Panagioti and colleagues write that "Burnout is prevalent in physicians and can have a negative influence on performance, career continuation, and patient care." These are group findings from studies of workers, and they say nothing certain about one person. Common effects, as people describe them and not findings from these papers: dreading work, short temper, less patience at home, and flatness about what used to bring joy. None of this is a reason for alarm, and it is a reason to rest and to ask for help. Burnout is not laziness, and it is nothing to be ashamed of. The Gita names what an unbalanced life costs. 6.16: "those who eat too much or too little, sleep too much or too little, cannot attain success in Yog." 18.28 describes a worker in the mode of ignorance: "A performer in the mode of ignorance is one who is undisciplined, vulgar, stubborn, deceitful, slothful, despondent, and a procrastinator." This is related to burnout and not identical to it. 18.28 is a description of a kind of work in the Gita's system of modes, and its words ("vulgar", "deceitful") are the translator's. They should not be read as a description of people who are exhausted. Reading the verses as effects of burnout is ours. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist, and exhaustion that is heavy or lasting is worth telling someone about.

The Upanishads name what depletion does. Chandogya 7.9: "if a man abstain from food for ten days, though he live, he would be unable to see, hear, perceive, think, act, and understand." The Buddhist texts show the pull to quit. In AN 6.55 the monk Soṇa, who is "one of the Buddha's most energetic disciples", thinks: "Why don't I resign the training and return to a lesser life, so I can enjoy my wealth and make merit?" SN 46.51 names dullness and drowsiness as what grows when "discontent, sloth, yawning, sleepiness after eating, and mental sluggishness" are fed. This is related to burnout and not identical to it. Soṇa's thought comes from his sense that his effort is not freeing him, and the text does not call it exhaustion. Reading the passages as effects of burnout is ours. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist, and exhaustion that is heavy or lasting is worth telling someone about.

Seneca names the effect of unbroken work: "continuous toil produces a sort of numbness and sluggishness." And: "the liveliness of our minds will be destroyed by unceasing labour, but they will recover their strength after a short period of rest and relief". Aristotle names the cost of making amusement the aim: "it would, indeed, be strange if the end were amusement, and one were to take trouble and suffer hardship all one's life in order to amuse oneself." This is related to burnout and not identical to it. Seneca is writing about the mind and Aristotle about the purpose of amusement, and neither describes a syndrome. Reading them as effects of burnout is ours. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist, and exhaustion that is heavy or lasting is worth telling someone about.

The research read here finds that remedies help a little, and that the setting matters. Panagioti and colleagues, reviewing trials in physicians, found "small significant reductions in burnout" overall (a standardised mean difference of -0.29), with organisation-directed interventions (-0.45) doing better than physician-directed ones (-0.18). Their conclusion: "recent intervention programs for burnout in physicians were associated with small benefits that may be boosted by adoption of organization-directed approaches." Maslach and colleagues point to "engagement, the positive antithesis of burnout". The steps below are common advice. Name it and check. Say "I am burnt out" (words of our own), and see a doctor, who can check for illness or depression. That is a standard statement, not drawn from the papers. Rest properly. Sleep, real breaks and days off. That is common advice. Change the load where you can. Talk to a manager, hand tasks on, say no. This follows the review's finding that changes to the setting did better than changes to the person, and the review is of physicians. Keep something that gives energy back. A walk, a friend, a hobby, with no target. That is common advice. Do not carry it alone. Tell someone. That is common advice. Get help. Burnout is not laziness, and it is nothing to be ashamed of. The Gita counsels balance and a steady mind. Keep a moderate rhythm. 6.17: "those who are temperate in eating and recreation, balanced in work, and regulated in sleep, can mitigate all sorrows by practicing Yog." Avoid both extremes. 6.16: "those who eat too much or too little, sleep too much or too little, cannot attain success in Yog." Work steadily, and let go of the result. 2.48: "Be steadfast in the performance of your duty, O Arjun, abandoning attachment to success and failure. Such equanimity is called Yog." This is related to burnout and not identical to it. These verses are about the discipline of yoga and do not speak of overload, and they should not be read as telling a worn-out person to work on with a calmer mind. Reading them as a way through burnout is ours, and nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist. The Buddhist texts counsel tuning energy like the strings of a harp. Tune it. AN 6.55: "when energy is too forceful it leads to restlessness. When energy is too slack it leads to laziness. The philosophers' counsel is to rest in order to work, and to alternate. Rest so that you can act. Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 10.6: "to amuse oneself in order that one may exert oneself, as Anacharsis puts it, seems right; for amusement is a sort of relaxation, and we need relaxation because we cannot work continuously." Do not force the field. Seneca, Of Peace of Mind: "We must not force crops from rich fields, for an unbroken course of heavy crops will soon exhaust their fertility". Alternate. Same passage: "pass our lives alternately in solitude and among throngs of people". This is related to burnout and not identical to it. Both are advice for a healthy mind, and neither describes recovery from exhaustion. Reading them as a way through burnout is ours, and nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist. Note: This is an invented composite story, not a real case. It is built from patterns people commonly describe, so you can see how burnout works and how people recover. Nadia's story Nadia led a small team. After two years of covering gaps, answering messages at night and skipping breaks, she began waking tired and dreading Mondays. Things she had enjoyed felt flat, and she snapped at a colleague over nothing. What helped: She named it and checked. She told her doctor she thought she was burnt out. The doctor asked about her sleep and mood, and ruled out illness. She rested properly. She took the leave she had been saving, and slept. She changed the load. She told her manager what she was carrying, handed two tasks on, and stopped answering messages after seven. She kept something that gave energy back. A Saturday walk with a friend, with no target. She did not carry it alone. She told her sister, and then the team. She asked for more help. The flatness lingered for weeks, so she saw a counsellor. It took months, and some weeks she slipped back into old habits. What it shows: Nadia did not fix it by pushing harder. Rest, a lighter load and someone to tell mattered more than another resolution.

The regulated life Two verses of the Gita draw the picture. 6.16: "those who eat too much or too little, sleep too much or too little, cannot attain success in Yog." 6.17: "those who are temperate in eating and recreation, balanced in work, and regulated in sleep, can mitigate all sorrows by practicing Yog." What it shows: The life that works is neither overdone nor underdone, in food, sleep and work. This is a picture drawn from two verses and not a tale of a person, and linking it to burnout is ours. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist, and exhaustion that is heavy or lasting is worth telling someone about.

Narada on power and food In Chandogya 7 Narada asks again and again: "Sir, is there something better than" the last thing? In 7.8 Sanatkumara says: "Power (bala) is better than understanding. One powerful man shakes a hundred men of understanding." Then, in 7.9: "Food (anna) is better than power. Therefore if a man abstain from food for ten days, though he live, he would be unable to see, hear, perceive, think, act, and understand. But when he obtains food, he is able to see, hear, perceive, think, act, and understand." What it shows: In the teaching, power depends on food, and when the body is emptied the mind goes with it. This is a moment in a dialogue and not a tale of burnout, and linking it to burnout is ours. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist, and exhaustion that is heavy or lasting is worth telling someone about.

Moses and Jethro In Exodus 18 Moses sits as judge "from morning until evening". His father-in-law Jethro asks: "Why do you sit alone, while all the people stand around you from morning until evening?" Moses explains: "Because the people come to me to inquire of God." Jethro says: "What you are doing is not good. You will surely wear yourself out, both you and these people with you, for the task is too heavy for you; you cannot do it alone." He advises that Moses teach the people, and "look for able men among all the people" and set them over groups: "let them bring every important case to you but decide every minor case themselves. So it will be easier for you, and they will bear the burden with you." "So Moses listened to his father-in-law and did all that he had said." What it shows: The remedy is to share the work. The story is about judging a people and not about burnout as such; the link is ours. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist, and exhaustion that is heavy or lasting is worth telling someone about.

Soṇa and the harp In AN 6.55 the monk Soṇa thinks: "I am one of the Buddha's most energetic disciples. Yet my mind is not freed from defilements by not grasping." He considers going back to a lesser life. The Buddha knows his thought, appears before him and asks: "When you were still a layman, weren't you a good player of the arched harp?" "When your harp's strings were tuned too tight, was it resonant and playable?" "No, sir." The same for too slack. "But when your harp's strings were tuned neither too tight nor too slack, but fixed at an even tension, was it resonant and playable?" "In the same way, Soṇa, when energy is too forceful it leads to restlessness. When energy is too slack it leads to laziness. So, Soṇa, you should focus on energy and serenity, find a balance of the faculties, and learn the character of this situation." "After some time Soṇa focused on energy and serenity, found a balance of the faculties, and learned the pattern of this situation." What it shows: The Buddha's answer to a man tempted to quit is to tune his effort. The sutta is about a monk's practice and not about burnout as such; the link is ours. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist, and exhaustion that is heavy or lasting is worth telling someone about.

The rested field Seneca gives a picture. "Men's minds ought to have relaxation: they rise up better and more vigorous after rest. We must not force crops from rich fields, for an unbroken course of heavy crops will soon exhaust their fertility, and so also the liveliness of our minds will be destroyed by unceasing labour, but they will recover their strength after a short period of rest and relief: for continuous toil produces a sort of numbness and sluggishness." What it shows: The mind is pictured as a field that gives more when it is allowed to lie fallow. It is an argument in an essay and not a tale of a person, and linking it to burnout is ours. Nothing here replaces a doctor or therapist, and exhaustion that is heavy or lasting is worth telling someone about.
